families.name: KRAB zinc-finger proteins (KZFPs)
families.def: The large, rapidly evolving KRAB-ZNF family; long idiosyncratic motifs, frequently derived from transposable elements. Most ZNF### genes without a separate entry.
families.short: KRAB zinc-finger proteins (KZFPs) are the largest family of DNA-binding proteins in the human genome: roughly 350 to 380 genes, most named only ZNF followed by a number. Each combines a KRAB repression domain, which recruits the corepressor TRIM28/KAP1 and the histone methyltransferase SETDB1, with a tandem array of C2H2 zinc fingers that reads a long, protein-specific stretch of DNA. Most of those stretches lie inside transposable elements, and the family has expanded and diversified alongside successive waves of element invasion. This atlas entry is therefore a bucket, not a motif: its 587 matrices come from 304 different proteins, run from 4 to 38 bp, and mostly do not resemble one another. A hit identifies one protein's site, not a family motif.
families.long:
## The factors

Human KZFPs number about 350 in the original survey and 378 in the most complete census, the largest group of transcription factors encoded by tetrapods (Imbeault et al. 2017; de Tribolet-Hardy et al. 2023). The architecture is uniform: an N-terminal KRAB domain, a variable linker, and a tandem array of 4 to more than 30 C2H2 fingers. The KRAB domain binds the corepressor KAP1/TRIM28 (Friedman et al. 1996), which in turn scaffolds the H3K9-specific methyltransferase SETDB1, HP1 proteins and DNA methyltransferases, producing H3K9me3 heterochromatin over the bound site (Schultz et al. 2002). The genes sit in clusters, heavily on chromosome 19, built by repeated gene and segment duplication; the family traces back more than 400 million years, to a common ancestor of coelacanths and tetrapods (Imbeault et al. 2017). Selection has acted specifically on the finger residues that touch DNA, so recent paralogues diverge in specificity while their scaffolds stay similar (Emerson and Thomas 2009). Not all are simple repressors: across 101 KZFP interactomes, those conserved up to placental mammals essentially recruit KAP1, while a subset of more ancient ones interact instead with genome-architecture and RNA-processing factors (Helleboid et al. 2019). Expression is not restricted to stem cells. This entry carries 304 distinct gene symbols, 191 of which have two or more matrices.

## The motif

There is no family consensus and one should not be invented. Every protein's finger array differs, and each finger specifies roughly three base pairs through a few residues in its recognition helix, so a 10-finger protein can specify 30 bp. That is what the data show: median consensus length 17 bp, 360 of 587 matrices at least 15 bp, 214 at least 20 bp, median information content 16.3 bits, and 149 matrices above 20 bits. The longest is a 31 bp, 50.7-bit model for ZNF550. Family cohesion is 0.37, against values above 0.8 for entries that really are one motif, and the listed representative (CIS-BP M07723, GCTCCCTGC) is just the matrix nearest the centre of a diffuse cloud. Typical examples: ZNF558 ATTTGATGAAAGACATAAATCTACAAATC (29 bp), ZNF611 TCTGGGATGTGAGGAGCGCCTCTGC (42 bits), ZNF75D TGTAATGAATGTGGGAAAGCCTTCA. Recent paralogue pairs are not separable: ZNF417 and ZNF587 share TGGCGCCCAACATGGG, and the same holds for ZNF75A/ZNF75D, ZNF354A/ZNF354B and the ZNF33A/ZNF33B archetypes. A minority of matrices have the opposite problem, being short or low-complexity and therefore non-specific: 24 are under 8 bp, and models for ZNF212 (a TC repeat), ZNF613 (poly-T) and ZNF746 (poly-C) carry high nominal information but no factor-specific content.

## Where it acts

Overwhelmingly inside transposable elements: endogenous retroviral LTRs, L1, SVA and Alu. Most KRAB-containing C2H2 proteins bind specific endogenous retroelements, from currently active families to ancient ones, and also show widespread binding at regulatory regions (Najafabadi et al. 2015). Critically, most element targets have lost all transposition potential, so KZFPs are using conserved element fragments as regulatory platforms long after any arms race ended, creating a largely species-restricted layer of epigenetic regulation (Imbeault et al. 2017). The chromatin context is usually H3K9me3-marked and closed: many KZFPs bind within closed chromatin, each recognizing a distinct set of repeats (Razavi et al. 2026), so these sites are routinely absent from accessibility-based catalogues. A separate niche is the 3' end of the zinc-finger genes themselves, where ZNF274 recruits KAP1 and SETDB1 (Frietze et al. 2010). Occurrence counts track the copy number of the target element subfamily, from hundreds to tens of thousands of loci.

## Biology and disease

Depleting TRIM28 in human or mouse embryonic stem cells derepresses a broad range of transposable elements, which is the baseline phenotype for the family (Imbeault et al. 2017). Individual proteins show how element control becomes gene control. ZNF558 evolved as an L1 suppressor but now regulates a single target, the mitophagy gene SPATA18, in human but not chimpanzee forebrain progenitors, with its own expression set by a variable tandem repeat that differs between the two species (Johansson et al. 2022). More broadly, KZFPs act as context-specific switches that gate element-derived regulatory modules, and mutations in KZFP genes are an emerging cause of human developmental disorders (Davis et al. 2026); Bruno et al. 2019 review the arms race and its consequences for mammalian traits. Imprinting (ZFP57), pancreatic development (ZNF808) and the SVA/L1 restriction factors ZNF91 and ZNF93 have separate entries.

## Reading a hit

Start from the gene symbol on the matrix, not the family. Then check the evidence: of the 285 HOCOMOCO models here, 224 are ChIP-only (evidence code P) and 160 are graded C, with only 49 at grade A, and in vitro codes (S, M) are rare. A ChIP-derived KZFP motif is in practice the consensus of the element the protein sits on, so a match may mean only "this is that element". Long, high-information motifs will not arise by chance in a small interval, but they will match every copy of the parent element, so genome-wide enrichment is usually a statement about repeat content. Seventeen matrices here have their closest neighbour in a different family: three resemble ETS motifs, two each MAZ, CTCF, ZNF24 and TBX, and one each STAT, YY1, HNF4, E2F, ZNF384 and ZFP57. That is the expected failure mode of ChIP-derived models, and a reason to check short KZFP hits against the better-characterized families. Finally, most KZFPs are expressed at low levels in restricted contexts, so a sequence match without expression evidence in your cell type is weak.
families.caveats: This entry is a family of proteins, not a motif: cohesion 0.37, with 587 matrices from 304 genes whose sites are largely unrelated. Never report it as a consensus. Most models are ChIP-derived (224 of 285 HOCOMOCO entries, 160 graded C), and for KZFPs that usually means the matrix is the consensus of a transposable element, so a hit may amount to repeat annotation rather than evidence of binding. Recent paralogue pairs such as ZNF417/ZNF587 share a motif outright. Seventeen matrices most closely resemble motifs of other families, including ETS, CTCF and MAZ. Check the gene symbol, the evidence code, the repeat track, and whether the protein is expressed in your cells.

families.name: Q50 homeodomain (DLX/MSX/LHX-type, TAATTA)
families.def: Palindromic TAATTA read by homeodomains with glutamine at position 50, grouped by that specificity rather than by gene family: DLX1-6, MSX1-3, LHX1-9, ALX1/3/4, PRRX1/2, SHOX/SHOX2, EMX1/2, VAX1/2, EN1/2, GBX1/2, BARHL1/2, BARX1/2, UNCX, ARX, ESX1, HLX, HMX1-3, MEOX1/2, MNX1, NOTO, HESX1, ISL1/2, ISX, LBX1/2, LMX1A/1B, DBX1/2, EVX1/2, GSX1/2, TLX1-3, and the Q50 paired-like factors VSX1/2, RAX/RAX2, PHOX2A/2B, NOBOX, MIXL1, VENTX, PROP1, DRGX, BSX, OTP, SEBOX, PDX1.
aka: Q50 paired-like factors (RAX, VSX, PHOX2, PROP1)
families.short: About half of the roughly 200 human homeodomain proteins carry glutamine at position 50 of the domain and read the palindromic hexamer TAATTA. This family gathers 275 published motifs for 89 gene symbols: DLX1-6, MSX1-3, the LIM-homeodomain proteins LHX1-9 and ISL1/2, ALX1/3/4, ARX, PRRX1/2, EMX, EN, GBX, BARHL, LMX, SHOX, VAX and TLX, plus the paired-like factors VSX1/2, RAX/RAX2, PHOX2A/2B, NOBOX, MIXL1, VENTX, PROP1, DRGX, BSX, OTP and SEBOX and, from another family again, PDX1. Grouping follows the specificity a protein actually has rather than its gene family. Many of these proteins also bind cooperatively as dimers on TAATNNNATTA palindromes, which is where most real discrimination lies; a single TAATTA match carries almost no information.
families.long:
## The factors

The homeodomain is a 60-residue module: three alpha-helices around a hydrophobic core, with helix 3 in the major groove and a flexible N-terminal arm in the adjacent minor groove. The human genome carries about 235 functional homeobox genes, and roughly half of the encoded homeodomains have glutamine at position 50, the last residue of the recognition helix - the residue this family is named for.

Eighty-nine gene symbols and 275 motifs are grouped here. The core set is expected: DLX1-6; MSX1-3; the LIM-homeodomain proteins LHX1-6, LHX8/9 and ISL1/2, which contact DNA through the homeodomain but assemble via LIM domains and LDB1; the aristaless-related ALX1/3/4, ARX and PRRX1/2; and EMX, EN, GBX, BARHL, BARX, DBX, GSX, EVX, HMX, LBX, LMX, MEOX, SHOX, TLX, VAX, UNCX, MNX1, HLX, ESX1, HESX1, ISX and NOTO.

The family also holds proteins whose gene families would suggest otherwise: the paired-like factors VSX1/2, RAX/RAX2, PHOX2A/2B, NOBOX, MIXL1, VENTX, PROP1, DRGX, BSX, OTP and SEBOX, plus PDX1. In standard classifications these sit beside OTX, CRX, PITX and GSC, but they carry glutamine at position 50, not lysine, and their measured motifs are TAATTA-type; the atlas groups by the specificity a protein actually has, so they belong here rather than in HD_K50.

## The motif

Position 50 is a specificity switch: substituting it in Drosophila Paired transfers the preference of Fushi tarazu or Bicoid onto that protein, and the reciprocal change in Bicoid converts it into an Antennapedia-class binder. Site selection with six different residues at position 50 each gave a distinct specificity, all sharing the TAAT core and differing only in the bases immediately 3' of it.

Structurally, the invariant Asn51 hydrogen-bonds the second adenine of 5'-TAAT-3' while Arg3 and Arg5 of the N-terminal arm read the minor groove there; the position-50 side chain points at the next two. Glutamine accommodates T:A, giving TAATTA and TAATTG; lysine instead contacts C:G, giving TAATCC. Information is confined to those six base pairs, so most models here are 6-8 columns wide.

Longer models are dimeric. Paired-like homeodomains bind palindromes with two TAAT half-sites three base pairs apart (the P3 site, TAATNNNATTA) cooperatively, with up to 300-fold enhancement; residue 50 sets the spacing and the central bases, and the rules for which homeodomains can do this have recently been derived. Thirty-five of the 112 HOCOMOCO models here are 11 bp or longer: ALX4, PHOX2B, PROP1 and MIXL1 TAATTAGATTA, ARX TAATCTAATTAG, LMX1B TTAATTAATT, DRGX and PHOX2A TAATTTAATTA.

Paralogues are not separable. Cohesion is 0.84 across 275 models, the medoid is GBX1 (JASPAR MA0889.2), and the data consensus reads CTAATTA - the same site with one flanking base. Real outliers exist: BARHL1/2 prefer TAAACG, HMX1-3 and ISL1/2 give NKX-like TAAGTG models, MEOX1/2 TAATGA, VSX1/2 a distinctive TAATTAGC, and methyl-HT-SELEX models for LHX1/6/8/9, LBX2 and PRRX2 a CpG-containing TAACGA variant. Surveys quantify the point: 168 mouse homeodomains resolve into at least 65 binding activities and 84 Drosophila homeodomains into 11 specificity groups - real variation, but finer than a PWM resolves.

## Where it acts

TAATTA sites sit in AT-rich distal enhancers rather than CpG-island promoters, and occupancy is strongly cell-type restricted. The motif is extremely common: at human base composition this self-complementary 6-mer is expected some two million times in 3.1 Gb, so even restricting to the ~4.5 million mapped DNase I footprints leaves far more matches than any factor occupies. Members share enhancers and compete on the same sites: DLX and MSX are the classic antagonistic pair in craniofacial and limb enhancers, while VSX1/2 and RAX act in retinal progenitors, PHOX2A/2B in autonomic neurons and NOBOX in oocytes. Characterized enhancers usually contain double TAAT cores or several cores within a few hundred base pairs; one archetype here is named EMX/PAX.

## Biology and disease

Human mutations are typically heterozygous and dosage-sensitive, and produce sharply localized defects. An MSX2 homeodomain substitution causes autosomal dominant craniosynostosis and MSX2 haploinsufficiency enlarged parietal foramina; MSX1 causes selective tooth agenesis, DLX3 tricho-dento-osseous syndrome, recessive ALX3 frontorhiny, SHOX deletion the short stature of Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis and Turner syndrome, LMX1B nail-patella syndrome, LHX3 combined pituitary hormone deficiency, HESX1 septo-optic dysplasia and ARX X-linked lissencephaly. The paired-like members add PHOX2B in congenital central hypoventilation syndrome and neuroblastoma predisposition, VSX2 in microphthalmia, RAX in anophthalmia and NOBOX in premature ovarian failure. Many pathogenic substitutions lie inside the homeodomain and alter DNA binding or cooperativity directly.

## Reading a hit

A TAATTA match says a Q50-class homeodomain could bind, and little else. No published matrix separates DLX5 from LHX2 or EN1 from MSX1; report the hit as a Q50 homeodomain site, not a gene. The site is too common to be informative on its own, so a bare hit means little without expression data, accessibility and ideally a second TAAT core three to five base pairs away. Evidence that these proteins bind TAATTA is strong: 107 of 112 HOCOMOCO models have in vitro HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX support and only five are ChIP-only. That is not the same as saying their ChIP peaks sit on TAATTA; peak sets routinely carry other factors' motifs, and two members are flagged for that reason: a ChIP-derived VENTX model reads AATTTGCATA, the POU octamer, and a low-information CIS-BP VSX2 model (TATATT) matches WT1. Six CIS-BP entries (DBX1, DBX2, LHX3, HLX, OTP, SEBOX) are transferred from mouse orthologues, SEBOX at only 79% domain identity; archetype names such as DLX/LHX are majority labels, not claims of separability.
families.caveats: Trust the family, not the member. A TAATTA match identifies a Q50-class homeodomain site; the 89 gene symbols here are not distinguishable by matrix, and the expected genome-wide frequency of the hexamer (order 10^6) means an isolated hit is close to uninformative. Require expression, accessibility and preferably a dimeric TAATNNNATTA arrangement. In vitro support for the motif is strong (107 of 112 HOCOMOCO models have SELEX evidence), but ChIP-derived peaks often carry other proteins' motifs - one VENTX model here is in fact the POU octamer. Membership follows measured specificity, not gene family: VSX1/2, RAX/RAX2, PHOX2A/2B, NOBOX, MIXL1, VENTX, PROP1, DRGX, BSX, OTP, SEBOX and PDX1 are paired-like or CDX/PDX genes that carry Q50 and read TAATTA.

families.name: Unnamed zinc-finger archetypes
families.def: Archetype motifs whose only label is the generic token ZNF, so nothing is claimed beyond the structural class. This is not one motif: it is a set of long, distinct zinc-finger matrices, many of them matching transposable-element sequence.
families.short: Not a motif but a label gap. The Vierstra footprint atlas groups redundant matrices from several databases into archetypes, each named after the factor groups whose motifs clustered into it. For 256 of the 693 archetypes in this atlas that name collapses to a generic token, ZNF, ZFP, ZBTB, ZSCAN or ZKSCAN, so the only claim being made is that some C2H2 zinc finger binds here. These 256 matrices are long, high-information and almost entirely unrelated to one another: not one has a close match to another member of this entry. A hit means you matched a specific, reproducible zinc-finger matrix whose protein was never named, and the useful next step is to find that matrix's nearest named neighbour.
families.long:
## The factors

None is named, and that is the point of the entry. Human C2H2 zinc fingers number around 700, the largest structural class of transcription factors in the genome, and roughly half carry a KRAB, SCAN, BTB or SET domain in addition to their finger array (Schmitges et al. 2016; Lambert et al. 2018). Specificities for most of them were determined in bulk screens rather than by individual study (Najafabadi et al. 2015; Schmitges et al. 2016), and several hundred putative human transcription factors had no motif of any kind until very recently (Jolma et al. 2026). An archetype is a cluster of similar matrices drawn from several source collections, built to remove redundancy before annotating DNase I footprints genome-wide; the reference footprint atlas delineated about 4.5 million footprints across 243 human cell and tissue types and used archetypes as the motif vocabulary for them (Vierstra et al. 2020). An archetype identifier encodes accession, factor-group label and structural class, as in AC0403:ZNF:C2H2_ZF. Here the label field is generic for all 256 members: ZNF for 226, ZBTB for 12, ZFP for 9, ZSCAN for 5, ZKSCAN for 2, and mixed generic tokens for 2. The class field is C2H2_ZF for 248 of them. The only assertion any of these names carries is the protein fold.

## The motif

There is no consensus: 256 matrices here are 256 different things. Median consensus length is 14 bp, with 116 members at 15 bp or longer and 40 at 20 bp or longer; median information content is 15.3 bits, with 50 members above 20 bits and a maximum of 45.9 bits over 28 bp. Cohesion is 0.33, the lowest kind of value in this atlas, and the diagnostic number is starker still: of the 218 members that have any within-entry neighbour, not one scores above 0.9 similarity and 184 score below 0.7. The listed representative AC0620 (CCTCAGCCTCC) is a centroid, not a consensus. What an individual matrix is, however, is often recoverable from the data even though the label withholds it. AC0403 (TTGCGCCACTGCACTCCAGCCTGGGCAA, 45.9 bits) is essentially the CIS-BP matrix for ZNF496; AC0286 (AGTGGCTTTTTCTACCTCACAATACAAC, 43.3 bits) is essentially the CIS-BP matrix for ZNF737; AC0408 is the CIS-BP matrix attributed to ZNF445 and AC0339 is the ZSCAN29 site, an inverted pair of GTCTAC hexamers. More generally, 206 of the 250 archetypes that have a cross-family neighbour match it at 0.9 or better, so an unnamed archetype is usually a named protein's motif with the name dropped. Base composition is 55% GC overall, and the long, high-information members have the profile expected of transposable-element sequence read by KRAB zinc fingers (Imbeault et al. 2017).

## Where it acts

Archetypes were built to annotate accessible, footprinted DNA, so an archetype in this set was seen in DNase I cleavage data in at least some of the 243 profiled cell and tissue types (Vierstra et al. 2020). That is real evidence that a protein occupies some of its matches, without saying which protein. Beyond that, distribution follows the matrix. The GC- and CT-rich members, of which the representative CCTCAGCCTCC is one, will accumulate at promoters and CpG islands and will be difficult to separate from the SP/KLF, MAZ, VEZF1 and E2F pools. The long AT-containing members will accumulate in repeat-rich intronic and intergenic DNA. Many zinc fingers of this kind bind within closed chromatin at protein-specific sets of repeats and are therefore systematically under-represented in accessibility-based catalogues (Razavi et al. 2026).

## Biology and disease

This entry cannot support a biological claim, and treating it as though it could is the main way to misuse it. The processes the underlying proteins control are described in the entries that do have names: transposable-element silencing and its domestication for the KRAB zinc fingers, imprinting for ZFP57, promoter regulation for the SCAN and BTB groups. What can be said is that the gap is closing. Systematic in vitro and in vivo screens have produced motifs for just over half of 332 previously uncharacterized human transcription factors, adding roughly 130 distinct motifs to the known vocabulary, most of them associated with a single protein (Jolma et al. 2026). Some archetypes here will become assignable to one of those proteins, but the archetype label will not change until the clustering is rebuilt.

## Reading a hit

Do not report "a ZNF motif". Report the archetype accession, its length and its information content, then do three things. First, look for the nearest named matrix in JASPAR, HOCOMOCO or CIS-BP: for 82% of the members here that neighbour scores 0.9 or better, and it usually supplies the protein name the archetype lacks. Second, check the repeat annotation, because a matrix longer than about 20 bp is frequently a fragment of a transposable element, in which case matches are element copies rather than independent regulatory sites. Third, look at base composition: a GC- or CT-rich archetype cannot be separated from the general GC-box pool and should not be attributed to a specific protein. Two members are explicitly flagged as belonging elsewhere, AC0408 to the ZFP57 entry and AC0339 to the ZNF24/ZSCAN29 motif. And keep the semantics straight: the archetype name is a statement about which matrices clustered together, never a claim that a protein called ZNF binds this sequence.
families.caveats: This is a label gap, not a motif family: 256 archetypes whose names carry no information beyond "C2H2 zinc finger". Cohesion is 0.33 and no member resembles another above 0.9 similarity, so there is no consensus and the representative matrix is only a centroid. A hit tells you which archetype you matched and nothing about which protein. Resolve it by finding the nearest named matrix, which scores 0.9 or better for 206 of the 250 members that have a cross-family neighbour. Check the repeat track, since many of the long members are transposable-element sequence and their matches are element copies. GC- and CT-rich members cannot be separated from the general GC-box pool.

families.name: Other C2H2 zinc fingers
families.def: C2H2 factors and archetypes that are not KZFPs and have no dedicated entry.
families.short: The remainder of the C2H2 zinc-finger class: factors that are neither KRAB zinc-finger proteins nor members of a family with its own entry. Ninety-six named genes appear here, from well-studied cases such as ZNF335, ZNF341, ZFAT and ZFTA to dozens of ZNF numbers with almost no literature. What they share is the fold, and little else: the 168 matrices in this entry are mutually unrelated, with a cohesion of 0.38 and a median length of 12 bp. The evidence behind them is nonetheless much better than for the KRAB group, with 39 of 93 HOCOMOCO models at the top grade and many supported in vitro. A hit here identifies one named protein at best, never a family motif.
families.long:
## The factors

About 700 human proteins carry C2H2 zinc fingers, the largest structural class of transcription factors in the genome, and roughly half also carry a KRAB, SCAN, BTB or SET domain (Vaquerizas et al. 2009; Schmitges et al. 2016; Lambert et al. 2018). This entry holds most of the remainder that lack a dedicated family: 96 named genes plus two generic archetype labels, heterogeneous in every respect other than the fold. A few are well characterized. ZNF335/NIF-1 is a component of a vertebrate-specific trithorax H3K4-methylation complex. ZNF341 is a nuclear transcription factor that binds the STAT3 promoter. ZFTA, formerly C11orf95, is best known as a fusion partner in ependymoma. Others carry different modules: ZXDA, ZXDB and ZXDC; ZFP64 and ZFP91; ZNF423, a relative of the EBF-binding zinc fingers; MZF1, which has a SCAN domain but is filed here; and the NET-family proteins ZNF503 and ZNF703, with only one or two fingers. Most of the rest, from ZNF16 through ZNF865, received their motifs from bulk C2H2 screens rather than individual study (Najafabadi et al. 2015; Schmitges et al. 2016). Zinc fingers with distinctive, well-mapped sites — CTCF, EGR, WT1, KLF/SP, MAZ, VEZF1, ZNF143, ZNF263, ZNF281, ZNF384, ZNF410 and ZNF768 — have their own entries and are not included here.

## The motif

There is no family consensus; cohesion is 0.38 and the representative (CIS-BP M08388, CCCGGCCTCC) is only a centroid. Median consensus length is 12 bp and median information content 13.9 bits, with 59 matrices at 15 bp or more, 33 at 20 bp or more, and 26 above 20 bits. In practice they fall into three groups. First, long element-like matrices: ZNF146 (OZF) CTTTTTTATGGCTGCATAGTATTCC at 41 bits, with ZNF260 giving nearly the same sequence, so those two are not distinguishable; also ZNF280A TCTCTCCAGTGTGAATTCTCTGAT and ZNF121 CCTGGGCAACATAGCAAGACCCC. Second, simple-repeat matrices, which look informative but are not specific: ZNF646 and ZNF865 are both (TG)n at 31 and 27 bits, and ZNF48 is a GA repeat. Third, and hardest, short GC-rich matrices: ZNF740 GTGGGGGGGG, ZNF395 and SLC2A4RG both GCCGGCCGG, ZNF575 GCTGCGGCAGCAG, RLF CCGCCGCTTTT, ZXDA GCAGGGGC and ZXDB CAGGGG. These are near-indistinguishable from one another and from the SP/KLF, MAZ, VEZF1, ZNF281, EGR and GLI motifs, each of which has its own entry. Twenty-one matrices have their nearest neighbour outside the family: four are essentially a KLF/SP GC-box (three ZNF574 models and the archetype AC0466), two the SIX homeodomain motif (both ZNF32 models), two the BCL11 motif (both ZNF296 models), and single cases point to ZNF281, VEZF1, GLI, YY1, EBF, ZIC, PRDM, NFKB, ETS, ETV2/ETV6, posterior HOX and ZNF384. The clearest single case is basonuclin 2: the JASPAR BNC2 matrix is TGAGTCA, the canonical AP-1 site, at 0.99 similarity to the AP-1 entry.

## Where it acts

Mostly promoters and promoter-proximal regions. The GC-rich majority lands in CpG islands, joining a crowded pool of interchangeable GC-box models; the small number of long, element-like matrices lands in repeat-rich sequence. Systematic profiling of 166 poorly characterized human transcription factors found that nearly half associate with known promoters and enhancers, often co-localizing at conserved motif matches, while the other half bind largely non-overlapping sites in repeat-rich closed chromatin (Razavi et al. 2026). Members of this entry are split across both behaviours and mostly unassigned.

## Biology and disease

Three members have clear, mapped human phenotypes. Biallelic ZNF335 mutations cause severe microcephaly with small somatic size and neonatal death; Znf335-null mice are embryonic lethal, the protein is required for neural progenitor self-renewal and neuronal differentiation, and it directly regulates REST/NRSF (Yang et al. 2012). Loss-of-function mutations in ZNF341 cause a recessive form of hyper-IgE syndrome: ZNF341 binds the STAT3 promoter, and its loss lowers basal STAT3 mRNA and protein, abolishes STAT3 autoinduction, and removes T helper 17 cells while leaving an excess of T helper 2 cells (Béziat et al. 2018). ZFTA is the 5' partner of the recurrent ZFTA(C11orf95)-RELA fusion that drives oncogenic NF-kB signalling in supratentorial ependymoma; the driver is the fusion, not the wild-type factor (Parker et al. 2014). For most members here no loss-of-function phenotype has been published, which reflects absence of study rather than absence of function; these are the proteins recent systematic efforts were designed to characterize (Jolma et al. 2026).

## Reading a hit

Identify the protein, then ask whether the matrix can carry the identification. Three checks settle most cases. Is it GC-rich and shorter than about 12 bp? Then it is one of many interchangeable GC-box models and should not be attributed to a specific protein without orthogonal evidence. Is it a simple repeat, as for ZNF646, ZNF865 or ZNF48? Then it is not a motif in any useful sense. Does it have a high-similarity neighbour in a different family? Twenty-one matrices do, and for those the label should be treated as unresolved. Evidence here is comparatively good: 39 of 93 HOCOMOCO models are grade A and many carry in vitro codes (S or M) alongside ChIP, so a grade-A model with both kinds of support, such as ZFAT's GCAGATTCGTCA or ZFTA's GTGGCCCC, deserves more weight than a grade-C ChIP-only model such as ZNF711's. Two CIS-BP models, for ZNF652 and ZNF691, are transferred from mouse orthologues at 0.97 to 0.99 DNA-binding-domain identity, a safe transfer. Finally, because many of these proteins co-localize at the same conserved sites, a match in an occupied promoter does not tell you which zinc finger made the contact.
families.caveats: This entry is the leftover of a structural class, not a motif: 96 named proteins, 168 matrices, cohesion 0.38, no consensus. Read a hit as naming one protein at best. Short GC-rich members are interchangeable with each other and with the SP/KLF, MAZ, VEZF1, ZNF281, EGR and GLI motifs, and simple-repeat members such as ZNF646, ZNF865 and ZNF48 carry no factor-specific information. Twenty-one matrices most closely resemble a motif from another family; the clearest is the JASPAR BNC2 model, which is the AP-1 site. Evidence is better than in the KRAB group, with 39 of 93 HOCOMOCO models at grade A, so check the evidence code before trusting any label.

families.name: RXR and its heterodimers
families.def: DR1-DR5 direct repeats of AGGTCA. RXRA/B/G, RARA/B/G, THRA/THRB, VDR, PPARA/D/G, NR1H2/3 (LXR), NR1H4 (FXR), NR1I2/I3 (PXR/CAR).
families.short: This family covers retinoid X receptors (RXRA/B/G) and the receptors that heterodimerize with them: retinoic acid receptors (RARA/B/G), thyroid hormone receptors (THRA/THRB), the vitamin D receptor (VDR), the PPARs, the liver X receptors (NR1H2/NR1H3), FXR (NR1H4) and the xenobiotic sensors PXR and CAR (NR1I2/NR1I3). Every member reads the same hexameric half-site, AGGTCA (more precisely RGKTCA), so the half-site sequence tells you nothing about which receptor bound. What does carry information is how two half-sites are arranged: direct repeats separated by 1 to 5 bp (DR1 through DR5), inverted repeats and everted repeats. Spacing and orientation, not half-site identity, are the readable signal here.
families.long:
## The factors

RXRA, RXRB and RXRG are the shared partner of much of the nuclear receptor superfamily (Mangelsdorf and Evans 1995; Evans and Mangelsdorf 2014). The partners collected here are RARA/RARB/RARG (retinoic acid), THRA/THRB (T3), VDR (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3), PPARA/PPARD/PPARG (fatty acids, fibrates), NR1H3/NR1H2 (LXRalpha/beta, oxysterols), NR1H4 (FXR, bile acids) and NR1I2/NR1I3 (PXR, CAR, xenobiotics). All share a C4 double-zinc-finger DNA-binding domain (DBD) with a C-terminal extension (CTE). Heterodimers are permissive (PPAR:RXR, LXR:RXR, FXR:RXR, where an RXR ligand alone activates) or non-permissive (RAR:RXR, THR:RXR, VDR:RXR); RXR also homodimerizes. Expression ranges from near-ubiquitous (RXRA, RARA) to narrow (PPARG in adipocytes; PXR and CAR in liver and intestine). It is the largest family here: 106 models, 19 gene symbols.

## The motif

The half-site is AGGTCA, written RGKTCA when the degeneracy is spelled out (Moutier et al. 2012). It is the same hexamer the estrogen receptor reads; two hexamers make an element, and the variables are orientation and gap:

- Direct repeat (DRn): both half-sites on the same strand, AGGTCA-(n)-AGGTCA. Heterodimers read n = 1 to 5 (Rastinejad et al. 1995).
- Inverted repeat (IRn): head to head, AGGTCA-(n)-TGACCT. IR0 is the classic palindromic thyroid element; IR1 is the FXR element.
- Everted repeat (ERn): tail to tail, TGACCT-(n)-AGGTCA. ER6 is a documented PXR and thyroid element.

The gap is read by the CTE: in the RXR-THR DBD heterodimer on a DR4 the thyroid receptor's CTE lies in the minor groove across the spacer, measuring its length directly (Rastinejad et al. 1995); five residues in the second zinc finger set the tolerated spacing (Umesono and Evans 1989). The intact PPARgamma-RXRalpha complex shows the same asymmetry in full-length receptors (Chandra et al. 2008).

The usual assignments are the 3-4-5 rule: DR3 for VDR, DR4 for THR, DR5 for RAR, established by showing that adding or removing one spacer base converts a thyroid element into a retinoic acid or vitamin D element and abolishes the original response (Umesono et al. 1991). DR1 is used by PPAR:RXR and RXR homodimers; the PPAR element also needs a 5' extension (the malic enzyme PPRE is AACTAGGTCAAAGGTCA) and has fixed polarity, PPAR on the 5' half-site and RXR on the 3' (IJpenberg et al. 1997) - visible in the HOCOMOCO PPARA/PPARG models, acTaGGtcAAAGGTCA. LXR:RXR uses DR4; the FXR (NR1H4) models here are inverted repeats with a single-base spacer, AGGtCAnTGACCt. The PXR, CAR and VDR models drift from AGGTCA towards a GTTCA-type half-site (JASPAR NR1I2 tGAACTcnaTGAACT, VDR GAGTTCA). In vivo the rule is looser than it sounds: RAR-RXR occupies DR0, DR2, DR5, DR8 and IR0 elements in mouse cells and binds these non-canonical spacings about as well as DR2 and DR5 (Moutier et al. 2012).

What is distinguishable is the spacing class, and only sometimes the receptor. The JASPAR DR1 matrices for RXRA, RXRB, RXRG, PPARD and THRB are 0.997-0.998 similar - effectively one model. By contrast the THRB everted-repeat and PXR/CAR/VDR GTTCA models sit far from anything outside the family (best outside match 0.62-0.70), so those two shapes genuinely separate.

## Where it acts

Mostly distal enhancers, with some promoter-proximal elements such as the VDR sites at CYP24A1. Occupancy is ligand-modulated re-use of pre-existing sites, and is small relative to motif counts: 2,776 VDR-occupied positions after calcitriol in lymphoblastoid cells, with 229 genes changing expression (Ramagopalan et al. 2010). Sharing between heterodimers is extensive - in mouse liver PPARalpha occupies 71-88% of LXR-RXR binding regions, and sequential ChIP indicated they use degenerate shared elements mutually exclusively (Boergesen et al. 2012). Co-occurring motifs are typically CEBP in adipocytes (Nielsen et al. 2008) and liver, SPI1 in macrophages.

## Biology and disease

Retinoid signalling through RAREs patterns the anteroposterior axis, limbs and face; the PML-RARA fusion in acute promyelocytic leukemia blocks it and is treated with all-trans retinoic acid. THRB mutations cause resistance to thyroid hormone, VDR mutations hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets, and PPARG mutations familial partial lipodystrophy type 3; VDR binding regions are enriched near autoimmune and cancer association loci (Ramagopalan et al. 2010). PPARgamma and PPARalpha are the targets of thiazolidinediones and fibrates, LXRs drive reverse cholesterol transport, FXR agonists treat cholestatic liver disease, and PXR and CAR induce CYP3A4 and CYP2B6, a major source of drug-drug interactions.

## Reading a hit

Report the architecture, not the label. A bare AGGTCA occurs roughly a million times per haploid genome and means nothing on its own. Measure the gap between the two hexamers and state DR1-DR5, IRn or ERn; that narrows the candidates more than any motif name here does. Then accept the limit: a DR1 is compatible with RXR homodimers, PPAR:RXR, HNF4, COUP-TF/NR2F and TR2/TR4, and no PWM separates them. Watch the counting convention - the same 13 bp element is DR1 if the half-site is called as AGGTCA and 'GGTCA with a 2 bp gap' if it is called as GGTCA. JASPAR's explicit dimer entries (RXRA::VDR MA0074.1, Pparg::Rxra MA0065.3) name both partners but still cannot say which heterodimer bound a site. Prefer in vitro evidence codes (S, M, SM) for claims about direct binding: ChIP-only models here often carry flanking or partner signal, for instance RXRA.H14CORE.3.P.B (gGGkganvvagAGGTCAaGG). One Vierstra archetype here, AC0094:NR1H/WT, is the AT-rich model TATTATAT with no half-site at all - a clustering artefact, and a reminder that archetype names describe a majority of members, not a verified specificity (Vierstra et al. 2020).
families.caveats: Treat a hit here as evidence for the superfamily half-site plus a spacing class, never for a receptor. Many DR1 matrices for RXRA/B/G, PPARD and THRB in this collection are 0.997 similar - effectively interchangeable - and the same DR1 is used by HNF4, COUP-TF and TR2/TR4 outside this family. Only the THR everted repeats and the PXR/CAR/VDR GTTCA-type half-sites separate cleanly. A lone AGGTCA occurs about a million times per haploid genome and is not evidence of anything. ChIP-derived models frequently include partner or flanking signal, and one Vierstra archetype placed here (AC0094:NR1H/WT, TATTATAT) contains no half-site at all.

families.name: Forkhead (FOX)
families.def: RYAAAYA core. FOXA1-3, FOXB1/2, FOXC1/2, FOXD1-4, FOXE1, FOXF1/2, FOXG1, FOXH1, FOXI1, FOXJ1-3, FOXK1/2, FOXL1/2, FOXM1, FOXN1-4, FOXO1/3/4/6, FOXP1-4, FOXQ1, FOXR1/2, FOXS1.
families.short: Forkhead box (FOX) proteins are a family of about 50 human transcription factors that bind DNA as monomers through a ~100-residue winged-helix domain, named for the two loops, or wings, that flank its three-helix core. Nearly all of them read the same seven-base element, RYAAAYA, usually written GTAAACA or, on the opposite strand, TGTTTAC. The family includes the FOXA pioneer factors that engage nucleosomal DNA and open liver, prostate and breast enhancers; the insulin- and stress-controlled FOXO proteins; FOXC, FOXE, FOXG and FOXL factors needed for eye, thyroid, forebrain and ovary development; and the proliferation factor FOXM1. Because the DNA-contacting residues are almost invariant across the family, a forkhead match tells you that a FOX protein could bind there, but rarely which one.
families.long:
## The factors

The human genome carries about 50 forkhead box genes in 19 subfamilies, FOXA through FOXS. Each
encodes one copy of the forkhead (winged-helix) domain: roughly 100 residues in which three
alpha-helices pack against a short three-stranded beta-sheet. Helix H3 lies in the major groove
and supplies the base-specific contacts, while two extended loops - wing 1, between strands
beta2 and beta3, and wing 2 at the C-terminus - fold over the phosphate backbone and reach into
the flanking minor groove. The first co-crystal structure, of HNF-3gamma (FOXA3) on DNA, showed
that this fold is essentially that of linker histone H5 and that it bends DNA by about 13
degrees. Binding is monomeric in the usual case, but FOXO1 (and, in the same assays, FOXO3,
FOXM1 and FOXI1) also homodimerizes on a palindromic element using wing 1. Expression ranges
from near-ubiquitous (FOXK1/2, FOXO1/3, FOXJ3) to sharply restricted: FOXA1-3 in endoderm-
derived epithelia, FOXE1 in thyroid, FOXG1 in telencephalon, FOXL2 in granulosa cells and
eyelid, FOXI1 in inner ear and renal intercalated cells, FOXM1 in cycling cells.

## The motif

The literature consensus is RYAAAYA (R = A/G, Y = C/T), seven base pairs, most often realized as
GTAAACA; the medoid model of the 106 collected here is exactly GTAAACA, matching the databases.
Specificity comes almost entirely from H3 contacts to the central AAA run and the following
pyrimidine, several of them water-mediated, which is why that core tolerates so little variation
and the flanks so much. The FOXO field calls the same element the DAF-16 binding element, core
TTGTTTAC, and distinguishes it from the weaker insulin-response sequence in the IGFBP1 promoter.
Longer models in the data are one of three things: an extended monomeric site with AT-rich
flanks (HOCOMOCO FOXA1, TTGTTTACTTAA); a perfect palindrome, GTAAATATTTAC, which is two RYAAAYA
half-sites head-to-head with no spacer and corresponds to the wing-1 homodimer site (HOCOMOCO
FOXD3, FOXD2, FOXB1, FOXC1; CIS-BP FOXC2); or a composite with a partner, as in the JASPAR
models FOXO1::ELK1, FOXO1::ELK3, FOXO1::ELF1 and FOXO1::FLI1, where most of the information
content is the ETS GGAA core, not the forkhead site. Two members are real exceptions. FOXM1
models carry almost no information (2.1 bits in CIS-BP) because FOXM1 reaches chromatin mainly
through cofactors and non-canonical sequences. FOXH1 (FAST-1/FAST-2) models read AATCCACA,
equivalently TGTGGATT - the activin/Smad response element - and not RYAAAYA at all. Otherwise
FOXA, FOXB, FOXC, FOXD, FOXI, FOXK, FOXL, FOXO, FOXQ, FOXR and FOXS are not separable by
sequence.

## Where it acts

Forkhead sites are AT-rich and enhancer-biased: depleted from CpG-island promoters, enriched in
distal tissue-specific elements, and frequently on nucleosomal rather than naked DNA. FOXA1 and
FOXA2 bind a nucleosomal site that overlaps the linker-histone position, displace H1, and hold
liver enhancers in an accessible but nucleosome-occupied state. ChIP-seq typically recovers tens
of thousands of FOXA1 sites per cell type, most of them distal, and which ones are used depends
on the partner present: androgen receptor in prostate, estrogen receptor alpha and GATA3 in
luminal breast, HNF4A and CEBP in liver. FOXA1 is required for almost all ER-chromatin contacts
and for tamoxifen-dependent ER activity. FOXO sites sit at insulin- and oxidative-stress-
responsive promoters and enhancers (IGFBP1, G6PC, SOD2) and are switched off by AKT-driven
nuclear export, not by loss of the site. RYAAAYA is short - with two degenerate positions it is
expected on the order of three million times in a 3.1 Gb double-stranded genome - so occupancy
is set by chromatin and partners, not by the element.

## Biology and disease

Forkhead loss-of-function is usually severe. FOXC1 mutations cause Axenfeld-Rieger malformations
and early-onset glaucoma; FOXL2 mutations cause blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus
syndrome, and the recurrent FOXL2 C134W substitution is present in most adult granulosa cell
tumors; FOXE1 variants affect thyroid development; FOXG1 mutations produce a Rett-like
encephalopathy. FOXA1 is the clearest cancer story. It is altered in roughly a third of prostate
cancers, and the most common class of activating mutation clusters inside the wing-2 loop of the
forkhead domain, increasing chromatin mobility and driving a luminal androgen-receptor program;
other classes truncate the C-terminus or rearrange the locus. FOXA1 is also amplified or mutated
in breast, bladder and salivary tumors and sets the response to endocrine therapy. FOXM1 is
overexpressed in most carcinomas and drives cell-cycle gene expression.

## Reading a hit

A GTAAACA/TGTTTAC match identifies a forkhead site, not a forkhead protein. All of FOXA, FOXO,
FOXK, FOXC and FOXD read this element with the same residues, the models in all four databases
collapse onto one cluster (cohesion 0.78, no member with out-of-family nearest neighbors), and
the archetype names make the point explicitly: AC0042 is "FOXA/FOXB", AC0039 is "FOXD/FOXK",
AC0093 is "FOXC/HOXA". Deciding which FOX protein is involved requires expression data, ChIP, or
a partner site. The element is common enough to occur millions of times by chance, so a single
match in a region of unknown function is weak evidence. Prefer the in vitro models when you need
"this protein binds this sequence": 24 of the 30 HOCOMOCO entries here carry HT-SELEX or methyl-
HT-SELEX evidence (S or M in the fourth field), and only six are ChIP-only. Treat the FOXO1::ETS
and FOXJ2::ELF1 composite models as ETS motifs with a forkhead flank, and treat FOXM1 and FOXH1
models as not representing RYAAAYA.
families.caveats: High confidence that a match is a forkhead site; very low confidence about which of the ~50 FOX proteins binds it. Sequence cannot separate FOXA from FOXO, FOXC, FOXD, FOXI, FOXK, FOXL or FOXQ, and the Vierstra archetype names (FOXA/FOXB, FOXD/FOXK, FOXC/FOXK) reflect that rather than resolving it. The element is short and AT-rich, so it occurs millions of times by chance; treat matches as candidates that need chromatin or expression evidence. Two labels in this family do not represent RYAAAYA: FOXM1 models are near-uninformative, and FOXH1 models are the activin/Smad response element. Four CIS-BP entries are mouse-derived (FOXJ1, FOXM1, and the inferred FOXS1 and FOXB2 models at 79% and 93% DBD identity).

families.name: KLF / SP (GC-box)
families.def: GC-box GGGGCGGGG and CACCC-box. KLF1-17, SP1-9.
families.short: The SP and KLF proteins are about 26 human transcription factors that each use three C2H2 zinc fingers to read a nine- to ten-base GC-rich element. Two classical forms of that element exist: the GC-box GGGGCGGGG, found in the SV40 21-bp repeats and in most CpG-island promoters, and the CACCC-box CCACACCC of erythroid promoters such as beta-globin. In vitro selection puts the family consensus at CCACGCCC, which is the same site read from the other strand. Because all 26 proteins share the same finger code, sequence alone cannot say which one is bound; a GC-box hit identifies the family and, given how common GC-rich sequence is in promoters, often identifies very little else.
families.long:
## The factors

The mammalian SP/KLF family comprises roughly 26 genes - SP1 to SP9 and KLF1 to KLF17/18 - unified under a single nomenclature by Suske et al. (2005). Each protein carries three Cys2-His2 zinc fingers at its C terminus; the SP subgroup additionally has the Sp-box and a buttonhead box, while the KLF subgroup is more variable outside the fingers. SP1 was the first mammalian sequence-specific activator purified, isolated as the factor that activates the SV40 early promoter through its 21-bp repeats (Dynan and Tjian 1983), and its DNA-binding activity was mapped to the C-terminal zinc-finger region (Kadonaga et al. 1987). The KLF branch was opened by the cloning of erythroid Kruppel-like factor, KLF1/EKLF, as a CACCC-element-binding protein (Miller and Bieker 1993). Older aliases persist: KLF1 = EKLF, KLF2 = LKLF, KLF4 = GKLF, KLF9 = BTEB1, SP7 = Osterix. Expression splits the family into broadly expressed members (SP1, SP2, SP3, KLF6, KLF7, KLF9-KLF11, KLF13, KLF16) and restricted ones (KLF1 in erythroid cells, KLF2 in lymphocytes and endothelium, KLF4 and KLF5 in gut and skin, SP4 in neurons, SP7 in osteoblasts, SP8 and SP9 in limb bud and forebrain, KLF17 in oocytes). They bind DNA as monomers.

## The motif

Three fingers read nine to ten bases, three per finger, following the Zif268 code. Two canonical forms are described in the literature. The GC-box, GGGGCGGGG, is the Sp1 site. The CACCC-box, CCACACCC, is the erythroid form found in the beta-globin promoter. The 100 matrices collected here converge on a third way of writing the same thing: the medoid (SP3, JASPAR MA0746.3) is GCCACGCCCAC, and in vitro selection models across the family read CCACGCCC or, on the opposite strand, GGGCGTGG. Which of these a given paralogue prefers is a graded matter, not a switch. Matrices for SP1-SP4 and most KLFs keep a CpG in the central triplet (GGGGCGGGG, GGGCGTGG), whereas KLF1, KLF3, KLF4 and KLF5 tolerate A or T there and yield the CACCC-type models seen in this atlas (KLF4: TGGGTGTGGC; KLF9: GCCACACCCAC). Structurally, the Klf4 three-finger domain has been solved bound to fully methylated DNA at 1.85 A, where an arginine and a glutamate contact the 5-methyl group and binding to methylated DNA is only slightly tighter than to unmodified DNA (Liu et al. 2014); methyl-SELEX across 542 human factors confirmed that many C2H2 proteins, KLFs included, are methylation-tolerant rather than methylation-blocked (Yin et al. 2017). Several HOCOMOCO models here span 18-23 positions and contain two copies of the core, reflecting how often these sites occur in tandem. With 100 matrices from 27 gene labels and a cohesion of 0.84, the honest summary is that this family has one motif: no matrix distinguishes SP1 from SP3, or KLF10 from KLF11.

## Where it acts

GC-boxes are the characteristic element of CpG-island promoters and are the reason many housekeeping promoters have no TATA box. They cluster with NRF1, NFY and ETS sites in the same promoters, while CACCC-type sites dominate erythroid regulatory elements such as the beta-globin promoter and locus control region. The family's real problem is neighbors, not partners. The gastrin EGF-response element GGGGCGGGGTGGGGGG binds Sp1 and, independently, ZBP-89/ZNF148 (Merchant et al. 1996). When the CT/GC-rich element of the IL-3 promoter was used as a bait, the clones recovered were EGR1, EGR2 and DB1/VEZF1 (Koyano-Nakagawa et al. 1994). In other words, a single GC-rich element can be a legitimate binding site for members of four or five different families in this atlas.

## Biology and disease

Sp1-null mouse embryos are retarded and die around day 11, yet Sp1-/- cells grow and differentiate, so the requirement is developmental rather than cell-autonomous (Marin et al. 1997). KLF1 is required for beta-globin transcription and activates the beta-globin promoter through its CACCC box but not the gamma-globin promoter, whose CACCC sequence differs (Asano and Stamatoyannopoulos 1998); dominant human KLF1 mutations cause severe anemia, including congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type IV (Kulczynska-Figurny et al. 2020). KLF4 is one of the four factors in the original reprogramming cocktail for induced pluripotent stem cells. SP7/Osterix is required for osteoblast differentiation, and its mode of action is unusual (below).

## Reading a hit

A hit identifies the GC-box family and nothing narrower. Beyond that, ask three questions. Is the site informative at all? GGGGCGGGG and CCACGCCC are very common in GC-rich sequence, so a match inside a CpG-island promoter carries little information by itself. Which matrix matched? Of the 100 profiles here, 45 come from HOCOMOCO and many rest on ChIP-seq evidence at grade B or C; the grade-A models (KLF3-KLF5, KLF10, KLF12-KLF14) carry in vitro support and are the ones worth trusting for "this protein binds this sequence". Two HOCOMOCO models are not GC-box motifs at all: SP7.H14CORE.0.P.B and SP9.H14CORE.0.P.B are AT-rich (TAATTACAGGTT). For SP7 this is understood - amino-acid differences in the Sp7 zinc-finger domain reduce its affinity for the GC-box, and Sp7 reaches osteoblast enhancers inside Dlx-containing complexes bound to AT-rich motifs (Hojo et al. 2016) - which makes the SP7 ChIP motif a textbook case of a factor "having" its recruiter's motif. One CIS-BP matrix labelled SP5 (M03682_2.00) is not from a human protein at all: it is transferred from a Drosophila melanogaster protein at 94% DNA-binding-domain identity. Finally, MAZ/PATZ1, ZNF281/ZNF148, VEZF1, EGR and WT1 all read GC- or GA-rich sequence, and where a match scores well against both a GC-box and a GGGAGGG model, sequence cannot decide between them.
families.caveats: A match tells you the GC-box family, not the member: 100 matrices from 27 gene labels share essentially one motif. GC-rich nine-mers are also very common, so a hit in a CpG-island promoter may be no more than a statement about base composition. Most matrices are ChIP-derived at grade B or C; prefer the grade-A in vitro models. Two HOCOMOCO models labelled SP7 and SP9 are AT-rich and are not this motif - for SP7, indirect recruitment by Dlx factors explains it - and one CIS-BP matrix labelled SP5 is inherited from a Drosophila protein. Overlap with MAZ, ZNF281/ZNF148, VEZF1, EGR and WT1 is frequently unresolvable from sequence alone.

families.name: SOX (HMG box)
families.def: AACAAT / (A/T)(A/T)CAA(A/T)G. SOX1-21, SOX30, SRY; plus SOX-OCT composite sites.
families.short: SOX proteins are the 20 human transcription factors built around a single SRY-type HMG box, a 78-residue L-shaped domain that binds DNA entirely in the minor groove, wedges a hydrophobic residue between base pairs and bends the double helix by 70-80 degrees. They read a six- to seven-base core usually written AACAAT, or CATTGTT/ATTGTT on the opposite strand. A SOX protein bound alone does little; transcriptional output comes from a partner factor on an adjacent site, most famously OCT4 in the SOX-OCT composite element of pluripotency enhancers, and from dimeric palindromic sites used by SOX8, SOX9 and SOX10. The family covers sex determination (SRY, SOX9), cartilage (SOX9, SOX5, SOX6), neural stem cells (SOX2), neural crest and melanocytes (SOX10) and endothelium (SOX17, SOX18).
families.long:
## The factors

Humans have 20 SOX genes: SRY (group A), SOX1/2/3 (B1), SOX14/21 (B2), SOX4/11/12 (C), SOX5/6/13
(D), SOX8/9/10 (E), SOX7/17/18 (F), SOX15 (G) and SOX30 (H). Each carries one HMG box of about
78 residues folded into a twisted L: three alpha-helices whose concave face lies against DNA.
Unlike almost all other transcription factors, recognition happens entirely in the minor groove.
Side chains intercalate between base pairs - isoleucine 13 in SRY - widening the groove,
unwinding the helix and bending it by 70-80 degrees. That distortion is the point: SOX proteins
are as much architectural as regulatory, and one bound alone generally neither activates nor
represses. Output depends on a partner factor at an adjacent site, which is why the same SOX
protein behaves differently in different tissues. Two subgroups add dimerization hardware. SOXD
proteins (SOX5, SOX6, SOX13) carry a coiled-coil that makes them obligate dimers or
heterodimers; SOXE proteins (SOX8, SOX9, SOX10) carry a short DIM domain immediately N-terminal
to the HMG box that supports cooperative homo- and heterodimers. SOX2 and SOX11 can also bind
DNA on the nucleosome surface and are bona fide pioneer factors.

## The motif

The core is six to seven bases, conventionally written AACAAT and equivalently ATTGTT or CATTGTT
on the other strand; the medoid of the 87 models here is CATTGTT, the reverse complement of
AACAATG. The SRY consensus determined by site selection is (A/T)(A/T)CAA(A/T)G. Information is
concentrated on the CAA/TTG centre, which is where the intercalating residue inserts and where
groove width is most constrained; the outer positions are AT-preferring largely because AT-rich
DNA is easier to bend. Site selection on Sox4, Tcf1 and yeast Ste11 showed the functional
element is really 10-12 base pairs, with residues C-terminal to the HMG box reading the 3'
flank. Many models here are dimeric: CIS-BP SOX8 AACAATGTGCAGTGTT (28.8 bits), CIS-BP SRY,
SOX15, SOX7 and SOX2 AACAAT(A/G)(n)CATTGTT, HOCOMOCO SOX9 ATSAATTGCAGTSAT. All are head-to-head
inverted repeats of the core with a two- to four-base spacer, consistent with the finding that
SOXE dimers tolerate a range of spacings rather than a fixed one. Within the family sequence
does not separate members: SOX1, SOX2 and SOX3 are interchangeable on DNA, as are SOX8, SOX9 and
SOX10 apart from their preference for dimeric sites, and the Vierstra archetypes are labelled
"SOX" or "SOX/SRY", not a protein. One overlap reaches outside the family: HOCOMOCO SOX4, SOX11,
SOX13 and one SOX2 model read CCTTTGTT, whose reverse complement AACAAAGG also satisfies the
TCF/LEF Wnt response element CTTTGWW. SOX and TCF/LEF share the HMG fold and their consensus
sequences differ at essentially one position, so CTTTG-type hits are genuinely ambiguous between
the two families.

## Where it acts

SOX sites are enhancer-biased and usually appear as one half of a composite element. The best
characterized is the SOX-OCT element, where a SOX core abuts the octamer ATGCAAAT: SOX2 and OCT4
occupy it at the FGF4, UTF1, NANOG and POU5F1 enhancers, and the crystal structure of the
POU/HMG/DNA complex showed that the two proteins assemble in different conformational
arrangements depending on which enhancer's spacing they are given. Other named partnerships
include SOX2 with PAX6 at the lens DC5 element, SOX9 with SOX5/SOX6 at the COL2A1, COL9A2 and
COL11A2 enhancers, SOX10 with MITF at melanocyte enhancers, and SOXF factors with ERG and FLI1
in endothelium. Because AACAAT is only six bases it is expected roughly 1.5 million times in a
3.1 Gb double-stranded genome, far more often than it is occupied; nucleosome position matters,
since SOX2 and SOX11 bind at superhelical location 2, distort the DNA there and help detach the
terminal nucleosomal DNA.

## Biology and disease

SRY is the testis-determining gene, and HMG-box point mutations that abolish DNA binding or
bending cause 46,XY sex reversal. SOX9 mutations cause campomelic dysplasia with XY sex
reversal; Sox9 is required for cartilage formation, and a mutation in the dimerization domain
alone gives skeletal disease without sex reversal, showing that the dimeric and monomeric
activities are separable. SOX10 mutations cause Waardenburg syndrome type 4 (Waardenburg-
Hirschsprung disease) and peripheral demyelinating neuropathy, and SOX10 is the lineage-
dependency factor of melanoma. SOX2 mutations cause bilateral anophthalmia, SOX2 is one of the
four Yamanaka reprogramming factors, and its locus is amplified in squamous carcinomas of lung
and esophagus. SOX17 and SOX18 are required for endothelial and lymphatic development, and SOX11
is a diagnostic marker in mantle cell lymphoma.

## Reading a hit

A CATTGTT/AACAAT match identifies a SOX-family site, not a SOX protein: all 20 members read it
with the same fold and the same contacts, and the archetype labels ("SOX", "SOX/SRY") say so.
Expression data is the practical discriminator. Even the family assignment is soft at the
boundary with TCF/LEF, because CTTTG-type variants fit both. The core is short enough to occur
by chance more than a million times, so an isolated match means little; look for a partner site
- an octamer, a second SOX core in inverted orientation, a MITF E-box - before treating it as
functional. Of the 36 HOCOMOCO models here, 27 carry HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX evidence and
nine are ChIP-only; the ChIP-only ones (SOX5, SOX6, SOX11, SOX13, SOX30, some SOX2 and SOX17
models) are the likeliest to have absorbed a partner's preference. Two CIS-BP entries (SOX1,
SOX11) are mouse-derived at 100% DNA-binding-domain identity, which does not affect specificity;
no member of the family has out-of-family nearest neighbors.
families.caveats: A hit tells you a SOX-family HMG box could bind; it does not tell you which of the 20 proteins. SOX1/2/3, SOX8/9/10 and SOX4/11/12 are mutually indistinguishable from sequence, and the Vierstra archetypes are named "SOX" or "SOX/SRY" for that reason. The core is six bases and occurs over a million times by chance, so isolated matches are weak evidence; SOX proteins also need a partner factor to do anything, so a lone SOX site rarely predicts regulation. CTTTG-type variants overlap the TCF/LEF Wnt response element and cannot be confidently assigned to either family. Nine of the 36 HOCOMOCO models are ChIP-only and may reflect a partner's specificity.

families.name: NeuroD / Atonal / ASCL
families.def: Class II neural E-box CAGATG / CAGCTG. NEUROD1/2/4/6, NEUROG1-3, ATOH1/7/8, ASCL1/2, OLIG1-3, PTF1A, FERD3L, BHLHA9/15, BHLHE22/23, MSGN1, FIGLA, NHLH1/2.
families.short: Class II basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) proteins of the Atonal, achaete-scute, Olig and NSCL groups — NEUROD1/2, NEUROG1-3, ATOH1/7/8, ASCL1/2, OLIG1-3, PTF1A, BHLHA15, FIGLA, MSGN1, NHLH1/2 and relatives — bind DNA only as heterodimers with the broadly expressed class I E-proteins TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12. The dimer reads a six-base E-box, CANNTG; this group prefers CAGATG (CATCTG on the opposite strand), with CATATG and CAGCTG as the two common variants. These factors are commitment switches for progenitors in the nervous system, inner ear, retina, pancreas, intestine and presomitic mesoderm, and several of them — ASCL1, NEUROD1, NEUROG2, ATOH1 — are the active ingredients of direct reprogramming protocols that convert fibroblasts into neurons.
families.long:
## The factors

This family collects the tissue-restricted ("class II") bHLH proteins whose DNA-binding domains are closest to *Drosophila* atonal and achaete-scute. In the atlas it spans NEUROD1/2 (and NEUROD4/6), NEUROG1/2/3, ATOH1/7/8, ASCL1/2, OLIG1/2/3, PTF1A, FERD3L, FIGLA, BHLHA9, BHLHA15 (MIST1), BHLHE22/23, MSGN1 and NHLH1/2 — around twenty human genes. The binding unit is a ~60-residue basic helix-loop-helix domain: a basic segment that lies in the major groove, followed by two helices separated by a loop that pack into a parallel four-helix bundle with the partner subunit. Almost none of these proteins binds DNA usefully on its own. The functional species is a heterodimer with a class I E-protein — TCF3 (E12/E47), TCF4 (ITF2) or TCF12 (HEB) — which are expressed in nearly every cell type. The crystal structure of the E47-NEUROD1 bHLH dimer on the insulin-gene E-box shows why heterodimers dominate: the E47-NEUROD1 interface is as extensive as the E47 homodimer interface, while NEUROD1 homodimers are unstable. Expression of the class II partners is narrow and largely non-overlapping: NEUROG1/2 in neural progenitors, NEUROD1 in newly born neurons and pancreatic islets, ATOH1 in cerebellar granule, inner-ear hair-cell and intestinal secretory progenitors, ASCL1 in ventral telencephalon and autonomic and neuroendocrine lineages, OLIG2 in motor-neuron and oligodendrocyte precursors, PTF1A in pancreas and cerebellum, BHLHA15 in exocrine secretory cells, FIGLA in oocytes, MSGN1 in presomitic mesoderm. "Neural" describes most of the family, not all of it.

## The motif

The site is a six-base E-box, CANNTG, an imperfect palindrome in which each monomer reads one CAN half-site. A glutamate in the basic region hydrogen-bonds the cytosine and adenine of its half-site and an adjacent arginine contacts the guanine on the complementary strand; these contacts are what make CA...TG invariant. The central two positions are the variable ones, and in the E47-NEUROD1 structure no side chain contacts them directly — specificity there comes from backbone contacts, DNA deformability and flanking sequence. That is the single most important fact for interpreting hits: CAGATG, CAGCTG and CATCTG (the reverse complement of CAGATG) differ at positions the protein barely touches.

The data reflect this. The representative model is `gaCAGATGG`, and the 82 motifs split into three overlapping groups: CAGATG (mostly ChIP-derived, for NEUROD1/2, NEUROG2, ATOH1, PTF1A), CATATG (almost all HT-SELEX or methyl-SELEX models, covering NEUROG1/2/3, OLIG1/2/3, ATOH1/7, BHLHE22/23, NEUROD1/2, BHLHA15) and CAGCTG (ASCL1/2, NHLH1/2, PTF1A, FERD3L, ATOH8, BHLHA9), with a CACCTG minority for FIGLA and some ASCL1 and PTF1A models. Genome-wide comparison of NEUROD2 and MYOD binding found CAGCTG shared between them and CAGATG as the NEUROD2-preferred site, so CAGCTG is the least diagnostic of the three. The flanks add a little: FERD3L models read GTAACAGCTGTTGC, NHLH models CGCAGCTGCG, and PTF1A ChIP gives an E-box followed after about five bases by a TTC, the TC-box of the trimeric PTF1 complex with RBPJ or RBPJL. Overall cohesion is 0.81 and no member is flagged as belonging elsewhere, but the CATATG and CAGCTG subgroups are separated by more than the usual paralogue-level noise.

## Where it acts

These are enhancer factors. Sites are distal, AT-rich rather than CpG-island-associated, and binding is largely confined to E-boxes that are already in accessible chromatin, so the same motif is used by different family members in different cell types with little overlap. Typical genome-wide occupancy is thousands to tens of thousands of sites per factor, a small fraction of the available E-boxes. Frequent neighbours are SOX (SOX2, SOX10), POU (POU3F2/BRN2), LHX and RFX motifs in neural enhancers, and in the pancreas FOXA, PDX1 and RBPJ/RBPJL. The named composite element in this family is the PTF1 site: an E-box and a TC-box about one helical turn apart, bound by PTF1A together with RBPJ (PTF1-J) or RBPJL (PTF1-L).

## Biology and disease

These factors are commitment switches. *Atoh1* loss removes cerebellar granule neurons, inner-ear hair cells and the intestinal secretory lineage; *Neurog3* loss removes all four pancreatic endocrine cell types; *Olig1* and *Olig2* couple motor-neuron and oligodendrocyte specification, and *Olig2* loss removes both; *Neurog1/2* are required for cranial and dorsal root sensory neurons. ASCL1 also drives progenitor proliferation, not only differentiation, which is why proneural activity and cell-cycle exit are not synonymous. In humans, biallelic *PTF1A* mutations cause pancreatic and cerebellar agenesis. ASCL1 and NEUROD1 define transcriptional subtypes of small-cell lung cancer and OLIG2 marks oligodendroglial tumours. The same commitment function underlies direct reprogramming: ASCL1 with POU3F2 and MYT1L converts fibroblasts to functional neurons, and NEUROD1, NEUROG2 and ATOH1 are used in comparable protocols.

## Reading a hit

A CAGATG, CATATG or CAGCTG match tells you a class II bHLH-E-protein heterodimer could bind, and nothing about which one. All ~20 members are indistinguishable from sequence; the Vierstra archetype `AC0084:OLIG/NEUROG:bHLH` says so in its name. Chance matters: a fixed six-mer is expected roughly 750,000 times per strand of a 3.1-Gb genome, so a bare E-box hit is close to uninformative without conservation, accessibility or expression evidence. Which motif version you scan with changes the answer — the in vitro (HT-SELEX) models say CATATG while the ChIP models say CAGATG or CAGCTG. Members with only ChIP evidence (HOCOMOCO fourth-field `P`, e.g. `NDF1.H14CORE.0.P.B`) support "this factor occupies these regions", not "this factor binds this sequence"; the S and M models do the latter. One outlier deserves naming: the Vierstra archetype `AC0461:ASCL:bHLH` has the consensus ACACGACGC, which is not an E-box and matches nothing else in the family.
families.caveats: A hit identifies the family, not the factor: all twenty-odd members read the same six-base E-box and cannot be told apart from sequence, which is why one Vierstra archetype here is named OLIG/NEUROG rather than after a protein. The three variants CAGATG, CATATG and CAGCTG differ at positions the protein does not directly contact, so a scan tuned to one will miss or misrank the others, and CAGCTG in particular is shared with E-protein homodimers, MYOD, TWIST and TCF21. Six-mers are far too common to be evidence on their own. ChIP-only models (HOCOMOCO evidence letter P) show occupancy, not binding specificity.

families.name: POU (octamer)
families.def: Octamer ATGCAAAT and MORE/PORE dimer sites. POU1F1, POU2F1-3, POU3F1-4, POU4F1-3, POU5F1/OCT4, POU5F1B, POU6F1/2.
families.short: The octamer ATGCAAAT is the site read by the 16 human POU-domain factors, including OCT1/POU2F1, OCT2/POU2F2, PIT1/POU1F1, the BRN2/BRN1 group (POU3F1-4), the BRN3 group (POU4F1-3) and OCT4/POU5F1. What makes the family unusual is the binding unit: a POU-specific domain and a homeodomain joined by a flexible linker, so the two halves of the site can be re-arranged. The same proteins therefore also form dimers on the PORE and MORE elements and sit next to SOX partners in the SOX-OCT composite elements that control pluripotency genes. Hits matter because octamer elements drive immunoglobulin and snRNA promoters and because OCT4 occupancy of SOX-OCT sites is a defining feature of pluripotent cells. The motif is short and AT-rich, so it is common.
families.long:
## The factors

Sixteen human POU genes fall into six classes: POU1F1 (PIT1), POU2F1-3 (OCT1, OCT2, OCT11/SKN-1a), POU3F1-4 (OCT6, BRN2, BRN1, BRN4), POU4F1-3 (BRN3A/B/C), POU5F1 (OCT4) together with the retrogene-derived POU5F1B locus, and POU6F1/2. All of them use one composite DNA-binding unit, described from sequence in 1988 and named after PIT1, OCT1, OCT2 and *C. elegans* UNC-86: an N-terminal POU-specific domain (POU-S), a four-helix bundle whose helix-turn-helix resembles the bacteriophage lambda and 434 repressors, tethered by a flexible 15-27 residue linker to a C-terminal POU-homeodomain (POU-HD), a conventional 60-residue three-helix homeodomain. Expression is class-restricted. POU2F1 is essentially ubiquitous; POU2F2 is lymphoid; POU5F1 is confined to pluripotent and germ cells; POU3F and POU4F members mark defined neural, retinal and inner-ear lineages; POU1F1 is restricted to the anterior pituitary.

## The motif

The core is the 8-bp octamer ATGCAAAT, first noted as a conserved element upstream of immunoglobulin genes. The 1994 crystal structure of the OCT1 POU domain on an octamer site showed why the site is bipartite: POU-S grips the 5' ATGCA half and POU-HD the 3' AAAT half, the two domains bind opposite faces of the duplex, and the linker is disordered and contacts no bases. The 3' half is a TAAT-type homeodomain site read in the reverse orientation; POU-S contributes most of the base-specific contacts, which is why the ATGC block is the least tolerant part of the site. Because the linker tethers rather than spaces, the half-sites can be rearranged: two POU domains dimerize on the PORE (ATTTGAAATGCAAAT) or on the MORE (ATGCATATGCAT) using two non-overlapping surface patches, and only the PORE arrangement recruits the coactivator OBF-1/POU2AF1. Pooled across JASPAR, HOCOMOCO, CIS-BP and the Vierstra archetypes, this family's consensus is tTATGCaAATt - the octamer plus its usual flanking T - but cohesion is only 0.68, because many HT-SELEX models for POU3F, POU4F and POU6F members report homeodomain-half arrangements (TGCATAAT, ATTAATTATGCA, TAATTA, TCATTA) instead of the full octamer. Those are configuration variants of one binding unit, not separate specificities.

## Where it acts

Octamer sites are classically promoter-proximal, in immunoglobulin heavy- and light-chain promoters, the histone H2B promoter and snRNA promoters. The best-characterized POU enhancer elements are composite: an OCT4 octamer immediately adjacent to a SOX HMG site. OCT4 and SOX2 dimerize in different relative orientations on the FGF4 and UTF1 enhancers, and it is the arrangement of the two boxes in the DNA, not a switch in the proteins, that sets the geometry. The Vierstra archetype set recovers POU5F/NANOG and POU2F/POU3F clusters, reflecting how routinely these sites are found with partner motifs. Because the octamer is only 8 bp and AT-rich, an exact match is expected on the order of 10^5 times in 3.1 Gb, so the great majority of matches are unoccupied in any one cell type; occupancy tracks which POU class is expressed. Methyl-SELEX places several POU factors among those whose affinity is changed by CpG methylation in flanking positions, although the octamer core itself has no CpG.

## Biology and disease

POU5F1/OCT4 maintains the pluripotent state and is one of the four factors that reprogram human fibroblasts to induced pluripotent stem cells. POU2F2 with OBF-1 drives immunoglobulin promoter activity in B cells, and the PORE-versus-MORE distinction is the structural explanation for that coactivator dependence. POU3F2 and POU3F3 pattern the neocortex; POU4F1-3 specify sensory neurons, retinal ganglion cells and inner-ear hair cells; POU1F1 controls the growth hormone and prolactin genes. Mendelian loss of POU1F1 causes combined pituitary hormone deficiency, and mutations in POU3F4 and POU4F3 cause X-linked and autosomal dominant deafness respectively. In cancer, POU2F3 defines a tuft-cell-like subtype of small-cell lung carcinoma, and POU5F1 is re-expressed in germ cell tumors.

## Reading a hit

A good octamer match tells you that a POU factor could bind; it does not tell you which one. The in vitro models for POU2F1, POU2F2, POU2F3, POU3F1-4 and POU5F1 are all the same 8-9 bp, so treat a hit as "POU family" unless expression data narrow it. Do not read a bare TAATTA or TCATTA match as POU: that is the homeodomain half alone and is shared with most of the homeodomain superfamily, which is exactly why two low-information CIS-BP and Vierstra entries in this family have nearest neighbours in the HOX and Q50 groups. Conversely, a full PORE, MORE or SOX-OCT composite is much stronger evidence, because the spacing constraint is specific. HOCOMOCO ids are informative here: PO2F1.H14CORE.0.PS.A and PO5F1.H14CORE.2.SM.B carry in vitro (S/M) support, whereas the P-only models such as PO3F2.H14CORE.0.P.B come from ChIP alone and may reflect co-binding.
families.caveats: A hit identifies the POU family, not a paralogue: the octamer models for OCT1, OCT2, OCT4 and the BRN proteins are interchangeable at 8-9 bp. The family is only moderately cohesive (0.68) because HT-SELEX returns several linker configurations, and the lowest-information members reduce to TAAT cores indistinguishable from the rest of the homeodomain superfamily; three entries here have nearest neighbours in other homeodomain families. ChIP-derived (P-grade) POU models can capture partner motifs, particularly SOX sites in pluripotent cells. Exact octamers occur roughly 10^5 times genome-wide, so a match alone is weak evidence without expression or footprint support.
