families.name: ATF6 / CREB3 (ER stress)
families.def: ERSE / UPR elements, TGACGTGG-like. ATF6, ATF6B, CREB3, CREB3L1-L4, XBP1.
families.short: This group collects the endoplasmic-reticulum-tethered basic region-leucine zipper factors ATF6 and ATF6B together with the CREB3 (OASIS/Luman) family - CREB3, CREB3L1, CREB3L2, CREB3L3 and CREB3L4 - and XBP1. All are made as inactive precursors and released by regulated proteolysis or, for XBP1, by IRE1-mediated mRNA splicing, so their activity reports stress in the secretory pathway rather than a signaling kinase. They bind an asymmetric, CRE-like element, TGACGTGG, equivalently CCACGTCA on the opposite strand, whose CCACG half is the ATF6-contacted part of the ER stress response element ERSE (CCAAT-N9-CCACG). Their targets are ER chaperones, ERAD components and secretory-pathway genes. The members are not separable by sequence, and several of their matrices are indistinguishable from an ordinary CRE or a CACGTG E-box.
families.long:
## The factors

Two related sets of bZIP proteins share this element, and both are membrane-tethered. ATF6 (ATF6A) and ATF6B (CREB-RP) are type-II transmembrane proteins of the ER; accumulation of unfolded protein in the ER lumen releases them for transport to the Golgi, where site-1 and site-2 proteases cleave off a soluble nuclear fragment, the 50 kDa p50ATF6. The CREB3 family - CREB3 (Luman/LZIP), CREB3L1 (OASIS), CREB3L2 (BBF2H7), CREB3L3 (CREB-H) and CREB3L4 (AIbZIP) - is processed the same way, but the members are tissue-restricted: CREB3L1 in osteoblasts and other secretory cells, CREB3L2 in chondrocytes, CREB3L3 in liver and intestine, CREB3L4 in prostate, while CREB3, ATF6 and ATF6B are broad. XBP1 groups here by motif but is produced differently: IRE1 excises 26 nucleotides from its mRNA, shifting the reading frame to yield the active bZIP XBP1s. Because the bZIP domains are closely related, all of these proteins dimerize with one another to varying degrees, and ATF6-XBP1s heterodimers are documented.

## The motif

The element is best written as the 8 bp TGACGTGG, or CCACGTCA reading the other strand. It is asymmetric: one half is the CRE half-site TGACG, the other is CCACG (CGTGG on the top strand), so a single subunit reads a CRE-like half and the other reads a G-rich half. The functional promoter element in which ATF6 acts is composite. The ER stress response element ERSE has the consensus CCAAT-N9-CCACG, and p50ATF6 binds CCACG only when the general factor NF-Y occupies the CCAAT box nine bases away; a second element, ERSE-II, has the shorter arrangement ATTGG-N-CCACG and is also ATF6-dependent. The mammalian UPRE, used in reporter work, is the TGACGTG(G/A) core alone. The 26 models collected here give a consensus of GGTGACGTGGC, with the highest-information examples (JASPAR ATF6 MA1466.2, CIS-BP ATF6 and ATF6B) reading TGATGACGTGGCA. Members are not distinguishable: the ATF6, ATF6B, CREB3, CREB3L3, CREB3L4 and XBP1 models sit above 0.95 similarity to one another, and the Vierstra archetype AC0633 is named CREB3L/XBP precisely because their motifs clustered. Two kinds of drift within the family matter in practice. Some entries collapse to a plain CRE - the HOCOMOCO ATF6A HT-SELEX model is TGATGACGTCAT and JASPAR CREB3L4 MA1475.2 is GTGACGTCA - and are then indistinguishable from CREB/ATF. Others collapse to a CACGTG E-box - JASPAR Creb3l2 MA0608.1 is GCCACGTGT and the CIS-BP CREB3L1 model is TGCCACGTGTAC - and are then indistinguishable from USF, MITF or TFE3 motifs. Both drifts follow from the shared ACGT core.

## Where it acts

This family works mainly at promoters, and its canonical targets are the ER chaperone and quality-control genes: HSPA5 (GRP78/BiP), HSP90B1 (GRP94), CALR, and ERAD components including HERPUD1, SEL1L and EDEM1. These promoters are CpG-island-associated and the elements are promoter-proximal rather than distributed across enhancers, which distinguishes this family's genomic distribution from AP-1. XBP1s occupancy is nonetheless condition- and cell-type-specific, with distinct target networks in different tissues, so the shared motif does not imply a shared target set. The obligate partner for ERSE function is NF-Y at the CCAAT box; ATF6 and XBP1s also co-occupy UPR promoters with ATF4, whose amino-acid response elements lie at overlapping loci. CREB3-family factors additionally act at secretory-pathway and lipid-metabolism promoters outside the classical chaperone set.

## Biology and disease

These factors implement the transcriptional arm of the unfolded protein response and, more broadly, adjust secretory capacity to demand. XBP1 is required for plasma cell differentiation, the extreme case of secretory expansion, and Xbp1-null mice also fail in hepatocyte development. CREB3L1/OASIS is required for bone formation in mice, and biallelic CREB3L1 loss causes a recessive form of osteogenesis imperfecta in humans. CREB3L2 is the 3-prime partner of the recurrent FUS-CREB3L2 fusion that defines low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma, in which the CREB3L2 bZIP supplies DNA binding to a chimeric activator. Biallelic ATF6 variants, including multi-exon deletions, cause achromatopsia with foveal hypoplasia, a phenotype that localizes an ER-stress transducer to cone photoreceptor development. Prolonged signaling through this arm, with ATF4 and CHOP, drives apoptosis rather than adaptation.

## Reading a hit

A TGACGTGG match is a reasonable family call and no kind of member call: ATF6, ATF6B, CREB3, CREB3L1 to CREB3L4 and XBP1 are interchangeable at this resolution, and only expression data can narrow it. Before trusting the call, check which half-sites you actually matched. If the 3-prime half is GTCA rather than GTGG, you have a plain CRE and CREB/ATF is at least as likely; if the match is CACGTG with no TGAC half, you have an E-box and the USF/MITF/TFE families are better explanations. A functional ATF6 site normally comes with context: look for a CCAAT box about nine bases away (ERSE) or an ATTGG one base away (ERSE-II), and for promoter proximity. All ten HOCOMOCO models here carry in vitro evidence in their code (S or M), which supports direct binding, but three members - CREB3L1, CREB3L2 and CREB3L4 - also contribute truncated models such as ACGTGG and ACGTGGC that will match far too often to interpret on their own.
families.caveats: The family is internally cohesive, but its motif is the least distinctive in the bZIP set because it is built on an ACGT core shared with the CRE and with CACGTG E-boxes. Several matrices in this collection have drifted to one or the other: two read as plain CREs and two as E-boxes, so an unqualified hit may not even be in the right family. A match also does not tell you which of the eight proteins is bound, nor that any of them is expressed, nor whether the ER stress pathway is active. Because ATF6 needs NF-Y at a CCAAT box to work at ERSE, an isolated CCACG with no CCAAT nearby is weak evidence of a functional UPR element.

families.name: TWIST / HAND
families.def: E-box CATCTG/CAGATG bound by TWIST1/2, HAND1/2, TCF21, MESP1/2, SCX.
families.short: TWIST1/2, HAND1/2, TCF21, SCX and MESP1/2 are class II basic helix-loop-helix factors of mesoderm and neural crest. They bind the E-box CANNTG as heterodimers with the ubiquitous E-proteins TCF3/TCF4/TCF12, with each other, or as homodimers, and this group prefers CAGATG (CATCTG on the opposite strand). Because the two central E-box bases are barely contacted by the protein, the distinction from the muscle E-box CAGCTG and the neural CATATG is weak. TWIST has one genuinely diagnostic feature: a double E-box with the two boxes five bases apart, which aligns two TWIST-E47 dimers on one face of the helix so they can tetramerise. The family runs craniofacial, cardiac, tendon and epithelial-mesenchymal transition programmes.
families.long:
## The factors

TWIST1, TWIST2 (DERMO-1), HAND1 (eHAND/Thing1), HAND2 (dHAND/Thing2), TCF21 (capsulin/epicardin/POD1), SCX (scleraxis) and MESP1/MESP2 make up this family. All are class II bHLH proteins of mesodermal and neural-crest lineages, and all bind DNA as dimers: heterodimers with the ubiquitous class I E-proteins TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12, homodimers, and heterodimers with each other. The TWIST1-HAND2 pairing matters functionally, because different dimer species have different activities and the balance between them is set post-translationally. Phosphorylation of two conserved residues in helix I by protein kinase A and protein kinase C, reversed by protein phosphatase 2A, shifts TWIST1 and HAND2 dimer choice, and mutations that alter that balance produce limb and craniofacial phenotypes overlapping the TWIST1 loss-of-function syndrome. TWIST1 additionally carries a C-terminal WR ("Twist-box") domain that dimerises, allowing two TWIST1-E47 dimers to assemble into a tetramer. Expression is lineage-restricted but broad within those lineages: TWIST1/2 in cranial and limb mesenchyme, dermis and many mesenchymal tumours; HAND1 in extraembryonic mesoderm, left ventricle and trophoblast; HAND2 in right ventricle, branchial arches and sympathoadrenal cells; TCF21 in epicardium, kidney, lung mesenchyme and vascular smooth muscle; SCX in tendon; MESP1/2 in nascent mesoderm.

## The motif

The core is again a six-base E-box, CANNTG, with each monomer reading one CAN half-site. This family's preference is written CAGATG, or equivalently CATCTG read on the other strand, and that is what the data give: the representative model is `CCAGATGT` (CIS-BP TWIST1 and JASPAR TWIST1 MA1123.3 agree exactly), with HOCOMOCO TWIST1 ChIP models reading ACATCTG. The distinction from the muscle E-box CAGCTG and the neural CAGATG/CATATG is weak by construction — the two central bases are the ones that vary, and in the one solved class I/class II structure on an asymmetric E-box (E47-NEUROD1 on CATCTG) no side chain contacts the central base pairs directly. Expect substantial cross-matching.

The one feature in this family with real discriminating power is architectural rather than compositional. High-resolution mapping of TWIST occupancy in human and *Drosophila* genomes found that TWIST, and not other bHLH proteins tested, prefers a double E-box with the two boxes separated by five nucleotides; the spacing aligns two TWIST-E47 dimers on the same face of the helix so that the WR domains can contact each other and form a stable tetramer. The data carry that signature: `TWST2.H14CORE.0.P.B` reads CAGCTGGNNNCCAGATGT, two E-boxes five bases apart, in a single model.

Cohesion here is the lowest of the E-box families at 0.76, and label agreement is poor for most members. TCF21 has one high-grade model reading AACAGCTGG (a myogenic-type site) and another reading CATATGGT (a NeuroD/Atonal-type site). MESP1/MESP2 models read CATATG or CACCTG. The HAND models are the weakest: `HAND1.H14CORE.0.P.B` and `HAND2.H14CORE.0.P.B` are nearly identical to one another (TCTGGNTTNTGTCA) but resemble nothing else, and JASPAR's Hand1 MA2123.1 (CCAGACCT) and Hand1::Tcf3 MA0092.2 (GTCTGGCA) are not recognisable E-boxes at all, while the one HT-SELEX HAND2 model reads GCACCTGC. Three mutually inconsistent HAND2 models exist across the four databases.

## Where it acts

These are enhancer factors in mesenchymal, cardiac and neural-crest chromatin, not CpG-island promoter factors. TWIST1 sites occur in epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) programmes alongside SNAI, ZEB, TEAD and AP-1 motifs; the double E-box is the TWIST-specific arrangement. HAND2 sites sit in the core regulatory circuitry of the adrenergic/noradrenergic state of neuroblastoma, co-occurring with PHOX2B, GATA3, ASCL1 and TBX2 motifs in large super-enhancer clusters, and the same circuit can switch to a mesenchymal state with an entirely different motif complement. TCF21 acts in smooth-muscle and fibroblast enhancers; the coronary artery disease association at 6q23.2 maps to an enhancer regulating *TCF21* expression rather than to coding variation.

## Biology and disease

TWIST1 haploinsufficiency causes Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, with coronal craniosynostosis, facial asymmetry and limb anomalies; both founding reports identified loss-of-function and missense changes clustered in the bHLH domain. TWIST1 is also required for EMT-associated metastasis in mammary tumour models. *Hand1*-null mouse embryos die with extraembryonic and cardiac defects; *Hand2* (dHAND) loss disrupts right ventricle and branchial-arch development and sympathetic neuron differentiation. *Mesp1* is expressed in heart precursors and required for a single heart tube. HAND2 is a dependency of adrenergic neuroblastoma. TCF21 variation contributes to coronary artery disease risk through smooth-muscle phenotype.

## Reading a hit

A CAGATG or CATCTG match says a class II bHLH-E-protein dimer of this general kind could bind. It does not tell you which factor, and the separation from the NEUROD/ATOH family (CAGATG/CATATG) and the MYOD family (CAGCTG) is one or two bases at positions the protein barely touches. If you want evidence that a site is genuinely TWIST-type rather than generically bHLH, look for the double E-box with a five-base spacer; a single E-box will not settle it. Treat HAND1 and HAND2 models with particular caution: all of the HAND ChIP-derived models in this family are HOCOMOCO grade B with `P` (ChIP-only) evidence, they do not look like E-boxes, and they match nothing else in the collection, which is the expected signature of an indirect or low-quality model rather than of a HAND recognition sequence. One CIS-BP TWIST2 model is inherited from the mouse protein at 100% DBD identity, which is harmless. Because the family's own members disagree about their preferred site, do not use a hit to assign a specific paralogue.
families.caveats: This is the least cohesive of the E-box families in the atlas (cohesion 0.76), and its members disagree with each other. TCF21 has one high-grade model reading a myogenic AACAGCTGG and another reading a NeuroD-type CATATGGT; HAND2 has three mutually inconsistent models across the four databases. The HAND1 and HAND2 models from ChIP are nearly identical to one another, are not recognisable E-boxes, and resemble nothing else in the collection — treat them as unreliable rather than as HAND recognition sequences. A single CAGATG or CATCTG hit identifies the general class II bHLH site, not the factor. Only the five-base-spaced double E-box discriminates TWIST specifically.

families.name: HES / HEY (N-box)
families.def: Class C bHLH-Orange repressors reading CACGYG (and the N box CACNAG); the CACGTG form is shared with the MYC/USF/MITF/CLOCK E-box families. HES1-7, HEY1/2, HEYL, HELT.
families.short: HES1-7, HEY1/2, HEYL and HELT are the vertebrate hairy/Enhancer-of-split relatives: bHLH repressors with an Orange domain that sets partner choice and a C-terminal WRPW or YRPW peptide that recruits TLE/Groucho corepressors. Most are direct Notch targets, so their activity reports Notch signalling. They read a genuinely different site from the class II bHLH activators — a proline in the basic region shifts preference away from CANNTG. Two sites are described: the functionally defined N box CACNAG, and the higher-affinity CACGYG (CACGTG or CACGCG) that the database matrices actually capture. HES1 autorepression through N boxes generates a two-hour expression oscillation; HES7 drives the somite segmentation clock.
families.long:
## The factors

HES1-HES7, HEY1, HEY2, HEYL and HELT are the vertebrate relatives of *Drosophila* hairy and Enhancer of split, and they are structurally distinct from the class I and class II bHLH proteins that read E-boxes. Three features define them. First, a proline in the basic region, which is why this group is sometimes called the proline-bHLH class and why its sequence preference differs from CANNTG. Second, an Orange domain, a two-helix module immediately C-terminal to the bHLH that restricts which partners a given member will dimerise with. Third, a C-terminal tetrapeptide — WRPW in HES proteins, YRPW in HEY proteins — that recruits TLE/Groucho corepressors. They are repressors, not activators. Most are direct transcriptional targets of Notch signalling through RBPJ/CSL, so their expression reports Notch activity: HES1 broadly, HES5 in neural progenitors, HES7 in presomitic mesoderm, HEY1/HEY2/HEYL in cardiovascular and endothelial tissue. HES2, HES3, HES4 and HES6 are divergent; HES6 does not behave like a canonical repressor. Crucially, these proteins repress by two routes. They bind DNA and recruit corepressors, and they also sequester class II activators: HES1 reduces E47-driven transcription and blocks MyoD- and MASH1-driven differentiation, which requires no HES site at all.

## The motif

Two different sites are attributed to this family, and the distinction matters. The site defined functionally is the N box, CACNAG, the Enhancer-of-split recognition sequence through which HES1 represses transcription. *Drosophila* hairy was then shown to prefer a non-canonical site, CACGCG, and mutating a single CACGCG in the *achaete* promoter abolishes hairy-mediated repression in cells and produces ectopic sensory organs in flies. Different papers call this site a class C site or a class B E-box; the nomenclature is not consistent, so it is safer to write the sequence than the class name.

What the databases contain is neither of these. Twenty-four of the 26 motifs assigned here read CACGTG or CACGYG, usually with GG/CC flanks: GGCACGTGCC. The representative model is JASPAR HEY1 MA0823.1 (CACGTGCC), and almost all the HOCOMOCO models carry in vitro evidence (`S` or `SM`), so this is a real binding preference measured in vitro, not an artefact. Genome-wide, HEY1, HEY2 and HEYL bound preferentially to CACGYG, but a large fraction of efficiently bound promoters contained no E-box at all, implying additional, loosely defined binding modes. The honest summary is that the high-affinity in vitro site is CACGYG, the classical repression site is the lower-affinity N box CACNAG, and the database matrices capture only the former. The atlas's data consensus CACGTGCC therefore disagrees with the ontology definition's N box for a documented reason rather than by error.

CACGTG is a problem sequence. It is the canonical palindromic E-box of MYC/MAX, USF1/2, TFE3/TFEB/MITF, SREBF1/2, BHLHE40/41, ARNT and the CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer. The Vierstra archetype `AC0068:HEY/CLOCK:bHLH` states this in its name. Two further Vierstra archetypes here, `AC0263:HES` and `AC0264:HES`, have low-information consensuses (CACACTT, CNCACGT) that resemble nothing else in the family and should not be used as HES models. Two CIS-BP entries, for HES4 and HEYL, are inferred from mouse proteins at 91% DNA-binding-domain identity.

## Where it acts

Unlike the E-box families, HES/HEY sites are promoter-proximal. Chromatin immunoprecipitation of HEY factors in HEK293 cells, cardiomyocytes and mouse hearts found binding clustered in proximal promoter regions, disproportionately at genes encoding transcriptional regulators and developmental control proteins. CACGTG contains a CpG, so these sites are enriched in CpG islands and their occupancy is sensitive to DNA methylation. HES1 binds N boxes in its own promoter, and that negative feedback loop, combined with short protein and mRNA half-lives, generates a roughly two-hour oscillation in HES1 expression. Neighbouring RBPJ/CSL sites are common, because these genes and their targets are Notch-responsive.

## Biology and disease

HES and HEY proteins are the main transcriptional output of Notch signalling. Hes1 and Hes5 maintain neural progenitors and delay neuronal differentiation; removing them causes premature neurogenesis and progenitor depletion. Hes7 drives the segmentation clock in presomitic mesoderm, and its loss disorganises somite formation; in humans, *HES7* mutations cause spondylocostal dysostosis with vertebral and rib malformations. HEY1, HEY2 and HEYL are strikingly redundant, which is why single knockouts are often mild and combined losses phenocopy each other in the heart. HES1 acts downstream of activated NOTCH1 in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

## Reading a hit

A CACGTG hit is one of the least specific results a scan can return: on sequence alone it is compatible with at least eight other families, several of which (MYC/MAX, USF, MITF, CLOCK-BMAL1) are far more abundantly expressed in most cell types than HES or HEY. Treat a CACGTG match as a "class B E-box" hit and resolve it with expression and co-factor evidence, not with motif scores. If you are specifically after Notch-effector repression, the functionally validated site is the N box CACNAG, which the database matrices will not find for you; scan for it separately and expect weak scores. The individual HES and HEY paralogues cannot be distinguished. Finally, remember that these proteins can repress without binding DNA, by titrating E-proteins and class II activators, so the absence of a site is not evidence that HES or HEY is not acting on a gene.
families.caveats: The site the databases model, CACGTG, is the canonical palindromic E-box shared with MYC/MAX, USF1/2, TFE3/TFEB/MITF, SREBF, BHLHE40/41, ARNT and CLOCK-BMAL1 — one Vierstra archetype here is named HEY/CLOCK for exactly that reason — so a hit is weak evidence for HES or HEY specifically. The classically defined repression site, the N box CACNAG, is lower affinity and is not represented by these matrices, so a scan will miss it. Two low-information Vierstra HES archetypes resemble nothing else in the family. HES4 and HEYL models are inferred from mouse proteins. HES and HEY also repress without binding DNA, by sequestering E-proteins, so absent sites do not exclude their involvement.

families.name: STAT
families.def: GAS TTCnnnGAA and ISRE-like. STAT1-4, STAT5A/B, STAT6.
families.short: The seven human STAT proteins - STAT1, STAT2, STAT3, STAT4, STAT5A, STAT5B and STAT6 - sit latent in the cytoplasm until a receptor-associated JAK kinase phosphorylates a single C-terminal tyrosine. Two phosphorylated monomers then pair through reciprocal SH2-phosphotyrosine contacts and clamp around DNA at a gamma-interferon activation site (GAS): the short inverted repeat TTCNNNGAA. Spacing is almost the only sequence feature that distinguishes them, with STAT6 preferring a four-base spacer and the rest a three-base spacer, so a GAS match names the family and not the member. STATs convert essentially every cytokine, interferon and several growth factor signals into transcription, and germline or somatic STAT mutations cause immunodeficiency, allergy, growth failure and leukemia.
families.long:
## The factors

Seven genes: STAT1, STAT2, STAT3, STAT4, STAT5A, STAT5B and STAT6. All share one architecture - an
N-terminal domain, a coiled-coil, a DNA-binding domain built on an immunoglobulin fold like those of
NF-kappaB and p53, a linker, an SH2 domain, and a C-terminal transactivation domain carrying the
conserved tyrosine. The protein is latent in the cytoplasm; a receptor-associated JAK phosphorylates
that tyrosine, and two monomers pair by reciprocal contacts between the SH2 domain of one and the
phosphotyrosine tail of the other, producing a C-shaped clamp that encircles the DNA. The
phosphotyrosine site of the SH2 domain is structurally coupled to the DNA-binding domain, so
dimerization and DNA binding are not independent. Which STAT is active is set by the cytokine, not by
the DNA: STAT1 homodimers by interferon gamma, STAT1-STAT2 plus IRF9 (ISGF3) by type I interferons,
STAT3 by the IL-6 family, STAT4 by IL-12, STAT5A and STAT5B by the IL-2 family, growth hormone,
prolactin and erythropoietin, and STAT6 by IL-4 and IL-13. STAT5A and STAT5B have no measured
difference in DNA-binding specificity.

## The motif

The GAS element is TTCNNNGAA: two TTC/GAA half-sites facing each other across a three-base spacer,
often written TT(N)5AA. Spacer width is the only substantial selectivity available. STAT6 prefers
four spacer bases, TTCNNNNGAA, but still binds three-base sites reasonably well; STAT1 and STAT5
prefer three, and STAT5A tolerates four weakly; none of them binds a lone half-site. In reporter
assays, a five-base TT-to-AA spacing is generally permissive, four favors STAT3-containing complexes
and six favors IL-4-activated complexes. Within the three-base class, STAT1, STAT3, STAT4 and STAT5
are not separable by sequence, and the consensus that the models here agree on, TTCCTGGAA, is
compatible with all of them. Two further arrangements matter in practice. First, tetramers: contacts
between N-terminal domains let two dimers bind tandem, individually weak GAS sites cooperatively, so
genuine STAT5 targets are often clusters of poor matches rather than one good one, and scanning for a
single strong site will miss them. Second, ISGF3: when STAT1 and STAT2 act with IRF9 they read an
ISRE rather than a GAS, with the STAT pair on the 5' GGAA and IRF9 on the second GAAA repeat. That is
why several STAT-labelled models here look like ISREs - HOCOMOCO STAT1.H14CORE.1.P.B
(TCAGTTTCRTTTTCC), HOCOMOCO STAT2.H14CORE.0.P.B (GGAAANHGAAACTGA) and JASPAR STAT1::STAT2.

## Where it acts

STAT occupancy is signal-dependent and transient: sites become occupied within minutes of cytokine
exposure and are vacated as the STAT is dephosphorylated and exported. Targets are both
cytokine-inducible promoters and, more often, enhancers, where STATs cooperate with the
lineage-defining factors of the responding cell. The practical consequence is that a GAS match in an
unstimulated cell type usually corresponds to nothing: the motif is present in the genome whether or
not the pathway is on. Type I interferon signaling shifts the element as well as the factor, from GAS
to ISRE, so the same STAT1 protein leaves different footprints depending on which interferon acted.

## Biology and disease

Human genetics has produced an unusually clear catalogue. Gain-of-function STAT1 mutations impair
IL-17 immunity and cause chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Dominant-negative mutations in the STAT3
DNA-binding domain cause hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome - a disease of DNA binding specifically, since the
mutant protein dimerizes but cannot read its site. Somatic STAT3 mutations, mostly in the SH2 domain,
occur in large granular lymphocytic leukemia, and activating STAT5B mutations recur in T-cell
leukemias. Loss-of-function STAT5B mutations cause growth hormone insensitivity with severe short
stature and immune dysfunction. Germline gain-of-function STAT6 mutations cause severe early-onset
allergic disease. Together these establish that STAT dosage and DNA-binding competence, not just
pathway activation, are rate-limiting in vivo.

## Reading a hit

Be conservative. TTCNNNGAA specifies only six bases, so it is expected on the order of several
hundred thousand times per strand in a 3.1-Gb genome; STAT matches are among the least specific in
this atlas, and this family is the least internally cohesive of the ETS/IRF/STAT group. The evidence
behind the models is also weaker than elsewhere: every HOCOMOCO model assigned here is ChIP-derived
(evidence letter P, grade B) with no in vitro HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX model, all nine JASPAR
models are ChIP-seq, six of them from mouse rather than human experiments (Stat2, Stat4, Stat5a,
Stat5b, Stat6, Stat5a::Stat5b), and two CIS-BP entries are transferred from mouse proteins on
DNA-binding-domain similarity - one of which is the motif this atlas selects as the family
representative. "This protein binds this sequence" therefore rests largely on in vivo co-occupancy
plus older in vitro studies. Expect confusion with IRF: the ISRE-shaped STAT models cross-match IRF
motifs, and in this atlas most nearest neighbours of STAT1.H14CORE.1.P.B, STAT2.H14CORE.0.P.B and
JASPAR STAT1::STAT2 are labelled IRF, while the JASPAR mouse Stat2 model's best match anywhere lies
outside the STAT family. The discriminator is orientation: a GAS is an inverted repeat (TTC facing
GAA), an ISRE is a direct repeat of GAAA. Finally, no STAT paralogue can be named from sequence -
STAT5A versus STAT5B is impossible - so use the cytokine, the time point and the cell type.
families.caveats:
A GAS match names the family, never the member: STAT1, STAT3, STAT4 and STAT5 read
the same three-spacer inverted repeat, STAT5A and STAT5B have no measured specificity difference, and
only STAT6's preference for a four-base spacer gives partial leverage. The element is short enough to
occur hundreds of thousands of times by chance, and occupancy is signal-dependent, so a hit in an
unstimulated cell type usually means nothing. Evidence is weaker here than for most families: all
HOCOMOCO models assigned to STAT are ChIP-only, all JASPAR models are ChIP-seq and two-thirds of
them are mouse, and two CIS-BP entries - including the family representative - are inferred from
mouse proteins. Expect overlap with IRF, since ISGF3 (STAT1-STAT2-IRF9) reads the ISRE, not a GAS.

families.name: C/EBP
families.def: TT(G/A)CGCAA palindrome. CEBPA/B/D/E/G, and DDIT3 (CHOP) heterodimer sites.
families.short: The C/EBP family - CEBPA, CEBPB (NF-IL6), CEBPD, CEBPE, CEBPG, with DDIT3 (CHOP) as a heterodimer partner - binds the palindromic element TT(G/A)CGCAA, most often written as the 10-mer ATTGCGCAAT. These are basic region-leucine zipper proteins; the leucine zipper itself was first described in C/EBP, and the family's distinctive DNA contacts centre on an arginine that is conserved in C/EBPs but not in other bZIPs. Family members control hepatic and adipose metabolism, the acute-phase response, and granulocyte maturation, and CEBPA and CEBPE are mutated in human myeloid disease. The paralogues are indistinguishable from sequence. The boundary with the CREB/ATF family is genuinely blurred: CHOP-containing dimers and ATF4 read a hybrid half-C/EBP, half-CRE site, and CpG methylation converts a CRE into a C/EBP-alpha site.
families.long:
## The factors

Five C/EBP proteins bind DNA as this family: CEBPA, CEBPB (also NF-IL6 or LAP/LIP), CEBPD, CEBPE and CEBPG. All are basic region-leucine zipper (bZIP) factors, and the leucine zipper was in fact first proposed from the C/EBP sequence, with the scissors-grip model of DNA recognition advanced for the same family a year later. CEBPA, CEBPB, CEBPD and CEBPE have N-terminal activation domains; CEBPG has essentially none and works mainly through heterodimers. Expression differs sharply even though the motif does not: CEBPB and CEBPG are broad, CEBPA is concentrated in liver, adipose tissue, lung and granulocytes, CEBPD is stress- and cytokine-inducible, and CEBPE is restricted to the granulocyte and eosinophil lineages. Alternative translation initiation produces short LIP isoforms of CEBPA and CEBPB that dimerize and occupy sites without activating, so the same motif can be read as an activator or a competitive repressor depending on isoform ratio. DDIT3 (CHOP/GADD153) is included here because it is an obligate C/EBP partner, but its basic region is substituted at positions that matter for C/EBP-site contact, so CHOP-C/EBP heterodimers bind a different, hybrid sequence rather than the C/EBP palindrome. C/EBPs also pair outside the family, notably with ATF4 and with NF-kappa-B subunits.

## The motif

The consensus is the palindrome TT(G/A)CGCAA, usually presented with flanks as ATTGCGCAAT. It is an inverted repeat of the half-site TTGC, one half per subunit. The C/EBP-alpha crystal structure resolved the contacts across ATTGCGCAAT and identified Arg289 as the keystone residue: it hydrogen-bonds to an adenine in the half-site, to the DNA backbone, and to Asn292, the asparagine invariant across bZIPs. A second residue explains the family boundary. Val296, which is alanine in most other bZIPs, discriminates against purines and restrains the invariant Arg300; mutating it to alanine strongly increased C/EBP-alpha binding to CRE sites while leaving C/EBP-site affinity intact. In other words a single side chain, not a different reading frame, separates the C/EBP site from the cyclic-AMP response element. Common variants replace the central CG: ATTGCACAAT and ATTGCGTAAT are both well represented among the 25 models here, as are half-degenerate forms in which only one TTGC half is intact. Methylation adds a twist in the same direction: CpG methylation of the CRE TGACGTCA, and of the half-sites CGTCA and CGCAA, increases C/EBP-alpha binding, and methylated promoters bound by C/EBP-alpha lose that binding when demethylated. The paralogues are not distinguishable - JASPAR CEBPB MA0466.4 and CEBPE MA0837.3 are 0.997 similar, and every CEBPA, CEBPD and CEBPG model here falls within 0.95 of the family medoid. What does look different is the CHOP-partnered and ATF4-adjacent set: JASPAR Ddit3::Cebpa, HOCOMOCO DDIT3 and JASPAR CEBPG MA1636.2 all read ATGATGCAAT-like sequences, which is the C/EBP-ATF composite element (CARE), half CRE and half C/EBP.

## Where it acts

C/EBP sites occur at both promoters and enhancers, with less CpG-island bias than the CRE. In macrophages and adipocytes they are among the motifs that lineage-determining factors use when priming enhancers, and C/EBP-beta co-occupies acute-phase promoters with NF-kappa-B while C/EBP-alpha and C/EBP-beta act with PPARG at adipocyte enhancers and with RUNX1 and SPI1 at myeloid enhancers. The named composite element is the CARE, TTGCATCA or TGATGCAAT, at integrated-stress-response genes including DDIT3 itself, TRIB3, ASNS and ATF3; there C/EBP-family proteins and ATF4 occupy the same element. On frequency: the exact palindrome TTGCGCAA is expected of order 10^4 times in 3.1 Gb before allowing for the genome's CpG depletion, while its non-CpG relatives TTGCACAA and TTGTGCAA are several-fold more common, so scans at usual thresholds return large numbers of C/EBP-like matches.

## Biology and disease

Cebpa-null mice die soon after birth from hypoglycemia, with no hepatic glycogen and disrupted adipose tissue. Cebpb-null mice survive but their macrophages fail at bacterial killing and tumor cytotoxicity. Cebpe-null mice have impaired granulopoiesis, myelodysplasia and early lethality, and in humans loss-of-function CEBPE mutation causes neutrophil-specific granule deficiency, a disorder of defective secondary granules and recurrent bacterial infection. Dominant-negative CEBPA mutations that truncate the N-terminus define a recurrent subtype of acute myeloid leukemia, and germline CEBPA variants cause familial AML. C/EBP-beta and C/EBP-delta are the transcriptional arm of the IL-6 acute-phase response. DDIT3/CHOP, acting with ATF4, raises protein synthesis during sustained ER stress to the point of cell death, which makes the CARE element a control point for stress-induced apoptosis.

## Reading a hit

A full ATTGCGCAAT palindrome is among the more distinctive bZIP matches: TTGC half-sites are not shared with AP-1, CREB/ATF, MAF or NFE2/BACH, so the family call is comparatively safe. The member call is not available at all. CEBPA, CEBPB, CEBPD, CEBPE and CEBPG give one motif, and which of them is bound is a question about expression, not sequence. A lone TTGC half-site is not interpretable. The real ambiguity is with the C/EBP-ATF composite: if your match reads ATGATGCAAT or TTGCATCA, it is a CARE, and ATF4 in the CREB/ATF family accounts for it as well as any C/EBP does; the DDIT3 and CEBPG matrices here are the same element. Methylation cuts both ways: a methylated CRE can be a genuine C/EBP-alpha site, and a CGCAA-containing hit may require methylation to be occupied. None of the 25 models is flagged as belonging elsewhere, and the in vitro (HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX) models agree with the ChIP-derived ones, which is the reassuring case for a ChIP-heavy family.
families.caveats: C/EBP is one of the more trustworthy family calls in this atlas: the motif is cohesive across all four databases, its in vitro and ChIP-derived models agree, and the TTGC half-site is not shared with the other bZIP families. Do not read a member into it - the five paralogues are identical at this resolution, and the biological consequence differs between them and between full-length and LIP isoforms of the same protein. Two caveats are specific. Matches of the form ATGATGCAAT are C/EBP-ATF composites and are equally well explained by ATF4. And because methylated CpG creates C/EBP-alpha sites at half-CRE and half-C/EBP sequences, a scan run without methylation data will both miss real sites and over-call unmethylated ones.

families.name: ETS epithelial (ELF/EHF)
families.def: AACCGGAAGT with distinct 5' preference. ELF1-5, EHF, ELF2.
families.short: ELF1, ELF2, ELF3, ELF4, ELF5 and EHF are the ELF branch of the ETS family. They bind the same GGA(A/T) core as every other ETS protein through the same winged helix-turn-helix domain, but prefer a C where class I ETS factors prefer an A three bases 5' of the core, giving the ten-base site ACCCGGAAGT. ELF3, ELF5 and EHF are the epithelium-specific "ESE" members, expressed in gut, salivary gland, breast, airway, cornea, prostate and bladder epithelium; ELF1, ELF2 and ELF4 are broader, with strong hematopoietic expression. These factors set and maintain epithelial differentiation - mammary alveolar cell fate, intestinal goblet cells, airway CFTR expression - and are recurrently mutated or silenced in carcinomas of the bladder, biliary tract, cervix and breast.
families.long:
## The factors

Six human genes make up this group: ELF1, ELF2 (NERF), ELF3 (ESE-1/ESX), ELF4 (MEF), ELF5 (ESE-2)
and EHF (ESE-3). Each has a single ETS domain of about 85 residues - three alpha-helices on a
four-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet, a winged helix-turn-helix - that binds DNA as a monomer,
with no obligate dimerization partner of the kind GABPA requires. Binding profiles of all human
and mouse ETS proteins place the ELF proteins in class II (subclass IIa), separate from the large
class I group and from ETV6/ETV7. Expression splits the group in two. ELF3, ELF5 and EHF, together
with SPDEF, form the epithelium-specific ETS ("ESE") subfamily: ELF3 is highest in
gastrointestinal tract, salivary gland, bladder, liver and prostate; ELF5 is restricted to
salivary gland, breast and bladder with some lung, kidney and skin; EHF covers salivary gland,
esophagus, prostate, colon, skin, bladder and breast. ELF1, ELF2 and ELF4 are more widely
expressed, with prominent hematopoietic and lymphoid expression.

## The motif

The literature writes the class II site as CCCGGAAGT, differing from the class I consensus
ACCGGAAGT at a single position: the base three steps 5' of the GGA core, where class I strongly
disfavors C and the ELF group accepts or prefers it. With the extra 5' adenine that most
in vitro models here include, the site reads ACCCGGAAGT, which is what the motifs assigned to this
family agree on. The recognition chemistry is identical to the rest of the family: two invariant
arginines in helix H3 hydrogen-bond the two guanines of GGA, a wing lysine contacts DNA 5' of the
core and a turn lysine contacts the opposite strand 3' of it, so the core is read directly and the
flanks through backbone geometry. That makes the discriminating information one or two low-content
positions, and the six ELF/EHF proteins are not distinguishable from each other by sequence: the
JASPAR models for EHF (MA0598.4) and ELF3 (MA0640.3) have the identical consensus CACTTCCTG.
One variant is worth recognizing. CCGGAAGT contains a CpG, and methylating that CpG blocks ETS
binding; the methylation-aware HOCOMOCO models for ELF2, ELF3 and ELF4 in this family instead read
CAGGAAGT, a form with no CpG. Whether that is cause or coincidence, both forms are in wide use and
a scan should allow CAGGAAG as well as CCGGAAG.

## Where it acts

Two contexts dominate. ELF1, ELF2 and ELF4 contribute to the redundant ETS occupancy of
CpG-island promoters, where a strong consensus 20-40 bp upstream of the transcription start site is
bound interchangeably by many ETS proteins; a hit there is a poor basis for naming a factor. The
ESE members act mostly at epithelial enhancers and tissue-specific promoters, where their sites
are frequently non-consensus and sit among other epithelial regulators. Documented examples
include EHF at the CFTR promoter in bronchial epithelium, where it acts as a repressor and is
induced by inflammatory mediators; EHF across enhancers that define corneal epithelial identity;
and ELF5 at genes of the mammary alveolar program, including repression of SNAI2. Because the
motif is short and its family-discriminating positions weak, cell type - which ELF genes are
actually expressed - is usually more informative about which protein is bound than the sequence is.

## Biology and disease

The ESE factors maintain epithelial differentiation. Elf5-null mouse embryos die by about E7.5
from a trophoblast defect, and loss of a single Elf5 allele blocks mammary alveolar development in
pregnancy; ELF5 also holds cells in an epithelial state by repressing SNAI2, and its loss promotes
epithelial-mesenchymal transition and metastasis in breast cancer models. About 30% of Elf3-null
embryos die around E11.5 and survivors have abnormal small intestinal epithelium with reduced
goblet cells. The consequences in human cancer are mostly loss of function: ELF3 is recurrently
mutated in roughly 6% of bladder cancers, mucinous ovarian cancers, cholangiocarcinomas and
gallbladder cancers, about 10% of ampullary carcinomas and about 13% of cervical adenocarcinomas,
with a large share of inactivating alleles; EHF is downregulated with promoter methylation in
prostate cancer. An Ehf knockout phenotype has not been reported.

## Reading a hit

A match identifies an ELF/EHF-type ETS site, and it does so only weakly. The sequence separating
this family from class I ETS is a single flanking base, so a hit that scores well for ELF3 will
almost always also score well for ETS1, ERG or ELK1, and the reverse; if you need to know which
protein is bound, use expression and ChIP data, not the motif. The GGAA core is expected millions
of times per strand in a 3.1-Gb genome, so context - accessibility, conservation, an epithelial
enhancer, neighboring sites - has to carry the inference. Evidence quality is uneven within the
family: ELF1, ELF2, ELF3, ELF4 and ELF5 all have in vitro (HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX) HOCOMOCO
models, but EHF's only HOCOMOCO model here is ChIP-derived, so "EHF binds this sequence" rests on
weaker evidence than for its relatives. Two of the three Vierstra archetypes grouped here
(AC0452:ELF, AC0645:ELF) have GGAT-containing consensus sequences and match motifs outside this
family better than motifs inside it; treat them as loosely attached. Consensus strings also appear
on either strand - CACTTCCTG and CAGGAAGTG are the same site.
families.caveats:
The one base that distinguishes this family from class I ETS is a low-information
flanking position, so in practice a hit means "an ETS site" and not "an ELF site", let alone a
specific ELF protein; the JASPAR EHF and ELF3 models are literally the same consensus. Which of
the six proteins is bound has to come from expression or ChIP, not from sequence. Within the
family, EHF's only HOCOMOCO model here is ChIP-derived rather than in vitro, so its label carries
less weight than ELF1-ELF5, which have HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX support. Two of the three
Vierstra ELF archetypes in this family have GGAT-type consensus sequences and their nearest
neighbours lie outside the family. Allow both CCGGAAG and the CpG-free CAGGAAG form when scanning.

families.name: HSF
families.def: Heat-shock element, inverted nGAAn repeats. HSF1/2/4/5, HSFY1/2.
families.short: Heat shock factors bind the heat shock element (HSE), an array of the 5-base unit nGAAn in alternating orientation: nTTCn-nGAAn-nTTCn and longer runs. The DNA-binding domain is a winged helix, and HSF proteins trimerize through a coiled coil so that three subunits each read one 5-base unit, with further trimers loading cooperatively onto longer arrays. Humans have HSF1, HSF2, HSF4, HSF5 and the Y-linked HSFY1/HSFY2. HSF1 is the stress-inducible member, held inactive as a monomer until proteotoxic stress triggers trimerization. HSEs drive heat shock protein genes, and HSF1 activity also supports malignant transformation; HSF4 mutations cause congenital cataract.
families.long:
## The factors

Human HSF1 is the stress-responsive member, kept as an inactive monomer by intramolecular
coiled-coil interactions and by chaperone binding, and converted on proteotoxic stress into a
DNA-binding trimer that is further tuned by phosphorylation, acetylation and SUMOylation. HSF2 is
developmentally and differentiation-regulated, binds many of the same elements, and forms
heterotrimers with HSF1. HSF4 is expressed mainly in lens and other epithelia and, unlike HSF1, is
constitutively trimeric and can act as a repressor at HSF1 targets. HSF5 is poorly characterized
and largely testis-restricted. HSFY1 and HSFY2 lie in multicopy on the Y chromosome within the
AZFb interval and are expressed in testis. All members share an N-terminal winged-helix DNA-binding
domain followed by hydrophobic repeats (HR-A/B) that mediate trimerization; the domain is among the
most conserved DNA-binding domains in eukaryotes.

## The motif

The recognition unit is 5 bases, nGAAn, and a functional heat shock element is an inverted array of
at least three of them. The classical rendering is nTTCnnGAAnnTTCn; the two permutations,
head-to-head and tail-to-tail repeats of the 5-bp unit, bind with similar affinity and with
striking two-fold symmetry, which was the original evidence that the unit and not a longer
palindrome is the recognition module. HSF binds arrays cooperatively, so four, five or six units
give progressively higher affinity and are common in strongly inducible promoters. The crystal
structure of an HSF DNA-binding domain showed a three-helix bundle capped by a four-stranded
antiparallel beta sheet, a winged-helix variant of the helix-turn-helix motif, and the human HSF1
structure in complex with DNA showed how the trimer positions three such domains around the helix.
Each domain reads GAA in the major groove, so the information sits on the GAA/TTC triplets while
the two flanking bases of each unit are nearly free. That is why database models for HSF1, HSF2 and
HSF4 look like TTCTAGAA-cg-TTC or aGAA-cg-TTCTAGAA: they are the same three-unit array written with
different phase and strand. The HSFY and HSF5 models are different in a real way, favoring TTCGAA
and CGTTCGAA arrangements, so the family separates loosely into an HSF1/2/4 group and an
HSFY/HSF5 group; overall cohesion (0.66) is the lowest in this batch. Within the HSF1/2/4 group no
member is distinguishable from sequence.

## Where it acts

HSEs are promoter-proximal at the classic targets: HSPA1A/HSPA1B, HSP90AA1, DNAJB1, HSPB1 and the
other chaperone and co-chaperone genes carry clustered HSEs within a few hundred bases of the
start site, usually with a paused RNA polymerase already engaged so that induction is a release
step rather than a recruitment step. HSF1 is also found at thousands of distal enhancers, and the
enhancer repertoire differs between stress types: heat shock and oxidative stress drive HSF1 and
HSF2 to partly distinct gene and enhancer sets. GAGA-type factors and, in mammals, SP1 and NF-Y
occupy the same promoters; NF-Y binds the CCAAT boxes of several heat shock promoters. In cancer
cells, HSF1 occupies a large set of non-chaperone genes that is distinct from the classical heat
shock program, and in tumor stroma it drives a separate program in cancer-associated fibroblasts.
HSF1 also localizes to sex chromatin during meiotic repression.

## Biology and disease

Hsf1-null mice are viable but lack thermotolerance, show tissue-specific failure of stress-inducible
chaperone expression, and develop demyelination and protein aggregate accumulation in the CNS;
Hsf1 is also required for oocyte meiosis. HSF1 activity extends lifespan in C. elegans together
with chaperones, linking the pathway to proteostasis in aging. In cancer, HSF1 supports malignant
transformation through a transcriptional program distinct from the heat shock response, high
nuclear HSF1 predicts poor outcome in breast cancer, and loss of Hsf1 suppresses lymphoma in
p53-deficient mice. HSF4 mutations in the DNA-binding domain cause autosomal dominant lamellar and
Marner cataract, and a homozygous splice mutation causes recessive congenital cataract; Hsf4-null
mice develop cataract with reduced gamma-S-crystallin. HSF2 contributes to inducible hsp expression
through heterotrimerization with HSF1 rather than acting alone. HSFY copy loss accompanies AZFb
deletions in azoospermia, though targeted studies argue HSFY genes are not themselves required for
spermatocyte maturation, so the association may be positional.

## Reading a hit

A three-unit HSE is reasonably informative, and models here reach 17-21 bits, so a good match is
worth following up. Two specific traps make this family riskier than that number suggests. First,
nGAAn arrays overlap other purine-rich motifs. A GGAA core is the ETS recognition sequence and
GGAAA is the NFAT core, so loose HSF models score on ETS and NFAT sites and vice versa; one
Vierstra archetype in this family is explicitly labelled HSF/NFATC for that reason. A single
nGAAn unit is worthless as evidence. Second, and more concretely, several ChIP-derived HSF1 models
in these collections are not HSEs at all but resemble the tRNA internal B-box promoter element
(GTTCGAANNC): consensus strings such as GGGTTCGAATCCC appear in CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO and Vierstra
entries labelled HSF1 or HSF, and these are the entries whose label agreement with the rest of the
family is lowest. Treat a GGGTTCGAATCC-like match as a possible tRNA gene rather than an HSE. The
evidence codes help: HSF1, HSF2 and HSF4 grade-A or grade-B models built on SELEX plus methyl-SELEX
(PSM, SM) give the canonical three-unit HSE, while the B-box-like models are ChIP-only (P). Finally,
a genuine HSE hit does not mean the gene is stress-inducible, because HSF2 and HSF4 occupy the same
elements constitutively and HSF4 can repress there.
families.caveats: The 5-base unit nGAAn is useless alone; require at least three alternating units. nGAAn arrays cross-score with ETS (GGAA) and NFAT (GGAAA) sites, and one archetype here is labelled HSF/NFATC for that reason. Several ChIP-only models labelled HSF1 or HSF match the tRNA B-box (GGGTTCGAATCC) rather than an HSE and have the lowest label agreement in the family; a hit of that shape may be a tRNA gene. The family also splits into an HSF1/2/4 group and a distinct HSFY/HSF5 group, and cohesion is the lowest in this batch. A hit does not imply stress-inducibility, since HSF2 and HSF4 bind the same elements constitutively.

families.name: ZIC
families.def: GLI-like CCTGCTGNG. ZIC1-5.
families.short: ZIC1 to ZIC5 are five-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger proteins whose DNA-binding domains are the closest relatives of GLI outside the GLIS subfamily, and which read a GLI-like site. In vitro selection gives an optimal ZIC site almost identical to the GLI consensus but bound with lower affinity; modern high-throughput measurements extend it to GACCCCCCGCTGTG, whose reverse complement, CACAGCAGGGGGT, is how several databases write the same motif. ZIC proteins also bind GLI zinc fingers directly and can raise or lower GLI-dependent transcription. They act mainly in dorsal neural tube, neural crest, somites and cerebellum, and human mutations cause holoprosencephaly (ZIC2), X-linked heterotaxy (ZIC3) and Dandy-Walker malformation (ZIC1 with ZIC4).
families.long:
## The factors

The ZIC family has five human members, ZIC1 to ZIC5, each with a tandem array of C2H2 zinc fingers
that is more similar to the GLI fingers than to any other vertebrate zinc-finger class. ZIC1 and
ZIC4 are a divergently transcribed pair on chromosome 3q24; ZIC2 and ZIC5 are a similar pair on
13q32; ZIC3 sits alone on Xq26. They bind as monomers. In addition to binding DNA, ZIC proteins
associate physically with GLI zinc fingers and, depending on cell type, either enhance or suppress
GLI-dependent transactivation, so part of their activity is exerted as a GLI cofactor rather than
through their own site. Expression is largely neural and paraxial: dorsal neural tube and roof
plate, neural crest, somites, and, postnatally, cerebellar granule cells. ZIC2 is also expressed in
early epiblast and embryonic stem cells.

## The motif

The first systematic definition of the ZIC site used gel-shift-based target selection with ZIC1,
ZIC2 and ZIC3 and recovered a sequence almost identical to the GLI binding sequence, but bound with
lower affinity than GLI; consistently, reporter activation by ZIC proteins depended less on the
presence of a GLI site than GLI1 activation did, and ZIC proteins activated many promoters lacking
one. Circular-dichroism comparisons of ZIC, GLI and GLIS finger domains on DNA support a shared
recognition mode.

High-throughput SELEX extends the site to a 13-14 base element usually written GACCCCCCGCTGTG. Its
5' half, GACCCCCC, is the GLIS-like version of the GLI core, and the 3' extension GCTGTG is what
distinguishes ZIC from GLI and GLIS in practice. Several databases write the same element on the
other strand, as CACAGCAGGGGGT or the shorter CNCAGCAGG, and the ontology form CCTGCTGNG is the
reverse complement of that short core; none of these is a different motif. The data consensus here,
CNCAGCAGGGGGCC, is the reverse-strand form of the full site. One real subtlety is visible in the
collection: the HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX versions of the ZIC motif differ at a central CpG
(CAGCGGGGGG versus CAGCAGGGGG), so cytosine methylation shifts the measured preference at that
position, and different database entries for the same protein can look inconsistent for that reason.
No experiment distinguishes ZIC1 from ZIC2, ZIC3, ZIC4 or ZIC5 by sequence; the JASPAR
Zic1::Zic2 entry is modeled as a dimer but its consensus is the same short core.

## Where it acts

ZIC sites are enhancer elements. In mouse embryonic stem cells ZIC2 occupies thousands of
enhancers, is required for their activity, and cooperates with the Mediator and elongation
machinery; later work describes ZIC2 acting first as a priming factor on closed chromatin during
neural induction and then as an activator at established enhancers. In the cerebellum and dorsal
neural tube ZIC occupancy overlaps with GLI-responsive elements, which is expected given the shared
core, and ZIC and GLI compete or cooperate at the same sequences. Because the informative part of
the site is roughly nine to thirteen bases with a GC-rich core, matches are common in GC-rich
regulatory DNA, and the motif overlaps in scoring space with GLI, GLIS and, at the CAGCAGG core,
with simple CAG-repeat and E-box-adjacent sequence.

## Biology and disease

Gli/Zic factors together pattern the vertebrate neural plate by defining domains of differentiation,
with ZIC activity dorsal to the SHH-dependent ventral domains. Heterozygous ZIC2 loss-of-function
causes holoprosencephaly type 5, characteristically with a middle-interhemispheric variant and
distinctive facial features; ZIC3 mutations cause X-linked heterotaxy with complex congenital heart
defects and laterality reversal; heterozygous deletion of the linked ZIC1 and ZIC4 pair causes
Dandy-Walker malformation, and mouse work shows that combined Zic1 and Zic4 loss disturbs several
developmental programs in the cerebellar anlage rather than one. ZIC5 was identified in Xenopus as a
neural-crest regulator. Beyond development, ZIC family members are recurrently deregulated in
tumors, most consistently by promoter hypermethylation and silencing.

## Reading a hit

Treat a ZIC match as "ZIC family", never as a specific paralogue: all five members share one motif.
Then treat it cautiously as "ZIC rather than GLI". The two families were defined on essentially the
same 5' core, and separating them depends on the 3' GCTGTG extension, which carries relatively
little information; a short or weak match can belong to either, and a ZIC hit inside a
Hedgehog-responsive enhancer is as likely to be a GLI site. Note also that a real ZIC effect need
not require a ZIC site at all, since ZIC proteins act as GLI cofactors and in reporter assays
activate promoters lacking the site. The GC-rich core makes the motif frequent in GC-rich
regulatory DNA, so isolated matches are weak evidence. In the data behind this family, one Vierstra
archetype labelled ZIC (AC0536) has the consensus GACCACCC and matches the GLI family better than
its own; that is the expected failure mode for this pair, not a claim that the label is wrong.
families.caveats: The five ZIC paralogues are indistinguishable by sequence, so a hit names the family only. The larger problem is the GLI boundary: ZIC and GLI were defined on nearly the same core, ZIC binds the GLI consensus in vitro (with lower affinity), and the two are separated only by a weakly informative 3' extension, so weak matches cannot be assigned to one family. One Vierstra archetype labelled ZIC in these data in fact scores closest to GLI. In vitro entries for the same ZIC protein can also disagree at a central CpG because the methyl-SELEX and standard SELEX preferences differ there. Finally, ZIC can act on GLI-dependent transcription without occupying its own site.

families.name: ZNF24 / ZSCAN-type promoter ZFs
families.def: SCAN-domain zinc fingers with defined promoter motifs. ZNF24, ZSCAN4, ZKSCAN1/3, ZSCAN21/22/29.
families.short: A small group of SCAN-domain C2H2 zinc fingers with defined, experimentally supported binding sites at promoters and microsatellites: ZNF24 (also known as ZNF191 and ZSCAN3), ZSCAN4, ZSCAN21, ZSCAN22, ZSCAN29, ZKSCAN1 and ZKSCAN3. They are grouped by domain architecture and a promoter-proximal style of binding, not by a shared motif: the seven proteins read at least five unrelated sequences. ZNF24 binds a TCAT tetranucleotide repeat, ZSCAN4 a CA-repeat core, ZSCAN29 an inverted pair of GTCTAC hexamers, ZKSCAN3 GGCTAGCCC and ZKSCAN1 CCTACTATG. Reported functions are equally varied, from repressing VEGFA transcription to repressing autophagy genes and protecting telomeres in early embryos.
families.long:
## The factors

Seven proteins, all C2H2 zinc fingers with an N-terminal SCAN domain, an approximately 80-residue leucine-rich module that mediates self-association and selective association with other SCAN proteins (Williams et al. 1999). The NMR structure of the MZF1 SCAN domain is a domain-swapped dimer of five-helix monomers, with helix 3 forming the core of the interface and a dissociation constant near 600 nM (Peterson et al. 2006), so these factors are expected to act at least partly as dimers. ZKSCAN1 (7q22.1, formerly ZNF139/ZNF36) and ZKSCAN3 (6p22.1, formerly ZNF306) additionally carry a KRAB domain and can recruit TRIM28. ZNF24 (18q12.2) has been published under several names, including ZNF191, mouse Zfp191 and the alias ZSCAN3, and is 94% identical to its mouse orthologue (Li et al. 2006). SCAN genes generally sit in tandem clusters and carry between 3 and 14 fingers (Edelstein and Collins 2005). The wider SCAN group is split across this atlas: other ZSCAN and ZKSCAN genes have a separate entry, and MZF1 itself is filed under other C2H2 zinc fingers.

## The motif

Not one motif. Cohesion is 0.44, and the 24 matrices form roughly seven tight per-protein clusters. Every matrix has a near-identical partner in the family (median best within-family similarity 0.96), but that partner is almost always the same protein measured again in another database. ZNF24 reads a TCAT tetranucleotide repeat: JASPAR MA1124.1 and CIS-BP M08093 both give CATTCATTCATTC and the HOCOMOCO model is TGAATGAATGAATG, the reverse complement. That agrees with the literature, in which ZNF191/ZNF24 binds the polymorphic intronic TCAT repeat HUMTH01 of the tyrosine hydroxylase gene, and allele length changes both the amount and the pattern of binding (Albanese et al. 2001). ZSCAN29 reads GTCTACAC; its methyl-SELEX model is ATAAACGTCTACAC and the related unnamed archetype AC0339 reads GCGTAGACGTCTACAC, that is GTAGAC followed by GTCTAC, an inverted repeat of the same hexamer. That is the arrangement a SCAN-mediated dimer contacting two half-sites would produce, but no structure or mutagenesis has tested it. ZSCAN4 reads GCACACVCTGAAA, whose core is a CA repeat, consistent with mouse Zscan4 recognizing a subset of (CA)n microsatellites (Srinivasan et al. 2020). ZKSCAN3 reads GGCTAGCCC, ZKSCAN1 CCTACTATG (its JASPAR entry gives the reverse complement), ZSCAN22 the CT-rich CCTCCTCCCTCAGAC, and ZSCAN21 a weak nine-bit CTCAGCACT. Two pairs are inseparable: ZSCAN1, in the other SCAN entry, matches the ZSCAN4 motif at 0.95, and a grade-A HOCOMOCO model for the KRAB zinc finger ZNF500 is GCGTCTACACTANCC, the ZSCAN29 site.

## Where it acts

TCAT and CA repeats are ubiquitous microsatellites, so ZNF24- and ZSCAN4-type matches are common and mostly lie outside regulatory elements. ZNF24 has one precisely mapped functional site, an 11 bp element in the proximal VEGFA promoter (Jia et al. 2013). ZKSCAN3 occupies the promoters of more than 60 autophagy and lysosome genes, with MAP1LC3B and WIPI2 confirmed as direct targets, and responds to starvation in the opposite direction to TFEB (Chauhan et al. 2013). Mouse Zscan4 is restricted to two-cell embryos and a small, transient subpopulation of embryonic stem cells, where it localizes to telomeres and to nuclease-resistant, histone-dense microsatellite regions (Zalzman et al. 2010; Srinivasan et al. 2020).

## Biology and disease

Zfp191-null mouse embryos are severely growth-retarded and die around embryonic day 7.5, and no homozygous embryonic stem cell lines can be derived; tyrosine hydroxylase expression is unaffected, so the phenotype is a proliferation defect rather than a TH defect (Li et al. 2006). ZNF24 represses VEGFA: overexpression produces VEGF-like vascular defects in zebrafish that VEGF rescues, reduces tumour angiogenesis in a breast cancer xenograft, and ZNF24 and VEGF levels are inversely correlated in human breast tumours (Jia et al. 2013). Silencing ZKSCAN3 induces autophagy and lysosome biogenesis (Chauhan et al. 2013). Zscan4 knockdown shortens telomeres, raises sister chromatid exchange and karyotype abnormalities, and drives embryonic stem cells to crisis by passage eight (Zalzman et al. 2010); its loss also increases DNA damage in two-cell embryos in a transcription-dependent manner (Srinivasan et al. 2020).

## Reading a hit

Which protein the hit belongs to matters much more than the family label. Repeat-based matches, ZNF24's (TCAT)n and ZSCAN4's (CA)n core, will number in the tens of thousands genome-wide and are not evidence of occupancy; for ZNF24, repeat length is part of the signal, so genotype the repeat rather than scoring a fixed-width matrix. ZSCAN4 and ZSCAN1 share a motif, and so do ZSCAN29 and ZNF500, making those labels interchangeable from sequence alone. The evidence is mixed: five of the seven HOCOMOCO models are ChIP-only (evidence code P), while ZSCAN4 and ZSCAN29 have in vitro support (codes SM and M). The ZSCAN21 model carries about nine bits and should not be scanned by itself. The ZSCAN22 matrix is CT-rich and hard to separate from the many other CT- and GC-rich zinc-finger matrices in this atlas.
families.caveats: This entry holds seven proteins with at least five unrelated motifs; cohesion is 0.44 and there is no family consensus, so read a hit as a hit to the named protein. Two of the motifs, ZNF24's TCAT repeat and ZSCAN4's CA-repeat core, are microsatellites that match tens of thousands of loci by chance. ZSCAN4 cannot be distinguished from ZSCAN1, nor ZSCAN29 from the KRAB zinc finger ZNF500. Five of seven HOCOMOCO models are ChIP-only, so for those the enriched sequence may belong to a partner rather than the tagged protein. The ZSCAN21 model is too weak to scan on its own.

families.name: Grainyhead (GRHL)
families.def: AACCGGTT. GRHL1-3, TFCP2, TFCP2L1, UBP1.
families.short: The Grainyhead/CP2 family binds the palindrome AACCGGTT through an immunoglobulin-like DNA-binding domain that shares a fold with p53 but differs from it in important details. Six human members split into two branches: the epithelial GRHL1, GRHL2 and GRHL3, and the more broadly expressed TFCP2 (LSF/CP2), TFCP2L1 and UBP1 (LBP-1a). They bind as dimers, and many real elements are doubled, giving 16-26 bp tandem sites. GRHL factors control epidermal barrier formation, neural tube and palate closure, and epithelial identity, and they sit at the epithelial end of EMT regulation. Human mutations cause Van der Woude syndrome and nonsyndromic cleft palate.
families.long:
## The factors

Six human genes belong to this family. The grainyhead-like branch, GRHL1, GRHL2 and GRHL3, is
epithelial: GRHL1 and GRHL3 in epidermis and periderm, GRHL2 in most simple and stratified
epithelia including airway, gut and bladder. The CP2 branch, TFCP2 (also LSF or CP2), TFCP2L1
(CRTR-1) and UBP1 (LBP-1a), is more broadly expressed and includes the factor originally
characterized on the alpha-globin promoter. All six share a roughly 250-residue region that carries
both DNA binding and dimerization, inherited from Drosophila Grainyhead (also called NTF-1 and
Elf-1), and the Drosophila and human domains are interchangeable enough that the family was
recognized by that conservation. Crystal structures of the GRHL1 and GRHL2 DNA-binding domains
showed a closely similar immunoglobulin-like core sharing the overall fold of the p53 DNA-binding
domain while differing in the DNA-contacting elements. GRHL1 binds its recognition element as a
dimer, and target-site selection is parsimonious: two conserved arginine residues make most of
the base-specific contacts.

## The motif

The consensus is the 8-bp palindrome AACCGGTT, often written with flanking A/T as AAACCGGTTT.
Because selection rests on a small number of arginine contacts, the central CCGG is the most
constrained part and the flanking AA/TT contribute the rest. The palindrome means the two halves
are equivalent, and dimer binding is the normal mode. A conspicuous feature of this family's
models is doubling: HOCOMOCO entries for TFCP2, TFCP2L1, UBP1 and GRHL3 span 15-26 columns and
contain two AACCGGTT-like units, sometimes in the arrangement AACCGGTT-N(2)-AACCGGTT. That is a
genuine property of Grh/CP2 elements rather than a modelling artifact, and it is why the highest
information content in this family (about 20 bits) comes from CP2-branch models rather than from
the single-site GRHL models. Degenerate variants are common and legitimate: AACAGGTT, AACTGGTT and
AACCAGTT all appear as database consensuses, reflecting tolerance at the central positions. No
member is reliably distinguishable from another by sequence. The GRHL and CP2 branches are similar
enough that Vierstra collapses them into archetypes named GRHL/TFCP, and this family's cohesion
(0.78) is limited mainly by the mixture of single-site and doubled models, not by disagreement
about the core.

## Where it acts

Grh/CP2 sites occur at both promoters and enhancers, with a strong bias toward epithelial
differentiation loci: the epidermal differentiation complex, tight junction and desmosome genes,
transglutaminases, and the genes of the cornified envelope. GRHL3 binding is highly dynamic, with
enhancer usage rearranging as keratinocytes move between proliferative and differentiating states.
GRHL2 also occupies enhancers in pluripotent cells during exit from naive pluripotency and in
airway basal cells during mucociliary regeneration. Common neighbors are KLF4 and TP63 in
keratinocytes, IRF6 in periderm (GRHL3 and IRF6 act in the same genetic pathway for oral periderm),
and AP-1 at differentiation enhancers. GRHL factors recruit Trithorax-group complexes to switch on
differentiation genes, and in cancer they sit in a mutually repressive loop with ZEB1 and the
miR-200 family that keeps cells epithelial. The palindrome is 8 bp, so chance matches are frequent;
doubled sites are much rarer and much more indicative.

## Biology and disease

Grhl3-null mice fail to form a skin permeability barrier and develop spina bifida that is
resistant to both inositol and folate supplementation, identifying Grhl3 as the gene behind the
long-studied curly tail mouse. Grhl3 is also required for eyelid closure and urothelial
differentiation. In humans, dominant GRHL3 mutations cause Van der Woude syndrome, the commonest
syndromic form of cleft lip and palate, in families without IRF6 mutations; separate GRHL3 coding
variants, including a common susceptibility allele and rare truncating variants, cause and predispose
to nonsyndromic cleft palate. GRHL2 variants are associated with age-related hearing impairment,
and GRHL2 has both oncogenic and tumor-suppressive effects depending on context, promoting the
epithelial phenotype in breast, ovarian and prostate cancer while restraining metastatic
dissemination. TFCP2 appears in cancer as a fusion partner: EWSR1-TFCP2 and FUS-TFCP2 fusions define
an aggressive intraosseous spindle and epithelioid rhabdomyosarcoma with frequent ALK
overexpression, often in the jaw and skull.

## Reading a hit

An AACCGGTT match identifies the Grh/CP2 family and no individual member. That matters because the
two branches have different biology: a hit could correspond to epithelial GRHL2 or to broadly
expressed TFCP2, and only expression or ChIP data can tell you which. At 8 bp with a palindromic
core, single matches occur often by chance, so treat a lone AACCGGTT the way you would treat any
8-mer: as a hypothesis. A doubled site, two AACCGGTT-like units within about 20 bp, is a much
stronger signal and is the form in which many validated elements occur. Also note that models in
this family differ in width by a factor of three, from 8 to 26 columns, so scores from different
databases are not comparable and a "weaker" hit may simply reflect a narrower model. The evidence
base is mixed but reasonable: several HOCOMOCO models for GRHL1, GRHL3, TFCP2, TFCP2L1 and UBP1
rest on in vitro selection (evidence codes SM, SB, S), which supports direct binding, whereas the
GRHL2 models here are ChIP-only (P) and their degenerate variants (AACAGGTT, CCGGTTTGGCCAG) should
be read as descriptions of GRHL2 peaks rather than of GRHL2's intrinsic specificity.
families.caveats: A hit names the family, not the member, and the family spans two branches with different expression: epithelial GRHL1-3 versus broadly expressed TFCP2, TFCP2L1 and UBP1. The 8-bp palindrome occurs frequently by chance, so single matches are weak; doubled AACCGGTT units within about 20 bp are much more convincing. Model widths in this family range from 8 to 26 columns, so scores across databases are not comparable. Degenerate variants such as AACAGGTT come mostly from ChIP-only GRHL2 models and describe peak composition rather than intrinsic specificity; the in vitro-supported models converge on AACCGGTT.

families.name: AP-2 (TFAP2)
families.def: GCCYGCRGGC. TFAP2A-E.
families.short: The five human TFAP2 proteins (TFAP2A-E, historically AP-2 alpha through epsilon) bind a pseudo-palindrome made of GCC and GGC triplets separated by exactly three bases. Each subunit contributes a basic region that inserts a loop into the major groove, and the two subunits are held together by a helix-span-helix domain; the factors are constitutive dimers even off DNA, and all paralogue combinations heterodimerize. The site is GC-rich and sits in GC-rich promoters and neural crest enhancers. TFAP2 factors behave as pioneer factors during neural crest specification, and mutations cause branchio-oculo-facial syndrome (TFAP2A) and Char syndrome (TFAP2B). A hit identifies the family, not a paralogue.
families.long:
## The factors

Five human genes encode this family: TFAP2A, TFAP2B, TFAP2C, TFAP2D and TFAP2E, still widely
called AP-2 alpha, beta, gamma, delta and epsilon. Each protein has an N-terminal proline- and
glutamine-rich activation domain, a basic region, and a C-terminal helix-span-helix (HSH)
dimerization domain: two amphipathic helices separated by a long span. The HSH domain drives
dimerization on its own and can be transplanted onto a foreign basic region, but it cannot bind
DNA without an adjacent basic region. AP-2 is a dimer in solution as well as on DNA, and all of
the paralogue pairs can heterodimerize; in neural crest development TFAP2A switches partners from
TFAP2C to TFAP2B as specification proceeds, and the two heterodimers open different sets of
elements. Expression is restricted rather than housekeeping: TFAP2A and TFAP2B in neural crest,
surface ectoderm, facial mesenchyme and kidney; TFAP2C in trophoblast, germ cells and luminal
breast epithelium; TFAP2D mainly in retina and midbrain; TFAP2E in olfactory epithelium. TFAP2D
is the outlier, with a divergent basic region and weaker transactivation.

## The motif

The functional element is a pseudo-palindrome of two triplets, GCC and GGC, with a three-base
spacer: GCC(N3)GGC. Older literature writes the same site as GCCYGCRGGC or in specific promoters
as GCCTGAGGC and CCCCAGGC, and databases here report both a 9-mer form (GCCTGAGGC, GCCTCAGGC) and
an extended 11-12-mer form (GCCCTBAGGGCA), which is the same core with an extra C/G pair on each
flank. The data consensus for this family, GCCTCAGGGCA, is that extended form; it does not
conflict with GCC(N3)GGC but simply includes flanking positions that are only partly informative.
The crystal structure of the TFAP2A DBD-HSH tandem domain on DNA explains the geometry: the two
flat amphipathic HSH helices stack against each other through hydrophobic contacts, and a
stabilized loop from each DBD inserts into one of two neighboring major grooves. Because the two
loops are a fixed distance apart, spacer length, not just spacer sequence, determines binding: a
three-base gap is strongly preferred and altering it costs affinity. This makes the informative
positions the GCC and GGC triplets, with the central three bases nearly free (commonly written
YAG or TCA/TGA). The five paralogues are not separable from sequence. Every model in this family's
data, across all four source databases, converges on the same GCC-N3-GGC pattern with 7-15 bits.

## Where it acts

AP-2 sites are GC-rich, so they are enriched in GC-rich and CpG-island promoters, where they can
be hard to distinguish from SP/KLF GC-boxes on loose models. The functionally important sites,
however, are largely distal: TFAP2A occupies thousands of enhancers at the neural plate border and
in specified neural crest, acting as a pioneer factor that remodels chromatin ahead of the
lineage program. In melanocytes TFAP2 paralogues bind in parallel with MITF at pigmentation genes.
In luminal breast cancer cells TFAP2C co-occupies enhancers with estrogen receptor and FOXA1 and
regulates ESR1 itself. Co-occurring motifs therefore depend on the tissue: SOX and PAX motifs in
neural crest, MITF E-boxes in melanocytes, ERE and forkhead sites in breast. AP-2 sites are common
enough in GC-rich sequence that a genome-wide scan returns very large numbers of matches; the
constraint on real occupancy is TFAP2 expression, which is narrow.

## Biology and disease

Tfap2a-null mice fail cranial neural tube closure and have severe craniofacial defects, matching
AP-2's expression in ectoderm and migrating cranial neural crest. In humans, heterozygous TFAP2A
mutations, mostly missense changes in the basic region and HSH domain, cause branchio-oculo-facial
syndrome: cervical and infra-auricular skin defects, ocular anomalies, cleft lip or palate, and
sometimes inner ear malformation and deafness. Mutations in TFAP2B cause Char syndrome, a dominant
condition combining patent ductus arteriosus, a distinctive face and hand anomalies, with a
genotype-phenotype relationship that tracks with how much DNA binding is lost. TFAP2C is amplified
and overexpressed in a subset of breast cancers, where it governs the luminal epithelial phenotype
and hormone response and higher expression predicts worse outcome on anti-hormonal therapy.
TFAP2A and TFAP2C are also required in trophoblast and germ cell programs. A structural survey of
disease mutations concluded that reduced or abolished DNA binding is the primary mechanism in
TFAP2-associated disease.

## Reading a hit

A GCC(N3)GGC match tells you that a TFAP2 dimer could bind, and nothing about which one. The five
paralogues share one matrix; assign a member from expression, and remember that the biologically
active species is often a heterodimer, so the question may have no single answer. Check the spacer
before believing a match: GCC and GGC separated by two or four bases is a much weaker site than one
separated by three, and permissive scanning tools will happily report the wrong spacing. Because
the site is GC-rich, the main false-positive risk is confusion with other GC-binding families. A
loose AP-2 model will score on SP1/KLF GC-boxes (GGGGCGGGG) and on CpG-island sequence generally;
conversely, GC-box models score on AP-2 sites. Require the discontinuous GCC...GGC arrangement
rather than a continuous GC run before calling a hit AP-2. The evidence base here is comparatively
clean: HOCOMOCO models for AP2A and AP2C are grade A with combined ChIP-seq and in vitro selection
(PSM), and the AP2B and AP2E models rest on in vitro selection alone (SM), so the family's
specificity does not depend on ChIP data. The one provenance caveat is the CIS-BP TFAP2D entry,
which is transferred from a mouse protein at 80% DNA-binding-domain identity.
families.caveats: All five TFAP2 paralogues share one matrix and heterodimerize freely, so a hit identifies the family only. The three-base spacer is part of the motif: check it, because loose scans report mis-spaced matches. The biggest practical risk is GC-richness. AP-2 models cross-score with SP/KLF GC-boxes and with CpG-island sequence, so a GC-rich promoter hit needs the discontinuous GCC...GGC arrangement to be credible. Genome-wide matches vastly outnumber occupied sites because TFAP2 expression is narrow. In vitro evidence supports the core specificity; the CIS-BP TFAP2D model is inferred from mouse at 80% domain identity.
