families.name: NF-kB / Rel
families.def: kB site GGGRNNYYCC. NFKB1, NFKB2, RELA, RELB, REL.
families.short: The kB site is the element read by the five mammalian Rel/NF-kB proteins: NFKB1 (p105/p50), NFKB2 (p100/p52), RELA (p65), RELB and REL (c-Rel). They bind DNA only as dimers, through a shared Rel-homology region, so the site is pseudo-palindromic and is usually written GGGRNNYYCC, each subunit reading one guanine-rich half. What makes these factors unusual is that they are pre-made and held in the cytoplasm by IkB proteins, then released within minutes by inflammatory cytokines, microbial sensing, antigen receptors or DNA damage. The same kB site can therefore be empty in a resting cell and heavily occupied after stimulation. kB sites lie in promoters and enhancers of cytokine, chemokine, adhesion-molecule and pro-survival genes, and are the usual first evidence that a regulatory region is inflammation-responsive.
families.long:
## The factors

Humans have five Rel/NF-kB proteins. RELA (p65), RELB and REL (c-Rel) are synthesised in mature form and carry C-terminal transactivation domains. NFKB1 and NFKB2 are made as the longer precursors p105 and p100 and are processed to p50 and p52, which lack transactivation domains; p50 and p52 homodimers are therefore usually repressive unless they recruit a coactivator such as BCL3. All five share an N-terminal Rel-homology region of roughly 300 residues built from two immunoglobulin-like beta-barrel domains, with a nuclear localisation signal at its C-terminal end. The same region performs both jobs: the N-terminal barrel makes most base-specific contacts and the C-terminal barrel forms the dimer interface. Five subunits allow fifteen dimers in principle; the abundant ones are p50:RELA (the "classical" NF-kB of canonical IKK signalling), p50:REL, and p52:RELB, which is the output of the non-canonical, NIK-dependent pathway. RELA and NFKB1 are broadly expressed; REL and RELB are enriched in lymphoid cells and dendritic cells. Activity is controlled after translation rather than by transcription: IkBa, IkBb and IkBe, and the unprocessed p105 and p100 tails, mask the nuclear localisation signals, and signal-induced IKK phosphorylation triggers their degradation. The IkBa/NF-kB crystal structure showed how one IkB simultaneously blocks the NLS and distorts the DNA-binding surface.

## The motif

The kB site is 9-11 bp and is conventionally written GGGRNNYYCC; a recent structural review writes it GGGRNNNYCC, and the difference is real: the number of central, low-information positions depends on which dimer is bound. Crystal structures of the p50 homodimer, the p52 homodimer, and the p50:p65 heterodimer on the interferon-beta kB site show that each subunit reads one half-site, with conserved arginine, histidine and glutamate residues from loop L1 hydrogen-bonding the 5' GGG triplet. p50 and p52 prefer a 5-bp guanine-rich half-site, giving longer and more nearly symmetric sites such as GGGGATTCCCC; RELA, RELB and c-Rel prefer a 4-bp half-site (GGAA), giving shorter sites such as GGGAATTTCC. All the information sits in the GGG and in the CC of the opposite half; the middle two or three positions are close to free. A protein-binding-microarray and surface-plasmon-resonance survey of eight dimers found three specificity classes rather than five, and showed that dimers readily occupy "non-traditional" sites that contain only one good half-site - so NF-kB binding in vitro is more permissive than the palindromic consensus implies. The four databases assembled here agree closely (cohesion 0.83) and their NFKB1, NFKB2, RELA, RELB and REL models differ mainly in half-site length, not in the recognised bases. Two entries, JASPAR RELB (MA1117.2) and CIS-BP M08161, are half-site-only models (ATTCCCC); most of their nearest neighbours in motif space fall outside this family, and they should not be used for scanning.

## Where it acts

kB sites occur in both promoters and enhancers, and are not associated with CpG islands. In a stimulated macrophage or lymphocyte, NF-kB occupies thousands of sites, a small fraction of the hundreds of thousands of consensus matches in the genome; occupancy is largely confined to chromatin already made accessible by lineage-determining factors, so the cell type, not the motif, decides which kB sites are usable. The best-characterised composite element is the interferon-beta enhancer (the PRDII kB site together with IRF3/IRF7 and ATF2/JUN sites), whose assembled enhanceosome has been modelled atomically. More generally, kB sites co-occur with AP-1 (TGASTCA), IRF/ISRE, STAT (GAS) and C/EBP sites at inflammatory enhancers, and in myeloid cells with SPI1/PU.1.

## Biology and disease

NF-kB was found as an activity binding the immunoglobulin kappa light-chain enhancer and was soon recognised as the general transcriptional output of innate and adaptive immune signalling: cytokine and chemokine induction, antigen-receptor responses, lymphoid organogenesis and germinal-centre B-cell programmes through RELB/p52, osteoclast differentiation downstream of RANK, and survival genes including BIRC3 and BCL2L1. Mouse knockouts separate the subunits: loss of Rela causes mid-gestation lethality from TNF-driven hepatocyte apoptosis, Relb-null mice develop multiorgan inflammation with defective dendritic cells, and Nfkb1-null mice have selective B-cell and immune-response defects. In humans, heterozygous loss-of-function NFKB1 variants are among the more frequent monogenic causes of common variable immunodeficiency, and NFKB2 variants cause hypogammaglobulinaemia with adrenal insufficiency. Constitutive NF-kB activity is a defining feature of activated-B-cell diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and multiple myeloma, where NIK and TRAF3 lesions activate the non-canonical pathway.

## Reading a hit

A kB match says a Rel dimer could bind, not that one does. Because NF-kB is regulated by nuclear entry, a kB site in an unstimulated cell is usually unoccupied; a match is therefore a statement about potential, and it should be checked against accessibility or ChIP data from the relevant stimulus and cell type. The element is also common: with four strongly constrained positions and a degenerate centre, 10-bp matches occur many thousands of times per genome, so match count alone carries little weight. The subunits are not separable from sequence. At most, a long, symmetric site with a 5-bp GGGGA half-site slightly favours p50- or p52-containing dimers, and a short GGAA half-site favours RelA, RelB or c-Rel; no model distinguishes RELA from REL. Evidence codes help: the HOCOMOCO NFKB1 and NFKB2 core models carry in vitro SELEX or methyl-SELEX support (PS, PSM), whereas the RELA, RELB and REL models are ChIP-only, grade B, and describe where those proteins were found rather than what they bind directly. Since NF-kB works within enhanceosomes, ChIP-derived NF-kB models can be pulled toward IRF, AP-1 or STAT sequences contributed by partners.
families.caveats: Treat a kB hit as family-level and conditional. It identifies Rel/NF-kB, never which of the five subunits: the databases' NFKB1, NFKB2, RELA, RELB and REL models differ mainly in half-site length. Because NF-kB activity is controlled by nuclear entry rather than by expression, most matches in any given cell state are unoccupied, and a match is not evidence of an active site without accessibility or stimulus-matched ChIP data. The RELA, RELB and REL models in HOCOMOCO are ChIP-derived only (grade B), so partner motifs from enhanceosome co-binders can bleed into them. Avoid the half-site models (JASPAR MA1117.2, CIS-BP M08161) for genome scans; they match promiscuously.

families.name: RUNX
families.def: TGTGGT core (ACCACA). RUNX1/2/3 with CBFB.
families.short: RUNX sites are read by RUNX1, RUNX2 and RUNX3 through the Runt domain, a 128-residue immunoglobulin-like fold in the same structural class as NF-kB and p53. The core is a six-base element, TGYGGT, written ACCRCA on the other strand, and it is the retroviral enhancer "core" site originally described for core-binding factor. None of the three proteins binds efficiently alone: all require the non-DNA-binding subunit CBFB, which clamps the Runt domain into its DNA-bound conformation and raises affinity substantially. RUNX1 is the hematopoietic member and one of the most frequent targets of chromosomal translocation in leukemia; RUNX2 controls osteoblast differentiation and RUNX3 gut and immune programmes. The three paralogues are indistinguishable by sequence preference.
families.long:
## The factors

RUNX1 (AML1, CBFA2), RUNX2 (CBFA1) and RUNX3 (CBFA3) each carry one Runt domain near their N terminus. The domain is about 128 residues and adopts an s-type immunoglobulin fold, placing RUNX in the same structural superfamily as NF-kB, NFAT, STAT and p53 rather than with any classical helix-turn-helix family. It binds DNA as a monomer, but not effectively on its own: the shared subunit CBFB (CBFbeta, PEBP2beta) makes no DNA contact yet is required in practice. Two crystal structures of the Runt domain-CBFB-DNA ternary complex showed how - CBFB stabilises the DNA-bound conformation of the domain's C-terminal "tail" and "wing", which together clamp the phosphate backbone across both grooves, and the extended tail contributes most of the NF-kB-like base-specific major-groove contacts. Expression is largely complementary: RUNX1 in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and lymphocytes, RUNX2 in osteoblasts, chondrocytes and some epithelia, RUNX3 in gut epithelium, sensory neurons and T and NK cells. All three interact with CBFB and with the same corepressor and coactivator machinery, so which one is present is usually a matter of cell type rather than of DNA sequence.

## The motif

The core is six bases. Binding-site selection with core-binding factor gave the consensus PyGPyGGTPy, most compactly written TGYGGT, and its reverse complement ACCRCA is equally common in the literature. The Y at position three is the one genuinely ambiguous base, and it explains a discrepancy visible in these databases: ChIP-derived models for all three paralogues read TGTGGTT (ACCACA), whereas HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX models for RUNX2 and RUNX3, the JASPAR RUNX2 model, and the Vierstra archetypes read TGCGGTT (ACCGCA). Both are correct readings of TGYGGT; in vitro selection favours the C variant, genomic occupancy the T variant. Structurally, the guanines of the GG step are read by arginine and lysine side chains from the Runt domain tail in the major groove, while the flanking T and the distorted, bent B-form geometry of the site account for the rest of the specificity. Six informative positions is little, and the databases compensate in two ways. Several models are tandem repeats of the core (AACCGCAAAAACCGCA, GTGGTTTTTGTGGTTT), which reflects the real tendency of RUNX enhancers to carry paired sites rather than any dimeric binding by the protein. Others extend one or two positions into the flank. No model distinguishes RUNX1, RUNX2 and RUNX3 - family cohesion is 0.86 and the three ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO consensuses are character-for-character identical. Note also that one CIS-BP RUNX1 entry was measured on the mouse protein, whose Runt domain is identical to the human one at 100% identity.

## Where it acts

RUNX motifs are enhancer features more than promoter features, and are not enriched in CpG islands. In hematopoietic cells RUNX1 occupies tens of thousands of sites, and its motif is one of the commonest in the accessible chromatin of blood lineages; RUNX2 shows the same pattern in osteoblasts. The characteristic arrangement is a composite with ETS. Cooperative binding of ETS1 and core-binding factor to adjacent sites was described at the T-cell receptor enhancers, and genome-wide work later showed that the ETS-RUNX composite is what distinguishes ETS1's T-cell-specific enhancer occupancy from its redundant, consensus-driven occupancy at housekeeping promoters. RUNX sites also co-occur with GATA (the GATA-RUNX pairing at hematopoietic enhancers), with SPI1/PU.1 in myeloid cells, with TCF/LEF and with AP-1.

## Biology and disease

Runx1-null mice fail definitive hematopoiesis and die in mid-gestation with central nervous system hemorrhage; the Cbfb knockout reproduces this, which was the genetic demonstration that the partner subunit is required in vivo. Runx2-null mice have no bone formation at all because osteoblasts arrest before maturation, and heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in human RUNX2 cause cleidocranial dysplasia. RUNX3 silencing by promoter hypermethylation and loss of expression was linked causally to gastric carcinoma. RUNX1 is among the most frequently rearranged genes in human leukemia: t(8;21) creates RUNX1-RUNX1T1 in acute myeloid leukemia, t(12;21) creates ETV6-RUNX1 in the commonest subtype of childhood B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and inv(16) fuses CBFB to MYH11; germline RUNX1 mutations cause familial platelet disorder with predisposition to myeloid malignancy. Most of these lesions keep an intact Runt domain and convert RUNX1 into a repressor at its normal sites.

## Reading a hit

TGYGGT is short. Expect roughly one match every few hundred base pairs per strand, so an isolated hit is close to meaningless; weight matches by clustering, by conservation, and above all by the presence of a partner site. An adjacent ETS core (GGAA/GGAT) within a few base pairs, or a nearby GATA site, turns a weak RUNX match into a plausible composite element. The hit cannot name the paralogue, and it cannot distinguish RUNX from CBFB-containing complexes generally, since CBFB has no motif of its own - a "CBFB site" in any database is a RUNX site. Decide which variant to scan with deliberately: an in vitro TGCGGT model will score differently from a ChIP-derived TGTGGT model on the same sequence, and neither is wrong. The HOCOMOCO RUNX1, RUNX2 and RUNX3 primary models are ChIP-only (grade B); because RUNX travels in composites with ETS and GATA, ChIP-derived RUNX models can absorb flanking partner information, and conversely ETS models derived from T-cell ChIP can absorb the RUNX core.
families.caveats: A six-base core means chance matches dominate: treat a lone TGYGGT as no evidence and look for a composite, most often an ETS core within a few base pairs or a nearby GATA site. The three paralogues cannot be told apart - the ChIP-derived RUNX1, RUNX2 and RUNX3 models here are identical, so a hit is RUNX-family and the responsible protein follows from cell type. CBFB has no motif of its own, so any database entry labelled for it is a RUNX motif. Be deliberate about the variant: in vitro models read TGCGGT, ChIP models TGTGGT, and they score real sequence differently. All three primary HOCOMOCO models are ChIP-only.

families.name: CENP-B / pogo / Tigger
families.def: CENP-B box TTCGTTGGAA and related pogo-family transposase-derived domains. CENPB, TIGD1-7, POGK, JRK, CENPBD1.
families.short: The third and largest of the atlas's domesticated-transposase families. CENP-B, the Tigger-derived TIGD1 to TIGD7 proteins, POGK, JRK and CENPBD1 all carry DNA-binding domains descended from pogo, a Drosophila DNA transposon whose Tigger relatives left more than a hundred thousand fossil copies in the human genome. CENP-B itself recognizes the 17-base-pair CENP-B box, which recurs in alpha-satellite DNA - so a CENP-B box match is almost always centromeric or pericentromeric, not a regulatory site. Sixteen motifs cover twelve symbols, most of them sharing a bipartite pattern of a TTCG/CGAA block and a CCCG/CGGG block read by two helix-turn-helix domains. Cohesion is low at 0.48 and one model is flagged suspect.
families.long:
## The factors

In 1996 a survey of human interspersed repeats identified two roughly 2.5 kb elements with coding capacity, Tigger1 and Tigger2, that closely resemble pogo, a DNA transposon of Drosophila, and that probably mobilised at least fourteen families and more than a hundred thousand degenerate short copies carrying 14 to 25 base-pair terminal inverted repeats. The deduced pogo and Tigger transposases turned out to be very similar to CENP-B, the major mammalian centromere protein - the observation that first suggested CENP-B has a transposase origin. This family collects the human descendants of that lineage: CENPB itself, the Tigger transposable element derived proteins TIGD1 through TIGD7, POGK, JRK (jerky) and CENPBD1. TIGD7 was in fact isolated as a Jerky/JRK-like gene, and the wider pogo group also contains POGZ, which is not filed here.

Their host functions have diverged completely. CENP-B is a centromeric chromatin protein. Jerky, in Drosophila, facilitates cell-specific Wnt/Wingless signalling by modulating beta-catenin-TCF activity, and in mouse it is associated with translationally inactive neuronal mRNA. Several TIGD genes have no characterised function at all. What they retain in common is the recognition module, which is exactly what makes this family readable as a motif family and unreadable as a functional one.

## The motif

CENP-B binds a 17 base-pair sequence in centromeric alpha-satellite (alphoid) DNA, purified from HeLa nuclear extract as the protein that recognizes it, with an affinity of about 6 x 10^8 M^-1, and the major protein-DNA complex contains two DNA molecules. The 129-residue DNA-binding region forms two helix-turn-helix domains that occupy adjacent major grooves; the DNA is kinked at both recognition-helix contacts, the larger kink reaching 43 degrees through an arginine-rich helix that bridges the phosphate backbone, giving an overall bend of 59 degrees. The box recurs in alpha-satellite at regular intervals, roughly every other repeat unit.

The atlas models for CENPB, tCCCGCaTnntACGAA in HOCOMOCO and CCCGcdTnnwaCGAA in CIS-BP and Vierstra, are written on the strand opposite the way the box is conventionally quoted: the CCCG block at their 5' end corresponds to the CGGG block at the 3' end of the box, and their 3' CGAA corresponds to the box's 5' TTCG. Read in either orientation the bipartite architecture is visible, two conserved blocks separated by a tolerant spacer, exactly matching the two-helix-turn-helix structure. The same signature runs through the family: JRK gives CCTCgrTTAACCGGAA, TIGD7 ttCnnTAATTCGGAC, TIGD4 ACCCCGTTAaTAcGAaC, TIGD3 TATGCAGgTAAcCGda, TIGD5 cccbtTATAACGC and POGK TCGACcTtAgGTCGACa. These are long, information-rich models of 12 to 26 bits with grade A HOCOMOCO evidence, but they are not the same site as each other, which is why family cohesion is only 0.48. The tail is weak: TIGD1 gives TATTGCG, CENPBD1 TACGta at 4.1 bits, TIGD6 aaCGAA at 3.4 bits, and the Vierstra archetype AC0265 collapses to CG and is flagged suspect with SAND as its alternative family. Two CIS-BP models, for TIGD2 and TIGD6, are transferred from Monodelphis domestica, and a third for POGK is a PBM construct at only 73 percent domain identity.

## Where it acts

For CENP-B the answer is unusually definite: its sites are in alpha-satellite arrays at centromeres and pericentromeric regions, distributed through higher-order repeat units, and they are functional there. Both the CENP-B box and alphoid sequence context are required for de novo centromere chromatin assembly on synthetic repeats in the human artificial chromosome assay, including recruitment of CENP-A, CENP-C and CENP-E; combining CENP-B box positive and negative synthetic repeats improves artificial chromosome formation further. Alpha-satellite arrays differ in their CENP-B box content, and the box has arisen independently more than once - it is present in some New World monkey satellite lineages with separate origins. The other members are nuclear proteins of unremarkable distribution whose genomic occupancy is poorly mapped.

## Biology and disease

The centromeric role of the box is not matched by a requirement for the protein: Cenpb null mice are viable with no apparent abnormalities, so CENP-B is best understood as facilitating centromere assembly rather than being essential to it. This is the standard picture for domesticated transposases, whose retention reflects opportunistic recruitment rather than indispensability. Jerky loss in mouse produces an epilepsy phenotype, and the fly orthologue modulates Wnt signalling through beta-catenin-TCF. The Tigger and POGK members remain largely uncharacterised; POGZ, a pogo relative outside this family, is a well-established neurodevelopmental disorder gene, which is a reason to expect more phenotypes here.

## Reading a hit

Check repeat annotation first. A CENP-B box match will nearly always fall inside alpha satellite, and in that context it is a structural feature of the centromere, not a candidate enhancer; counting matches is effectively counting satellite repeat units, and satellite arrays are poorly resolved in most reference assemblies, so occurrence counts are unreliable. For the rest of the family, the long grade A models for JRK, POGK, TIGD3, TIGD4, TIGD5 and TIGD7 are individually specific and mutually distinct, so a hit can be assigned to a member rather than only to the family - but almost nothing is known about what those sites do, and there is no occupancy evidence to corroborate them. Discard the CENPBD1, TIGD6 and TIGD1 models, the cross-species transfers, and the suspect CG archetype.
families.caveats: This is a low-cohesion family (0.48) whose members do not share one site: only CENPB, and the models labelled CENPB, correspond to the CENP-B box, and those are written reverse-complement to the usual rendering of the box. A CENP-B box hit is almost always inside alpha satellite and should be read as centromeric structure, not regulation; match counts there track satellite copy number and assembly quality rather than biology. Four models are effectively uninformative (CENPBD1 4.1 bits, TIGD6 3.4 bits, the suspect CG archetype AC0265, and TIGD1's seven-base TATTGCG). Two CIS-BP models are transferred from Monodelphis domestica and one POGK model from a PBM construct at 73 percent domain identity. No member except CENPB has published occupancy data to corroborate its motif.

families.name: PRD-like / primate-specific (CRX-like)
families.def: Divergent paired-like homeodomains of germline and early embryo: DPRX, LEUTX, TPRX1, ARGFX, RHOXF1/2, DUX-like TPRX paralogs.
families.short: PRD-like homeobox genes are a small set of rapidly evolving, single-homeodomain factors, ARGFX, DPRX, LEUTX, TPRX1 and RHOXF1/2 among them, that are expressed almost exclusively in the oocyte, the cleavage-stage embryo and the germ line. Several arose by retrotransposition of a CRX-like ancestor within mammals, and several have been lost or pseudogenised in other lineages, so there are no mouse orthologues for much of the group. Most of them select a short K50-type homeodomain site, TAATCC, in vitro; ARGFX instead prefers a TAATTA palindrome. They are candidate drivers of human zygotic genome activation, acting at promoters derived from endogenous retroviral repeats. The evidence base is thin and largely in vitro, and the motifs are short.
families.long:
## The factors

The PRD-like class, as defined in the standard classification of human homeobox genes, contains ARGFX,
DPRX, LEUTX, TPRX1 and its relatives, RHOXF1 and RHOXF2, and several others. Their names record features of
the domain itself: ARGFX is "arginine-fifty homeobox" and LEUTX is "leucine-twenty homeobox", after the
residue at those positions of the homeodomain. Each protein is small, carries one homeodomain, and has no
other recognisable DNA-binding or dimerisation module. Evolutionarily this is the most volatile corner of
the homeobox repertoire: the genes arose in eutherian mammals, several by retrotransposition from a
CRX-like ancestor, and they have been repeatedly pseudogenised or deleted, so there is no one-to-one mouse
counterpart for ARGFX, DPRX or LEUTX. Expression is correspondingly narrow. LEUTX, TPRX1, DPRX and ARGFX
are detected in the oocyte and in 4- to 8-cell human embryos and essentially nowhere else; RHOXF1 and
RHOXF2 are expressed in human oocytes and male germ cells. Because the genes are off in every accessible
adult tissue, almost nothing is known about them from conventional cell-line work.

## The motif

Most members select TAATCC, written GGATTA on the other strand: a canonical homeodomain TAAT core followed
by two positions specified by residue 50 of the recognition helix, which is the position that separates
K50-type factors (TAATCC) from Q50-type factors (TAATTG or TAATTA). DPRX and RHOXF1 models extend this to
GATAATCC, and TPRX1 to AWCGGATTA. ARGFX is the exception and reads CTAATTAG, a TAAT/ATTA palindrome of the
Q50 type, consistent with its unusual residue 50. Information content is low throughout. The strongest
model in the family carries about 15 bits, most carry 8 to 13, and several are 6-mers or shorter; one
CIS-BP TPRX1 entry has 2 bits and reduces to "At", which is why the representative consensus computed from
the data is uninformative and should not be used. There is no single family consensus: the honest
description is two shapes, a K50 TAATCC site shared by most members and an ARGFX-specific TAATTA
palindrome. Crucially, the TAATCC form is not distinguishable from the site of the much better known K50
factors CRX, OTX1/2, PITX1-3 and GSC; nearest-neighbour similarity to motifs outside this family reaches
0.99 for several members.

## Where it acts

What is known comes from early-embryo transcriptomics rather than from chromatin maps. PRD-like binding
sequences are enriched at transcription start regions active at the 4-cell stage in human embryos, and a
substantial fraction of the promoters concerned are derived from repeat families, including MLT2A1/HERVL
long terminal repeats and Alu elements. Overexpression of nine of these genes in human cells activated
overlapping sets of embryo-specific targets, and LEUTX and the TPRX proteins converge on the 8-cell-stage
program. Outside those windows the sites are not occupied by these factors, because the proteins are
absent; any match in somatic chromatin is far more likely to be read by a K50 factor such as CRX in
photoreceptors, OTX2 in brain and retina, or PITX proteins more broadly. No composite element involving a
PRD-like factor has been named and characterised.

## Biology and disease

The central proposal is that these factors help drive human zygotic genome activation, the handover from
maternal transcripts to embryonic transcription that in humans occurs around the 4- to 8-cell stage.
LEUTX is expressed in a sharp pulse at that point and its manipulation changes 8-cell-stage gene
expression; depletion of the TPRX proteins impairs zygotic genome activation and subsequent development,
which is currently the strongest functional evidence in the group. The RHOXF cluster is regulated by DNA
methylation and histone H1, is imprinted in mouse, and its methylation state and expression have been
associated with human male infertility, but no PRD-like gene is an established Mendelian disease gene. The
absence of mouse orthologues for most members means there are no informative knockouts, and human
embryo work is limited in scale, so almost every functional statement in this family rests on a small
number of studies.

## Reading a hit

Treat a TAATCC match as a K50 homeodomain site and stop there. It does not identify a PRD-like factor; the
same sequence is read by CRX, OTX and PITX proteins, which are expressed in far more tissues and have far
more supporting data. Almost all motif evidence for this family is in vitro: HOCOMOCO models for ARGFX,
DPRX, RHOXF1 and RHOXF2 are built on HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX only, with quality grade B, and the
JASPAR models are HT-SELEX. Only TPRX1 and LEUTX have HOCOMOCO models with any in vivo component. One
JASPAR entry labelled RHOXF1 in this family is in fact the mouse Rhox11 protein-binding-microarray motif,
consensus CGCTGTAAA, which resembles nothing else here; the mouse Rhox cluster is a lineage-specific
expansion rather than a set of RHOXF1/2 orthologues, and that model should not be transferred to human
sequence. Unless your material is oocyte, cleavage-stage embryo or germ line, the prior on PRD-like
occupancy is very low.
families.caveats: Low-confidence family. The shared motif is a 6-base K50 homeodomain site, TAATCC, that occurs by chance roughly every few kilobases and is indistinguishable from the CRX, OTX and PITX site, so a hit almost never identifies a PRD-like factor. Several models in the family carry under 3 bits and cannot be scanned meaningfully. The evidence is overwhelmingly in vitro selection on recombinant protein; only TPRX1 and LEUTX have any in vivo support. One JASPAR entry labelled RHOXF1 is a mouse Rhox11 microarray motif with an unrelated consensus. Because the genes are expressed only in the oocyte, early embryo and germ line, matches in somatic data should be attributed elsewhere.

families.name: PAR bZIP (HLF/NFIL3/DBP)
families.def: Proline- and acidic-rich bZIPs binding TTATG(T/C)AA. HLF, NFIL3/E4BP4, DBP, TEF.
families.short: The PAR bZIP group contains three proline- and acidic-amino-acid-rich basic region-leucine zipper activators - DBP (albumin D-site binding protein), HLF (hepatic leukemia factor) and TEF - together with NFIL3 (E4BP4), which lacks the PAR domain, represses rather than activates, and yet reads the same site. That site is the palindrome TTACGTAA, written in much of the literature as TTATG(T/C)AA. It differs from the cyclic-AMP response element at only the outermost bases of each half-site, TTAC in place of TGAC. DBP, HLF and TEF accumulate with circadian rhythms in liver and suprachiasmatic nucleus, and NFIL3 oscillates in antiphase, so the same element can be activated or repressed depending on time of day. This is the most internally consistent bZIP family in the collection, and its four members are indistinguishable by sequence.
families.long:
## The factors

PAR stands for proline- and acidic-amino-acid-rich, the character of the region N-terminal to the basic region in DBP, HLF and TEF (also called VBP). All three are bZIP activators. NFIL3, better known as E4BP4, is grouped with them because its DNA-binding specificity is the same, but it is structurally distinct: it has no PAR domain and it carries a repression rather than an activation function, so the two halves of this family do opposite things at identical sites. Expression is informative. DBP, HLF and TEF accumulate with high-amplitude circadian rhythms in tissues where clock gene expression cycles strongly, notably liver and the suprachiasmatic nucleus, while remaining near-constant in most other brain regions. NFIL3 cycles in antiphase to DBP, which makes the pair a repressor-activator switch running on one element. NFIL3 is broadly expressed and prominent in immune cells; HLF is largely restricted, and in human hematopoiesis its expression marks the stem cell state. Dimerization matters for interpretation: the bZIP class heterodimerizes extensively, and systematic interaction surveys show these networks are highly partner-specific and have been rewired repeatedly over evolution, so which sites a PAR protein occupies depends on the partner it has.

## The motif

The palindrome is TTACGTAA: two TTAC half-sites in opposed orientation, one per subunit, usually with A, T or G immediately outside, giving GTTACGTAAT and ATTACGTAAC in the highest-information models here. Much of the older literature writes the site as TTATG(T/C)AA; that form is the same element with one half-site degenerate, and both appear in this collection - HOCOMOCO and JASPAR HLF and NFIL3 models read TTATGTAAC and TTATGCAAC, while the DBP and TEF models read TTACGTAA. The distinction from the cyclic-AMP response element is two bases and no more: TTAC against TGAC at the outer edge of each half-site, with the ACGT core shared. That difference is real but slim, and truncated matrices lose it. This family is unusually coherent. Across 15 models from four databases its internal cohesion is 0.94, the highest of the bZIP families here, and every JASPAR and CIS-BP model in the family sits above 0.97 similarity to another member. Four of the six HOCOMOCO models carry in vitro evidence (HT-SELEX or methyl-SELEX), so the claim that these proteins bind this sequence directly rests on more than ChIP. No member is distinguishable, and the family data flags no member as belonging elsewhere and contains no cross-species inferred model. The one model that drifts is CIS-BP M04016 for HLF, GTGACGTAA, which is half a PAR site and half a CRE; the same is true of CIS-BP M04034 for NFIL3, ATGACGTAAT.

## Where it acts

The founding site is the D-site of the rat albumin promoter, from which DBP takes its name, and the family's best-characterized targets are hepatic metabolic genes, including cytochrome P450 enzymes and pyridoxal kinase. DBP, HLF and TEF have similar circadian and tissue-specific expression but measurably different promoter preferences, so a shared matrix does not imply a shared target list. Because occupancy is rhythmic and NFIL3 occupies the same elements at the opposite phase, a site can be an activator target in one part of the day and a repressor target twelve hours later; a static motif scan cannot express this. In immune cells NFIL3 acts at lineage-specification loci rather than at metabolic promoters. On frequency: the AT-rich 8-mer is expected of order 10^5 times in 3.1 Gb of human sequence, so an isolated match carries little weight.

## Biology and disease

Single knockouts of Dbp, Hlf or Tef in mice are mild, which is the expected signature of factors that share an element. Mice lacking all three are viable but highly susceptible to spontaneous and audiogenic generalized seizures that are frequently lethal; the mechanism was traced to reduced expression of pyridoxal kinase and hence lower brain pyridoxal phosphate, serotonin and dopamine. NFIL3 has non-redundant immune roles: it is required for commitment to the natural killer cell lineage, where it directly regulates Eomes and Id2, and for the development of a common innate lymphoid cell precursor. HLF is the 3-prime partner of the t(17;19) TCF3-HLF fusion in a rare and aggressive pro-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia, in which the HLF bZIP supplies dimerization and DNA binding to a chimeric activator. In normal human hematopoiesis, HLF expression defines the stem cell compartment.

## Reading a hit

A TTACGTAA match is a clean family call by the standards of this class, because the family is cohesive, its models agree across databases, and several rest on in vitro binding data. It is not a member call at all, and here that matters more than usual: DBP, HLF and TEF activate while NFIL3 represses, so the same match is consistent with opposite outcomes, and which applies depends on cell type and on time of day. Check the outer bases before accepting the family. TTAC is PAR bZIP; TGAC is AP-1, CREB/ATF or ATF6/CREB3, and the shared ACGT core means a matrix scan will happily return CREs under a PAR model and vice versa. Two CIS-BP models filed here, for HLF and NFIL3, are themselves half-PAR and half-CRE hybrids. The 8-mer is AT-rich and common, so require accessibility or phase-resolved occupancy data before calling a site functional. Finally, treat a hit in a non-liver, non-immune, non-clock tissue with caution: expression, not sequence, is what limits this family's activity.
families.caveats: Of the eight bZIP families in this atlas, this is the one whose motif models agree best with each other and with in vitro binding data, and no member is flagged as belonging elsewhere. The limits are elsewhere. The site differs from a cyclic-AMP response element by only the outermost base of each half-site, so truncated or low-information matrices will not separate them, and two CIS-BP models here are already half-CRE hybrids. The 8-mer is AT-rich and occurs of order 100,000 times genome-wide. Most importantly, a hit does not indicate direction: DBP, HLF and TEF activate, NFIL3 represses, they occupy the same element in antiphase across the day, and sequence cannot distinguish them.

families.name: SAND domain (AIRE/SP100/GMEB)
families.def: GMEB1/2 (GRE-modulating), SP100, SP140, AIRE, DEAF1-like SAND factors.
families.short: The SAND domain is a small DNA-binding fold named after the four proteins in which it was first recognized: Sp100, AIRE, NucP41/75 and DEAF1. Sequence-specific binding depends on a conserved KDWK motif on the domain's surface, and only some SAND proteins have it. The best-defined members are GMEB1 and GMEB2, which bind as a heterodimer, also known as parvovirus initiation factor, to two CpG-containing tetranucleotide half-sites with flexible spacing: ACGY-N(1-9)-RCGY, with an optimum spacer of six bases. Binding is abolished by methylation of the CpG in either half-site. AIRE and the speckled proteins SP100 and SP140 lack the KDWK motif and are recruited through chromatin rather than sequence, so motif models attributed to them should be treated as descriptions of where they were found.
families.long:
## The factors

SAND is a fold, not a functional group. The domain was named from Sp100, AIRE-1, NucP41/75 and
DEAF1, and its NMR structure showed a novel alpha-beta fold whose DNA-binding activity maps to a
conserved surface motif, KDWK, which gives the family its alternative name. Human SAND proteins
fall into distinct groups. GMEB1 and GMEB2 (p96 and p79) were identified twice over: as the
heterodimer that binds the glucocorticoid modulatory element upstream of the tyrosine
aminotransferase gene, and as parvovirus initiation factor, the host factor required for
minute virus of mice origin nicking. They carry the KDWK motif, bind DNA cooperatively, and are
ubiquitously expressed. DEAF1 (NUDR) is a related KDWK protein that binds TTCG-containing repeats;
notably, it has no motif in any of the four databases used here despite being named in this
family's definition. The speckled proteins SP100, SP110, SP140 and SP140L are nuclear-body
components that combine a SAND domain with PHD fingers and bromodomains and act as chromatin
readers in immune cells. AIRE, the autoimmune regulator, is the most important special case: its
SAND domain lacks the KDWK residues required for sequence-specific DNA contact and instead mediates
homodimerization, while its two PHD fingers read histone H3, PHD1 binding H3 tails that are
unmethylated at lysine 4. AIRE is essentially restricted to medullary thymic epithelial cells.

## The motif

For GMEB1/GMEB2 the site is well defined and unusual. Degenerate oligonucleotide selection showed
that the heterodimer, and each homodimer, binds two tetranucleotide half-sites conforming to
ACGY-N(1-9)-RCGY, with an optimum spacer of six bases; the spacing is genuinely flexible, so the
element is a pair of short half-sites at variable distance rather than a fixed-width motif. The
invariant feature is the CpG in each half-site, and 5-methylation of those cytosines abolishes
binding completely, which makes GMEB an unusual example of a factor whose occupancy is directly
methylation-sensitive at its core. Because CpG is suppressed in vertebrate genomes, such sites
should be rare, yet over half of a sample of 100 human promoters contained at least one, often
within 100 bases of the start site. The models in these databases capture only part of this
grammar. Most GMEB matrices collapse the pair into a single half-site region: the representative
model here is TACGTAA, and JASPAR's GMEB1 and GMEB2 matrices are tACGTa and TACGTAA. One CIS-BP
model, M05735_2.00, does show the doubled form (TACGTACGGTACGTA), which is the two half-sites
resolved. The consequence for scanning is severe: a six- or seven-base ACGT-centered model sits in
the middle of the sequence space used by bZIP factors, since TACGTA, TGACGT and CACGTG all contain
ACGT, and the data reflect this directly. Two GMEB1 models have a higher similarity to their
best out-of-family neighbour than to any in-family motif, and the family's cohesion is only 0.70
across 15 motifs. The remaining models are not ACGT elements at all: the ChIP-derived GMEB models
are GCGTCAGCGCG-like, the HOCOMOCO SP100 model is AACGGTTA and the SP140 model is GTCGTCACTA, each
with zero label agreement, and the Vierstra AIRE archetype (AC0160) is a CCAAT-containing element
rather than anything resembling a SAND site.

## Where it acts

GMEB sites are promoter-proximal and, by construction, CpG-containing, so they concentrate in
CpG-island promoters where their methylation sensitivity could make them responsive to DNA
methylation state. The glucocorticoid modulatory element itself modulates the sensitivity of a
glucocorticoid-responsive promoter rather than driving it, so GMEB acts as a modifier of another
factor's output. AIRE acts in a completely different regime: in medullary thymic epithelial cells
it associates with super-enhancers and with thousands of promoters of tissue-restricted antigen
genes, and its principal mechanism is releasing stalled RNA polymerase II rather than recruiting it
to a specific sequence. SP140 occupies and maintains repressed loci in macrophages, including
lineage-inappropriate developmental genes.

## Biology and disease

Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in AIRE cause autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal
dystrophy (APECED, also APS-1), a monogenic autoimmune disease; Aire-deficient mice lose promiscuous
expression of thousands of tissue-restricted antigens in the thymus and develop multi-organ
autoimmunity, which established the central-tolerance model of negative selection. Missense
mutations in the SAND domain of DEAF1 cause intellectual disability with severe speech impairment
and behavioral problems. Variants at SP140 and SP110 are associated with Crohn disease, multiple
sclerosis and chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and SP110 mutations cause hepatic venoocclusive disease
with immunodeficiency. GMEB proteins have no established monogenic disease link, but they are
required for parvovirus DNA replication.

## Reading a hit

The central caution is that this key mixes proteins that read sequence with proteins that do not. A
match to a GMEB model is a real, if weak, claim: look for the second CpG half-site within nine bases
and check the methylation state, because an unmethylated CpG is part of the site rather than
incidental. A match to an AIRE, SP100 or SP140 model is much harder to interpret. None of these
proteins has the KDWK motif required for sequence-specific SAND binding, their models here come from
integrative and ChIP-based evidence, their nearest neighbours lie in other families, and in AIRE's
case the archetype is a CCAAT-type element. The general risk for the ACGT-centered GMEB models is
confusion with bZIP sites, which share the same four-base core and are far more abundant; a TACGTA
match in a promoter is more likely to be a CRE-like or MAF-like element than a GMEB site.
families.caveats: Split this family in two before trusting anything. GMEB1 and GMEB2 have the KDWK motif and a real, if unusual, site: two CpG-containing half-sites with a 1-9 base spacer, abolished by CpG methylation. But the matrices compress this to a six- or seven-base ACGT core that overlaps bZIP space, and two GMEB1 models here match an out-of-family motif better than any relative. AIRE, SP100 and SP140 lack the KDWK residues needed for sequence-specific SAND binding; their models come from ChIP and integrative evidence, carry zero label agreement, and the Vierstra AIRE archetype is a CCAAT-type element. Treat those as records of where the protein was found. DEAF1 has no motif here at all.

families.name: EGR
families.def: GCGTGGGCG. EGR1-4, WT1.
families.short: EGR1 to EGR4 are immediate-early transcription factors whose three C2H2 zinc fingers read a nine-base GC-rich site, GCGTGGGCG, also written GCGGGGGCG. The first of these proteins, EGR1, is better known to structural biologists as Zif268: its complex with DNA was the crystal structure that established how zinc fingers recognize DNA, three bases per finger, and it remains the reference for the C2H2 recognition code. EGR proteins are induced within minutes by growth factors, serum and neuronal activity, so their sites sit in the promoters of rapidly inducible genes. All four paralogues share the same matrix, and the WT1 tumor suppressor binds essentially the same sequence, so a hit names a site rather than a protein.
families.long:
## The factors

EGR1, EGR2, EGR3 and EGR4 are four paralogous immediate-early transcription factors, each with three Cys2-His2 zinc fingers and a set of aliases reflecting their independent discovery: EGR1 is also Zif268, NGFI-A, Krox-24 and zif/268; EGR2 is Krox-20; EGR4 is NGFI-C (Christy and Nathans 1989; Patwardhan et al. 1991). Their mRNAs are induced within minutes of exposure to growth factors, serum, mitogens or neuronal activity, which is what "immediate-early" means here: the protein is largely absent from unstimulated cells. EGR1 is broadly inducible; EGR2 is prominent in Schwann cells and the developing hindbrain; EGR3 in neurons and muscle spindles; EGR4 is largely restricted to brain. All four bind DNA as monomers. One further protein must be kept in mind: the Wilms tumor suppressor WT1 has a closely related four-finger domain and recognizes essentially the same site (Rauscher et al. 1990). WT1 is a separate family in this atlas, but it is not separable from EGR by sequence alone.

## The motif

The site is nine base pairs, usually written GCGTGGGCG or GCGGGGGCG; the reverse-complement form, CGCCCACGC, is how several matrices in this atlas are stored (the medoid, CIS-BP M04461_2.00, is CCGCCCACGCA, which is TGCGTGGGCGG read from the other strand). Recognition is the textbook case. The 2.1 A crystal structure of the three Zif268 fingers bound to a consensus site showed the fingers lying in the major groove and wrapping part way around B-DNA, each finger contacting a three-base subsite through residues at positions -1, 3 and 6 of its recognition helix (Pavletich and Pabo 1991); the structure was later refined to 1.6 A (Elrod-Erickson et al. 1996) and became the basis of the general C2H2 code (Wolfe et al. 2000; Zhang et al. 2024). Random-site selection showed that EGR1, EGR2, EGR3 and EGR4 all bind and activate from GCGGGGGCG and from a family of closely related variants, with only modest differences among them (Swirnoff and Milbrandt 1995). The atlas data agree emphatically: 15 matrices, four gene symbols, cohesion 0.90, and the JASPAR profiles for EGR1, EGR2, EGR3 and EGR4 are all the same 11-mer, ACGCCCACGCA. Nothing distinguishes the paralogues. The useful comparison is outward, to the other GC-rich families. EGR's signature is the CACGC / GCGTG triplet immediately adjacent to a GGGCG block; the KLF/SP GC-box, GGGGCGGGG, lacks it, and the KLF/SP in vitro consensus CCACGCCC shares the pentamer CCACG with the reverse complement of the EGR site but places it differently. Where a nine-mer matches both models at comparable scores, sequence cannot decide, and that situation is common.

## Where it acts

EGR sites are promoter-proximal and GC-rich, concentrated near CpG islands and in the promoters of rapidly inducible genes. Because EGR protein appears only after stimulation, occupancy is condition-dependent in a way that the sequence does not reveal: the same site can be empty in a resting cell and bound minutes after serum addition. The classic co-occurrence problem is with the GC-box factors. When the CT/GC-rich element of the human IL-3 promoter (positions -76 to -47) was used as bait in an expression screen, the clones recovered were EGR1, EGR2 and the unrelated zinc-finger protein DB1/VEZF1; in gel-shift assays DB1 bound the element constitutively while EGR1 bound only after T-cell activation (Koyano-Nakagawa et al. 1994). That single experiment is a compact demonstration of both the overlap and its resolution: the same element, different factors, distinguished by condition rather than by sequence. EGR sites also overlap WT1 sites directly, and the two proteins compete at shared sequences.

## Biology and disease

Egr1-null mice are viable but females are infertile because of a specific failure to produce luteinizing hormone beta, identifying EGR1 as the factor required for LH-beta expression (Lee et al. 1996). Egr2/Krox-20 null mice fail to myelinate peripheral nerves, establishing EGR2 as a control point for Schwann cell myelination (Topilko et al. 1994), and human EGR2 mutations cause hereditary myelinopathies in the Charcot-Marie-Tooth and congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy spectrum (Warner et al. 1998). EGR1 has been implicated in growth-factor responses, apoptosis and tumor suppression in various tissues, though the direction of effect is context-dependent and the literature is not settled. EGR3 and EGR4 have narrower documented roles, largely neuronal.

## Reading a hit

A match identifies the EGR site, not an EGR protein - and possibly not even an EGR protein, since WT1 binds the same sequence. The evidence that EGR factors really bind this sequence is unusually good: the HOCOMOCO models for EGR1, EGR2 and EGR3 carry combined ChIP and HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX evidence at grade A, so the label is in vitro supported, not ChIP-inferred. Two entries in the family are weaker and should not be used alone: EGR4.H14CORE.0.S.B is an eight-position model whose nearest neighbors across the databases lie outside this family, and the Vierstra archetype AC0262:EGR carries only 5.6 bits, too little to call anything. One archetype is explicitly named AC0519:EGR/WT, which is the clustering telling you that the EGR and WT1 motifs merged. Practically: a nine-base GC-rich site is common in promoters, so treat an isolated hit as weak evidence; and because EGR proteins are stimulus-induced, a real site may be unoccupied in whatever cell state you sampled.
families.caveats: EGR1 to EGR4 share one matrix, so a hit names the family at best. Worse, WT1 binds essentially the same nine-base site, and one Vierstra archetype in this family is explicitly labelled EGR/WT - a strong EGR match is also a candidate WT1 site. Overlap with the KLF/SP GC-box is frequent and often unresolvable from sequence. The in vitro evidence behind the EGR label is good (grade-A HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX models for EGR1-EGR3), but the EGR4 HT-SELEX model and the low-information AC0262 archetype should not be used on their own. Because EGR proteins are stimulus-induced, occupancy depends on cell state, not sequence.

families.name: MITF / TFE (CLEAR)
families.def: CLEAR/M-box GTCACGTGAC. MITF, TFE3, TFEB, TFEC.
families.short: MITF, TFE3, TFEB and TFEC are bHLH-LZ factors that dimerize only with each other, because a three-residue insertion kinks their leucine zipper. They read a canonical E-box core with a strict flanking requirement, giving the palindromic 10-mer GTCACGTGAC - the same element known as the melanocyte M-box (TCATGTGA) in pigmentation genes and as the CLEAR box in lysosomal and autophagy promoters. MITF is the lineage factor of melanocytes and is mutated in Waardenburg syndrome type 2A and predisposes to melanoma; TFEB and TFE3 run the lysosome-autophagy program downstream of mTORC1 and are recurrently rearranged in renal cell carcinoma. The four paralogues cannot be told apart from sequence.
families.long:
## The factors

MITF, TFE3, TFEB and TFEC form the MiT/TFE family of basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-LZ) factors. MITF was identified from the mouse microphthalmia locus, where mutations cause loss of melanocytes, deafness and small eyes; the three TFE genes were then recognized as a discrete family that dimerizes internally - each member homodimerizes and heterodimerizes with the others, but not with MYC, MAX or USF. The structural basis is a three-residue insertion that kinks the leucine zipper, which excludes the other bHLH-ZIP proteins from the dimer interface and explains why MiT/TFE factors, despite reading the same DNA core, form a closed dimerization set. Expression is what separates them: MITF is restricted (melanocytes, mast cells, osteoclasts, retinal pigment epithelium) and has multiple isoforms driven from alternative promoters, TFE3 and TFEB are broadly expressed and act as the general lysosomal-autophagy arm, and TFEC is largely myeloid. All four are regulated post-translationally rather than only transcriptionally; TFEB in particular is phosphorylated by mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface and held in the cytoplasm until nutrient stress releases it. The atlas assigns 14 motifs here (4 JASPAR, 6 HOCOMOCO, 4 CIS-BP) across all four symbols, cohesion 0.94, with TFE3.H14CORE.0.PSM.A as the representative.

## The motif

The core is the canonical E-box CACGTG, read as two CAC half-sites by the histidine-glutamate-arginine triad in each basic region, exactly as in MAX. What distinguishes MiT/TFE is an absolute-looking flanking requirement: these proteins need a T immediately 5' of the core (and the reciprocal A 3'), giving the palindromic 10-mer GTCACGTGAC. The same preference, written as TCATGTGA, defines the classical melanocyte M-box of the tyrosinase promoter, which uses the CATGTG rather than the CACGTG half-site; MITF binds TCATGTGA but not CATGTG without the T. In the lysosomal literature the identical 10-mer is called the CLEAR element (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression And Regulation), GTCACGTGAC, found in the promoters of most lysosomal hydrolase, subunit and trafficking genes. So the M-box and the CLEAR box are the same motif described in two fields. Two consequences follow. First, MITF, TFE3, TFEB and TFEC are not separable from one another by sequence: pairwise similarity among their models in this atlas is 0.97-0.995. Second, the motif is essentially identical to the USF motif, and very close to BHLHE41 and CLOCK-BMAL1 models, so the T/A flanks buy discrimination against MYC-MAX but not against those. The family data also contains lower-information, ChIP-derived variants (a grade-C TFEB model reading gTCACATG) that lose the 3' half entirely.

## Where it acts

MiT/TFE sites are promoter-proximal and CpG-island-associated. The CLEAR network was defined as a few hundred coordinately regulated lysosomal and autophagy genes carrying the element within the first few hundred base pairs of the transcription start site, and TFEB ChIP-seq recovers that set plus autophagosome-formation genes. MITF occupancy is layered on top of a melanocyte-specific accessibility landscape: the same GTCACGTGAC sequence is used at pigmentation genes (TYR, DCT, TYRP1, PMEL), at lysosome-related genes in melanosome biogenesis, and at proliferation genes, and MITF co-occupies melanocyte enhancers with SOX10 and the AP-1 machinery. TFEB and TFE3 occupancy is switched by subcellular localization rather than by motif availability - the sites are present and often accessible even when the factor is cytoplasmic.

## Biology and disease

MITF is the lineage-determining factor of the melanocyte: loss-of-function alleles cause the mouse microphthalmia phenotypes and, in humans, Waardenburg syndrome type 2A (deafness with pigmentary anomalies) and Tietz syndrome. The recurrent MITF E318K substitution, which impairs SUMOylation, raises melanoma risk and also associates with renal cell carcinoma. TFEB and TFE3 drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy downstream of mTORC1 and starvation, and are involved in lysosomal storage disease biology as therapeutic targets. Translocations involving these genes are diagnostic in cancer: promoter substitution at t(6;11)(p21;q13) drives TFEB overexpression in a distinct renal cell carcinoma subtype, and TFE3 fusions define another renal carcinoma group and alveolar soft part sarcoma.

## Reading a hit

A GTCACGTGAC or TCATGTGA hit identifies a T/A-flanked E-box. That is a real narrowing - it argues against MYC-MAX - but it does not name the factor: USF1/USF2, BHLHE41, CLOCK-BMAL1 and all four MiT/TFE proteins share it. Within the family, a hit cannot distinguish MITF from TFE3, TFEB or TFEC; the usual discriminator is expression, so a hit in melanocyte data suggests MITF and a hit in a starvation experiment suggests TFEB, and neither inference comes from the sequence. ChIP-derived MiT/TFE models are additionally biased toward active CpG-island promoters. Prefer the HOCOMOCO models with in vitro (S or M) support.
families.caveats: The T/A flanks make this motif distinguishable from MYC-MAX but not from USF1/USF2, BHLHE41 or CLOCK-BMAL1, which prefer the same extended palindrome; a GTCACGTGAC hit therefore names a group, not a protein. Within the family MITF, TFE3, TFEB and TFEC share one motif at 0.97-0.995 similarity, so assignment relies entirely on which factor is expressed and, for TFEB/TFE3, on whether it is nuclear at the time. Several models here are ChIP-only and low grade (a grade-C TFEB model reduces to gTCACATG), so they encode promoter context as much as intrinsic specificity. Prefer HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX-supported models when the question is direct binding.

families.name: YY1 / YY2
families.def: AAnATGGCggc. YY1, YY2, ZFP42/REX1.
families.short: YY1 is a ubiquitously expressed zinc-finger protein that binds a short CCAT-centered site, usually written CGCCATNTT or, on the other strand, AANATGGCGGC. It sits at or just inside the transcription start site of a large fraction of CpG-island promoters, works as an activator at some and a repressor at others, and is found on both the enhancer and the promoter side of enhancer-promoter contacts. Two retrogenes derived from YY1, YY2 and ZFP42/REX1, share the same zinc-finger domain; YY2 binds the same consensus more weakly, and REX1 prefers divergent sites that still contain the CCAT core. Because the motif is short and concentrated in CpG islands, a YY1 match is one of the most common hits in promoter sequence.
families.long:
## The factors

YY1 (Yin Yang 1) has four C2H2 zinc fingers at its C terminus and belongs to the GLI-Kruppel class;
its Drosophila counterpart is Pleiohomeotic (Pho). It was described independently in the same period
as a repressor whose activity is relieved by adenovirus E1A and as an initiator-binding protein that
directs and activates transcription in vitro, and it also appears in the older literature as NF-E1,
delta factor and UCRBP. It binds DNA as a monomer and is expressed in essentially all cell types.

The family in these databases has three human members. YY2 and ZFP42 (REX1) are both retrogenes
generated from YY1 in placental mammals, and their zinc-finger domains remain highly similar to
YY1's. Motif measurements show that YY2 binds the same consensus as YY1 but with much lower
affinity, while REX1 binds sequences divergent from YY1's that nevertheless share the CCAT core.
ZFP42/REX1 is best known as a pluripotency marker in embryonic stem cells. All three are assigned
here to a single family because their matrices are not separable.

## The motif

The literature core is CCAT. The short consensus most often quoted is CGCCATNTT, and the
reverse-strand form AANATGGCGGC is what several databases show, including the form used in the
ontology entry for this family. Selection experiments give a longer high-affinity version,
GCCGCCATTTTG, and the endogenous sites at Peg3 (GGCGCCATNTT) and Xist (CCGCCATNTT) are longer than
the classic motif. Substituting three residues in the first zinc finger, to mimic Drosophila Pho,
collapses specificity to a bare GCCAT, showing that the four fingers contribute jointly rather than
modularly and that the flanking information depends on finger one. The data consensus here,
CCGCCATYTT, is the same site.

The cocrystal structure of the YY1 zinc fingers on the adeno-associated virus P5 initiator explains
an unusual property. Upstream of the start sites the protein contacts both strands, whereas
downstream the contacts are essentially restricted to the template strand, leaving the non-template
strand free. That asymmetry is what allows YY1 to sit over an initiator, support TBP-independent
initiation with a fixed direction, and bind a preformed transcription bubble or a DNA/RNA hybrid.
Functionally the site is orientation-sensitive in context: in the c-fos promoter YY1 bends DNA and
its effect depends on which way the site points. Sequence alone does not distinguish YY1 from YY2,
and only partially separates ZFP42.

## Where it acts

YY1 is a promoter factor first. Its motif is strongly enriched at CpG-island promoters, where it
co-occurs with a characteristic set of partners at active promoters, including HCFC1, ZNF143,
THAP11 and GABP, and it binds within a few tens of base pairs of the transcription start site far
more often than at a distance. It is also present at active enhancers, and the observation that it
occupies both sides of many enhancer-promoter pairs led to the proposal that YY1 acts as a general
structural contributor to enhancer-promoter loops, in loose analogy to CTCF at structural loops.
YY1 is additionally reported as a CTCF cofactor at the X-inactivation choice, and as the mammalian
Pho counterpart that helps recruit Polycomb complexes, an activity that requires both DNA binding
and interaction with YAF2. Because the informative site is short and CpG islands are the preferred
context, matches are extremely dense in promoter sequence: a YY1 hit near a TSS is close to the
default expectation rather than a discovery.

## Biology and disease

YY1 is dosage-sensitive in humans: de novo heterozygous variants and deletions cause Gabriele-de
Vries syndrome, an intellectual-disability syndrome with movement abnormalities in which patient
cells show transcriptional and chromatin dysfunction, consistent with partial loss of a general
promoter factor rather than a tissue-restricted one. Mouse YY1 mutants show homeotic transformations
of the axial skeleton and interact genetically with the Polycomb gene Ring1, placing YY1 in the
PcG-dependent regulation of Hox genes. At the molecular level YY1 has been assigned both activating
and repressing roles at different promoters, often through the cofactor it recruits (HDACs and
Polycomb components on one side, coactivators and the basal machinery on the other), which is why
the same motif cannot be read as a sign. YY1 is frequently reported as overexpressed in tumors,
though the causal claims there are much less settled than the developmental genetics.

## Reading a hit

A YY1 match is common enough that on its own it is close to uninformative, particularly inside a
CpG island. Treat it as a family-level call: YY1, YY2 and ZFP42 are not separable by sequence, and
YY2 in particular binds the same consensus. A hit tells you nothing about direction of effect,
because YY1 activates at some promoters and represses at others. Position matters more than score:
a site within tens of base pairs of a TSS, in the orientation seen at initiators, is a more credible
YY1 element than a stronger match in intergenic DNA. Finally, YY1 has been used as a positive
control in so many ChIP experiments that the motif is over-represented in derived models generally;
if a ChIP-derived matrix for some unrelated factor looks like AANATGGCGGC, indirect or
co-occupancy-driven enrichment at active promoters is the first explanation to consider, not a new
specificity.
families.caveats: The site is short, CpG-island-associated and present at a large share of active promoters, so a hit is expected rather than informative and should be weighted by position relative to the TSS. YY1, YY2 and ZFP42/REX1 all descend from the same zinc-finger domain and cannot be told apart from sequence; YY2 binds the identical consensus with lower affinity. A match says nothing about activation versus repression, since YY1 does both depending on the cofactor recruited. And because YY1 sits at essentially all active promoters, an AANATGGCGGC-like motif recovered from another factor's ChIP data is more likely promoter co-occupancy than that factor's own specificity.

families.name: E-proteins (TCF3/4/12)
families.def: Class I bHLH E-box CAGCTG/CACCTG heterodimer partners. TCF3/E2A, TCF4/ITF2, TCF12/HEB, TCF15, TCFL5.
families.short: TCF3 (E2A/E12/E47), TCF4 (E2-2) and TCF12 (HEB) are the broadly expressed class I bHLH proteins that serve as the general dimerization partners for tissue-restricted bHLH factors - MYOD in muscle, ASCL and NEUROD in neurons, TWIST in mesenchyme, TAL1 in blood - and are sequestered by ID proteins. They bind the class-A E-box, written CACCTG or equivalently CAGGTG, and also CAGCTG. Because most functional sites are heterodimeric, only one half-site is read by the E-protein itself. E2A loss abolishes B-cell development; TCF4 haploinsufficiency causes Pitt-Hopkins syndrome, TCF12 loss causes coronal craniosynostosis, and TCF3 is a recurrent fusion partner in pre-B leukaemia.
families.long:
## The factors

The E-proteins are TCF3 (E2A, whose splice isoforms are E12 and E47), TCF4 (E2-2, ITF2) and TCF12 (HEB, HTF4). They are class I basic helix-loop-helix proteins: broadly expressed, lacking a leucine zipper, and defined by the fact that they are the general dimerization partners for the class II, tissue-restricted bHLH factors. The HLH motif itself was recognized by comparing the immunoglobulin enhancer-binding E12/E47 proteins with Drosophila daughterless, MyoD and MYC, and the following paper showed the central property directly: heterodimers between different HLH proteins form readily and bind a common DNA sequence. That is what E-proteins do. TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12 heterodimerize with MYOD and MYF5 in muscle, ASCL1, NEUROD and ATOH in neural tissue, TWIST1 and HAND in mesenchyme, TAL1 and LYL1 in blood, PTF1A in pancreas, and OLIG proteins in glia, as well as with each other. They are also the targets of the ID proteins (ID1-ID4), which have an HLH but no basic region and therefore sequester E-proteins into non-binding dimers. This family also collects TCFL5, a more distant protein, and the ontology lists TCF15; in the current data, motifs exist for TCF3, TCF4, TCF12 and TCFL5. The atlas assigns 13 motifs here (5 JASPAR, 4 HOCOMOCO, 4 CIS-BP), cohesion 0.87, representative TCF4 (MA0830.3).

## The motif

E-proteins read the class-A E-box, most often written CACCTG or, equivalently, CAGGTG - these are the same six base pairs read from opposite strands, which is worth keeping in mind when comparing database consensus strings. The other class-A variant, CAGCTG, is also bound; together the preference is CAG[C/G]TG on one strand. The immunoglobulin enhancer sites that defined the family, muE5 and kappaE2, are of this type. The E47 crystal structure showed how the site is read: a parallel four-helix bundle with one basic helix per monomer in the major groove, a glutamate contacting the CA of each half-site and an arginine the guanine on the complementary strand - the same chemistry as MAX, with the residue at one position determining class A versus class B preference. Because heterodimers are the functional unit, the real in vivo site is often asymmetric: one half-site is read by the E-protein and the other by the tissue partner, so MyoD-E47 and TAL1-TCF3 sites differ from E-protein homodimer sites mainly in one half. Systematic binding-site selection comparing MyoD and E2A complexes established this early, and it is the reason paralogue assignment from sequence fails here. In the atlas data, TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12 models are mutually similar at 0.96-0.995, so they are one motif. Two entries are not: the TCFL5 models read tCACGCGC, which is not an E-box, and the JASPAR Tcf12 model MA0521.3 is a bare CAGCTG whose nearest neighbour across all four databases lies outside this family. These two account for the modest cohesion score.

## Where it acts

E-protein sites are found at both promoters and enhancers, but the striking pattern is that their genomic distribution is essentially that of whichever partner is expressed. In B cells, TCF3 occupies the immunoglobulin heavy- and light-chain enhancers and the B-lineage gene set; in muscle, E-protein occupancy coincides with MyoD enhancers; in the T-lineage, TCF12 and TCF3 sit at TAL1 and thymocyte enhancers. Because CAGCTG and CACCTG contain no CpG, they are not depleted in mammalian DNA and occur very frequently - a 6-bp palindrome is expected roughly every 4 kb. The practical consequence is that E-proteins appear in an unusually large number of ChIP datasets, both as the tagged factor and as the apparent motif inside someone else's peaks, because they are physically present at almost every class-II bHLH site in every tissue that expresses one.

## Biology and disease

E2A/TCF3-null mice lack B cells entirely and fail to initiate immunoglobulin gene rearrangement, which established E-proteins as required for lymphoid specification rather than merely modulatory. Human disease follows the paralogues. TCF4 haploinsufficiency causes Pitt-Hopkins syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy and autonomic dysfunction, and common TCF4 variants are among the strongest transcription-factor associations with schizophrenia. TCF12 loss-of-function, acting through its partnership with TWIST1, is a frequent cause of coronal craniosynostosis. TCF3 is a recurrent fusion partner in pre-B acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, where the t(1;19) translocation joins the TCF3 activation domain to the PBX1 homeodomain. ID protein overexpression, which titrates E-proteins away from DNA, is a common feature of tumours and of proliferating progenitors.

## Reading a hit

A CACCTG or CAGCTG match identifies a class-A E-box. It does not identify an E-protein, and it certainly does not identify which one: TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12 share a single motif. Worse, the same core is read by MYOD, NEUROD/ATOH, ASCL, TWIST/HAND, TAL1/LYL1, TFAP4, ZEB1/2 and SNAI-associated E-boxes. Most real E-protein sites are occupied by a heterodimer, so only one half of the match belongs to the E-protein at all. Treat an E-protein motif inside someone else's ChIP peaks as expected co-occupancy rather than evidence of indirect binding artifact - and treat an E-protein ChIP peak as most likely marking the partner's locus. The TCFL5 models here are not E-boxes and should not be scanned as such.
families.caveats: TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12 share one motif at 0.96-0.995 similarity, so a hit names the E-proteins at best, never a paralogue. The class-A core is also read by MYOD, NEUROD/ATOH, ASCL, TWIST/HAND, TAL1/LYL1, TFAP4 and ZEB, contains no CpG and is not depleted, so it occurs by chance every few kilobases. Most genuine sites are heterodimeric, meaning half the match belongs to the partner. E-proteins consequently show up in a very large number of ChIP datasets as the apparent motif inside other factors' peaks; that is real co-occupancy, not necessarily mislabelling. The TCFL5 models assigned here read tCACGCGC, which is not an E-box, and one JASPAR Tcf12 model is a bare CAGCTG whose nearest neighbours lie outside this family.

families.name: p53 family
families.def: Two decamers RRRCWWGYYY. TP53, TP63, TP73.
families.short: The p53 response element is bound by three paralogues - TP53, TP63 and TP73 - through a shared, structurally unusual DNA-binding domain that works only as a tetramer. The element is built from two decamers of the form RRRCWWGYYY, usually adjacent but tolerating a spacer, so a full site is 20 bp or more. Each decamer is read by a p53 dimer, and the CATG core at its centre is the part that matters: three of the four hotspot residues mutated in human cancers contact exactly this DNA. Because the element is long and its core is well defined, p53 sites are among the more specific vertebrate motifs, and a good double-decamer match is genuinely informative. What a match cannot tell you is which of the three paralogues is responsible.
families.long:
## The factors

Three human genes encode this DNA-binding domain: TP53, TP63 and TP73. The domain is a beta-sandwich carrying a loop-sheet-helix motif and two large loops held together by a structural zinc ion, a fold shared with no other vertebrate transcription factor family. It works only as a tetramer, assembled through a separate C-terminal oligomerisation domain, and the tetramer is best described as a dimer of dimers: two dimers bind the two decamer half-sites and are further stabilised by protein-protein and base-stacking contacts between them. TP53 is ubiquitously expressed and normally short-lived, kept low by MDM2-mediated degradation until stress stabilises it. TP63 and TP73 are expressed more narrowly - TP63 in basal keratinocytes and other stratified epithelia, TP73 in ciliated epithelia and neurons - and both produce N-terminally truncated dominant-negative isoforms (dNp63, dNp73) that compete for the same element without activating it. All three share a near-identical DNA-contacting surface, which is why they read the same sequence.

## The motif

The consensus was defined by selecting genomic fragments that bind p53: two copies of 5'-PuPuPuC(A/T)(T/A)GPyPyPy-3', now usually written RRRCWWGYYY, separated by 0-13 bp. One decamer alone was insufficient for binding in that assay, and small alterations of the decamer abolished affinity even in multiple copies. The crystal structure of the p53 core domain on DNA explained why: arginine 280 hydrogen-bonds the invariant guanine, lysine 120 and alanine 276 read the adjacent bases, and arginine 248 tracks the minor groove - residues 248, 273 and 282 are among the most frequently mutated in human tumours, so the hotspots are literally the DNA-reading apparatus. Information is concentrated in the central CWWG (in practice mostly CATG) and in the purine and pyrimidine runs that flank it; the outer positions are looser. Spacing is genuinely contested. The original definition allowed up to 13 bp, but a systematic transactivation study found that even small increases in spacer length sharply reduce activity, while separately reporting substantial transactivation from non-canonical half-sites (a single decamer) and three-quarter sites. Solution and crystal work has since shown that p53 tetramers can form hemispecific complexes in which one dimer sits on a specific half-site and the other on adjacent spacer sequence, with comparable affinity - which reconciles the two observations without settling how much of the genome's real regulation runs through half-sites. Practically, the databases here are split the same way: the high-information models are full double decamers (for example ACATGTCC..GACATGT, 16-20 positions), while several HOCOMOCO secondary models are single decamers or less, and those have markedly lower label agreement. TP53, TP63 and TP73 models are not separable from one another; the family's cohesion is 0.81 mainly because half-site and full-site models are mixed together.

## Where it acts

p53 elements are found at promoters and at distal enhancers in roughly comparable numbers, and are not CpG-island-associated. The first genome-wide map put the number of high-confidence sites in the low hundreds to about 1,600 depending on threshold, far fewer than for most families, and curated censuses converge on a core set of a few hundred directly regulated genes that is largely shared across cell types and stresses. Unlike many factors, p53 does not require a partner site to bind: its element is self-sufficient and often sits in closed chromatin that p53 can open. Co-occurrence is therefore weaker and less stereotyped than for NF-kB or NFAT, though p53 sites are enriched near CCAAT boxes and E2F sites at cell-cycle genes, and p63 sites in keratinocytes co-occur with AP-1, KLF and GRHL motifs.

## Biology and disease

p53 activation by DNA damage, oncogene signalling, ribosomal stress or nucleotide depletion drives cell-cycle arrest (CDKN1A), apoptosis (BBC3, PMAIP1, BAX), senescence, DNA repair and metabolic adjustment. TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer, and the common mutations are missense changes in the DNA-binding domain rather than truncations - they produce a full-length protein that cannot read the element and can act dominant-negatively over the tetramer. Germline TP53 mutation causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome. The paralogues are developmental: Trp63-null mice lack limbs and stratified epithelia entirely, and human TP63 mutations cause EEC and related ectodermal dysplasia syndromes; TP73 loss affects ciliogenesis and neuronal survival. TP63 and TP73 are rarely mutated in cancer but their dominant-negative isoforms are frequently overexpressed.

## Reading a hit

A full double-decamer match is one of the more trustworthy motif hits available, because 20 constrained positions are rare by chance. A single decamer is not: it occurs frequently enough to be uninformative on its own, and the half-site models in these collections will match tens of thousands of times per genome. Always check whether the model you scanned with is a full site or a half site. The hit does not identify the paralogue - TP53, TP63 and TP73 read the same element, and in a keratinocyte or a basal breast tumour the more likely occupant is p63. Be aware of provenance: the CIS-BP TP53 motif M03439 is transferred from the mouse protein (91% DNA-binding-domain identity), which is harmless here but is the same mechanism that produces bad motifs elsewhere. ChIP-derived p53 models are relatively clean, since p53 binds its element directly and largely without partners, but the ChIP-only HOCOMOCO models still favour the subset of sites occupied in whichever cell line was assayed. Spacer-containing matches should be treated as plausible but weaker than adjacent decamers.
families.caveats: Trust full sites, distrust half sites. Two adjacent RRRCWWGYYY decamers are specific enough that a match means something; a single decamer is common and several models in these databases are single-decamer or shorter, with correspondingly low label agreement. A hit identifies the p53 family, not the member: TP53, TP63 and TP73 share the element, so in stratified epithelia p63 is often the likelier occupant. Spacer length is unsettled - the original definition allowed 0-13 bp, but transactivation falls off quickly as the spacer grows, so spaced matches deserve less weight than abutting ones. One CIS-BP TP53 entry is inherited from mouse rather than measured on the human protein.
