families.name: DUX / DUXA
families.def: Double homeodomain TAATCTAATCA. DUX4, DUXA, DUXB.
families.short: DUX4 and its relatives DUXA and DUXB carry two homeodomains in tandem within a single polypeptide, an architecture found only in placental mammals and derived from a retrotransposed copy of an ancestral homeobox gene. The two domains bind side by side, head to head, and together read an eleven-base site, TAATCTAATCA, that is far longer and more specific than a single homeodomain site. These genes are normally expressed only for a few cell divisions after fertilisation, where they help switch on the embryonic genome and a set of endogenous retroviral promoters. Misexpression of DUX4 in skeletal muscle causes facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, and DUX4 rearrangements define a subtype of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, so this motif marks one of the better understood pathogenic regulatory programs.
families.long:
## The factors

DUX genes exist only in eutherian mammals. Each encodes two complete homeodomains in tandem, joined by a
short linker, in a protein of a few hundred residues. Human DUX4 is encoded inside the D4Z4 macrosatellite
repeat at 4q35, with a nearly identical array at 10q26 and many DUX4L pseudogenes elsewhere; DUXA and DUXB
are single-copy genes. The mouse counterpart is *Dux*. DUX4 has a C-terminal transactivation domain that
binds p300/CBP, so it is a strong activator; DUXA is transcriptionally inert but binds an overlapping set
of sequences and competes with DUX4, and because DUXA is itself a DUX4 target this constitutes a negative
feedback loop that limits the window of DUX4 activity. The ancestral state is a single homeodomain: the
platypus sDUX protein has one, binds DNA as a homodimer, and is already able to activate
zygotic-genome-activation genes and long terminal repeats. Expression of the human genes is confined to
the cleavage-stage embryo, testis and thymus.

## The motif

The site is TAATCTAATCA, about 11 informative positions. The crystal structure of the DUX4 tandem
homeodomains bound to DNA explained its shape. The two domains bind head to head, and the linker between
them makes anchoring minor-groove contacts plus protein-protein contacts that fix their relative
positions, so the spacing between the two half sites is not variable the way it is for two independent
homeodomain monomers. The surprise from that structure is that the two homeodomains, although tandem
duplicates of each other, do not read the same core sequence: an arginine-to-glutamate substitution unique
to primates repositions a key arginine side chain in one recognition helix. That is why the consensus is
not a clean palindrome but an asymmetric TAATC-TAATCA. The same divergence explains why mouse DUX and
human DUX4 have different motifs, and the difference tracks with which retrotransposon promoters each one
can activate. In the assembled data, DUX4 and DUXA models are similar but not identical: DUX4 models read
TAATTTAATCA or TGATTAGGTTA, DUXA models TGATTAAATTA or TGATTTAATCA, with within-family similarities from
0.84 to 1.0 and overall cohesion of 0.89. One low-information entry, a 5.8-bit CIS-BP DUXA model reading
only TGATTG, is flagged in the data as belonging with Q50 homeodomains instead: a six-base TGATTA fragment
is simply a generic paired-like homeodomain half site and carries no double-homeodomain information.

## Where it acts

DUX4 sites are overwhelmingly repeat-resident. DUX4 occupies MERVL/HERVL long terminal repeats,
ERVL-MaLR elements and other retrotransposon promoters, along with conventional promoters of
cleavage-stage genes including ZSCAN4, TRIM43, MBD3L family members, PRAMEF family members, KHDC1L and
LEUTX. Because the motif sits inside repeat families, the number of genomic matches is large, in the tens
of thousands, and DUX4 ChIP-seq peaks are heavily biased toward repeats. Where DUX4 binds it recruits
p300/CBP and deposits H3K27 acetylation, so the sites behave as bona fide enhancers and promoters rather
than as passive footprints. In adult somatic tissue these sequences are silent and the motif is not
occupied, because the factors are not expressed.

## Biology and disease

Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy is the clearest example of a disease caused by a single
transcription factor being switched on in the wrong tissue. In FSHD1, contraction of the D4Z4 array to
between one and ten units on a permissive 4qA haplotype, which supplies a polyadenylation signal
downstream of the last repeat, allows a stable DUX4 transcript to accumulate in muscle. In FSHD2 the same
end is reached through mutations in chromatin repressors such as SMCHD1. DUX4 expressed in myoblasts
activates germline and cleavage-stage genes, retroelements and immune mediators, and is cytotoxic.
In normal development, mouse Dux and human DUX4 activate cleavage-stage genes and MERVL/HERVL elements at
zygotic genome activation, and DUX4 also has roles in priming the human embryonic genome beyond
transcriptional activation. Rearrangements that place DUX4 under the IGH enhancer, and related DUX4
fusions, define a distinct subtype of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in adolescents and young
adults; the retained portion is the double homeodomain.

## Reading a hit

An 11-base double-homeodomain match is a distinctive shape, but three cautions apply. First, it does not
tell you which DUX protein. DUX4 and DUXA have overlapping specificity and opposite activity, so the same
site can be an activated enhancer or a competitively blocked one. Second, half-site-only matches, TAATCA
or TGATTA, fall straight back into the large generic paired-like homeodomain pool and are not DUX
evidence. Third, one JASPAR entry in this family is the mouse Dux motif, which is genuinely different from
the human one, and the JASPAR DUX4 model and one HOCOMOCO DUX4 model are ChIP-derived from overexpression
systems rather than from in vitro selection on the purified protein. Finally, a match in an ERVL or MaLR
repeat is expected by composition and says little on its own.
families.caveats: The motif shape is good but the label is not resolvable: DUX4, DUXA and DUXB bind overlapping sequences, and DUXA represses what DUX4 activates, so a hit does not predict direction of effect. One JASPAR entry here is mouse Dux, whose motif differs from human DUX4 because of a primate-specific change in one recognition helix; do not transfer it to human sequence. The best DUX4 models are ChIP-derived from forced expression, not from in vitro selection. Because the site lives inside MERVL/HERVL and MaLR repeats, matches are numerous and largely explained by repeat content; outside the cleavage-stage embryo, testis, thymus, FSHD muscle or DUX4-rearranged leukaemia, no DUX protein is present to occupy them.

families.name: MAZ / PATZ1
families.def: GGGAGGG G-rich sites. MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF278-like.
aka: TFClass: more than 3 adjacent zinc finger factors
families.short: MAZ, the Myc-associated zinc finger protein, and PATZ1 are broadly expressed C2H2 zinc-finger proteins that bind short G-rich runs, written GGGAGGG or GGGGAGGGG and read as CCCTCCCC on the opposite strand. MAZ was cloned as the protein binding ME1a1, an element between the c-MYC P1 and P2 promoters. Interest in the motif increased when MAZ turned out to be a second insulator-type element: it colocalizes with CTCF at chromatin boundaries, contacts the cohesin subunit RAD21, and deleting MAZ motifs at the Hox clusters disrupts boundaries much as deleting CTCF motifs does. The single-base difference from the SP1 GC-box, an A where the GC-box has a C, is the only sequence discriminator, and it is thin.
families.long:
## The factors

MAZ is a 477-residue protein with six Cys2-His2 zinc fingers, an N-terminal proline-rich region and several polyalanine tracts. It was cloned by screening with a concatemerized copy of ME1a1, a 16-bp element lying between the c-MYC P1 and P2 transcription start sites that is required for P2 activity, and was implicated in both transcriptional initiation and termination at c-MYC (Bossone et al. 1992). Older aliases include Pur-1 and ZF87. PATZ1 is grouped here because its motif is not separable from MAZ's. PATZ1 (also MAZR, ZNF278, ZSG) is a POK-family protein: a BTB/POZ domain, an AT-hook and a C-terminal zinc-finger array. The BTB domain forms a homodimer whose crystal structure has been determined, and PATZ1 is ubiquitously expressed with a documented role in T-lymphocyte development, where it targets the CD8 gene, and in interactions with p53 (Piepoli et al. 2020). Both proteins are broadly expressed, unlike most of the restricted factors elsewhere in this atlas.

## The motif

The site is short: GGGAGGG, often extended to GGGGAGGGG, and CCCTCCCC on the complementary strand. The data here agree - the medoid (CIS-BP M08290_2.00) is CCCCTCCCC and JASPAR MAZ (MA1522.2) is CCCCTCCC. Why so short for a six-finger protein? Mutational analysis showed that only two consecutive zinc fingers are essential for MAZ to engage its element, just as only two of Sp1's three are essential for the GC-box (Song et al. 2001); the additional fingers are not all contributing base contacts, so the footprint is 7-9 bp rather than 18. The same study states the two respective sites explicitly: GGGCGG for Sp1, GGGAGGG for MAZ. That single-base difference - A where the GC-box has C - is the practical discriminator between this family and KLF/SP, and it is a thin one. Against the other G-rich families it is thinner still. The HOCOMOCO VEZF1 model VEZF1.H14CORE.0.P.C (GGGGGAGGGGG) has its nearest neighbor across all four databases inside this family, so VEZF1's motif is effectively MAZ's. ZNF281 and ZNF148 models (GGGGGAGGGG) differ only by context, and the ChIP-derived WT1 models fall in the same cluster. Within the family, the labels are not clean either: JASPAR's PATZ1 profile (MA1961.2) is GGGGGCGGGGG, which is a GC-box and will behave like an SP1 matrix, not like a MAZ matrix. None of the four HOCOMOCO models for MAZ or PATZ1 carries in vitro evidence; all are ChIP-only at grade B or C, and for two of them the best-matching matrix elsewhere in the databases scores higher than the best match inside the family.

## Where it acts

MAZ and PATZ1 sites are promoter-proximal and concentrated in GC-rich, CpG-island promoters, starting with c-MYC itself. The more interesting location is chromatin boundaries. A genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen for genes required for CTCF boundary activity at the HoxA cluster identified MAZ; MAZ colocalizes with CTCF at chromatin borders, interacts with the cohesin subunit RAD21, and deletion of MAZ motifs disrupts gene expression and intra-domain contacts in a way that resembles deletion of CTCF motifs (Ortabozkoyun et al. 2022). A follow-up study extended this to a small array of zinc-finger proteins that specify distinct Hox boundaries: PATZ1 was required for the thoracolumbar boundary in differentiating motor neurons and in the mouse skeleton, and ZNF263 for cervicothoracic boundaries, each acting with cohesin, with or without CTCF (Ortabozkoyun et al. 2024). So a G-rich site next to a CTCF site is not necessarily noise.

## Biology and disease

MAZ's documented functions center on c-MYC promoter regulation and on insulation: MAZ knockout disrupts local contacts within topologically associating domains and the expression of genes inside them (Ortabozkoyun et al. 2022). PATZ1 has a wider documented range, reviewed for its physiological functions and disease involvement (Fedele et al. 2017): repression of CD8 in lymphocyte development, interaction with p53, and suppression of differentiation with effects on metabolism in human embryonic stem cells (Huang et al. 2024). The clearest disease link in the family is through PATZ1 gene fusions. EWSR1::PATZ1 defines a rare round-cell sarcoma that was newly categorized in the 2020 World Health Organization classification of soft tissue and bone tumors (Yagi et al. 2024), and MN1::PATZ1 fusions occur in a rare class of CNS neuroepithelial tumors. Note that in a fusion the PATZ1 contribution is usually the zinc-finger array, so the motif is still relevant even when the protein is chimeric.

## Reading a hit

Three cautions. First, the site is short and G-rich, so GGGAGGG occurs constantly by chance, and especially inside CpG islands and G-rich repeats; an isolated match is weak evidence of anything. Second, the family cannot be separated from its neighbors by sequence. A hit here is also a plausible ZNF281, ZNF148, VEZF1 or ChIP-derived WT1 site, and is one base away from an SP1/KLF GC-box. If the question is which protein binds, sequence will not answer it. Third, check which matrix matched: all HOCOMOCO models in this family rest on ChIP-seq alone, and the JASPAR PATZ1 matrix is a GC-box that will pull in SP-family sites. What does make a hit worth following up is context. A G-rich motif immediately adjacent to a CTCF site at a developmental cluster is the configuration in which MAZ and PATZ1 have demonstrable boundary function, and there the motif deletion experiments give the label real support.
families.caveats: A seven-base G-rich site carries little information and occurs frequently by chance, so treat an isolated hit as weak. The family is also not separable from ZNF281/ZNF148, VEZF1 or the ChIP-derived WT1 models - the HOCOMOCO VEZF1 matrix's nearest neighbor across all four databases lies inside this family - and it differs from the SP1 GC-box by a single base. All four HOCOMOCO models here are ChIP-only at grade B or C, and JASPAR's PATZ1 profile is in fact a GC-box. Context helps more than score: a G-rich motif beside a CTCF site at a Hox-type boundary is where MAZ and PATZ1 have demonstrated function.

families.name: HIC1 / HIC2
families.def: TGCC(A/G) HiRE sites. HIC1, HIC2.
families.short: HIC1 (hypermethylated in cancer 1) and HIC2 are BTB/POZ zinc-finger repressors with five Kruppel-like C2H2 fingers. Their optimal site, defined by site selection, is (C/G)NG(C/G)GGGCA(C/A)CC, with a GGCA core read by fingers 3 and 4; databases usually render the same element on the opposite strand as TGCC(A/G), which is why the family is often listed with a short TGCC consensus. The BTB domain blocks binding to a single site but supports cooperative binding to several, so genuine targets carry multiple sites. HIC1 sits at 17p13.3, is induced by p53, is frequently silenced by promoter hypermethylation in tumors, and represses SIRT1; heterozygous mouse mutants develop tumors.
families.long:
## The factors

Two paralogues: HIC1 and HIC2 (also HRG22). Each has an N-terminal BTB/POZ domain, a central region containing a conserved GLDLSKK motif that binds CtBP, and five Kruppel-like C2H2 zinc fingers at the C terminus. HIC1 was cloned from 17p13.3, a region frequently deleted or hypermethylated in human tumors and deleted in Miller-Dieker syndrome, and was identified as a p53-inducible gene. The BTB domain has an unusual and important effect on DNA binding: it inhibits binding of the full-length protein to an isolated site while mediating cooperative binding to probes carrying several concatemerized sites, a property shared with other BTB/POZ proteins. Repression works through CtBP and through recruitment of HDAC-containing complexes, and HIC1 also localizes to distinct nuclear bodies, into which it can sequester other proteins. HIC1 is widely expressed in adult tissues and silenced epigenetically in tumors; HIC2 is expressed in the developing cardiovascular system and is much less studied. There is no evidence that the two heterodimerize preferentially over homodimerizing.

## The motif

Selection and amplification of binding sites with recombinant HIC1 gave the optimal sequence 5'-(C/G)NG(C/G)GGGCA(C/A)CC-3'. In silico and functional follow-up narrowed the essential element to a GGCA core contacted by zinc fingers 3 and 4, so of the five fingers only two carry most of the base-specific contacts - which explains why the informative region is short even though the domain could cover more sequence. The database matrices all describe this same element on the complementary strand, which is why they look different at first glance: JASPAR Hic1 (MA0739.2) reads ATGCCAAC, JASPAR HIC2 (MA0738.2) and CIS-BP M02902 read ATGCCC, the HOCOMOCO HIC1 grade-A model reads ATGCCA, and the Vierstra archetype AC0477:HIC reads ATGCCCAC. Reverse-complementing ATGCCCAC gives GTGGGCAT, which contains the GGGCA of the selected consensus. This is a strand convention, not a conflict, but it does mean the widely quoted "TGCC(A/G)" form of the consensus is a four- or five-base fragment of a longer selected site and is far too short to scan with. Information content of the database models is low, 7-11 bits. HIC1 and HIC2 models are 0.98 similar and cannot be separated by sequence. One archetype in the family, AC0435:HIC reading GGCAACC, matches the main HIC cluster poorly (0.74) and should be treated as a divergent model rather than an independent confirmation.

## Where it acts

HIC1 sites occur in promoters of genes it represses, and because the full-length protein needs cooperativity, functional HIC1 elements usually come in clusters - a single TGCC match in a promoter is not a HIC1 element in any meaningful sense. Validated targets include SIRT1, ATOH1, EPHA2 and Wnt-responsive genes; HIC1 also attenuates Wnt signaling by a non-DNA route, recruiting TCF4 and beta-catenin into nuclear bodies away from their target promoters. The element is GC-rich and CpG-containing, so matches concentrate in CpG-island promoters, the same territory as SP/KLF and other GC-box readers. HIC2 sites, where studied, are in cardiovascular differentiation genes.

## Biology and disease

Hic1-null mice die perinatally with developmental defects - acrania, exencephaly and limb abnormalities - that overlap the structures affected in Miller-Dieker syndrome, consistent with HIC1 contributing to that contiguous gene deletion phenotype. Heterozygous Hic1 mice are viable but develop a sex-dependent spectrum of malignant tumors, with age-dependent hypermethylation and silencing of the remaining wild-type allele, which is a textbook demonstration of an epigenetically inactivated tumor suppressor. Mechanistically, HIC1 binds and represses the SIRT1 promoter; because SIRT1 deacetylates p53, loss of HIC1 raises SIRT1 and blunts p53-dependent responses to DNA damage, forming a regulatory circuit with p53 that also explains why HIC1 is p53-inducible. HIC1 promoter hypermethylation is among the more common epigenetic lesions across human carcinomas, medulloblastoma and leukemia. HIC2 has been shown to control isoform switching during cardiovascular maturation and lies in the distal 22q11 region, but its human disease role is not established.

## Reading a hit

The honest summary is that a short TGCC-type match is close to worthless on its own. The informative element is longer, the database matrices capture only 7-11 bits of it, and the sequence is GC-rich and CpG-island-associated, so it overlaps the recognition space of SP1-SP4, the KLFs and other C2H2 GC-box factors. Two things make a HIC call more credible: multiple sites in the same promoter, which is what the BTB-dependent cooperativity requires, and a target gene or cell context in which HIC1 is expressed rather than methylated. Within the family, HIC1 and HIC2 are indistinguishable at 0.98 similarity, and the Vierstra archetypes are named AC0435:HIC and AC0477:HIC without a paralogue assignment, so a hit identifies the pair. On provenance, the better entries are in vitro: JASPAR MA0739.2 and MA0738.2 are HT-SELEX matrices and the HOCOMOCO HIC1 model is grade A with PSM evidence. Two weaker entries deserve flags - JASPAR MA0739.2 is derived from mouse Hic1 rather than the human protein, a cross-species transfer that is unproblematic here given how conserved the fingers are but should be recorded; and the HOCOMOCO HIC2 model carries ChIP-only evidence (code P, grade B) and matches the rest of the family poorly (0.75), so it is the entry most likely to reflect indirect binding.
families.caveats: The short TGCC(A/G) form quoted for this family is a fragment of a longer selected consensus, (C/G)NG(C/G)GGGCA(C/A)CC, rendered on the other strand; the database matrices hold only 7-11 bits, are GC-rich and CpG-island-associated, and therefore overlap SP/KLF and other GC-box motifs. Single matches are not interpretable: the BTB domain blocks binding to isolated sites and supports cooperative binding to clustered ones, so look for several sites in one promoter. HIC1 and HIC2 are indistinguishable (0.98 similarity) and the Vierstra archetypes do not assign a paralogue. Note JASPAR MA0739.2 is a mouse Hic1 matrix, and the HOCOMOCO HIC2 model is ChIP-only and a poor fit to the rest of the family.

families.name: IKZF (Ikaros)
families.def: GGGAA core Ikaros sites. IKZF1-5.
families.short: The Ikaros family (IKZF1 Ikaros, IKZF2 Helios, IKZF3 Aiolos, IKZF4 Eos, IKZF5 Pegasus) are lymphoid zinc-finger proteins with an N-terminal C2H2 array that binds DNA and a C-terminal pair of fingers that mediates homo- and heterodimerization. They recognize a GGGAA core, present in lymphocyte-specific regulatory elements and also in pericentromeric satellite repeats, to which Ikaros localizes by direct DNA binding. IKZF1 is required for the development of all lymphoid lineages, is deleted in BCR-ABL1 and Ph-like B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia where it predicts poor outcome, and, with IKZF3, is the protein whose thalidomide-analog-induced degradation explains how lenalidomide works in myeloma. The GGGAA core is shared with ETS and NF-kB sites, which makes these motifs hard to trust.
families.long:
## The factors

Five human Ikaros-family proteins are encoded by IKZF1 to IKZF5: Ikaros, Helios, Aiolos, Eos and
Pegasus. Each has an N-terminal array of C2H2 zinc fingers that binds DNA and a separate C-terminal
pair of fingers that is not used for DNA contact but mediates homodimerization and heterodimerization
among family members. Alternative splicing of IKZF1 produces isoforms (Ik-1 through Ik-5 in the
original description) carrying different combinations of the N-terminal fingers; these differ in
sequence specificity and affinity, with the full-length forms binding the whole set of recognition
sequences found in lymphocyte-specific regulatory elements and the short forms binding only a subset.
The short forms are also poorly nuclear and are weak activators, which is the basis of their
dominant-negative behavior.

Expression is lymphoid and largely restricted: IKZF1 and IKZF3 across B and T lineages, IKZF2 in
regulatory T cells and some other compartments, IKZF4 in regulatory T cells, IKZF5 more broadly.
Only IKZF1, IKZF2 and IKZF3 have motif models in the databases behind this family. The proteins work
in complexes rather than alone, associating with NuRD (Mi-2/CHD4) and with histone deacetylases, and
they localize to pericentromeric heterochromatin.

## The motif

The agreed core is GGGAA, written TTCCC on the other strand. Extended forms appear in the databases
as TGGGAATAC and similar; the representative archetype for this family has that consensus. None of
these carries much information beyond the five-base core, and that is the central problem for this
family, because GGGAA is not distinctive. It is contained within the ETS core GGA(A/T) and within the
NF-kB half-site GGGRNNYYCC, so an Ikaros matrix, an ETS matrix and an NF-kB matrix can all score the
same DNA.

The collection makes this concrete. The JASPAR IKZF3 matrix has the consensus CAGGAAGTG, whose
nearest neighbors across all four databases are ETS models rather than Ikaros models; the JASPAR
IKZF2 matrix, AGGAAG, likewise resembles ETS more than it resembles the rest of its own family; and
two Vierstra archetypes in this family are explicitly named for mixed groups, IKZF with ZNF and IKZF
with NFKB. Family cohesion is correspondingly low. Ikaros also binds within centromeric DNA repeats,
and targeting to pericentromeric foci depends on the DNA-binding finger domain together with the
dimerization domain, so part of the genuine binding repertoire is repetitive sequence that motif
scanners will report en masse.

## Where it acts

Ikaros-family sites are found at promoters and enhancers of lymphoid genes, including the
immunoglobulin and T-cell-receptor loci, and co-occur with EBF1, PU.1/SPI1, RUNX1 and E2A at B- and
T-lineage regulatory elements. Because PU.1 is itself an ETS factor that prefers a purine-rich GGAA
core, Ikaros and PU.1 sites are often indistinguishable in sequence at the same elements, and
composite occupancy is common. The other distinctive location is pericentromeric heterochromatin,
where Ikaros accumulates in foci; this was shown to require direct DNA binding rather than
recruitment through Mi-2, and is consistent with Ikaros sites inside satellite repeats. Genome-wide,
a five-base core occurs on the order of a million times, so scanning alone cannot define an Ikaros
cistrome.

## Biology and disease

Ikzf1-null mice lack B cells and have profound defects across lymphoid lineages, establishing IKZF1
as required for the development of all lymphoid lineages; mice expressing dominant-negative isoforms
develop T-cell leukemia. In humans, focal deletions and point mutations of IKZF1 are a defining
feature of BCR-ABL1-positive B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and of Ph-like ALL, and IKZF1
deletion is associated with a substantially worse outcome, which is why it is now assayed in risk
stratification. Germline dominant-negative IKZF1 variants cause a combined T-, B- and myeloid-cell
immunodeficiency, and other IKZF1 variants cause common variable immunodeficiency.

The best-known pharmacology is degradation, not transcription. Thalidomide, lenalidomide and
pomalidomide act as molecular glues that recruit a zinc finger of IKZF1 and IKZF3 to cereblon, the
substrate receptor of the CRL4-CRBN ubiquitin ligase, causing their selective degradation; this
accounts for the activity of these drugs in multiple myeloma. A systematic screen of the human C2H2
zinc-finger proteome identified eleven such degrons and predicted that more than 150 zinc fingers can
engage the drug-CRBN interface, which turned the Ikaros story into a general strategy for targeting
zinc-finger transcription factors.

## Reading a hit

Treat an Ikaros hit as a weak, ambiguous call. Three problems stack. First, the informative core is
five bases, so matches are everywhere. Second, that core is shared with ETS and NF-kB, and the
databases themselves are contaminated: at least one JASPAR Ikaros matrix in this family is closer to
ETS models than to Ikaros models, and two archetypes are named for IKZF together with ZNF or NFKB.
If you get an Ikaros hit at a lymphoid enhancer, PU.1 or another ETS factor is at least as likely to
be the direct binder. Third, no sequence argument distinguishes IKZF1 from IKZF2 or IKZF3, and IKZF4
and IKZF5 have no models here. Ikaros models are ChIP- and selection-derived in these collections
rather than backed by a structure of the protein on DNA, and Ikaros works in NuRD and HDAC complexes,
so indirect binding is a live possibility for any individual peak. A credible Ikaros call needs
lineage-appropriate expression, a peak from a well-controlled experiment, and ideally loss of the
peak on IKZF1 degradation rather than a motif match.
families.caveats: The informative core is only GGGAA, which is shared with ETS (GGAA) and NF-kB (GGGAA) sites, so an Ikaros match is rarely attributable to an Ikaros protein. The databases show the contamination directly: the JASPAR IKZF3 matrix here has ETS models as its nearest neighbors across all four sources, the IKZF2 matrix also resembles ETS more than its own family, and two Vierstra archetypes are named IKZF/ZNF and IKZF/NFKB. Family cohesion is low as a result. No model distinguishes IKZF1 from IKZF2 or IKZF3, and IKZF4 and IKZF5 have none. Ikaros additionally binds satellite repeats and acts within NuRD and HDAC complexes, so peaks need not reflect its own specificity.

families.name: BCL11A / BCL11B
families.def: TGACCA-containing sites. BCL11A, BCL11B.
families.short: BCL11A and BCL11B (originally CTIP1 and CTIP2) are paralogous C2H2 zinc-finger repressors with six fingers, of which a C-terminal cluster binds DNA while the N-terminal region recruits NuRD. They are best known not as motif proteins but as switches: BCL11A silences the fetal gamma-globin genes and is the target of approved gene-editing therapies for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia, while BCL11B enforces T-lineage commitment, so that its loss converts T cells into natural-killer-like cells. Reported DNA preferences conflict. In vitro selection on BCL11A gave a GC-box-like GGCCGG core, whereas the site it occupies at the gamma-globin promoter is written TGACCA. The family's matrices are heterogeneous and several look like other factors' motifs.
families.long:
## The factors

BCL11A and BCL11B were isolated as COUP-TF-interacting proteins 1 and 2 (CTIP1 and CTIP2) and are
also known as EVI9 (BCL11A) and RIT1 (Bcl11b in mouse). Both are large C2H2 zinc-finger proteins with
six fingers: an N-terminal region that includes the COUP-TF interaction domains and a short
NuRD-interacting motif, and a C-terminal cluster of fingers that carries the DNA-binding activity.
Neither is a simple monomeric binder. BCL11A forms a tetramer through a single zinc finger (ZnF0),
and tetramer formation is required both for steady-state protein accumulation and for gamma-globin
repression, because an engineered monomer fails to engage its corepressor complex. BCL11A's original
in vitro selection likewise recovered binding by an oligomeric complex rather than a monomer.

Expression is tissue-restricted and largely complementary. BCL11A is expressed in B cells, adult
erythroid cells and brain; BCL11B is T-cell-specific among hematopoietic cells and is also expressed
in skin, tooth and central nervous system. Both repress transcription, and the repression seen in
reporter assays was not reversed by the class I/II HDAC inhibitor trichostatin A.

## The motif

The literature gives two answers and they do not agree. A selection procedure for high-affinity
CTIP1 (BCL11A) sites recovered the core GGCCGG, described at the time as closely related to the
canonical GC box. Separately, the functionally best-characterized BCL11A element is in the HBG1 and
HBG2 (gamma-globin) promoters about 115 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site, where
BCL11A binds directly and where naturally occurring hereditary-persistence-of-fetal-hemoglobin point
mutations disrupt binding and raise gamma-globin expression; the JASPAR matrix built from that class
of data has the consensus CTGACCA. The family data consensus here, TGACC, follows the second form,
and we give TGACCA as the headline consensus because it is the site with direct functional
validation. But the GGCCGG form is not an error: two of the eight matrices assigned to this family
(a CIS-BP BCL11B model with consensus TCCGGCC and a Vierstra archetype with THCGGCC) are
GGCCGG-related, and they are the ones that agree with the in vitro selection.

Cohesion in this family is the lowest in the zinc-finger set at 0.50, and the individual matrices are
worth listing because they illustrate what goes wrong. Besides the TGACC and GGCCGG groups, a CIS-BP
BCL11A model and a Vierstra archetype share the consensus TTTCACTTCCTC, and the archetype is named
BCL11A/IRF, reflecting the IRF/ISRE-like TTTC core. One Vierstra BCL11B archetype has a long,
high-information consensus (GTGAACGCNDNHGCTACAC) with no close neighbor anywhere in the four
databases. And the JASPAR Bcl11B matrix has the consensus AAACCACAA, whose reverse complement,
TTGTGGTTT, contains the RUNX core TGTGGT; its nearest neighbors across all four databases are RUNX
models rather than BCL11 models, and it is flagged in these data as belonging with RUNX. Since RUNX1
and RUNX3 are dominant occupants of T-cell regulatory elements, where BCL11B ChIP is performed, the
simplest reading is indirect binding or co-occupancy at RUNX sites rather than a genuine BCL11B
specificity; we are not aware of literature that settles this either way.

## Where it acts

BCL11A acts through a small number of intensively studied elements rather than a diffuse cistrome:
sites in the beta-globin cluster, its own erythroid-specific +58 intronic enhancer (whose common
variants set fetal-hemoglobin level), and B-lymphoid and neural regulatory regions. BCL11B occupies
T-lineage enhancers and promoters, frequently alongside RUNX, TCF7, GATA3 and ETS factors. Both
proteins sit in NuRD-containing complexes, so much of their genomic footprint is complex-driven.

## Biology and disease

BCL11A is the developmental-stage-specific repressor of fetal hemoglobin: it is expressed in adult
but not fetal erythroid cells, knockdown reactivates HbF, and it occupies discrete sites in the
beta-globin cluster. Because its erythroid enhancer is dispensable outside erythroid cells,
disrupting that enhancer raises HbF without compromising B-cell development, which is the basis of
the CRISPR-Cas9 therapy now approved for sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent
beta-thalassemia. Heterozygous BCL11A microdeletions and variants (2p15-p16.1) cause an
intellectual-disability and autism-spectrum phenotype (Dias-Logan syndrome) with persistent fetal
hemoglobin but otherwise near-normal blood counts.

BCL11B is the T-lineage commitment factor. It is first expressed immediately before commitment,
suppresses natural-killer-cell and progenitor programs, and is required for alpha-beta T-cell
differentiation and survival; deleting it converts T cells at all developmental stages into
natural-killer-like cells that retain cytotoxic activity. In disease, BCL11B is targeted by
enhancer-hijacking translocations in T-cell and T/myeloid acute leukemias, and germline heterozygous
variants cause immune dysregulation with severe atopic disease.

## Reading a hit

Do not trust a BCL11 motif hit. The family has no single validated consensus: the in vitro selection
and the functionally validated gamma-globin element point at different sequences, and both are short
(five to seven informative bases). Several matrices in the family are almost certainly other factors'
motifs recovered from ChIP data, most clearly the JASPAR Bcl11B matrix that scores as a RUNX site.
Nothing distinguishes BCL11A from BCL11B in sequence. And because BCL11A works as a tetramer bound to
a corepressor complex and BCL11B works within NuRD, occupancy in vivo depends on partners as much as
on sequence, so peaks are a poor guide to intrinsic specificity and motif hits are a poor guide to
peaks. Practical advice: for BCL11A, work from the known validated elements (the gamma-globin -115
region and the +58 enhancer) rather than from a genome-wide scan; for BCL11B, check whether your hit
is better explained as a RUNX site before attributing it here.
families.caveats: Trust this family least. There is no agreed consensus: in vitro selection on BCL11A gave a GC-box-like GGCCGG core, while the functionally validated site at the gamma-globin promoter is written TGACCA, and both appear among the family's matrices. Cohesion is 0.50. At least three matrices look like other factors: two Vierstra/CIS-BP models with an IRF-like TTTCACTTCC consensus (one archetype is named BCL11A/IRF), and the JASPAR Bcl11B matrix whose AAACCACAA consensus is the RUNX core and whose nearest neighbors in all four databases are RUNX models, most plausibly indirect binding at RUNX sites in T cells. BCL11A and BCL11B are not separable by sequence, and both act within corepressor complexes.

families.name: ZNF460 / ZNF317-like
families.def: Long composite KZFP motifs characterised by ChIP-exo; covers ZNF460 and the closely related ZNF317.
families.short: ZNF460 and ZNF317 are poorly characterized human C2H2 zinc-finger proteins grouped here because their database motifs cluster together, not because a published experiment showed they read the same sequence. The family is the least coherent in this part of the atlas: its eight matrices split into two unrelated groups, one a long AGTCTGCTGT-type word from ZNF317 in vitro data and the other a GC-rich GCCTCAGCCTCCC-type word from ZNF460 that closely resembles Alu consensus sequence. No single consensus is given here because the data do not support one. Almost everything known about either protein comes from high-throughput surveys of zinc-finger binding specificity rather than from focused study.
families.long:
## The factors

ZNF460 and ZNF317 are human C2H2 zinc-finger proteins with tandem finger arrays. Neither has been the subject of a dedicated structural or biochemical study, and the literature on them is thin enough that this entry is mostly a description of data quality rather than of biology. They are grouped as one family because their motifs are nearest neighbours across the four databases, not because anyone has demonstrated shared specificity; the pairing should be read as a statement about matrix similarity. Both fall within the broad class of zinc-finger proteins surveyed in genome-wide characterizations of human KRAB and non-KRAB zinc fingers, where hundreds of members were assayed at once by ChIP-exo and related methods. They are broadly but not highly expressed. There is no reported dimerization, no described cofactor, and no knockout phenotype in a mammalian model for either gene.

## The motif

This family has the lowest cohesion in the batch (0.49 on the atlas's internal scale), and the reason is visible in the matrices. They fall into two groups that have nothing in common. The first is long and AT/AC-mixed: the CIS-BP ZNF317 matrix reads GAGAAGTCAGCTGTCADTCTTAT, the Vierstra archetype AC0085 reads AGTCTGCTGT, one ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO ZNF317 matrix reads GAHTGACAGCTGACTTCTCA, and JASPAR MA1593.2 reduces this to ACAGCAGA. The second group is GC-rich: JASPAR MA1596.1 for ZNF460 reads GCCTCAGCCTCCCGAG, the CIS-BP ZNF460 matrix reads CGCCGCCTCCCC, and the low-grade HOCOMOCO ZNF460 matrix reads GGGGGGCG. The GCCTCAGCCTCCC word is worth naming for what it is: that sequence is a near-exact match to a well-known segment of the Alu consensus, so a matrix built on it will report Alu copies rather than a specific protein-DNA preference. The second ChIP-derived ZNF317 matrix (ATGGAAGCCAGAAGACAATGGAA) has no close neighbour anywhere in the collection. For this reason no `consensus` field is given for this family: quoting either group as the consensus would misrepresent the data, and averaging them would be meaningless.

## Where it acts

There is little to say that rests on evidence. If the GC-rich ZNF460 matrices are reporting Alu sequence, then matches will be distributed like Alus: hundreds of thousands of copies, concentrated in gene-rich, GC-rich regions and in introns, and heavily represented near promoters simply because Alus are. The AGTCTGCTGT-type ZNF317 word is longer and less repeat-like, and would be expected to occur at more modest frequency, but no published mapping study describes where ZNF317 actually binds in a genome or which genes it regulates. Neither protein has a named composite element or an established partner. Surveys of human zinc-finger proteins provide the only genome-scale occupancy context, and they treat these two as members of a large set rather than as individually characterized factors.

## Biology and disease

Direct functional work is limited to recent cancer and vascular papers, all of which study the protein rather than the motif. ZNF460 has been reported to inhibit HMGCL and activate PI3K signalling in colon cancer, to act downstream of KMT2D in a COL9A1-dependent extracellular-matrix stiffening mechanism that maintains a colorectal cancer stem-cell pool, and to promote GSDME-driven pyroptosis through transcriptional activation of PKM2 in aortic dissection. These studies identify target genes but do not establish a binding consensus, so they cannot be used to validate the matrices above. ZNF317 has no comparable literature. Neither gene is a recognized Mendelian disease gene or a recurrent cancer driver, and neither appears among the primate-specific KRAB zinc fingers whose control of endogenous retroviruses has been worked out in detail. Where the literature is this thin, the right summary is that these are annotated but essentially uncharacterized factors.

## Reading a hit

Be cautious to the point of scepticism. First, decide which of the two motif groups your hit belongs to, because they are not the same element and the family label hides that. If the match is to the GC-rich GCCTCAGCCTCCC-type word, check whether it falls in an Alu; if it does, the hit is almost certainly reporting the repeat and not ZNF460 occupancy. If the match is to the longer AGTCTGCTGT-type word, you have a more specific sequence but almost no functional literature to interpret it against. Second, look at the evidence codes. The ZNF460 HOCOMOCO matrix is grade C with in vitro (S) evidence only and is a low-information G-run; the ZNF317 HOCOMOCO matrices are ChIP-only (P, grade B) and disagree with each other. Third, do not report a hit as identifying ZNF460 versus ZNF317: the grouping itself is data-driven, and nothing in the literature says these two proteins share a site. A match in this family is best treated as a flag to inspect the underlying sequence manually rather than as an assignment to a factor.
families.caveats: Treat this family as unreliable. Its matrices split into two unrelated groups, a long AGTCTGCTGT-type ZNF317 word and a GC-rich ZNF460 word whose sequence (GCCTCAGCCTCCC) closely matches Alu consensus, so matches to the latter most likely report a repeat rather than protein occupancy. Internal cohesion is 0.49, the lowest in this batch, and the two ChIP-derived ZNF317 matrices disagree with each other; the ZNF460 HOCOMOCO matrix is grade C with low information content. The pairing of ZNF460 with ZNF317 is a clustering result, not a published finding of shared specificity. No consensus is quoted because the data do not support one, and there is no focused literature on either protein's DNA binding.

families.name: HINFP (MIZF)
families.def: Histone H4 promoter site GTCCGCGGTA. HINFP.
families.short: HINFP, also called HiNF-P and originally cloned as MIZF, is a seven-finger C2H2 zinc-finger protein that reads a short CGGAC core, usually written CGGACGTT. Its best-characterized job is at the replication-dependent histone H4 genes, where it binds a conserved cell-cycle element in the proximal promoter and, using the cyclin E/CDK2 substrate NPAT/p220 as coactivator, switches on H4 transcription at the G1-to-S transition. It is the endpoint of a linear pathway from growth-factor-induced cyclin E/CDK2 activity to histone synthesis. The same protein was independently identified as a partner of the methyl-CpG-binding protein MBD2 and acts as a repressor in that context, so the motif can mean activation or repression depending on the promoter.
families.long:
## The factors

HINFP is a single gene with no paralogue sharing its specificity. The protein has seven C2H2 zinc fingers; deletion analysis showed that five of the seven are required for DNA binding, so the array is used as one continuous reading head rather than as separable modules. It was discovered twice. As MIZF it was pulled out as a binding partner of MBD2, a methyl-CpG-binding protein, and characterized as a sequence-specific repressor that recruits MBD2-associated silencing activity. As HiNF-P it was purified as the factor required for E2F-independent activation of the replication-dependent histone H4 multigene family. The activating function depends on a coactivator rather than on a dimerization partner: HINFP binds NPAT/p220, a substrate of cyclin E/CDK2, and NPAT phosphorylation at the G1 restriction point converts the bound HINFP into an activator. HINFP is broadly expressed and conserved; the Drosophila homolog exists and is functional.

## The motif

The site is short. Cyclic amplification and selection of targets gave the consensus CGGACGTT, with a conserved CGGAC core that is the invariant part; the trailing GTT positions are preferred but not essential. Written on the other strand this is AACGTCCG, which is the orientation most database matrices use, and the family's dataConsensus GCGGACG is simply the core with an extra 5' guanine. Only about six to eight positions carry information, and the core sits within a CpG dinucleotide context, which matters because methylation of that CpG is relevant to the MBD2 connection. One feature of the data is worth flagging: the strongest archetype in this family, the Vierstra AC0649 matrix, reads GCGGACGTTCAACGTCCGC, which is two CGGAC cores in inverted orientation separated by five base pairs. Whether that reflects a genuine preference for a palindromic arrangement or simply the frequent occurrence of paired sites in the sequences used to build the archetype is not settled in the literature; treat the single core as the unit and the palindrome as a common arrangement. HINFP has no close paralogue, so there is no within-family ambiguity, but the CGGAC core is short enough to be a substring of longer GC-rich motifs from other families.

## Where it acts

HINFP sites are proximal promoter elements. The canonical location is Site II of the human histone H4 genes, a conserved element a short distance upstream of the start site that is present across the replication-dependent H4 multigene family; chromatin immunoprecipitation and genomic footprinting confirmed occupancy in vivo. In the nucleus this activity is spatially concentrated: the H4 gene clusters assemble into histone locus bodies, subnuclear structures where HINFP, NPAT and the histone genes co-localize during S phase. Beyond histone genes, database searches identified the CGGACGTT word in many human promoters, and HINFP was shown to bind and repress the RB1 promoter through it. The motif is common enough that most genomic matches are not functional elements, and published HINFP ChIP-derived matrices in HOCOMOCO differ noticeably from the in vitro word, which is a sign that some of those peak sets contain indirect or low-specificity binding.

## Biology and disease

The HINFP-NPAT axis is the link between the cyclin E/CDK2 restriction point and the burst of histone gene transcription that packages newly replicated DNA. Reducing HINFP slows entry into S phase; in mouse, Hinfp is required for early embryonic cell cycles, maternal Hinfp protein sustains pre-implantation development, and the histone H4 deficiency caused by Hinfp loss is made worse by removing p53, indicating that cells sense the shortfall as a checkpoint problem. In Drosophila, loss of Hinfp derepresses most transposable elements and causes DNA damage in somatic tissues; the key mediator is Histone1, the linker histone, whose expression collapses without Hinfp, so higher-order chromatin assembly fails. The same work found that Hinfp loss enhances Ras-driven tissue growth and ageing phenotypes. On the repression side, MIZF/HINFP-mediated silencing of RB1 was described during myogenic differentiation. There is no established Mendelian HINFP disease, and cancer associations are indirect, mostly through the histone gene/cell-cycle axis.

## Reading a hit

A match to CGGACGTT is only moderate evidence. Ask first whether the hit is in a proximal promoter, and second whether it is at a replication-dependent histone gene, where the prior probability of function is far higher than anywhere else. Isolated CGGAC cores in enhancers or gene bodies are usually chance matches. Because the protein has no paralogue, a real site means HINFP, but the converse trap is that the core is a substring of longer GC-rich words, so check whether a better-scoring motif from another family covers the same position. Direction of effect cannot be read from the sequence: the same element activates histone H4 genes with NPAT and represses RB1 with MBD2. The in vitro-supported HOCOMOCO matrix is the safer choice; the ChIP-derived ones in this family are internally inconsistent.
families.caveats: The core is short, so chance matches are frequent and a hit outside a proximal promoter usually means little. The strongest prior is a replication-dependent histone H4 promoter. HINFP has no paralogue, so a genuine site implicates one protein, but the CGGAC core sits inside many longer GC-rich motifs and can be claimed by other families. Evidence quality within the family is uneven: the in vitro matrix and the SELEX-derived consensus agree, while two ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO matrices give noticeably different words, one of them with low information content, which suggests indirect or poorly resolved binding in those peak sets. Finally, the motif does not predict direction, since HINFP both activates and represses.

families.name: GCM (glial cells missing)
families.def: GCM box ATGCGGGT. GCM1, GCM2.
families.short: GCM1 and GCM2 (glial cells missing 1 and 2) are the only human members of a small metazoan family that binds DNA through the GCM domain, a conserved 150-residue region with a fold unlike any other transcription factor class: two subdomains held together by structural zinc ions, reading the major groove with a five-stranded beta-sheet rather than an alpha-helix. They recognize an 8-bp GCM box, AT(G/A)CGGGT, as monomers, with no half-sites or spacing rules. Despite the name, the mammalian proteins are not gliogenic: GCM1 is required for placental labyrinth branching and trophoblast fusion, and GCM2 for parathyroid gland development, where loss-of-function and activating mutations cause hypoparathyroidism and hyperparathyroidism respectively.
families.long:
## The factors

GCM (glial cells missing) proteins are a small metazoan family with two human members, GCM1 (also GCMa) and GCM2 (GCMb); *Drosophila* has *gcm* and *gcm2*. They share a highly conserved 150-residue N-terminal region, the GCM domain, which carries all of the sequence-specific DNA-binding activity and sits next to a bipartite nuclear localization signal; the transactivation function maps to the divergent C-terminal half. There is no dimerization module — the GCM domain binds its site as a monomer — and no relationship to any other DNA-binding class. Expression is narrow. GCM1 is expressed in placental trophoblast, with lower levels in kidney and thymus; GCM2 is expressed in the developing parathyroid and, at lower levels, in a few brain regions. Despite the name, the mammalian proteins have no established role in gliogenesis: the glia-versus-neuron switch is the *Drosophila* function, and it was the fly gene that gave the family its name. With only two paralogues and highly restricted expression, GCM is one of the most self-contained families in this atlas.

## The motif

The GCM box is an 8-mer, AT(G/A)CGGGT, determined by binding-site selection for *Drosophila* GCM and reproduced for both mammalian proteins. The models here agree closely: JASPAR, CIS-BP and the Vierstra archetypes all give ATGCGGGT, and family cohesion is 0.92. Note that two of the HOCOMOCO entries (GCM1.H14CORE.0.S.B, GCM2.H14CORE.0.SM.B) report the consensus as ACCCGCAT, which is the reverse complement of the same element — an orientation convention, not a different specificity. One short CIS-BP profile (M02020_2.00, TGCGGG) is simply a trimmed version of the same core.

The structural story is what makes this family unusual. The crystal structure of the murine GCMa GCM domain bound to its octameric site, at 2.85 A, revealed a fold with no precedent: two subdomains tethered together by one of two structural zinc ions, and a five-stranded beta-sheet that protrudes into the major groove perpendicular to the DNA axis. Almost every well-known DNA-binding class reads the major groove with an alpha-helix; GCM does it with a beta-sheet, and the zinc ions are structural rather than part of a classical zinc finger. That is why the recognized sequence looks like nothing else: the GC-rich CGGGT half is read by beta-strand side chains in a geometry not available to helical readers. Because the element is a single 8-mer with high information content and no half-site structure, there are no spacing rules to worry about and no composite arrangements to score. GCM1 and GCM2 are not distinguishable from sequence.

## Where it acts

GCM boxes act in promoters and proximal enhancers of a small number of tissue-restricted genes. The best-documented GCM1 targets are the syncytin-1 (*ERVWE1*) promoter in human trophoblast, and *Itga4*, *Rb1* and syncytin A in mouse placenta; GCM1 activity is regulated by cAMP/PKA signaling in trophoblast. GCM2 acts in parathyroid precursor cells. Because both factors are so restricted, the great majority of sequence matches genome-wide are unoccupied in any given cell type. An exact 8-mer of this composition is expected tens of thousands of times in the human genome, and GC-rich promoter sequence produces additional weak partial matches, so the motif is informative only when paired with the right cell type. The GCM box is not part of any named composite element.

## Biology and disease

In *Drosophila*, *gcm* is a binary switch: cells that express it become glia, cells that do not become neurons. The mammalian phenotypes are entirely different. *Gcm1*-null mouse embryos fail to initiate chorioallantoic branching morphogenesis and die from a defective placental labyrinth; the fusion of trophoblast into syncytium depends on GCM1-driven syncytin expression. *Gcm2*-null mice have no parathyroid glands, yet remain viable with parathyroid hormone produced from the thymus. In humans, loss-of-function *GCM2* mutations, including substitutions that disrupt DNA binding by the GCM domain, cause autosomal recessive familial isolated hypoparathyroidism, while activating *GCM2* variants cause familial isolated hyperparathyroidism — a clean case of a transcription factor with disease alleles in both directions.

## Reading a hit

A GCM box match is one of the more trustworthy family-level calls in this atlas. The fold is unique, the element is an 8-mer with high information content, and no other human family in this collection reads it: across the eight member motifs, similarity to the nearest non-GCM motif (0.67-0.80) sits well below within-family similarity. The evidence is also good — the HOCOMOCO entries rest on in vitro selection (codes `S` and `SM`), not on ChIP alone, so the claim "these proteins bind this sequence" is directly supported rather than inferred from co-occupancy.

What the match does not license is a call on which paralogue, or on occupancy. GCM1 and GCM2 are indistinguishable by motif; the discriminator is tissue, and outside trophoblast and parathyroid neither is expressed at a level that would make a site functional. Watch for two practical traps: databases report this motif in both orientations (ATGCGGGT and ACCCGCAT), so a scan that only checks one strand will miss half the sites; and permissive thresholds on GC-rich promoter sequence will produce partial matches to the CGGGT half that have little to do with GCM.
families.caveats: The GCM box is a high-information 8-mer read by a structurally unique domain, so family-level assignment is reliable — nothing else in this atlas reads ATGCGGGT, and the HOCOMOCO models rest on in vitro selection rather than ChIP alone. GCM1 and GCM2 cannot be told apart from sequence; use tissue instead, since GCM1 is essentially trophoblast-restricted and GCM2 parathyroid-restricted, so most matches are unoccupied in most cell types. Two mechanical points: the element is reported in both orientations across databases (ATGCGGGT and its reverse complement ACCCGCAT), and permissive scoring on GC-rich promoter sequence yields partial matches to the CGGGT half that are not GCM sites.

families.name: PLAG / PLAGL
families.def: GRGGC(N6-8)GGG bipartite sites. PLAG1, PLAGL1/ZAC1, PLAGL2.
families.short: The PLAG proteins - PLAG1, PLAGL1 (also called ZAC1 or LOT1) and PLAGL2 - are C2H2 zinc-finger factors with seven fingers that read a bipartite G-rich site: a GRGGC core and a GGG cluster separated by roughly six to eight base pairs. Finger 3 contacts the G-cluster and fingers 6 and 7 contact the core, so the two halves are read by different parts of one protein. PLAG1 is the classic translocation target in salivary-gland pleomorphic adenoma, where promoter swapping with CTNNB1 or LIFR switches it on; PLAGL2 is also transforming, while PLAGL1/ZAC1 is an imprinted, maternally silenced growth suppressor whose loss of imprinting causes transient neonatal diabetes. All three activate IGF2.
families.long:
## The factors

Three human genes make up this family. PLAG1 (8q12) was identified as the gene activated by promoter
swapping in pleomorphic adenomas of the salivary gland carrying t(3;8)(p21;q12), which fuses the CTNNB1
promoter to the PLAG1 coding region; a second recurrent translocation, t(5;8)(p13;q12), puts PLAG1 under
the LIFR promoter. PLAGL1 (6q24), independently named ZAC1 for zinc finger with apoptosis and cell-cycle
arrest and LOT1 for lost on transformation, and PLAGL2 (20q11) complete the set. All three carry seven
Cys2-His2 zinc fingers in a conserved N-terminal DNA-binding domain plus a C-terminal
serine/threonine/proline-rich transactivation domain, and all bind DNA as monomers. The DNA-binding
domains are highly similar in sequence, which is the central problem for interpreting a hit. PLAG1 and
PLAGL2 are broadly expressed in embryonic tissues and largely silenced after birth; PLAGL1 is expressed
from the paternal allele only, in pituitary, brain, pancreatic islets and many embryonic tissues.
PLAG1 activity is further tuned by SUMOylation of its transactivation domain.

## The motif

The literature consensus is bipartite: GRGGC(N)6-8GGG, a GRGGC core and a GGG G-cluster separated by six
to eight unconstrained bases. The spacer length is permissive, which is unusual and means the element is
better described as two half-sites with flexible spacing than as a fixed-width matrix. Mutational and
binding work assigned the two halves to different fingers: finger 3 engages the G-cluster, fingers 6 and
7 engage the GRGGC core, so a single molecule bridges the gap.

The data in this atlas are consistent with that but compress it. The JASPAR PLAG1 model
(GGGGCCCAAGGGGG, 14 bp) and the equivalent CIS-BP and Vierstra models (CCCCCTTGGGCCCC) span the whole
bipartite element with the short end of the spacer; the PLAGL2 and PLAGL models collapse to an 8-bp
GGGCCCCC, effectively just the G-rich halves. The atlas medoid, GGGCCCCC, is therefore shorter than the
literature consensus rather than in conflict with it: fixed-width position weight matrices cannot
represent a variable spacer, so the databases store the tightest-spaced version. Expect real sites to be
longer and more variably spaced than any of these matrices.

The three paralogues are not equivalent in vitro. PLAG1 and PLAGL2 bind the same bipartite site and both
transform NIH3T3 cells, whereas PLAGL1/ZAC1 binds a distinguishable, more homogeneously G-rich sequence
and arrests rather than promotes growth. The CIS-BP PLAGL1 model here is a 4-bp CCCC inferred from mouse
Plagl1 at 88% DNA-binding-domain identity, so it carries almost no information and should not be used
for scanning.

## Where it acts

PLAG-family sites are G-rich and land preferentially in GC-rich, CpG-island promoters. The best-validated
target is IGF2: PLAG1 and PLAGL2 both bind the IGF2 P3 promoter region and up-regulate it, and IGF2
induction accompanies PLAG1- and PLAGL2-driven transformation. PLAGL1/ZAC1 sits at the top of an
imprinted gene network that includes IGF2, H19, CDKN1C, DLK1 and MEST, and coordinates their expression
during embryonic growth. Because the sites are G-rich, they overlap the binding preferences of KLF/SP
factors, EGR, MAZ, PATZ1 and other GC-box readers, and PLAG matches are common in the CpG-island
promoters of housekeeping genes where none of these factors is necessarily the functional occupant.

## Biology and disease

PLAG1 is the defining oncogene of salivary-gland pleomorphic adenoma and also of lipoblastoma, where
HMGA2-PLAG1 and related fusions (including CHCHD7-PLAG1) again act by promoter substitution rather than
by making a chimeric protein. PLAGL2 is amplified and overexpressed in glioma and colorectal cancer and
promotes proliferation partly through WNT-dependent and partly through IGF2/ASCL2-dependent routes.
PLAGL1/ZAC1 has the opposite behaviour: it induces apoptosis and G1 arrest, is imprinted with maternal
silencing, and relaxation of that imprint at the 6q24 HYMAI/PLAGL1 locus causes transient neonatal
diabetes mellitus. Zac1-null mice are growth-restricted, consistent with a network role in embryonic
growth. Outside disease, a regulatory variant at the bovine PLAG1-CHCHD7 interval is one of the largest
single-locus effects on stature and carcass weight in cattle, a reminder that PLAG1 dosage controls
growth in normal physiology.

## Reading a hit

A PLAG match is a G-rich, GC-box-like element, so the honest conclusion from sequence alone is "a G-rich
promoter element," not "a PLAG site." KLF, SP, EGR, MAZ, PATZ1 and ZNF263 all compete for the same
matches, and G-rich matrices produce many chance hits in CpG islands. Within the family, PLAG1 and
PLAGL2 cannot be told apart by sequence; PLAGL1 is somewhat distinguishable in vitro, but the PLAGL1
matrices available here are too short (4-8 bp) to exploit that. Because the true element is bipartite
with a 6-8 bp variable spacer, a fixed-width matrix will miss wider-spaced real sites and may score
contiguous G-runs that are not functional sites. Check for the two halves explicitly if the call
matters. Expression is the strongest discriminator: PLAG1 and PLAGL2 are largely embryonic, so in adult
tissue a PLAG match is more likely to be a generic GC-box unless a fusion or amplification is known.
families.caveats: The real element is bipartite with a variable 6-8 bp spacer, which no fixed-width matrix can represent, so the matrices here are truncated or tightest-spaced versions and will both miss wide sites and over-call plain G-runs. Matches overlap KLF/SP, EGR, MAZ and other GC-box factors, and G-rich models hit CpG-island promoters frequently by chance. PLAG1 and PLAGL2 share a specificity and cannot be separated by sequence; PLAGL1/ZAC1 differs in vitro, but its models here (CCCC, TGGGGCCA) are too short to use, and the CIS-BP PLAGL1 entry is inferred from mouse at 88% DBD identity. PLAG1 and PLAGL2 are largely embryonic, so adult-tissue matches deserve extra scepticism.

families.name: OSR1 / OSR2
families.def: Odd-skipped related zinc fingers; GC-rich sites. OSR1, OSR2.
families.short: OSR1 and OSR2 (odd-skipped related 1 and 2) are the two vertebrate members of the Odd family of C2H2 zinc-finger proteins, homologs of Drosophila odd-skipped. OSR1 carries three tandem C2H2 fingers and OSR2 five, and both bind the 8-mer GCTACTGT, established by in vitro selection. Despite the C2H2 class label, this motif is not GC-rich — the central TACTG carries most of the information. Both proteins are mesenchymal and developmentally restricted: OSR1 is required for the metanephric mesenchyme and hence for kidney formation, OSR2 for palatal shelf growth, and loss of either causes a distinct mouse malformation. A knock-in experiment showed the two coding sequences are functionally interchangeable, so their different phenotypes reflect where they are expressed rather than what they bind.
families.long:
## The factors

OSR1 and OSR2 (odd-skipped related 1 and 2) are the two vertebrate members of the Odd family of C2H2 zinc-finger proteins, named for *Drosophila* odd-skipped (*odd*), which together with *sob* and *bowl* forms a related fly group. The two human proteins are small and consist of little besides their finger array: OSR1 has three tandem C2H2 fingers (residues 175-253), while OSR2 has five (172-306), the fifth degenerate. That difference matters for the motif, since more fingers means more base pairs contacted. OSR2 additionally has isoforms differing at the N-terminus. Both act mainly as repressors in reporter assays and both are mesenchymal: OSR1 in intermediate mesoderm, the metanephric mesenchyme that gives rise to the kidney, and in cardiac and lateral plate mesenchyme; OSR2 in palatal mesenchyme and tooth germ. Neither is broadly expressed in adult tissues, and neither has a large paralogue set — with two genes, this is a two-member family in the strictest sense. A knock-in experiment in mice showed that Osr1 and Osr2 coding sequences are functionally interchangeable when expressed from each other's locus, so their distinct phenotypes come from expression pattern rather than from different biochemistry.

## The motif

The consensus supported by the data is GCTACTGT, an 8-mer derived from in vitro selection (HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX). Six of the eight models here — from JASPAR, CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO and the Vierstra archetypes — give GCTACTG or GCTACTGT, and family cohesion is 0.92, so this is a well-agreed motif.

It is worth stating plainly that this contradicts a common shorthand. C2H2 zinc-finger factors are often assumed to read GC-rich sequence, and this family is sometimes described that way, but GCTACTGT is not GC-rich; the central TACTG is the most distinctive part, and the informative positions span a mixed-composition 7-8-mer. Anyone scanning with a GC-rich expectation will look in the wrong places.

Two orientation and length details follow from the structure. The JASPAR OSR2 profile MA1646.2 has a consensus of CAGAAGC, which is the reverse complement of GCTTCTG — the same core with one substitution, reported on the opposite strand; databases are not consistent about strand here. And the longest model in the family, the HOCOMOCO OSR2 methyl-HT-SELEX matrix (tGCTACTGaagtaGC, 15 bp, 18.2 bits), reads as an inverted repeat: GCTACTG at the 5' end and, on the other strand at the 3' end, GCTACTT. That arrangement is consistent with OSR2's larger finger array or with two-site occupancy, but no structure of either protein on DNA has been reported, so which fingers make which contacts is not established. OSR1 and OSR2 are not distinguishable from sequence.

## Where it acts

Because both factors are mesenchymal and developmentally restricted, the sites that matter are developmental enhancers in mesenchyme rather than housekeeping promoters, and the motif is not CpG-island associated. No named composite element exists for this family, and no well-characterized partner motif has been established — a genuine gap rather than an omission. An exact 8-mer of this composition is expected on the order of tens of thousands of times in the human genome, which puts OSR matches firmly in the "too common to mean anything alone" category.

## Biology and disease

The mouse phenotypes are clean and non-overlapping. *Osr1*-null embryos fail to form the metanephric mesenchyme and have no kidney, along with heart and urogenital defects; conditional and lineage work has since shown that Osr1-expressing mesenchymal cells also initiate lymph node formation. *Osr2*-null mice have cleft palate, caused by reduced proliferation and disturbed patterning of the palatal shelf mesenchyme, and Osr2 also functions in tooth germ development. Human Mendelian disease links are weaker than the mouse data would suggest; the clearest reported human connection is regulatory rather than coding, with enhancer variation at *OSR2* associated with susceptibility to mandibular incisor agenesis.

## Reading a hit

A GCTACTGT match identifies the family, not the member. The mouse knock-in result makes this more than a technical caveat: the two proteins are biochemically interchangeable, so there is no reason to expect sequence to separate them, and any call between OSR1 and OSR2 has to come from expression data.

Three practical points. First, check strand — at least one database profile in this family is reported as the reverse complement (CAGAAGC), so a single-strand scan will miss half the matches. Second, weigh the evidence: the strongest models here are in vitro (HOCOMOCO codes `SM` for OSR1 and `PSM` for OSR2, the latter grade A), so the claim that these proteins bind this sequence is well supported and not a ChIP-only inference; the weakest, OSR2.H14CORE.1.M.C, is grade C and much longer, and the extra flanking positions in it should not be treated as a requirement. Third, the motif is short and common, so a hit is only informative in a mesenchymal context where one of the two genes is actually expressed. Outside kidney, palate, tooth and related mesenchyme, a match is very unlikely to be occupied.
families.caveats: The motif itself is well agreed (cohesion 0.92, six of eight models giving GCTACTG/GCTACTGT, with in vitro HOCOMOCO evidence at codes SM and PSM), so family assignment is sound. What it cannot do is name the protein: OSR1 and OSR2 read the same site, and a mouse knock-in showed their coding sequences are functionally interchangeable, so only expression data can separate them. The 8-mer is common enough to occur tens of thousands of times by chance, and both genes are restricted to developing mesenchyme, so matches outside kidney, palate, tooth or related mesenchyme are unlikely to be occupied. Check strand: one JASPAR profile reports the reverse complement (CAGAAGC). Do not expect a GC-rich site here.

families.name: RNA-binding proteins with inferred DNA motifs
families.def: Factors whose motif comes from an RNA-binding assay or from inference, so the DNA motif should be read with caution: CPEB1, LIN28B and MBNL2. MBNL1 has no matrix in these databases.
aka: RNA-binding proteins with inferred DNA motifs
RBP motifs in a DNA motif database
families.short: This is not a motif family. It is a warning label. The factors here have motifs that came out of RNA-binding proteins run through DNA assays, or out of inference, so the matrices filed under their names should be read with real caution. Three proteins are present - CPEB1, LIN28B and MBNL2, plus a generic MBNL archetype - across eight models, at cohesion 0.50. All three are bona fide RNA-binding proteins with well-mapped RNA elements, and for CPEB1 the DNA matrix is simply that RNA element with T written for U: its models read TTTTAT and AATAAAA, the cytoplasmic polyadenylation element and its own reverse complement. Scanning genomic DNA against these is usually a mistake. Read the RNA literature instead, and look up the RNA motif.
families.long:
## The factors

Three proteins, eight models. MBNL1 is named in the definition but has no model here, and the "and similar" resolves to nothing further: the bucket is smaller than its label implies.

CPEB1 was identified as the specificity factor for cytoplasmic polyadenylation during Xenopus oocyte maturation. It binds the cytoplasmic polyadenylation element, UUUUAU, in mRNA 3' untranslated regions using two RRMs and a ZZ zinc-binding domain that close on it in a fly-trap arrangement, and it lengthens poly(A) tails to control translation. MBNL2 is a muscleblind-like protein with tandem CCCH zinc fingers that read YGCY motifs - GC steps embedded in pyrimidines - in single-stranded pre-mRNA to control alternative splicing. LIN28B carries a cold-shock domain and a pair of CCHC zinc knuckles; the knuckles read a GGAG element in the preE loop of pre-let-7, the cold-shock domain contributes little sequence specificity, and the protein blocks let-7 maturation. Its documented nuclear activity is indirect: in neuroblastoma it occupies active promoters through protein-protein interaction with the zinc finger ZNF143.

## The motif

There is no consensus. The reported aATAAAA is only the medoid, CIS-BP M03581.

CPEB1 contributes three models: HOCOMOCO CPEB1.H14CORE.0.S.B reads TTTTAT (9.9 bits) and CPEB1.H14CORE.1.S.B reads TTTTATttTtTTt (15.1 bits), both from HT-SELEX alone at grade B, and CIS-BP M03581 reads AATAAAA (10.8 bits). TTTTAT is the CPE with T for U. ATAAAA is the exact reverse complement of TTTTAT, which is why those models agree at 0.94 - and it is also the whole problem in miniature. An RNA element is strand-specific; a DNA scan is not. Scan for the CPEB1 matrix and half your hits are reverse-complement copies that correspond to no RNA element at all.

MBNL contributes three: CIS-BP M04659 (MBNL2) cGCtTcGCtT at 8.8 bits, HOCOMOCO MBNL2.H14CORE.0.B.B cGCTT at 8.3 bits from a protein-binding microarray alone at grade B, and the Vierstra archetype AC0360:MBNL:CCCH_ZF, tGCtTcGCtT. Those contain CGCT, a YGCY motif. A microarray presents double-stranded DNA, so a real duplex preference was measured - for a protein whose physiological target is single-stranded.

LIN28B contributes two, CIS-BP M04663 and the Vierstra archetype AC0341:LIN28B:CSD, both reading CGCGATAtaaCaGCG at 16.6 and 15.9 bits. These are the most information-rich models here and the only ones with no match in any other family. Neither LIN28B's RNA specificity nor its documented nuclear mechanism predicts a 15-bp CG-flanked matrix, so do not read 16.6 bits of information as 16.6 bits of biological confidence.

There are four routes by which an RNA-binding protein acquires a DNA motif. First, direct DNA assay of a protein admitted to a transcription-factor census on the strength of a nucleic-acid-binding domain: HT-SELEX for CPEB1, a microarray for MBNL2. Second, inference by domain similarity, which propagates a measured matrix to relatives and across species. Third, indirect ChIP, where a protein tethered to chromatin by a partner yields the partner's motif. Fourth, archetype clustering, which merges similar matrices under a joint label.

## Where it acts

On RNA, in every case: CPEB1 at cytoplasmic polyadenylation elements in mRNA 3' untranslated regions, MBNL2 at YGCY in introns and around regulated exons, LIN28B on pre-let-7 and target mRNAs. No validated genomic DNA element exists for any of the three. The arithmetic is decisive: TTTTAT and its reverse complement are expected roughly four million times in 3.1 Gb at human base composition, and GCTT about twenty million times. No threshold localises anything. Restricting a scan to transcribed sequence does not help: a DNA-space match is blind to which strand is transcribed, to whether the position survives splicing, and to whether it lies in the 3' untranslated region where CPEB1 works.

## Biology and disease

The disease biology here is RNA biology. In myotonic dystrophy type 1, a CTG expansion produces CUG-repeat transcripts that recruit and sequester muscleblind proteins, and the resulting loss of MBNL activity misregulates splicing; that is a disease of an RNA element, which no DNA scan for an MBNL matrix would find. CPEB1 governs translational activation in oocyte maturation and local translation at synapses. LIN28B is an oncofetal factor overexpressed in neuroblastoma, where it potentiates MYCN-driven tumour formation partly by repressing let-7 and partly at promoters through ZNF143.

## Reading a hit

Treat a hit here as a red flag, not a result. Name the matrix, state which assay produced it - S is HT-SELEX and B is a protein-binding microarray in the HOCOMOCO model name - then ask which question you were answering. If you want to know whether the protein binds your sequence as RNA, take the RNA motif from an RNA motif compendium; large collections of RNA-binding specificities exist, and a CPEB1 or MBNL model from one is the right tool. If you want to know what bound your genomic site, discard these matrices and look at the next best hit.

Do not over-correct. Proteins that genuinely bind both exist, and the founding example is in this atlas: TFIIIA/GTF3A binds the internal control region of the 5S rRNA gene as duplex DNA and also binds the 5S RNA transcript, a dual specificity described in 1980; reviews of dual DNA- and RNA-binding proteins document many more. An RNA-binding label is not automatically disqualifying. The test is whether a duplex-DNA measurement exists for your protein, whether the candidate site sits where that protein is known to act, and whether the genomic context makes sense at all. For the three proteins here, at least one of those answers is no.
families.caveats: Not a family, and not really a set of DNA motifs. Three RNA-binding proteins are represented by eight models at cohesion 0.50: CPEB1 from HT-SELEX alone, MBNL2 from a protein-binding microarray alone, both at HOCOMOCO grade B, and LIN28B from CIS-BP plus its Vierstra archetype. Two of the CPEB1 models are the cytoplasmic polyadenylation element UUUUAU written as TTTTAT and its own reverse complement, which is the difficulty in miniature: RNA elements are strand-specific and DNA scanning is not. MBNL1, named in the definition, has no model here. Do not build a consensus, do not scan genomic DNA against these matrices, and if you need a CPEB1 or MBNL specificity take it from an RNA motif resource.
