families.name: AHR / AHRR
families.def: Xenobiotic response element TNGCGTG. AHR, AHRR (with ARNT).
families.short: The xenobiotic response element is the site bound by the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, AHR, paired with ARNT. Both are bHLH-PAS proteins. AHR sits in the cytoplasm in a complex with HSP90 and XAP2 until it binds a ligand: dioxins and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or endogenous tryptophan metabolites such as kynurenine. It then enters the nucleus, exchanges its chaperones for ARNT, and binds an asymmetric half-site pair in which AHR reads the 5' TNGC and ARNT reads the 3' GTG, giving the core TNGCGTG. The paralogue AHRR is induced by AHR and represses it by competing for ARNT and for the same element. Occupied sites drive the cytochrome P450 genes CYP1A1, CYP1A2 and CYP1B1, so this motif is the entry point of the classical xenobiotic-metabolism response.
families.long:
## The factors

AHR (aryl hydrocarbon receptor, also called the dioxin receptor) and AHRR (AHR repressor) are bHLH-PAS proteins: a basic helix-loop-helix DNA-binding domain followed by PAS-A and PAS-B. Unliganded AHR is cytoplasmic in a complex with HSP90, p23 and XAP2/AIP1, whose architecture has been resolved by cryo-EM with agonist bound (Gruszczyk et al. 2022). Ligand binding in the PAS-B pocket triggers nuclear translocation and heterodimerization with ARNT, the same beta subunit used by HIF, SIM1/2 and the NPAS factors; ARNT is the shared partner of the whole class, and its loss in mice is embryonic lethal (Maltepe et al. 1997). AHRR is an AHR-induced gene lacking a functional ligand pocket; it represses by competing with AHR for ARNT and for the response element, a negative-feedback circuit that helps set tissue-specific sensitivity to pollutants (Mimura et al. 1999). AHR is widely expressed, with highest levels in liver, lung, placenta and immune cells. This atlas family is small: five motifs, one from JASPAR, two from HOCOMOCO and two Vierstra archetypes, with no CIS-BP entry.

## The motif

The element has several names: xenobiotic response element (XRE), dioxin response element (DRE) and AH response element (AHRE). Its core was defined as 5'-TA/TGCGTG-3' in the dioxin-responsive enhancers of the CYP1A1 locus, with flanking bases needed for full enhancer function (Denison et al. 1988); it is conventionally written TNGCGTG. The two half-sites are not equivalent. Selection experiments assign high-affinity 5' half-sites T(C/T)GC to AHR and GT(G/A)C to SIM, and the 3' half-site GTG to ARNT, so ARNT contributes the same GTG in every complex and the partner supplies the discriminating 5' half (Swanson et al. 1995). Within that scheme the invariant string is GCGTG, and a single position, the base immediately 5' of CGTG, separates the XRE (G) from the hypoxia response element (A) and from the palindromic E-box CACGTG that ARNT homodimers prefer. The crystal structure of the AHR-ARNT heterodimer on the DRE shows ARNT curling around AHR in an intertwined, asymmetric architecture; specificity is set locally by the DNA-contacting residues that discriminate the DRE from the HRE and globally by the dimerization and interdomain interfaces (Seok et al. 2017). Systematic measurements across the family report 12-15 bp footprints in which flanking preferences, not the core, separate members that share a core (Bersten et al. 2026). Two presentation issues matter when reading the collected models. The pooled consensus for this family is CACGCaA, which is the reverse complement of TTGCGTG: the Vierstra archetypes here are written on the minus strand, and CACGCAA is not a separate motif. And de novo discovery in AHR ChIP-seq recovers a symmetrical variant, GTGCGTG (Lo and Matthews 2012). AHR and AHRR are not distinguishable: their HOCOMOCO models are TGCGTGC and TGCGTGCcA. The long archetype AC0516:AHR:bHLH (about 20 bits) is an outlier whose best within-family similarity is only 0.66, so it encodes flanking or composite information absent from the other four.

## Where it acts

In TCDD-treated MCF-7 cells, ChIP-seq found 2,594 AHR-bound, 1,352 ARNT-bound and 882 co-bound regions; about 60% of the co-bound regions contained at least one core GCGTG. Peak density was highest within 1 kb of transcription start sites, though some sites lay up to 100 kb away, and the same regions were enriched for FOXA1 and SP1 motifs, placing AHR in cell-type-specific enhancer contexts (Lo and Matthews 2012). Canonical targets are CYP1A1, CYP1A2, CYP1B1, NQO1, ALDH3A1, TIPARP and AHRR itself; the CYP1A1 enhancer carries several XREs. Occupancy is ligand-dependent, so in untreated cells most matches are unbound. The core contains a CpG and is methylation-sensitive; relatedly, a CpG in AHRR (cg05575921) is the strongest and most reproducible blood DNA-methylation marker of cigarette smoking (Joehanes et al. 2016).

## Biology and disease

AHR mediates the toxicity of dioxins and related planar aromatic pollutants. Ahr-null mice have reduced liver size, hepatic fibrosis and immune defects, and are resistant to TCDD (Fernandez-Salguero et al. 1995). It also responds to endogenous and diet-derived tryptophan metabolites: kynurenine produced by TDO in gliomas activates AHR and promotes tumor growth and immune suppression, making AHR an immuno-oncology target (Opitz et al. 2011). AHR contributes to barrier immunity and intestinal lymphocyte programs, and AHRR behaves as a candidate tumor suppressor in several epithelial cancers.

## Reading a hit

TNGCGTG carries roughly six informative base pairs, so chance matches are frequent and a hit alone licenses no conclusion. Separating an XRE from an HRE rests on one base plus weak flanking preferences, and the two are routinely confused by scanners. A hit cannot distinguish AHR from AHRR. Provenance here is thin: both HOCOMOCO models are ChIP-only (letter P) at grades B and C, the JASPAR entry is a dimer model, and the other two are Vierstra footprint archetypes, so nothing in the collection is in vitro evidence that AHR binds this sequence. That support comes from the older selection work and the crystal structure, not from these models. Roughly 40% of AHR/ARNT co-bound regions have no core AHRE, so indirect and tethered binding is common in ChIP-derived versions. Finally, the archetype label AC0073:AHR:bHLH names the factor group whose motifs clustered together; it is not a claim that AHR is separable from other bHLH-PAS proteins.
families.caveats: Every model in this family is ChIP-derived or footprint-derived, at grade B or C, so it evidences occupancy in cells rather than direct AHR binding; the in vitro anchor for TNGCGTG is the older selection literature and the AHR-ARNT crystal structure. About 40% of AHR/ARNT co-bound regions lack any core element, so indirect binding is well documented. AHR and AHRR share one motif and cannot be told apart. The XRE differs from the hypoxia response element at a single base 5' of CGTG, so XRE and HRE calls are easily swapped. Note also that the pooled consensus CACGCAA is simply TTGCGTG on the opposite strand, not a different site. Occupancy requires a ligand, so an unbound match in untreated cells is expected.

families.name: TBP / TATA
families.def: TATA box TATAWAWR. TBP, TAF1.
families.short: The TATA box is the oldest known eukaryotic core promoter element and the binding site of TBP, the TATA-box-binding protein. TBP is a saddle-shaped, internally pseudo-symmetric protein that straddles about eight base pairs of AT-rich DNA, reads them entirely from the minor groove, kinks the duplex at both ends and bends it by roughly 80 degrees. It works within TFIID for RNA polymerase II and within SL1 and TFIIIB for polymerases I and III, so a single protein serves all three. Because minor-groove contacts barely distinguish A:T from T:A, the element carries little information: the canonical TATAWAWR is present in only a small minority of human promoters, most of which are instead GC-rich and TATA-less. A TATA match on its own is therefore very weak evidence of anything.
families.long:
## The factors

TBP is a single small protein, about 180 residues in its conserved core, encoded by one gene. Its
fold is a pseudo-symmetric saddle: two structurally similar halves, each contributing a curved
beta sheet that forms the concave underside, with helices on the convex top surface where general
factors and activators dock. TBP does not act alone. For RNA polymerase II it is the anchoring
subunit of TFIID, a roughly one-megadalton complex of thirteen or more TAF subunits; for
polymerase I it sits in SL1 and for polymerase III in TFIIIB. Two paralogues exist, TBPL1
(TRF2/TLF) and TBPL2 (TRF3), which have the TBP fold but altered DNA-contacting surfaces and do
not bind TATA boxes; neither has a motif in the databases used here. TAF1, the largest TFIID
subunit, is included in this key because its motif models are attributed to a promoter-binding
component of the same machinery, but TAF1 is not a sequence-specific DNA-binding protein in the
way TBP is: its promoter contacts involve the initiator and downstream regions, and it carries
histone-acetyltransferase and bromodomain activities.

## The motif

The literature consensus is the eight-base TATAWAWR, most often realized as TATAAAAG or TATATAAG,
positioned roughly 25-30 bp upstream of the transcription start site in a focused promoter. The
co-crystal structures of human and yeast TBP on TATA DNA showed why the information content is
low: TBP makes no major-groove base contacts at all. It binds the minor groove, where an A:T and a
T:A base pair present nearly the same pattern of hydrogen-bond acceptors, and inserts pairs of
phenylalanine side chains between the first two and last two base pairs, kinking the helix at both
ends and bending the whole element by about 80 degrees while partially unwinding it. What TBP
really reads is a short run of deformable, narrow-minor-groove AT-rich DNA, and later work showed
that a wide range of AT-rich variants are bound with comparable affinity. The consequence for
motif models is direct: every matrix in this family is a low-information AT-rich model. The
representative here, the Vierstra archetype AC0057, is TATAAAAG; JASPAR MA0108.3 is TATAAAA;
HOCOMOCO's TBP model is CTATAAAAGG. There is no half-site structure and no spacing rule, and
because TBP is a monomer on a pseudo-symmetric site, orientation is only weakly determined by
sequence, which is one reason TATA-box orientation prediction is unreliable. Family cohesion here
is only 0.64, and two of the five motifs are flagged as belonging elsewhere, discussed below.

## Where it acts

TATA boxes belong to focused, or sharp-initiation, promoters: a single dominant start site,
AT-rich surroundings, no CpG island. These are a minority of mammalian promoters. A genome-scale
analysis found that about 76% of human core promoters have no TATA-like element, are GC-rich and
are enriched for SP1 sites; about 24% have something TATA-like, but only about 10% of those match
the canonical TATAWAWR, which puts canonical TATA boxes at a few percent of human genes. Broad,
dispersed-initiation promoters in CpG islands dominate the mammalian genome, and these use the
initiator, downstream elements and TFIID-DNA contacts rather than a TATA box. Functionally the
split is informative: TATA-less promoters skew toward housekeeping genes, while TATA-containing
promoters are enriched for highly regulated, stimulus-responsive and tissue-specific genes,
including many that are strongly induced by stress or hormones. Cryo-EM structures of
promoter-bound TFIID show TBP being loaded onto the TATA region while other TAFs contact the
initiator and downstream promoter, so the TATA box is one anchor point in an extended,
multi-contact interaction rather than the sole determinant of where transcription starts.

## Biology and disease

TBP is essential in every organism tested; there is no viable null. Its N-terminal region in
humans contains a polyglutamine tract, and expansion of that tract to roughly 43 repeats or more
causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 17, a rare autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder,
placing TBP among the polyglutamine diseases. Mutations in individual TAFs cause developmental
syndromes and intellectual disability, and TAF1 variants are associated with X-linked
neurodevelopmental disease. TATA-box variants in individual promoters cause disease in their own
right, the classic cases being promoter mutations that reduce beta-globin expression in
beta-thalassemia and the TATA-box polymorphism in the UGT1A1 promoter that contributes to
Gilbert syndrome.

## Reading a hit

Treat a TATA match as almost no evidence. TATAWAWR is an eight-base AT-rich pattern with two
degenerate positions, expected by chance roughly once every few kilobases on either strand, which
is hundreds of thousands of matches in a human genome, the overwhelming majority of them nowhere
near a promoter. A match is only interesting if it sits 25-30 bp upstream of an annotated or
measured start site in a promoter that otherwise looks focused and AT-rich. It also says nothing
about TBP itself, since TBP is present at essentially all active promoters, including TATA-less
ones, where it is positioned by TFIID rather than by sequence. This family is also a good place to
see what happens when a ChIP-derived matrix is assigned to the wrong protein. The HOCOMOCO model
TAF1.H14CORE.0.P.B is AAGATGGCGGC, which is the YY1 motif, not a TBP-like or TAF1-specific
sequence; YY1 sites are common at focused promoters, so a TAF1 ChIP experiment recovers them.
Likewise the CIS-BP TBP entry M08231_2.00 is TATTTGCATA, whose core ATTTGCAT is the POU octamer
read in reverse. Neither model should be used as a TATA box.
families.caveats: The TATA box is the least informative element in common use: eight AT-rich bases read entirely from the minor groove, where A:T and T:A are nearly interchangeable, so the matrix cannot be much better than the physics allows. Expect hundreds of thousands of chance matches per genome and only a few percent of human promoters to carry a real one. A match means nothing without position 25-30 bp upstream of a start site. Two of the five motifs under this key are not TATA boxes: the HOCOMOCO ChIP-derived TAF1 matrix is the YY1 motif, and the CIS-BP TBP entry M08231_2.00 is the POU octamer. Family cohesion is correspondingly low at 0.64.

families.name: WT1
families.def: EGR-like GC-rich site with distinct KTS-isoform preference. WT1.
families.short: WT1 is the Wilms tumor suppressor, a four-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger protein whose last three fingers are closely related to those of EGR1 and which binds essentially the same GC-rich site. In vitro selection also found a slightly different high-affinity site, GCGTGGGAGT, called the WTE. Alternative splicing inserts three amino acids (lysine-threonine-serine) between fingers three and four, and the +KTS form binds DNA poorly but binds RNA and localizes to splicing-factor compartments, so WT1 is a DNA-binding protein only in part. Expression is restricted to developing kidney and gonad, podocytes, mesothelium and epicardium. The WT1 matrices in motif databases are ChIP-derived and G-rich rather than EGR-like, which matters when reading a hit.
families.long:
## The factors

WT1 was isolated as a zinc-finger gene at the Wilms tumor locus on human chromosome 11p13, spanning about 50 kb (Call et al. 1990). The protein has four Cys2-His2 fingers; fingers 2-4 align with the three fingers of EGR1, and finger 1 adds further contacts. Two alternative splice events generate four main isoforms: insertion or omission of exon 5 (17 amino acids) in the N-terminal region, and insertion or omission of the tripeptide lysine-threonine-serine (KTS) between fingers 3 and 4. The KTS insertion is the consequential one. The -KTS protein localizes to nuclear compartments occupied by transcription factors, while the +KTS protein concentrates in splicing-factor domains (Larsson et al. 1995), and +KTS WT1 binds RNA (Caricasole et al. 1996) through a region that overlaps the DNA-binding fingers (Bardeesy and Pelletier 1998). So one gene produces a DNA-binding transcriptional regulator and an RNA-binding protein from the same finger array, and the ratio between them is under splice control. WT1 expression is restricted: nephron progenitors and podocytes in kidney, Sertoli and granulosa cells in gonad, mesothelium, epicardium and spleen, with additional roles in heart and nervous system (Hastie 2017). WT1 has no close paralogue; its nearest relatives by DNA-binding domain are the EGR proteins.

## The motif

WT1 binds the EGR-1 consensus, which was how its sequence specificity was first demonstrated: a bacterially expressed WT1 finger region bound the EGR-1 site (Rauscher et al. 1990). A whole-genome PCR selection later identified a distinct preferred 10-mer, GCGTGGGAGT, termed the WTE, which is similar to but not the same as the EGR-1 consensus GCG(G/T)GGGCG (Nakagama et al. 1995). The difference is the penultimate triplet: GGGAGT in the WTE against GGGCG in the EGR site. The four-finger domain has been solved on DNA by X-ray crystallography and NMR on both 14-bp and 17-bp duplexes, which resolved the position of finger 1 (Stoll et al. 2007). Here the atlas data and the literature do not agree, and the discrepancy is worth stating plainly. The five WT1 matrices collected here are not EGR-like. Both HOCOMOCO models (WT1.H14CORE.0.P.B, GGGGGAGGA; WT1.H14CORE.1.P.B, GCGGGGGAGG) and the JASPAR profile (MA1627.2, CCTCCCCCAC, which is GTGGGGGAGG on the other strand) are G-rich runs with no CACGC, placing them in the GGGAGGG cluster occupied by MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF281, ZNF148 and VEZF1 rather than with EGR. Family cohesion is correspondingly low, 0.57. The remaining two matrices carry no usable signal: the Vierstra archetype AC0095:WT/FOXC is an AT-rich model (ATATATT) whose nearest neighbors are K50-class homeodomain motifs, and the CIS-BP entry M00243_2.00 has 0.1 bits of information. In the other direction, a HOCOMOCO matrix labelled ZBTB17/MIZ1 (ZBT17.H14CORE.0.P.B, GTGGGGGAGGGG) has its nearest neighbor across all four databases in this family - another sign that what these ChIP-derived WT1 models capture is the generic G-rich promoter element, not a WT1-specific sequence.

## Where it acts

WT1 sites sit in GC- and GA-rich promoter-proximal sequence, and the genes WT1 controls are concentrated in the programs it is expressed in: nephron and podocyte differentiation, gonadal development, epicardial and mesothelial identity (Hastie 2017). Because WT1 and EGR1 recognize overlapping sequences, they compete at shared sites, and which one occupies a site is determined by which protein is present - EGR1 only transiently after stimulation, WT1 only in the restricted lineages that express it. The G-rich matrices in the databases, by contrast, point at CpG-island promoters generally, where MAZ-, ZNF281- and SP-family sites are also abundant.

## Biology and disease

Wt1-null mice fail at an early step of kidney development, with defective ureteric bud outgrowth and no metanephros, together with gonadal and mesothelial defects (Kreidberg et al. 1993). In humans, germline WT1 mutations cause two distinct syndromes that map onto the protein's two functions. Denys-Drash syndrome arises from germline missense mutations concentrated in the zinc fingers and combines urogenital malformation, nephropathy and Wilms tumor (Pelletier et al. 1991). Frasier syndrome arises from donor splice-site mutations in intron 9 that specifically abolish the +KTS isoform, producing gonadal dysgenesis and progressive glomerulopathy without the same Wilms tumor risk (Barbaux et al. 1997) - direct evidence that the KTS isoform ratio, not just total WT1, matters in vivo. Somatic WT1 mutations occur in a minority of Wilms tumors, and WT1 is also reported to be highly expressed in acute leukemias.

## Reading a hit

Be careful here, because the label and the matrix disagree. The structurally and biochemically characterized WT1 site is EGR-like (the EGR-1 consensus, or the WTE), but every informative WT1 matrix in these databases is a ChIP-derived G-rich model at grade B. A hit to one of those models tells you the sequence belongs to the GGGAGGG family of G-rich promoter elements - shared with MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF281, ZNF148, VEZF1 and at least one ZBTB17 matrix - and does not establish that WT1 binds there. Conversely, a strong hit to an EGR matrix is also a candidate WT1 site, and one Vierstra archetype is labelled AC0519:EGR/WT precisely because the two could not be separated. Ignore the two uninformative entries: AC0095:WT/FOXC is an AT-rich homeodomain-like model, and M00243_2.00 carries essentially no information. Two further constraints are biological rather than sequence-based. WT1 is expressed in few cell types, so in most samples there is no WT1 available to bind. And even in those cell types, roughly half the WT1 protein may be the +KTS isoform, whose documented high-affinity ligand is RNA rather than DNA.
families.caveats: The WT1 label and the WT1 matrices point in different directions. Biochemistry and structure say WT1 binds an EGR-like GC-rich site (the EGR-1 consensus, or the WTE GCGTGGGAGT); but all informative database matrices here are ChIP-derived, grade B, and G-rich (GGGGGAGGA), which places them in the MAZ/ZNF281/VEZF1 cluster instead. Family cohesion is only 0.57, one matrix has 0.1 bits, and one Vierstra archetype labelled WT is an AT-rich homeodomain model. A hit therefore identifies a G-rich promoter element, not WT1 occupancy. Also check that WT1 is expressed at all, and remember the +KTS isoform binds RNA.

families.name: ZEB
families.def: E-box-like CACCTG bound by ZEB1/ZEB2 zinc fingers.
families.short: ZEB1 and ZEB2 are large C2H2 zinc-finger repressors that bind the E-box-like sequence CACCTG, written CAGGTG when read on the other strand. Each protein carries two widely separated zinc-finger clusters, either of which can engage a site, so one molecule can hold two boxes at once. ZEB proteins contain no basic helix-loop-helix domain, yet they compete for the same CAGGTG boxes that bHLH activators use, so an E-box hit does not imply a bHLH factor. Both paralogues repress epithelial genes, E-cadherin (CDH1) above all, and are central to epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Loss-of-function mutations cause posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (ZEB1) and Mowat-Wilson syndrome (ZEB2), and high ZEB1 marks poorly differentiated carcinomas.
families.long:
## The factors

Humans have two paralogues: ZEB1 (also TCF8, deltaEF1, AREB6, ZFHX1A) and ZEB2 (SIP1, ZFHX1B, SMADIP1), each roughly 1,100-1,200 residues. Their architecture is atypical. Instead of one contiguous finger array, each protein carries two widely separated C2H2 clusters - three to four fingers near the N terminus and three near the C terminus - flanking a central region that includes a degenerate homeodomain which does not itself bind DNA. Remacle and colleagues showed that each cluster binds a target site on its own, so a single molecule works with two hands and can occupy two sites simultaneously. ZEB proteins do not dimerize through a leucine zipper or a helix-loop-helix; repression is delivered by recruited partners, chiefly CtBP through a central interaction domain, plus NuRD and HDAC complexes. ZEB2 was independently isolated as a SMAD-interacting protein, and both paralogues couple TGF-beta signaling to transcription. ZEB1 is expressed in mesenchymal tissue, T cells and corneal endothelium; ZEB2 in neural crest derivatives, the central nervous system and blood. Both are induced during epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and are restrained post-transcriptionally by the miR-200 microRNA family.

## The motif

The literature writes the site CACCTG, or equivalently CAGGTG on the opposite strand: a 6 bp member of the CANNTG E-box class, sometimes called the E2-box or Z-box. Essentially all the information sits in those six positions. Each three-finger cluster reads about one base triplet per finger from the major groove, which accounts for a footprint of roughly 6 bp and for the absence of strong flanking preference. The family data matches this: the CIS-BP and JASPAR models are rendered CACCTG and CTCACCTG while the HOCOMOCO models read CAGGTG and CAGGTGAG, which is the same motif on the other strand (the reverse complement of CAGGTGAG is CTCACCTG). This is a strand convention, not a disagreement. Information content is low, 10-12 bits, and the ZEB1 and ZEB2 models are effectively interchangeable, with cross-database similarities of 0.94-0.99, so sequence alone cannot tell the two paralogues apart. Because each protein has two independent hands, tandem CACCT(G) boxes bind more strongly than a single box, and validated targets such as CDH1 carry two or more; no fixed spacing is required.

## Where it acts

ZEB sites occur in proximal promoters of epithelial structural genes - the E-pal element of CDH1 is the textbook case - and in large numbers of distal enhancers in mesenchymal and carcinoma cells. CACCTG contains no CpG, so it is not depleted by genome-wide CpG loss: a strict 6 bp match occurs roughly once every 2 kb counting both strands, on the order of a million times in the human genome. Occupancy is therefore set by chromatin state and competition, not by site availability. ZEB1 ChIP-seq peaks overlap extensively with SNAI1/SNAI2 peaks and with bHLH factor peaks, because all of them use the same box. Functional partners include SMAD2/SMAD3 (especially for ZEB2), CtBP, NuRD and, in some settings, YAP; the best-characterized regulatory circuit is the mutual repression between ZEB1 and the miR-200 family.

## Biology and disease

ZEB1 and ZEB2 repress epithelial genes including CDH1, EPCAM, CRB3 and LGL2, and are required for EMT in gastrulation, neural crest migration and organ fibrosis. Mouse deltaEF1 (Zeb1) mutants show skeletal defects and impaired thymocyte development. Zeb1 also couples EMT to cellular senescence through the CDKN2A locus, so loss of Zeb1 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts triggers premature senescence. In humans, heterozygous ZEB1 mutations cause posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy type 3, with ectopic COL4A3 expression in corneal endothelium, while truncating mutations and deletions of ZEB2 cause Mowat-Wilson syndrome (intellectual disability, microcephaly, Hirschsprung disease and a distinctive face). In carcinomas, ZEB1 expression tracks with loss of apicobasal polarity and dedifferentiation. One honest qualification: ZEB-driven EMT is firmly established in culture and in development, but in human tumors the transition is usually partial, and how much full EMT contributes to metastasis is still argued; current consensus statements describe a spectrum of hybrid epithelial-mesenchymal states rather than a binary switch.

## Reading a hit

A CACCTG/CAGGTG match is among the least specific hits a scan can return. Plausible binders include the bHLH E-proteins TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12, MYOD and MYF, TWIST and HAND, NEUROD and ATOH, MAX and USF, and the C2H2 repressors SNAI1-3, SCRT1/2 and ZBTB18. An E-box hit therefore does not imply a bHLH factor. Nothing in the 6 bp core distinguishes ZEB from these alternatives; only context does. Two boxes within a short window, in a mesenchymal or TGF-beta-stimulated cell type, and near an epithelial gene, is a reasonable circumstantial case for ZEB. A single isolated box is not. Note also the evidence types: the HOCOMOCO ZEB1 and ZEB2 models are ChIP-seq-derived (evidence code P, grade B) and the JASPAR ZEB1 matrix MA0103.4 is ChIP-seq-derived, so they report where ZEB was found, not necessarily what ZEB binds directly; the CIS-BP entries for both genes are direct rather than inferred. Low label agreement in the family data (0.2-0.4) means the nearest neighbours of these matrices across databases are often non-ZEB E-box models, which is expected rather than a sign of error.
families.caveats: Trust the family, not the member, and not even the family without context. The 6 bp CACCTG core is shared with bHLH activators, SNAIL/SCRATCH, INSM and ZBTB18, so a hit licenses "E-box" and nothing more; ZEB1 and ZEB2 motifs are indistinguishable from each other at 0.94-0.99 similarity. The site is common enough to occur roughly a million times by chance in the genome, so single matches carry almost no evidence. HOCOMOCO ZEB1/ZEB2 and JASPAR MA0103.4 are ChIP-derived and can reflect indirect or co-binding. Paired boxes, an epithelial target gene and a mesenchymal or TGF-beta context are what make a ZEB call defensible.

families.name: ZNF384 / ZNF362
families.def: AT-rich TAAAAA-type site at extracellular-matrix gene promoters, shared by the near-identical paralogues ZNF384 and ZNF362.
families.short: ZNF384 and its near-identical paralogue ZNF362 are C2H2 zinc-finger proteins that bind homopolymeric runs of A on one strand and T on the other. They are unusual among zinc fingers in reading the minor groove of an A-tract rather than the major groove of a mixed sequence, and only three of their fingers contact DNA. ZNF384 was cloned twice, as CIZ, a partner of the adaptor p130Cas that activates matrix metalloproteinase genes, and as Nmp4, a nuclear matrix factor at the type I collagen alpha-1 promoter. In human leukaemia ZNF384 is a recurrent fusion partner: rearrangements joining its C-terminal region to EP300, TCF3, TAF15 and others define a subtype of B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
families.long:
## The factors

ZNF384 and ZNF362 are paralogues whose zinc-finger arrays are close enough that no assay distinguishes their sequence preferences; the family therefore has two members and one motif. Splice variants of ZNF384 contain between five and eight C2H2 fingers, together with an SH3-binding region overlapping a putative AT-hook and a polyglutamine-alanine repeat. Mapping the DNA-binding function showed that only fingers 2, 3 and 6 are needed for association with the A-tract element, so most of the array does something other than read bases. ZNF384 was described independently as CIZ, a protein that binds the focal-adhesion adaptor p130Cas and activates matrix metalloproteinase promoters, and as Nmp4, one of a set of nuclear matrix proteins occupying the rat COL1A1 promoter. The N-terminus carries a strong activation domain that is masked in the full-length protein and becomes productive once the fingers engage DNA, and the polyglutamine-alanine repeat then contributes to activation, suggesting an allosteric switch triggered by binding. Both proteins are broadly expressed.

## The motif

This is the atlas entry whose consensus is least word-like. The element is a homopolymeric (dA:dT) tract: eight or more consecutive adenines on one strand, equivalently eight or more thymines on the other. The literature usually writes it as poly(dA:dT) rather than as an IUPAC string, and the AT-rich promoter sites in COL1A1 and the MMP genes are described as TAAAAA-type runs. ZNF384 and ZNF362 are, as far as is known, the only C2H2 zinc-finger proteins that bind within the minor groove of such a tract, which is why only three fingers are involved: there are no distinguishing major-groove bases to read. All five matrices in this family are A- or T-runs of seven to twelve positions, differing mainly in run length and in whether they specify a flanking base; the HOCOMOCO ZNF362 matrix adds a 3' C and the ZNF384 matrix a 3' GT. Information content is therefore low in the usual sense while being high in a positional sense, because the requirement is a structural one: an uninterrupted, narrow-minor-groove A-tract. ZNF384 and ZNF362 cannot be distinguished from sequence at all.

## Where it acts

Occurrences are promoter-proximal in the characterized cases, notably the COL1A1 and MMP promoters in osteoblasts, and genome-wide mapping of Nmp4 in bone cells recovered a large target set biased toward extracellular-matrix and secretory-pathway genes. A-tracts are, however, everywhere: they are among the most abundant simple sequence features in mammalian genomes, occur heavily in intergenic and intronic DNA, and are also intrinsically nucleosome-disfavouring, which means they influence chromatin accessibility independently of any protein binding them. That double life is the central interpretive problem for this family. There is no named composite element with a partner factor, and the reported cofactor interactions are protein-protein rather than DNA-adjacent: p130Cas for CIZ, and the nuclear matrix for Nmp4.

## Biology and disease

Nmp4/ZNF384 is best understood in bone as a brake. Nmp4-null mice respond more strongly than wild type to anabolic parathyroid hormone therapy, gaining more trabecular bone, and their osteoblasts show enhanced secretory capacity; the factor has accordingly been described as closing the PTH anabolic window. Nmp4 loss also alters innate immune responses to influenza A and modifies serum-induced arthritis, so the effects are not skeletal alone. The prominent human disease link is oncogenic and structural rather than transcriptional-regulatory in the ordinary sense: ZNF384 is a recurrent fusion partner in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, with EP300, TCF3, TAF15, CREBBP and other 5' partners fused to a nearly complete ZNF384 coding region. These ZNF384-rearranged leukaemias form a distinct transcriptional subtype with a characteristic immunophenotype, they include mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia cases, and additional classes of ZNF384 aberration have since been described. Because the fusion retains the zinc-finger array, the chimeric protein is thought to redirect a strong heterologous activation domain to ZNF384's A-tract sites.

## Reading a hit

Treat a hit here as a statement about DNA structure first and about protein occupancy second. Eight-base A-tracts occur many hundreds of thousands of times in the human genome, so a match on its own is close to uninformative; conversely, a long A-tract found in an accessibility or ChIP dataset may reflect nucleosome depletion or an alignment artefact rather than ZNF384 binding. The family also overlaps other AT-rich motif families, and any tool that scans for homopolymer runs will find these sites regardless of which factor is labelled. ZNF384 and ZNF362 are indistinguishable, so a hit identifies the pair. HOCOMOCO's evidence codes for this family include in vitro data (S and M), so direct binding to A-tracts is real; what is not licensed by a hit is the conclusion that a particular tract is a regulated element.
families.caveats: This is a structural motif, not a word, and its abundance makes single hits nearly uninformative: eight-base A-tracts appear hundreds of thousands of times genome-wide. A-tracts are also intrinsically nucleosome-disfavouring, so their enrichment in open chromatin and in ChIP peak sets can arise without any ZNF384 binding, and an A-tract hit in an accessibility dataset should not be read as occupancy. ZNF384 and ZNF362 are indistinguishable from sequence, and the motif overlaps other AT-rich families. In vitro evidence supports direct minor-groove binding, so the protein-motif link itself is sound; only the interpretation of individual genomic matches is weak. Context, notably promoter position and extracellular-matrix or secretory target genes, does most of the work.

families.name: ZNF768
families.def: MYC-box-like TGGCAGCAGC repeat. ZNF768.
families.short: ZNF768 is a C2H2 zinc-finger protein whose binding site sits in the core region of mammalian-wide interspersed repeats (MIRs), an old family of SINE retrotransposons. The site is bipartite: GCTGTGTG and CCTCTCTG separated by about twenty unconstrained bases, so the two halves are usually reported separately and most motif databases hold only one of them. ZNF768 binding is concentrated in euchromatin and at promoters of expressed genes, and its own N-terminus contains a heptad repeat array structurally reminiscent of the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, which is where the frequent comparison to MYC-box-like repeats comes from. The literature is recent and small: two primary characterizations plus mouse work linking it to RAS-induced senescence and p53.
families.long:
## The factors

ZNF768 is a single human gene with no paralogue that shares its specificity, and the entire family here consists of its own matrices. The protein has a C-terminal C2H2 zinc-finger array and, unusually, an N-terminal region built from a heptad repeat array that is structurally related to the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II. That array evolved in placental mammals, is absent in marsupials and monotremes, and varies in length between species, which raises the possibility that it performs CTD-like scaffolding functions in gene regulation. The resemblance of these repeats to MYC homology boxes is the origin of the "MYC-box-like" description attached to this family in some annotations; the description refers to the protein's repeats rather than to a MYC-type DNA element, and no E-box-like binding has been reported. ZNF768 is broadly expressed, is a phosphoprotein, and is destabilized when RAS signalling is activated.

## The motif

The characterized site is bipartite. Affinity purification and genome-wide mapping identified specific binding to GCTGTGTG followed, about twenty base pairs later, by CCTCTCTG, with the intervening sequence unconstrained. This spacing is the reason the four databases disagree so visibly. The two ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO matrices, 23 and 21 base pairs long, are adjacent windows on the same long site and even share their overlapping flank: one contains CTCAGAGAGG (the reverse complement of CCTCTCTGAG) and the other ends in CACACAGC (the reverse complement of GCTGTGTG). The CIS-BP matrix and the Vierstra archetype both read CTTAACCTCTCTGAG, essentially the CCTCTCTG half with its native MIR flank, and JASPAR MA1731.2 reduces it to the eight-base CCTCTCTG core. No matrix in any of the four databases spans the whole bipartite element, because standard motif discovery does not model a twenty-base gap. The family consensus quoted here therefore writes the gap explicitly; the dataConsensus CTTAACCTCTCTGAG is the 3' half only. Because the site is embedded in a repeat family, the "flanks" that motif discovery recovers are MIR consensus sequence rather than base contacts, and should not be read as specificity determinants.

## Where it acts

ZNF768 occupancy tracks MIRs, and MIRs are old enough to be widely fixed and heavily fragmented, with hundreds of thousands of copies in the human genome. Binding is preferentially associated with euchromatin and with promoter regions of genes that are actively expressed, and in the two cell lines examined (the B-cell line Raji and the osteosarcoma line U2OS) it marked genes expressed in a cell-type-specific manner. Mass spectrometry of ZNF768 complexes recovered the Elongator components ELP1, ELP2 and ELP3 along with other nuclear factors, pointing to a role at expressed genes rather than in silencing. MIR-derived sequences are independently known to act as enhancers and to be rewired during changes in pluripotency, so the sequence class is regulatorily active with or without ZNF768. There is no named composite element pairing ZNF768 with another factor.

## Biology and disease

The functional literature is small and recent, and it is worth saying plainly that the connection between the DNA motif and the phenotypes below has not been closed. ZNF768 protein is destabilized when oncogenic RAS is activated, and its levels fall in replicative, stress-induced and oncogene-induced senescence. Depleting ZNF768 impairs proliferation and induces senescence, altering expression of cell-cycle effectors and established p53 targets; overexpressing it helps cells bypass RAS-induced senescence, and it interacts with p53 and suppresses p53 phosphorylation and activity. ZNF768 is amplified or overexpressed in a range of tumours. Mouse work supports this axis from both directions: ZNF768 loss amplifies p53 action and reduces lung tumorigenesis, and a Cre-inducible ZNF768 overexpression model has been generated. None of these studies identifies the MIR-embedded motif as the mediator, so the relationship between the binding site and the senescence phenotype is currently an open question rather than an established mechanism. There is no human Mendelian disease linked to ZNF768.

## Reading a hit

Expect a hit here to be a hit on a MIR. Because the recognized sequence lies in a repeat core, a match tells you first that you are in a MIR element and only second that ZNF768 might bind, and the two statements are not interchangeable: the great majority of MIR copies are not occupied. Only one half of the bipartite site is modelled by most matrices, and CCTCTCTG on its own is an eight-base CT-rich word that overlaps other CT-rich families, so a single-half match in non-repeat sequence is weak. Check whether the two halves occur with the expected spacing. All the direct evidence in this family is ChIP-derived (HOCOMOCO evidence code P for both matrices), with no HT-SELEX support, so direct binding by the purified protein is not independently confirmed here. Repeat-derived motifs are also a known source of artefacts in occupancy data, including spurious apparent binding at repetitive and organellar sequences, so verify mappability before interpreting a hit.
families.caveats: Two structural problems. The site is bipartite with an unconstrained twenty-base gap, and no database matrix models it, so every available matrix covers one half; scores are not comparable and half-site matches are weak. And the site lives inside MIR SINEs, which means a match mainly reports the presence of a MIR, not occupancy: MIR copies number in the hundreds of thousands and only a small subset is bound. Evidence in this family is ChIP-only (HOCOMOCO codes P, grade B), with no in vitro confirmation of direct binding to the motif, and the recovered flanks are MIR consensus sequence rather than demonstrated base contacts. The senescence and p53 biology is not yet tied to the motif.

families.name: MTF1
families.def: Metal response element TGCRCNC. MTF1.
families.short: MTF1 (MTF-1) is a six-finger C2H2 zinc-finger protein that binds the metal response element, a short TGCRCNC core first defined as the 12-base-pair repeat that makes metallothionein promoters metal-inducible. MTF1 is constitutively present but only becomes an activator when free zinc rises, so the same site is quiet in resting cells and strongly occupied after exposure to zinc, cadmium, copper or other heavy metals, and under oxidative and hypoxic stress. Metallothionein promoters carry several MREs in tandem, and that clustering, rather than any single site, is what produces a large induction. Mouse Mtf1 knockout is embryonic-lethal with liver degeneration. Because the core is only seven informative bases, isolated genomic matches are common and mostly meaningless.
families.long:
## The factors

MTF1 is a single gene with no paralogue that shares its specificity; the human protein was cloned in 1994 after the mouse factor was identified biochemically as the zinc-responsive activity binding the metallothionein-I enhancer. Its DNA-binding region is a tandem array of six C2H2 zinc fingers, and the fingers differ from each other in how tightly they hold zinc. That heterogeneity is the basis of metal sensing: at low free zinc some fingers are unloaded and the array binds DNA poorly, while rising zinc fills them and licenses binding. Three separate transactivation domains (acidic, proline-rich and serine/threonine-rich) lie C-terminal to the fingers, and nuclear import, phosphorylation and interaction with coactivators add further layers of regulation; the Hippo kinases LATS1 and LATS2 phosphorylate MTF1 and dampen the heavy-metal response. Homologues exist from Drosophila to mammals and the protein is broadly expressed, with the highest activity in liver.

## The motif

The metal response element was defined genetically before any protein was known: a 12-base-pair motif repeated several times in metallothionein promoters was shown to be sufficient to make a heterologous gene metal-inducible, and fine mapping narrowed the essential part to a core now written TGCRCNC (reverse complement GNGYGCA). Only about seven positions carry real information, and the strongest of these are the invariant TGC and the following purine. The in vitro matrices in this family extend the core with flanking preferences: the HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX word is GCCGTGTGCAAAA (reverse complement TTTTGCACACGGC), which is the TGCACAC core with a 5' GCC and a 3' A-tract, and JASPAR MA0863.1 is the same element written on the other strand. The family consensus quoted here is the literature core, TGCRCNC, because that is what functional work defines; the longer database words reflect flanking base preferences measured in vitro and should not be treated as required. Individual MREs vary considerably and have been grouped into subtypes with different affinities. There are no half-sites and no dimerization: MTF1 binds as a monomer to a single core, and the potency of a promoter comes from having several cores in a row.

## Where it acts

MREs sit in proximal promoters, typically within a few hundred base pairs of the start site, and the classic arrangement is a tandem cluster: the mouse and human metallothionein promoters carry five or more. Beyond metallothioneins, target-gene searches identified zinc transporters (including SLC30A1/ZnT1), selenoprotein and glutathione-pathway genes, and stress-response genes, so the element marks a metal-and-oxidative-stress promoter module rather than a tissue-specific enhancer. Occupancy is inducible, which sets this motif apart from most in the atlas: in unstressed cells many strong MREs are unoccupied, and the same promoter can go from no signal to heavy signal within an hour of zinc or cadmium exposure. MTF1 also handles the opposite extreme, activating a different gene set under copper starvation, so the direction of the response depends on context. No named composite element pairs MTF1 with another factor, but MREs frequently sit next to antioxidant response elements and major late transcription factor sites in the same promoters.

## Biology and disease

Cells lacking MTF1 lose both basal and metal-induced metallothionein expression and become hypersensitive to cadmium. Mouse Mtf1 knockout dies around embryonic day 14 with liver degeneration; Drosophila MTF-1 null flies are viable in normal conditions but cannot survive heavy-metal load or copper starvation, which frames the factor as a homeostatic buffer rather than a developmental regulator. In humans the interest is largely toxicological and oncological: MTF1 mediates cadmium responses implicated in prostate carcinogenesis, contributes to chemoresistance through metallothionein induction, and has been recovered in screens as a modifier of mutant huntingtin toxicity. There is no classical Mendelian MTF1 disease.

## Reading a hit

TGCRCNC is short. A genome of three billion base pairs contains millions of matches, the great majority of which are never bound, so a single MRE match in a promoter is weak evidence on its own. Two things strengthen it: a tandem cluster of two or more cores within about 100 base pairs, and a promoter whose expression is metal-, zinc- or cadmium-responsive. Conversely, absence of MTF1 signal in a resting-cell ChIP dataset says nothing, because occupancy requires induction. Paralogue ambiguity is not an issue here, since no other human factor is known to read this word, but the short core does overlap by chance with parts of longer GC-rich motifs, so check whether a hit is better explained by a neighbouring family. The in vitro (S/M) evidence behind the HOCOMOCO and CIS-BP matrices supports direct binding, so this is one motif where the label is well grounded.
families.caveats: The protein-to-motif link is solid: MREs were defined functionally, MTF1 was purified on them, and the database matrices rest on in vitro selection rather than ChIP alone. The weakness is length. With roughly seven informative positions, matches occur by chance throughout the genome and most are not bound, so a lone MRE is not evidence of regulation. Require a tandem cluster, or a demonstrated metal response, before calling a site functional. Occupancy is also conditional: MTF1 only binds when free zinc is elevated, so both positive and negative ChIP results depend entirely on the metal status of the cells assayed. The longer in vitro consensus adds flanking preferences that functional MREs frequently violate.

families.name: ZFP57 / imprinting
families.def: Methylated TGCCGC hexamer at imprinting control regions. ZFP57, ZNF445.
families.short: ZFP57 is a KRAB zinc-finger protein that reads a six-base sequence, TGCCGC, but only when the CpG inside it is methylated. That combination of a short site and a methylation requirement lets it mark the methylated parental allele at imprinting control regions, the germline-methylated switches that restrict about two dozen loci to expression from one parent's chromosome. ZFP57 binds together with the corepressor TRIM28/KAP1 and DNA methyltransferases, shielding those regions from the wave of demethylation that follows fertilization. The larger zinc finger ZNF445 reads the same element and covers most of the same regions, which is why loss of ZFP57 alone produces imprinting defects with incomplete penetrance. In humans, recessive ZFP57 mutations cause transient neonatal diabetes with hypomethylation at multiple imprinted loci.
families.long:
## The factors

ZFP57 (6p22.1, formerly C6orf40) is a KRAB zinc-finger protein with a short tandem array of C2H2 fingers, of which only the first two are needed for sequence recognition. Like other KZFPs it carries an N-terminal KRAB domain that binds the corepressor TRIM28/KAP1, and in mouse embryonic stem cells ZFP57 and KAP1 occupy imprinting control regions (ICRs) together with DNA methyltransferases and the hemimethylated-DNA-binding protein NP95/UHRF1 (Quenneville et al. 2011). ZFP57 is a maternal-zygotic effect gene: protein and transcript are supplied by the oocyte and the gene is also expressed in the embryo (Li et al. 2008). ZNF445 (3p21.31, also catalogued as ZKSCAN15/ZSCAN47) is a much larger zinc finger that binds the same regions, can be traced back to the origins of imprinting, and is expressed earlier in the embryo than ZNF/ZFP57 (Takahashi et al. 2019). This entry holds five matrices for the two proteins; a sixth label, the Vierstra archetype AC0364, is annotated only as "ZFP".

## The motif

The literature consensus is the hexamer TGCCGC carrying a methylated CpG. A 1.0 Angstrom crystal structure of the two relevant Zfp57 fingers on fully methylated DNA shows finger 1 contacting the 5' half (TGC) and finger 2 the 3' half (CGC). The two 5-methylcytosines are read asymmetrically: one packs against Arg178, which simultaneously contacts the neighbouring 3' guanine in a 5mC-Arg-G arrangement, while the other is read through a layer of ordered water. Affinity falls for unmodified DNA and for the oxidation products of 5mC, and two point mutations found in patients abolish binding (Liu et al. 2012). The atlas matrices agree with this. JASPAR MA1583.2 is TGCCGCA; HOCOMOCO, CIS-BP and the Vierstra archetype all give GCGGCA, which is the reverse complement of TGCCGC, so the apparent disagreement with the literature consensus is only a choice of strand. Family cohesion is 0.76, the highest value among the zinc-finger entries in this group and the level expected of a genuinely single motif. One member does not fit: the CIS-BP model for ZNF445 (M07674) is a 29 bp, 31-bit matrix unrelated to the hexamer, and nothing else in the atlas resembles it.

## Where it acts

ICRs, also called germline differentially methylated regions, number on the order of 20 to 25 in human and mouse and include the regions controlling SNRPN, KCNQ1OT1, H19/IGF2, GNAS and PLAGL1. ZFP57 and KAP1 bind only the H3K9me3-bearing, DNA-methylated allele, so occupancy is monoallelic by construction (Quenneville et al. 2011). Binding is not confined to ICRs: several tens of additional methylated loci carry the hexamer and lose methylation when ZFP57 is deleted in ES cells, and allele-specific ZFP57 binding also occurs at non-imprinted monoallelically expressed regions (Strogantsev et al. 2015). Real ICRs usually contain a cluster of hexamers rather than one copy, and clustering discriminates far better than any single match.

## Biology and disease

Mice lacking only zygotic Zfp57 show partial neonatal lethality; removing maternal and zygotic function together is close to fully embryonic lethal, and maternal methylation imprints fail to be established at the Snrpn region (Li et al. 2008). In humans, recessive ZFP57 mutations cause transient neonatal diabetes mellitus with mosaic hypomethylation at multiple imprinted loci, the first heritable multi-locus imprinting disorder compatible with life (Mackay et al. 2008), with long-term clinical follow-up reported later (Boonen et al. 2013). Penetrance is incomplete, which is what motivated the search that found ZNF445: in mice Zfp445 and Zfp57 together maintain all but one ICR, and in humans ZNF445 is intolerant of loss-of-function variation, suggesting it carries more of the load than ZFP57 (Takahashi et al. 2019).

## Reading a hit

A six-base site occurs by chance roughly once every few kilobases per strand, so an isolated TGCCGC match licenses no conclusion. Three things make a hit interesting: the CpG is methylated in your sample, several copies cluster within a few hundred bases, and the interval overlaps an annotated germline DMR. Position-weight-matrix scanning cannot see methylation, so a scan returns candidate sites only. ZFP57 and ZNF445 cannot be separated from sequence. Neither can every GCGGC-containing zinc-finger motif: the HOCOMOCO model for ZNF729, a KRAB zinc finger with no known imprinting role, is TGCGGCAG, and its nearest neighbour anywhere in the atlas is the ZFP57 matrix. The HOCOMOCO ZFP57 model itself is ChIP-derived (evidence code P, grade B), so confidence that this protein binds this sequence rests on the structure and biochemistry in the primary papers rather than on the motif model.
families.caveats: A TGCCGC match is a candidate, not a site. The hexamer is short enough to appear roughly a million times in the genome, and the property that makes it functional, CpG methylation, is invisible to motif scanning. Treat a hit as meaningful only with methylation data, clustered copies, or germline-DMR annotation. The motif does not distinguish ZFP57 from ZNF445, and short GCGGC-containing motifs of unrelated KRAB zinc fingers such as ZNF729 score almost as well. The ZFP57 models in HOCOMOCO and the Vierstra set are ChIP-derived or unnamed; the in vitro and structural support comes from the primary literature, not from these matrices.

families.name: Telobox (TERF1/TERF2/ZBTB48)
families.def: Telomeric TTAGGG repeat binders. TERF1, TERF2, ZBTB48/TZAP.
families.short: The telobox factors TERF1 (TRF1) and TERF2 (TRF2) bind the vertebrate telomeric repeat TTAGGG through a single Myb-type helix-turn-helix domain that is, structurally, a homeodomain-like fold. Both work as preformed homodimers, and the dimer reads two YTAGGGTTR half-sites whose spacing and orientation are almost unconstrained, so the footprint on a tandem repeat array is flexible rather than fixed. ZBTB48 (TZAP) is a zinc-finger protein that binds the same telomeric and subtelomeric variant repeats and triggers telomere trimming. Because the motif is the telomeric repeat itself, a match in the genome is almost always either a true telomere, a subtelomeric region, or an interstitial telomeric sequence - not a conventional regulatory element.
families.long:
## The factors

Human telomeres end in several kilobases of tandem TTAGGG repeats, bound by the six-protein shelterin
complex. Two shelterin subunits supply the double-stranded DNA contact: TERF1 (TRF1) and TERF2 (TRF2).
Each has an N-terminal domain (acidic in TRF1, basic in TRF2), a central TRFH homodimerization domain, and
a C-terminal Myb/SANT-type helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain. The Myb domain here is a single repeat, not
the three-repeat array of c-MYB, and crystal and NMR structures show that it adopts a homeodomain-like
fold, the same solution the budding-yeast telomere protein Rap1 uses. Both proteins bind DNA as preformed
homodimers in which the two DNA-binding domains are independent structural units on a flexible tether. The
family name comes from the telobox, a Myb-related telomeric DNA-binding motif recognized as a conserved
module across yeast, plants and humans.

ZBTB48, also called TZAP or HKR3, is grouped here because it binds the same sequence, but it is a
different protein class: a BTB/POZ zinc-finger factor, not a telobox protein. It binds telomeric and
subtelomeric variant repeats directly, competes with TRF1 and TRF2 for long telomeres, and also acts as a
conventional transcriptional activator at a small set of promoters. TRF1 and TRF2 are broadly expressed
and essential; ZBTB48 is a more transient telomere visitor.

## The motif

The literature consensus is the telomeric repeat itself, TTAGGG, and in practice the unit the protein
reads is the 7-9 bp half-site YTAGGGTTR. High-resolution crystal structures of the TRF1 and TRF2
DNA-binding domains on telomeric DNA show that both recognize the same TAGGGTT site, that two of the three
G-C base pairs characteristic of the repeat are read specifically, and that an unusually large number of
ordered water molecules mediate the protein-DNA interface. SELEX with dimeric TRF1 defined the site as
bipartite: two YTAGGGTTR half-sites with essentially no constraint on distance or relative orientation,
simultaneously contacted by one dimer, with the intervening DNA looped out. A tandem repeat array
therefore does not have one canonical binding register.

The matrices in this atlas all describe fragments of this repeat in one orientation or the other: AGGGTT
(HOCOMOCO TERF1), AACCCTA (CIS-BP TERF2), TCCCTAA and GGTCCCTDA (ZBTB48/TZAP), GGTCCCT (a Vierstra ZBTB
archetype). These are the same repeat unit read on opposite strands and phased differently, which is why
the atlas medoid, TCCCTAA, looks unlike TTAGGG at first glance - it is CCCTAA, the reverse complement,
shifted by one. Family cohesion is about 0.81, and the residual spread is phase and strand, not genuine
specificity differences. None of these short matrices captures the dimeric bipartite logic, so a scan
reports individual half-sites rather than functional dimer footprints. The members are not distinguishable
from sequence: TRF1, TRF2 and ZBTB48 all read the same repeat.

## Where it acts

Almost everywhere this motif occurs it is a telomeric repeat. ChIP-seq for TRF1 and TRF2 recovers
telomeres, subtelomeric regions, and a defined subset of interstitial telomeric sequences (ITSs) -
internal blocks of degenerate TTAGGG repeats scattered through the genome, many of them near or within
gene introns - plus some centromeric and pericentromeric satellite DNA. ITSs are themselves unstable and
are recombination-prone. ZBTB48 additionally binds subtelomeric variant repeats. So the honest description
of the genomic distribution is: chromosome ends, subtelomeres, ITSs and satellite arrays, with only a
small number of genuine promoter sites, such as the ZBTB48 target MTFP1. This motif is not a promoter
element in the ordinary sense, and CpG-island promoter enrichment is not expected.

## Biology and disease

TRF1 is a negative regulator of telomere length: overexpression shortens telomeres progressively and a
dominant-negative form lengthens them, in telomerase-positive cells. TRF2 protects chromosome ends from
being processed as double-strand breaks; its inhibition causes end-to-end chromosome fusions and triggers
an ATM-dependent damage response, and TRF2 is implicated in the t-loop structure at telomeres, although
the crystal structures show no DNA distortion that would explain that activity. ZBTB48/TZAP binds
preferentially to long telomeres, where shelterin density is low, and initiates telomere trimming - rapid
deletion of telomeric repeats - which sets an upper limit on telomere length; it is also a negative
regulator of telomere length in cancer cells regardless of their telomere-maintenance mechanism. Telomere
dysfunction through these routes connects to senescence, genome instability in cancer, and the
telomere-biology disorders, and TRF1 and TRF2 are reviewed as shelterin components in that context.

## Reading a hit

The practical rule for this family is different from every other family in the atlas: a match is a
telomeric repeat, so ask where it is before asking who bound it. If the hit is at a chromosome end or in a
subtelomere, it is telomeric. If it is internal, the most likely explanation is an interstitial telomeric
sequence or a satellite array, and a TTAGGG-rich internal block will score highly whether or not any
protein binds it. Only after excluding those should a hit be read as a regulatory element. The members
cannot be separated by sequence - TRF1, TRF2 and ZBTB48 all read TTAGGG - and the short matrices available
represent single half-sites rather than the flexible bipartite site a TRF dimer actually occupies, so
scores will not track dimer affinity. The CIS-BP TERF2 model is inferred from mouse Terf2 at 92%
DNA-binding-domain identity rather than measured on the human protein, the HOCOMOCO TZAP model is
ChIP-only (grade B), and the Vierstra archetype is labelled for the broad ZBTB group rather than for
ZBTB48 specifically.
families.caveats: This motif is the telomeric repeat, so most matches are telomeric, subtelomeric, interstitial telomeric sequence or satellite DNA rather than regulatory elements - check location before interpreting. TRF1, TRF2 and ZBTB48 all read the same TTAGGG repeat and cannot be separated by sequence. The available matrices (6-9 bp fragments in both orientations; the medoid TCCCTAA is the reverse complement, phase shifted) capture single half-sites, whereas TRF dimers bind two YTAGGGTTR half-sites with almost no spacing or orientation constraint, so scores do not track real affinity. The CIS-BP TERF2 model is inferred from mouse Terf2 (92% DBD identity), the HOCOMOCO TZAP model is ChIP-only at grade B, and the Vierstra archetype is labelled for ZBTB generally.

families.name: SRF
families.def: CArG box CCW6GG. SRF.
families.short: The CArG box is the site of a single protein, serum response factor, which binds as a homodimer through a MADS box - the same fold MEF2 uses, reading a different sequence. The element is CC(A/T)6GG: a ten-base near-palindrome in which the outer CC and GG carry the specificity and the six central A/T positions are effectively free, giving a well-defined but degenerate site. SRF is expressed almost everywhere and is constitutively bound to many of its sites; what changes with signalling is not occupancy but which coactivator family it recruits - the ETS-domain TCF proteins downstream of MAP kinase, or the actin-regulated MRTF proteins downstream of Rho. Both bind the same CArG box, so the motif does not tell you which programme is running.
families.long:
## The factors

SRF is one protein, encoded by one gene, and this family has one member. Its DNA-binding and dimerisation function sits in a MADS box of about 57 residues with two extensions: an N-terminal one that MEF2 lacks, and a C-terminal B-box that docks one class of cofactor. The crystal structure of the SRF core on a serum response element showed that the dimer binds an alpha-helix into the widened major groove of each half-site and that the recognised feature is as much DNA shape as base identity - the intrinsic and induced bend of the CArG box is what SRF reads. SRF is broadly and constitutively expressed, and its activity is set by cofactors rather than by its own abundance or nuclear entry. Two families compete for it. The ternary complex factors ELK1, ELK4 (SAP-1) and ELK3 dock on the B-box through a short peptide and simultaneously contact an adjacent ETS site with their own ETS domain; they are activated by ERK and p38 phosphorylation, and the ternary-complex structure showed that the B-box contact dominates their recruitment. The myocardin-related transcription factors MRTFA (MKL1/MAL), MRTFB and MYOCD instead bind the MADS domain itself, and MRTFA and MRTFB are sequestered by monomeric actin until Rho-driven actin polymerisation releases them.

## The motif

The CArG box is CC(A/T)6GG, ten bases, a near-palindrome. Nearly all of the information is in the outer CCW and WGG; the six central positions are constrained only to be A or T, which is why the element is often described as heavily degenerate - one genome-wide survey characterised it as a 1,216-fold degenerate cis element once CArG-like variants are included. Contacts from the MADS helix reach the guanines of the GG step and the adjacent bases, and basic residues clamp the phosphate backbone across the bend. Literature and data agree here: the four models (JASPAR, HOCOMOCO, CIS-BP and one Vierstra archetype) converge on CCATATATGG, with family cohesion 0.93, the highest in this batch. The useful contrast is with MEF2, the other vertebrate MADS family: both read a ten-base A/T-cored near-palindrome, but SRF requires CC and GG at the ends where MEF2 requires CTA and TAG. That difference is small in edit distance but large in practice; a few in vitro MEF2 models in these collections drift into CArG-like CCAAATATGG, so the database boundary is less clean than the protein boundary. One further practical point: the cofactor switch does not change the motif. A TCF-driven serum response element, such as the c-fos SRE, is a CArG box plus a nearby ETS site; an MRTF-driven CArG box, such as those in cytoskeletal genes, is frequently a CArG box with no ETS site at all. The presence or absence of the flanking ETS site, not the CArG itself, is what distinguishes the two.

## Where it acts

CArG boxes are predominantly proximal promoter elements, usually within a few hundred base pairs of the transcription start site, which sets SRF apart from the enhancer-biased MEF2. They are not CpG-island features. A comparative-genomics screen of conserved CArG elements near human and mouse orthologous transcription start sites recovered more than 100 candidate targets and validated 60 of 89 tested; 26 of those encode cytoskeletal, contractile or adhesion proteins. The characteristic composite is the serum response element itself - CArG plus an ETS site - at immediate-early genes including FOS and EGR1. In smooth muscle, CArG and CArG-like elements cluster in the promoters of ACTA2, MYH11, TAGLN and CNN1.

## Biology and disease

SRF sits at the junction of growth-factor signalling and the actin cytoskeleton. Deleting Srf in the mouse blocks mesoderm formation and is lethal in early gastrulation; conditional deletion in the developing heart produces myocardial defects and embryonic lethality. In fibroblasts, the immediate transcriptional response to serum is dominated by Rho-actin signalling to the MRTF coactivators rather than by the TCF arm, and conversely the TCF arm handles much of the ERK-driven immediate-early response. The target set explains the phenotypes: smooth muscle contractile genes, cytoskeletal and focal-adhesion genes, and the immediate-early genes. SRF has been implicated in cardiac hypertrophy and dilated cardiomyopathy, in vascular smooth-muscle phenotypic switching in atherosclerosis, and, through MRTFA, in tumour-cell migration and mechanotransduction. Sun and colleagues described SRF as an ancient regulator of the actin cytoskeleton.

## Reading a hit

A CArG hit is more interpretable than most, for three reasons: there is only one protein in the family, so there is no paralogue problem; the site is ten bases with four well-constrained positions; and SRF is expressed nearly everywhere, so a match is not disqualified by cell type. The limits are the degeneracy and the position bias. CCW6GG still occurs often by chance, and the A/T core means AT-rich regions produce false positives, so a match carries much more weight in a proximal promoter than in random intergenic DNA. Note one artefact of how this atlas is built: because SRF is a single-member family, every SRF model's nearest neighbours in motif space are mostly outside the family - label agreement is 0.3 for all four - and those neighbours are MEF2 and other MADS motifs. That is a property of a singleton family, not a sign the labels are wrong. Finally, the hit says nothing about which cofactor arm is active: for that, look for an ETS site within roughly 20 bp (TCF-type), or its absence at a cytoskeletal gene (MRTF-type).
families.caveats: Unusually for this atlas, there is no paralogue problem: SRF is the only member, so a CArG hit names the protein. The real limits are degeneracy and position. CC(A/T)6GG constrains only four bases, so chance matches are frequent and AT-rich sequence inflates them; weight a hit far more heavily in a proximal promoter, where real CArG boxes concentrate, than in intergenic DNA. A hit also says nothing about which coactivator arm is active, since TCF and MRTF use the same element - look for an adjacent ETS site to distinguish them. The low label-agreement values on all four SRF models reflect the family being a singleton surrounded by MEF2 and other MADS motifs, not mislabelling.

families.name: CSL / RBPJ
families.def: GTGGGAA. RBPJ (SUH), plus NOTCH-dependent dimer sites.
families.short: CSL is the DNA-binding transcription factor at the end of the Notch pathway, named for its three orthologues: CBF1/RBPJ in mammals, Suppressor of Hairless in Drosophila and LAG-1 in C. elegans. Humans have one broadly expressed gene, RBPJ, plus the pancreas-restricted paralogue RBPJL. RBPJ binds the seven-base element GTGGGAA, often written on the other strand as TTCCCAC, and does so whether or not Notch is active: without a Notch intracellular domain it recruits corepressors, and with one it assembles an activating ternary complex with Mastermind-like coactivators. Some Notch targets carry two sites in a head-to-head pair with fixed spacing, an SPS, which allows two Notch complexes to dimerize. Notch signaling through RBPJ controls lateral inhibition, T-cell specification and vascular development, and is constitutively activated in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
families.long:
## The factors

There is essentially one CSL protein per genome. In humans the gene is RBPJ (older names RBP-J,
RBPSUH, CBF1); the paralogue RBPJL (RBPSUHL) is restricted to pancreatic acinar cells, where it
replaces RBPJ in the PTF1 complex. RBPJ is expressed in nearly every tissue. It is not a
Notch-specific protein in the sense of being present only when Notch is: RBPJ is constitutive,
and Notch activation changes what RBPJ does rather than whether it exists. The DNA-binding
module has three parts: an N-terminal domain with a Rel-homology-like fold, a beta-trefoil
domain (BTD) and a C-terminal domain. The crystal structure of CSL on DNA showed that the
Rel-like domain and the BTD grip the site from opposite faces, with the BTD doing double duty as
the docking site for the RAM peptide of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD). On Notch
activation, NICD binds RBPJ and recruits a Mastermind-like coactivator (MAML1-3) to form the
ternary complex; in the absence of NICD, RBPJ binds corepressors such as SPEN/SHARP and
associated histone deacetylases and demethylases. So the same protein on the same sequence can
repress or activate.

## The motif

The literature consensus is GTGGGAA, usually written with a 5' pyrimidine as YGTGGGAA, and its
reverse-strand form is TTCCCAC. Only about six or seven positions carry information, and the
models in these databases are short accordingly: the representative motif here is TTCCCA, which
is simply the reverse complement of TGGGAA with the 5' GT trimmed off, and JASPAR's RBPJ matrix
(TGGGAA) is the same element on the forward strand. The GGG at the center is the least tolerant
part of the site. Only one symbol, RBPJ, appears across all four databases, so there is no
paralogue problem inside the family, and the four models agree closely (cohesion 0.93). The
difficulty is external. TGGGAA and its complement TTCCCA sit inside the purine-rich sequence
space used by ETS cores (GGAA), NFAT (GGAAA) and the half-sites of NF-kB and STAT models, and
the label-agreement statistics for all four RBPJ motifs are low (0.3) precisely because their
nearest neighbours across the four databases frequently belong to those families. A separate
feature is site architecture rather than sequence: some Notch-responsive promoters carry two
CSL sites in head-to-head orientation with a spacer of roughly 15-17 bp, the Su(H)-paired site
or SPS, first described in the Drosophila Enhancer of split complex. The spacing and orientation
matter because they allow the ankyrin repeat domains of two Notch molecules to contact each
other across the DNA, which sharpens the response. No PWM captures an SPS; you have to look for
two matches at the right distance and orientation.

## Where it acts

RBPJ sites are found in both promoters and enhancers, and the best-studied targets are the HES
and HEY families (HES1, HES5, HEY1, HEY2), DTX1, NRARP, and, in lymphoid cells, PTCRA, IL2RA and
MYC. Genome-wide, RBPJ and Notch1 occupy thousands of sites, and occupancy is dynamic: in
Drosophila, Su(H) binding at target enhancers is transient and only partly overlaps its
Notch-independent binding, and in mammalian cells RBPJ occupancy at many sites increases on
Notch activation rather than being fixed. Conversely, a subset of sites is occupied by CSL
without Notch and functions in default repression, keeping targets off in cells that have not
received a signal. RBPJ co-occurs with lineage factors that determine which of its sites are
used: TCF/LEF and GATA3 in T cells, ETS and RUNX factors at lymphoid enhancers, and PTF1A
through RBPJL in pancreas.

## Biology and disease

Rbpj-null mouse embryos die around embryonic day 10 with defects in somitogenesis and
vasculature, phenocopying loss of Notch1 more closely than any single ligand mutant. Through
Notch, RBPJ drives lateral inhibition in neurogenesis, T-cell versus B-cell specification,
arterial-venous specification and intestinal secretory-versus-absorptive choice. Activating
NOTCH1 mutations that stabilize NICD are the commonest genetic lesion in T-cell acute
lymphoblastic leukemia, and the resulting Notch1/RBPJ complexes bind a largely conserved set of
enhancers in human and mouse leukemia cells. Notch loss of function causes disease as well:
NOTCH3 in CADASIL, JAG1 and NOTCH2 in Alagille syndrome, and inactivating NOTCH1 mutations in
squamous carcinomas, where the pathway is tumor-suppressive. RBPJ itself is mutated in Adams-Oliver
syndrome.

## Reading a hit

The important caution is interpretive, not statistical: a match to the RBPJ motif, and even
measured RBPJ occupancy, does not mean Notch signaling is active at that site. RBPJ binds
constitutively and represses in the unsignaled state, so the sequence marks a potential Notch
response element, not a signaled one. To claim active signaling you need evidence for NICD or
MAML at the site, or a change in output on gamma-secretase inhibition. The site is also short:
six or seven informative bases occur often by chance, and the purine-rich core is easily
confused with ETS, NFAT or NF-kB half-sites, which is what the low label-agreement scores in
these data reflect. Two matches in head-to-head orientation about 15-17 bp apart are much
stronger evidence than one.
families.caveats: One factor, RBPJ, so a hit does not have a paralogue problem inside the family; the risk is outside it. The informative core is only six or seven bases and overlaps ETS, NFAT and NF-kB purine-rich half-sites, which is why all four RBPJ models here score low label agreement against the other databases. The HOCOMOCO model (SUH.H14CORE.0.P.B) is ChIP-derived, so it reports where RBPJ was found, not what RBPJ binds in isolation. Most importantly, RBPJ occupies sites constitutively and represses without Notch, so neither a sequence match nor a ChIP peak licenses the conclusion that Notch signaling is active.
