families.name: PROX1 (Prospero)
families.def: Prospero-domain homeodomain-like factor PROX1.
families.short: PROX1 is the human counterpart of Drosophila Prospero, and it binds DNA with a module unlike any other homeodomain: a highly divergent homeodomain fused to a conserved Prospero domain, the two folding into one structural unit called the homeo-prospero domain. That unit reads a non-canonical site, TAAGACG, rather than the TAAT core used by ordinary homeodomains, and the Prospero domain both aligns the protein on DNA and masks a nuclear export signal, coupling DNA binding to where the protein sits in the cell. PROX1 is essential for lymphatic endothelium, lens fibre elongation, liver and pancreas development and dentate gyrus identity, and it also works without its own site by tethering to nuclear receptors. A single human gene, so no paralogue ambiguity.
families.long:
## The factors

This family has effectively one member in human, PROX1, a 737-residue protein; PROX2 is a shorter relative
with much less supporting data. PROX1 was cloned as the vertebrate homologue of *Drosophila* Prospero, a
pan-neural factor required for proper differentiation of neuronal lineages. The DNA-binding module sits at
the C terminus and is unusual enough that standard domain annotation does not register a homeobox in PROX1
at all. It consists of a highly divergent putative homeodomain immediately followed by a conserved
Prospero domain, and the crystal structures showed that these two regions are not separable: they fold as a
single structural unit, the homeo-prospero domain. The homeodomain region retains a three-helix fold
similar to a canonical homeodomain, the Prospero domain is a four-helix bundle, and the recognition helix
bridges the two. PROX1 binds as a monomer through this unit; it has no zinc fingers, leucine zipper or
other dimerisation module. Both the fly and human proteins also act on other transcription factors: 
Prospero modulates the DNA-binding properties of conventional homeodomain proteins such as Deformed, and
PROX1 modulates nuclear receptors, in both cases through the same conserved C-terminal region that binds
DNA but through activities that are formally independent of it.

## The motif

The functionally validated Prospero target sequence is TAAGACG, which is not a homeodomain site: there is
no TAAT core, and the bases contacted are read by residues that do not correspond to the canonical
homeodomain specificity positions. The co-crystal structure of the homeo-prospero domain with DNA showed
Lys1290, Asn1294 and Asp1297, invariant across the family, making the specific contacts, and it reconciled
two different sequences that had previously been proposed as Prospero targets, the TAAGACG element and a
looser SELEX-derived pyrimidine-rich consensus. The Prospero domain does not itself contact many bases; its
job is to align the protein correctly on the site. In vitro selection on human PROX1 extends the site to an
eleven-position model, AAGACGCCTTA, whose reverse complement reads TAAGGCGTCTT; the TAAGACG core of the
literature consensus is contained in it, and the extra positions are a weakly specified 3' half that makes
the whole thing look like a loose near-palindrome of two AAG-type half sites. All four database models in
the family agree on this shape, with a cohesion of 0.89, and the only weak entry is a shortened HOCOMOCO
model reduced to CGTCTT. Because there is one gene, there is no paralogue problem: the motif and the
protein correspond one to one.

## Where it acts

PROX1 acts at promoters and enhancers of lineage genes in the tissues where it is expressed: lymphatic
endothelium, lens, liver, pancreas, heart, lymphocytes and dentate gyrus granule cells. A large part of its
genomic footprint, though, is not explained by its own site. PROX1 functions as a corepressor and
coregulator of nuclear receptors, including liver receptor homologue-1, the oestrogen-related receptor
ERRalpha with its coactivator PGC-1alpha, and the retinoic-acid-related orphan receptors; in these
complexes it is recruited to the receptor's own response element. So PROX1 ChIP peaks are expected to be
enriched for nuclear receptor half sites as well as for TAAGACG, and in bioenergetic gene programs the
nuclear receptor element may be the only motif present. There is no widely used name for a PROX1 composite
element.

## Biology and disease

Prox1-null mouse embryos fail to form a lymphatic vasculature: lymphatic endothelial cells do not bud from
the embryonic veins, which established PROX1 as the switch for lymphatic endothelial identity. Forced PROX1
expression in blood vascular endothelial cells reprogrammes them toward a lymphatic phenotype, and this
remains one of the cleaner examples of single-factor endothelial fate conversion. Prox1 loss also blocks
lens fibre elongation, causing a cataract-like phenotype, and blocks hepatocyte migration during liver
development. In the brain, Prox1 postmitotically specifies dentate gyrus granule cell identity in
preference to CA3 pyramidal identity. Through ERRalpha/PGC-1alpha, PROX1 restrains mitochondrial and
bioenergetic gene expression. In cancer the direction of effect is context-dependent and contested; in
intestinal tumorigenesis a PROX1-positive tumour stem or progenitor population has been described that
contributes to tumour growth, while other settings report tumour-suppressive behaviour.

## Reading a hit

A good TAAGACG or AAGACGCCTTA match is unusually informative for a homeodomain-class family, because the
site shares nothing with the TAAT core that hundreds of other homeodomain factors use, and because there is
only one human protein that reads it. Two limits. The site is short and only moderately constrained, so
chance occurrence is not negligible in a large search space, and matches should be weighted by whether
PROX1 is expressed in the tissue at all; it is off in most adult somatic cell types. More importantly, the
converse inference fails: a PROX1 ChIP peak with no TAAGACG is not evidence against PROX1 involvement,
because much of what PROX1 does genomically is tethered to nuclear receptors. The available models rest on
in vitro selection, which supports the statement that PROX1 binds this sequence, and the crystal structure
supports it independently; that is a stronger evidence base than most families in this atlas.
families.caveats: One gene, one motif, so no paralogue ambiguity, and the site is structurally validated by a co-crystal of the homeo-prospero domain with DNA. The limits are elsewhere. TAAGACG is only seven constrained positions, so chance matches are common in large searches and should be filtered by whether PROX1 is expressed. The database models come from in vitro selection, which is good evidence for sequence but not for occupancy. And a large fraction of PROX1 genomic action is indirect: it is recruited as a coregulator by nuclear receptors including LRH-1, ERRalpha and RORs, so PROX1 ChIP peaks are expected to carry nuclear receptor elements rather than, or in addition to, this motif.

families.name: Other HMG-box
families.def: HMG-box factors outside SOX and TCF/LEF: HMG20A/20B, BBX, HMGB-like archetypes.
families.short: This entry holds the HMG-box factors that are neither SOX nor TCF/LEF: HMG20A (iBRAF), HMG20B (BRAF35) and BBX (bobby sox homolog). They share only the fold. HMG20A and HMG20B are paralogous subunits of chromatin complexes - HMG20B of the LSD1-CoREST-HDAC complex that keeps neuronal genes off in non-neuronal cells, HMG20A of KMT2A/MLL complexes that turn them on - so their genomic distribution is largely set by whichever partner recruits the complex. BBX is a poorly characterized protein that groups phylogenetically with CIC rather than with SOX. The three measured motifs are unrelated to each other and to the SOX core, and this is the least coherent family in the HMG class; a hit here should be treated as a lead, not an identification.
families.long:
## The factors

Three proteins are collected here, and what they have in common is a single HMG box, not a site.
HMG20B, originally named BRAF35 (BRCA2-associated factor 35), is a core subunit of the BHC
complex that pairs LSD1 (KDM1A) and CoREST with histone deacetylases and represses neuronal
genes in non-neuronal cells. HMG20A, its paralogue, was named iBRAF for inhibitor of BRAF35: it
opposes that complex and instead recruits KMT2A/MLL to drive neuronal gene expression, and it is
also found in a KMT2A-associated PHF5A-PHF14-HMG20A-RAI1 subcomplex. HMG20B has a separate
mitotic function that depends on its interaction with the BRC repeats of BRCA2. Both are broadly
expressed. BBX is a larger, much less studied protein, broadly expressed with enrichment in the
central nervous system, which phylogenetic analysis places with CIC (capicua) in an HMG-box
subfamily distinct from both SOX and TCF/LEF. The important structural point is that most HMG
boxes are architectural rather than sequence-reading domains: the HMGB1/HMGB2 type binds and
bends DNA with little sequence preference, and only a minority of the superfamily - SOX,
TCF/LEF, CIC and a few others - has demonstrable sequence specificity. Nothing published
establishes that HMG20A or HMG20B selects a specific sequence in cells.

## The motif

There is no single consensus for this family, which is why none is given. The four models here
disagree with each other; cohesion is 0.45, the lowest of the HMG-class families. BBX gives the
most informative model, and it is the family medoid: CIS-BP reports TGAACRVCGTTCA (15.1 bits)
and the Vierstra archetype AC0363 independently reports TGAACRNYGTTCA (15.8 bits). These are the
same 13-base element - an inverted repeat, since TGAAC and GTTCA are reverse complements, with
three variable bases between them. The half-site resembles the TGAAT half of the dimeric,
palindromic sites that appear in SOX models (Vierstra TGAATGTGCAGTCA, HOCOMOCO SOX1
TGAATANCATTCAT), differing at one position, which is consistent with BBX reading DNA in the same
general way as other sequence-specific HMG boxes. HMG20A's single HOCOMOCO model,
HM20A.H14CORE.0.SB.A, reads TCCCTAGGC (11.5 bits); its fourth field carries S, so it rests on
HT-SELEX rather than on ChIP, and it is graded A. CCTAGG is itself palindromic but bears no
relation to the SOX or TCF/LEF core. The HMG20B model, CIS-BP M02487_2.00, is ATTATAT (10.5
bits) and is inferred from the mouse protein at 94% DNA-binding-domain identity; a short AT-rich
string of this kind is what a non-sequence-specific HMG box tends to produce in a selection
experiment, and it should not be read as a recognition sequence.

## Where it acts

For HMG20A and HMG20B the practical answer is: wherever the complex goes. LSD1-CoREST-HDAC is
recruited to neuronal gene promoters largely by REST binding its own RE1/NRSE element, and KMT2A
complexes are recruited by their own targeting subunits; HMG20A and HMG20B come along as
subunits. Locations reported for them therefore track partner occupancy - neuronal gene
promoters, pancreatic islet regulatory regions where HMG20A is required for beta cell
maturation, adipocyte loci where HMG20A acts through MEF2C, and KMT2A targets in pancreatic
cancer stem cells. BBX has been mapped less. Its 13-base palindrome is specific by the standards
of this atlas: with two degenerate inner positions, TGAACRVCGTTCA is expected only a few hundred
times in a 3.1 Gb genome, against tens of thousands for the nine-base HMG20A model and millions
for a bare six-base HMG core.

## Biology and disease

HMG20B is required for repression of the neuronal program in non-neuronal cells and for
completion of mitosis, and its splicing has been implicated in breast cancer; the HMG20A locus
is a genome-wide-association signal for type 2 diabetes, and HMG20A is needed for functional
maturity of pancreatic beta cells, restrains adipogenesis through MEF2C, and supports the stem-
cell state in pancreatic cancer. The HMG20A/HMG20B antagonism is a clean example of two
paralogues with the same DNA-binding domain having opposite effects by virtue of the complexes
they join. BBX has been linked to phosphate homeostasis through regulation of FGF23 in bone, and
is maternally expressed and CNS-enriched in zebrafish and mouse. None of the three has an
established monogenic human disease.

## Reading a hit

Treat this family as a fold, not a motif: the models do not resemble one another and the family
cohesion is 0.45. The BBX palindrome is worth taking seriously as a sequence - two databases
derived it independently and it is long enough to be rare - but the label rests on in vitro
selection with no structural or functional follow-up, so "BBX site" is provisional, and because
the half-sites resemble those of dimeric SOX sites you should exclude SOX before settling on
BBX. An HMG20A match does not license the conclusion that HMG20A occupies the site: the HT-SELEX
evidence supports "this protein can bind this sequence", while in cells HMG20A is a passenger in
LSD1-CoREST and KMT2A complexes whose distribution is set by REST and other partners, so check
for an RE1/NRSE element nearby. The HMG20B model is mouse-inferred and low in information; do
not use it to call sites. More generally, a weak AT-rich match labelled with an HMG-box protein
is more likely to reflect a shape preference than a recognition sequence.
families.caveats: Low confidence throughout. This is a fold-defined group with no shared consensus and the lowest cohesion in the HMG class (0.45) across only four models. The BBX 13-base palindrome is reproduced by two databases and is rare enough to be useful, but rests on in vitro selection alone and its half-sites overlap those of dimeric SOX sites. The HMG20A motif has HT-SELEX support, yet HMG20A acts as a subunit of LSD1-CoREST and KMT2A complexes, so genomic locations attributed to it may belong to REST or another recruiting factor. The HMG20B model is inferred from mouse at 94% DNA-binding-domain identity and is an uninformative AT-rich string.

families.name: REST (NRSF)
families.def: 21-bp RE1/NRSE TTCAGCACCACGGACAGCGCC. REST.
families.short: REST, also called NRSF, is a single zinc-finger protein that recognizes RE1 (the neuron- restrictive silencer element), a 21-base-pair site that is one of the longest and most information- rich transcription-factor motifs in the human genome. Eight of its nine zinc fingers read two half-sites separated by a two-base spacer, which is why the element is long and unusually specific. REST recruits SIN3-HDAC and CoREST-LSD1 complexes to silence neuronal genes in non-neuronal cells, and is removed or degraded as neurons differentiate. Human and mouse genomes contain roughly one to two thousand canonical RE1s, many spread by transposable elements, plus a larger set of weaker non-canonical variants. Unusually for a PWM, a strong RE1 match is good evidence of real REST binding.
families.long:
## The factors

This family has one member. REST (RE1-silencing transcription factor) was identified twice in 1995:
as NRSF, a coordinate repressor of multiple neuron-specific genes, and as REST, a silencer protein
that restricts type II sodium channel expression to neurons. It contains nine C2H2 zinc fingers,
eight of which form the DNA-binding array, plus a separate C-terminal finger. REST is not itself a
catalytic repressor; it carries two repression domains that dock different corepressor machinery, an
N-terminal region that binds SIN3A with HDAC1 and HDAC2, and a C-terminal region that binds
CoREST/RCOR1, which in turn brings the demethylase LSD1/KDM1A and associated activities such as
G9a, CTDSP1 and MeCP2. REST is expressed broadly in non-neuronal tissue and in neural stem cells,
and its protein level falls sharply at neuronal differentiation. A truncated splice variant, REST4,
lacks most of the finger array. There is no paralogue in these databases, so the family and the
protein coincide.

## The motif

The canonical RE1/NRSE is written TTCAGCACCACGGACAGCGCC, 21 base pairs. It is best read as two
half-sites, a left half around TTCAGCACC and a right half around GGACAGCGCC, separated by a
two-nucleotide spacer that carries almost no information. Separate groups of zinc fingers engage the
two halves, which is the structural reason a single monomer can specify 19 informative positions;
by contrast most vertebrate factors specify six to ten. The spacer explains a discrepancy readers
will notice: the canonical string has AC at those two positions, while the JASPAR and HOCOMOCO
matrices show a weak preference for at, and the data consensus for this family is
TCAGCACCatGGACAGCgcC. These are the same element, differing only where the model is uninformative.
Non-canonical RE1s are common and functionally important. They include half-site RE1s, in which only
the left or right half is present; compound elements with expanded spacers; and single-substitution
variants throughout. Binding-affinity work shows that canonical motifs give strong occupancy at
targets shared by all cell types, whereas atypical motifs give weak occupancy at cell- and
tissue-specific targets, and, unexpectedly, that the weak sites are the most evolutionarily
constrained.

## Where it acts

RE1 elements sit in promoters, first introns and distal regions of neuronal genes: ion channels,
synaptic vesicle proteins, neurotransmitter receptors, neuronal microRNAs and splicing factors.
Position-specific scoring searches of the human genome recover on the order of 1,300 canonical RE1s
(about 1,000 in mouse), and a comparative-genomics model built from conserved occurrences produced
842 high-confidence human sites at 733 genes; larger surveys that admit weaker matches reach a few
thousand. The number is small for a vertebrate motif, which is the practical consequence of the
element's length. RE1s are present in all sequenced vertebrate genomes and absent from invertebrates
and protochordates, as is REST itself. A substantial fraction lie in repeats, and many RE1s fall
into closely related families associated with transposable elements, implying that transposon-
mediated duplication carried the element to new target genes during vertebrate evolution. The REST
cistrome is not conserved in detail: it is substantially larger in human than in mouse embryonic
stem cells.

## Biology and disease

REST silences neuronal genes in non-neuronal cells and keeps them repressed in progenitors,
releasing them as neurons mature. Its regulation is therefore mostly post-transcriptional, through
splicing to REST4 and through ubiquitin-dependent degradation at differentiation. The first
mammalian ChIP-sequencing experiment was performed on NRSF, and the resulting maps established the
tight coupling between the motif and occupancy that makes this factor unusual.

Several diseases turn on REST dosage. Wild-type huntingtin sequesters REST in the cytoplasm; mutant
huntingtin fails to, so REST enters the nucleus, occupies RE1s and represses target genes including
BDNF, contributing to Huntington disease pathology. In the ageing human cortex, nuclear REST rises
and is required for stress resistance, and is lost in Alzheimer disease. Germline truncating REST
mutations predispose to Wilms tumor, and REST loss or degradation has been reported in epithelial
tumors, so it behaves as a tumor suppressor in some contexts while its gain of function drives
pathology in others.

## Reading a hit

This is the family where a PWM hit means the most. With about 19 informative positions, a full-length
canonical RE1 match essentially does not occur by chance in a three-gigabase genome, and the great
majority of strong matches are occupied wherever REST is expressed. There is no paralogue problem:
the motif belongs to one protein. Two caveats remain. First, half-site and other non-canonical RE1s
score poorly and will be missed by a threshold tuned to the canonical element, yet they carry the
cell-type-specific part of the regulon, so a negative result at a neuronal gene is weak evidence.
Second, occupancy is not the same as repression: REST is bound at many sites in cells where the
target is expressed anyway, and the functional output depends on which corepressor complex is
recruited and on REST protein level, which falls in neurons. Because the element is long and
distinctive, ChIP-derived REST models are relatively clean, and an RE1-like motif appearing in
another factor's ChIP data usually means that factor is part of a REST corepressor complex.
families.caveats: This is the best case for trusting a PWM hit: a full canonical 21-bp RE1 has roughly 19 informative positions, has no paralogue competing for the label, and is rare enough that chance matches are negligible. The failure mode is the opposite of usual: thresholds set for the canonical element miss half-site and other non-canonical RE1s, which are numerous, weakly bound and carry the tissue-specific part of the regulon. A hit also does not imply repression, since REST occupies sites in cells where the target is expressed and its protein level and corepressor choice determine the output. Conversely, an RE1-like motif recovered from another factor's ChIP data usually means that factor sits in a REST corepressor complex.

families.name: ZBTB33 (Kaiso)
families.def: KBS TCCTGCNA and methyl-CpG CGCG sites. ZBTB33.
families.short: ZBTB33, better known as Kaiso, is a BTB/POZ zinc-finger repressor with only three C2H2 fingers and two distinct ways of reading DNA. It binds the non-methylated consensus TCCTGCNA - the Kaiso binding site, or KBS, whose minimal core is CTGCNA - and, separately, methylated CpG dinucleotides, with higher affinity for the KBS of the two. Crystal structures show both modes use the same first two fingers, with methylcytosine read through CH-to-O hydrogen bonds. Kaiso was found as a partner of p120-catenin, which blocks its DNA binding, and it links adhesion to transcription. Note that all four database matrices for ZBTB33 describe a CGCG-containing palindrome, TCTCGCGAGA, not the KBS.
families.long:
## The factors

Kaiso is a single-gene family. ZBTB33 encodes a roughly 670-residue protein with an N-terminal BTB/POZ dimerization and repression domain and, unusually for a BTB-ZF factor, only three C2H2 zinc fingers at the C terminus plus a short C-terminal extension. It was isolated in a yeast two-hybrid screen for partners of the Armadillo-family adhesion protein p120-catenin, and independently in Xenopus as a methylation-dependent repressor that associates with the N-CoR corepressor. p120-catenin binding inhibits Kaiso's DNA binding in both of its modes, which is the mechanistic basis for the claim that Kaiso couples cadherin-based adhesion to transcriptional output: when p120 is released from junctions it can sequester Kaiso off DNA. Repression is delivered through recruited corepressors including N-CoR and the MTG16/CBFA2T3 corepressor; Kaiso is also regulated by phosphorylation, with modification at Thr606 driving cytoplasmic accumulation and reduced repression of CDH1. Kaiso is broadly expressed and is not restricted to a lineage.

## The motif

This is the family where the phrase "dual specificity" is literal, and where the databases and the literature describe different things. Site-selection experiments defined a sequence-specific consensus, TCCTGCNA, with a minimal sufficient core of CTGCNA; two copies occur in the human and mouse matrilysin (MMP7) promoters. The same work showed that Kaiso separately possesses a methyl-CpG-dependent binding activity, requiring consecutive methylated CpGs and biochemically distinct from KBS binding, and that affinity for the KBS is the higher of the two. Only zinc fingers 2 and 3 are needed for sequence-specific binding. Crystal structures of the Kaiso zinc-finger domain bound to the KBS and to a symmetrically methylated sequence from the E-cadherin promoter explain how one small domain does both jobs: bases are read in the major groove by residues in the first two fingers, using classical hydrogen bonds for the KBS and methyl CH-to-O hydrogen bonds for methylcytosine, while the C-terminal extension past finger 3 binds the opposing minor groove and is required for high affinity. That extension is disordered in the free protein and folds on binding. Now the discrepancy: all four matrices in this family - the JASPAR ENCODE-derived MA0527.2, both HOCOMOCO KAISO models (evidence P, grade B), and CIS-BP M08094 - read TCTCGCGAGA or a close variant. That palindrome is the CGCG element found at TATA-less, CpG-island-associated bidirectional promoters. It is CpG-containing, so it is compatible with the methyl-CpG mode, but it is not the KBS, and it is not what site selection returned. In other words, the collections capture one Kaiso mode and miss the other entirely. Genome-wide work with Kaiso-knockout cells as a control reports both: CGCG and CTGCNAT are the two principal enriched motifs, with about 60 percent of sites containing both.

## Where it acts

Kaiso sites are overwhelmingly promoter-proximal and CpG-island-associated. ChIP in Kaiso-knockout-controlled experiments places Kaiso at CpG islands with a preference for methylated ones and for islands with partial methylation at their 5' or 3' boundaries, including a class showing wave-like methylation. Canonical KBS-containing targets include MMP7 (matrilysin) and Wnt-pathway genes; the methylation-dependent mode has been studied at the CDH1 promoter. Because the CGCG element is a general bidirectional-promoter feature, Kaiso motif hits cluster where CpG-island promoters cluster rather than at tissue-specific enhancers. Named partners are p120-catenin (negative), N-CoR, MTG16, and, at Wnt targets, the TCF/LEF-beta-catenin machinery.

## Biology and disease

Kaiso-deficient mice are viable and fertile, and on an Apc(Min) background they show reduced intestinal tumor burden and longer survival, which put Kaiso forward as a tumor-promoting repressor rather than a suppressor. Much of the disease literature concerns Kaiso's subcellular distribution in carcinoma: nuclear versus cytoplasmic Kaiso correlates with p120-catenin status and with prognosis in several tumor types, and Thr606 phosphorylation shifts the balance toward the cytoplasm, releasing CDH1. Kaiso has also been linked to clonal hematopoiesis and myelodysplastic phenotypes, and to DNA-damage responses in breast cancer cells. The tumor-biology claims are more contested than the biochemistry: reported effects of Kaiso depletion vary between cell systems and between the two binding modes, and the field has not settled how much of Kaiso's function depends on methyl-CpG reading versus KBS binding.

## Reading a hit

First decide which motif you matched. A hit to a database ZBTB33 matrix is a hit to the TCTCGCGAGA CGCG element, which is a common CpG-island promoter feature also matched by other GC- and CpG-reading factors; on its own it is closer to evidence of "this is a CpG-island bidirectional promoter" than of Kaiso occupancy. A hit to TCCTGCNA is the literature KBS, but it is short, degenerate at one position, and therefore frequent by chance. Second, note that every matrix here is ChIP-derived: JASPAR MA0527.2 is ENCODE ChIP-seq and both HOCOMOCO models carry evidence code P at grade B, with no HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX model in this family's data. That is exactly the situation in which indirect binding cannot be excluded, and published Kaiso ChIP-seq datasets have been noted to conflict with the in vitro binding data. Third, methylation state is part of the specificity, and no PWM encodes it: a CpG-containing match that is unmethylated in your cell type may not be a Kaiso site at all, and vice versa. The practical recommendation is to pair a motif hit with methylation data and, where possible, with a knockout-controlled occupancy dataset.
families.caveats: Kaiso has two binding modes and the databases represent only one. All four ZBTB33 matrices here read the CGCG palindrome TCTCGCGAGA - a generic CpG-island bidirectional-promoter element - rather than the site-selection consensus TCCTGCNA, so the same gene symbol can mean two different motifs depending on the source. Every matrix in this family is ChIP-derived (ENCODE JASPAR; HOCOMOCO evidence P, grade B), with no in vitro model, and published Kaiso ChIP datasets are known to conflict with in vitro data, so indirect binding is a live possibility. Methylation state is part of the specificity and no position weight matrix captures it; interpret hits alongside methylation data.

families.name: MECOM / EVI1
families.def: Two-finger-cluster GATA-like and GACAAGATA sites. MECOM, PRDM16-EVI1 module.
families.short: MECOM, better known as EVI1, is a 145-kDa C2H2 zinc-finger protein with two separate finger clusters that bind two different sequences. The N-terminal cluster of seven fingers reads a 15-bp GATA-like site, GA(C/T)AAGA(T/C)AAGATAA, whose core is GACAAGATA; the C-terminal cluster of three fingers reads the unrelated GAAGATGAG. EVI1 is normally expressed in hematopoietic stem cells, kidney and lung, and is silenced in most differentiated blood cells. It is one of the strongest adverse prognostic markers in acute myeloid leukemia, where 3q26 rearrangements such as inv(3)(q21q26) do not create a fusion protein but move a GATA2 enhancer next to MECOM, switching the gene on. Germline MECOM mutations cause radioulnar synostosis with amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.
families.long:
## The factors

MECOM (MDS1 and EVI1 complex locus, 3q26.2) encodes EVI1, first found as the site of retroviral
integration in murine myeloid leukemia cell lines. The protein carries two physically separate arrays of
Cys2-His2 zinc fingers, seven at the N terminus and three near the C terminus, plus a CtBP-interaction
motif and an acidic domain; it can act as a repressor or an activator depending on partners. A longer
read-through transcript, MDS1-EVI1, adds a PR/SET domain and is the reason EVI1 was once numbered
PRDM3. Unlike the PRDM family proper, the two finger clusters of EVI1 are used as independent
DNA-binding modules, which is why this atlas treats MECOM separately. EVI1 binds as a monomer, not an
obligate dimer, and one protein can engage both site types. Expression is restricted: hematopoietic stem
and progenitor cells, kidney, lung and developing heart and limb, with silencing on myeloid and
lymphoid differentiation. There is only one human gene, so there is no paralogue ambiguity within the
family, but there is considerable ambiguity with GATA factors.

## The motif

The proximal (N-terminal, fingers 1-7) cluster recognizes a 15-nucleotide consensus,
GA(C/T)AAGA(T/C)AAGATAA, which contains a tandem pair of GATA-like half-sites. Fingers 4-7 make the
sequence-specific contacts; fingers 1-3 do not detectably bind DNA on their own but bias the first
position toward GACAA over GATAA and are needed for optimal occupancy of the full 15-mer. The functional
minimal core is GACAAGATA, and a single amino-acid change (R205N) abolishes high-affinity binding to it.
Because GATAA is embedded in the site, EVI1 and GATA factors have overlapping but not identical
preferences: EVI1 binds erythroid GATA-1 target sites only weakly, while GATA-1 can bind and activate
through a GACAAGATAA element. The distal (C-terminal, three-finger) cluster binds a completely different
and shorter consensus, GAAGATGAG.

The database consensus in this atlas, TTATCTTATCT (and the 14-bp TATCTTATCWTATC archetype), is the
reverse complement of the proximal site written as tandem AGATAAGATAA half-sites; JASPAR renders the
same thing as AGATAAGATAA. So the literature consensus and the data agree once strand and finger cluster
are accounted for, and the longer Vierstra archetype simply captures more half-site repeats. No
widely used matrix in these databases represents the distal GAAGATGAG site, which is worth remembering:
scanning with a MECOM matrix tests only one of EVI1's two specificities.

## Where it acts

EVI1 occupancy in fibroblasts and myeloid cells maps to conserved GACAAGATA-like motifs within about
10 kb of transcription start sites of a defined target set, including GATA2, ZFPM2/FOG2, GADD45G, SKIL,
KLF5, DCN and MAP3K14. Sites are found in both promoters and distal elements. Because the proximal site
is a doubled GATA half-site, EVI1 peaks overlap GATA1/GATA2 peaks in hematopoietic cells, and in
erythroid or megakaryocytic chromatin a WGATAA-rich region is ambiguous between the two families. EVI1
also functions through protein interactions with a large partner network, including CtBP and
polycomb-associated proteins, so a fraction of its ChIP signal is likely tethered rather than
sequence-driven.

## Biology and disease

Conditional deletion of Evi1 in mice depletes hematopoietic stem cells and impairs repopulation, and
also blocks transformation by leukemic fusion oncogenes, making EVI1 required for both normal and
malignant stem-cell self-renewal. High EVI1 expression marks roughly 6-11% of adult acute myeloid
leukemia and is associated with poor outcome. The clearest mechanism is enhancer hijacking: in
inv(3)(q21q26) and t(3;3)(q21;q26), the breakpoint does not create a fusion protein but relocates a
distal GATA2 hematopoietic enhancer to the MECOM locus, driving EVI1 expression while leaving the
other GATA2 allele haploinsufficient. Two independent studies established this, one by mapping the
rearranged enhancer in patient genomes and one by deleting the orthologous mouse enhancer. Germline
biallelic or dominant MECOM mutations cause radioulnar synostosis with amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia,
a bone-marrow-failure syndrome with a skeletal phenotype, confirming a developmental role beyond blood.

## Reading a hit

A MECOM match is a doubled GATA-like element, so the first alternative hypothesis is a GATA factor, not
EVI1 - especially in erythroid, megakaryocytic or endothelial cells where GATA1/GATA2 are abundant and
EVI1 is usually off. The 15-bp full site is long enough to be reasonably specific, but the shorter
matrices in these databases (10-11 bp, essentially two WGATAA half-sites) will match tandem GATA sites
indiscriminately. A hit on the distal GAAGATGAG specificity will not be found at all with the available
matrices. There is only one human MECOM gene, so a true EVI1 hit has no paralogue problem, but the
CIS-BP model is inferred from mouse Evi1 at 98% DNA-binding-domain identity rather than measured on the
human protein, and the Vierstra archetypes are named for MECOM without claiming separability from GATA.
Treat a hit as evidence for a GATA-type element and use expression data to decide whether EVI1 is a
plausible occupant.
families.caveats: The proximal EVI1 site is a tandem GATA-like element, so matches are shared with GATA1-GATA6 and TRPS1; in blood and endothelium a GATA factor is usually the more likely occupant, since EVI1 is off in most differentiated cells. The shorter matrices here are effectively two WGATAA half-sites and match tandem GATA sites indiscriminately. EVI1's second specificity, GAAGATGAG, is not represented by any matrix in these databases, so a MECOM scan tests only one of two binding modes. The CIS-BP model is inferred from mouse Evi1 (98% DBD identity), not measured on human EVI1. Part of EVI1's ChIP signal is likely tethered through its large protein-interaction network rather than direct.

families.name: ZFX / ZFY
families.def: CpG-island GGCCT core at promoters. ZFX, ZFY.
families.short: ZFX and its Y-linked paralogue ZFY are thirteen-finger C2H2 zinc-finger activators that bind a short GC-rich site containing a GGCCT core. Their placement is the interesting part: they bind inside CpG-island promoters a couple of hundred base pairs downstream of the transcription start site, between the open region at the TSS and the first downstream nucleosome, and they activate the promoters they occupy. Together with the related ZNF711, they occupy the majority of active CpG-island promoters in a cell. ZFX loss slows proliferation, which is why the gene recurs in growth-based CRISPR screens, and ZFX supports embryonic and hematopoietic stem-cell self-renewal. Germline ZFX variants cause an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder.
families.long:
## The factors

ZFY was cloned in 1987 from the sex-determining region of the human Y chromosome and proposed as the
testis-determining factor, a role later taken by SRY. Its X-linked paralogue ZFX has a similar gene
structure, escapes X inactivation, and was recognized early as a probable transcriptional activator
with alternative isoforms. The third member, ZNF711, is also X-linked and has an overlapping binding
pattern. All three are ubiquitously expressed, which is unusual among C2H2 factors and consistent
with a housekeeping role at promoters.

The proteins have an acidic N-terminal region and thirteen C2H2 zinc fingers. Mutational dissection
shows that fingers 11 to 13 are necessary and sufficient for DNA binding, and that these fingers
together with the N-terminal region constitute a functional transactivator; the remaining ten fingers
are not required for site recognition. In the databases behind this family, only ZFX has matrices,
and the four of them agree closely (cohesion 0.91), so this is one of the more internally consistent
zinc-finger families despite the short motif.

## The motif

The consensus is GC-rich and short. The core that all models share is GGCCT, and the fuller form used
by JASPAR and CIS-BP is GCCBMGGCCT, which is also the data consensus for this family; the HOCOMOCO
ChIP-derived version, CCAGGCCBCG, is the same core with different flanks. There is no crystal or NMR
structure of the ZFX fingers on DNA, so which bases the three DNA-binding fingers contact is inferred
from the standard C2H2 recognition rules rather than observed. With roughly five to eight informative
positions, the motif is one of the least specific in routine use, and it is intrinsically GC-rich, so
matches are dense wherever GC content is high. Reported analyses note that the GGCCT motif occurs
throughout the genome but at higher density inside CpG islands, which is where occupancy is found.

ZFX, ZFY and ZNF711 are not separable by sequence in practice, and their genomic binding patterns at
CpG-island promoters are essentially the same. ZNF711 also has its own reported motif, and where the
two are distinguished, ZFX appears to be the dominant of the pair, with ZNF711 playing a subordinate
role at shared promoters.

## Where it acts

This family is a promoter family, and the position of binding is its defining feature. ChIP in four
cancer cell lines recovered roughly 9,000 ZFX sites, most of them in CpG-island promoters, and genes
with ZFX-bound promoters were expressed at higher levels than unbound ones; knocking ZFX down
down-regulated many of them, so ZFX is an activator. The binding position is about 240 base pairs
downstream of the transcription start site of responsive promoters, and nucleosome-occupancy and
methylome sequencing places it between the nucleosome-free region at the TSS and the first downstream
nucleosome. Taking ZFX, ZFY and ZNF711 together, the union of their bound promoters covers on the
order of 10,000 CpG-island promoters, a large majority of the active CpG-island promoters in a cell.
Mechanistically, reducing ZFX lowers histone H4 acetylation and increases RNA polymerase II pausing
at target promoters, which is consistent with a role in promoter architecture and early elongation
rather than in enhancer-driven, cell-type-specific regulation.

## Biology and disease

Zfx-null mice are viable but smaller, with reduced self-renewal of embryonic and hematopoietic stem
cells, so the gene supports proliferative capacity rather than specifying a lineage. That fits the
cancer literature, in which ZFX expression correlates with proliferation and outcome across several
tumor types, and in which Zfx facilitates tumorigenesis driven by Hedgehog-pathway activation.
Because ZFX contributes to growth in many cell types, bi-allelic ZFX knockouts reduce cell growth and
combined ZFX/ZNF711 knockouts cause major proliferation defects, which is why ZFX turns up repeatedly
as a hit in growth-based genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens; readers should be aware that a ZFX hit
in such a screen usually reflects this general proliferative requirement rather than a
pathway-specific dependency. In human genetics, germline ZFX variants cause an X-linked
neurodevelopmental disorder with a recurrent facial gestalt. ZFY, on the Y chromosome, has a distinct
role in male germ-cell development.

## Reading a hit

A GGCCT-containing match is weak evidence by itself: the motif is short, GC-rich, and denser in CpG
islands, so hits accumulate in exactly the sequence people usually submit. Position is the most useful
filter. A match a couple of hundred base pairs downstream of a CpG-island TSS is a plausible ZFX site;
the same match in an intergenic or AT-poor enhancer is probably not. The hit identifies the family
rather than the protein: ZFX, ZFY and ZNF711 bind the same sequence, and which one matters depends on
the sex and expression of the cells. Note also that the CIS-BP human ZFX motif in this collection is
transferred from mouse Zfx rather than measured on the human protein, though at 99% DNA-binding-domain
identity that transfer is harmless. Finally, because ZFX sits at a large fraction of all active
promoters, a ZFX-like motif recovered from another factor's ChIP data is more likely to reflect
promoter co-occupancy than that factor's own specificity.
families.caveats: The motif is short (roughly five to eight informative positions) and GC-rich, so hits are dense in CpG islands and GC-rich sequence generally, and a match alone means very little. Position carries more information than score: credible sites lie a couple of hundred base pairs downstream of a CpG-island transcription start site. ZFX, ZFY and ZNF711 read the same sequence and cannot be separated, and only ZFX has matrices here; the CIS-BP entry is transferred from mouse Zfx, benign at 99% DNA-binding-domain identity. No structure of these fingers on DNA exists, so the base contacts are inferred. Because ZFX occupies most active CpG-island promoters, a ZFX-like motif in another factor's ChIP data usually means co-occupancy.

families.name: ZNF410
families.def: Long GC-rich site clustered at the CHD4 promoter. ZNF410.
families.short: ZNF410 is a five-finger C2H2 zinc-finger protein that recognizes a long, information-rich element, and it is the clearest known case of a mammalian transcription factor with essentially one target gene. Two conserved clusters near CHD4, which encodes the ATPase of the NuRD chromatin remodeling complex, together carry 27 copies of the motif; comparable clusters occur nowhere else in the genome. Removing ZNF410 lowers CHD4 protein by about 60 percent, which is enough to de-repress the fetal haemoglobin genes without obvious toxicity, and the factor was found in CRISPR screens for fetal haemoglobin silencers. Matches to the motif are therefore biologically meaningful mainly when they fall in those clusters, and isolated hits elsewhere rarely correspond to occupied, functional sites.
families.long:
## The factors

ZNF410 is a single, conserved protein with no close paralogue in the human genome: a tandem array of five C2H2 zinc fingers flanked by N- and C-terminal regions that are not themselves DNA-binding domains. It is broadly expressed. The pentadactyl array is the whole of the sequence-reading apparatus, and crystallographic and solution work shows it binds DNA as a monomer with 1:1 stoichiometry. An unusual regulatory feature sits outside the fingers: AlphaFold modeling combined with small-angle X-ray scattering indicates that an acidic, serine/threonine-rich hairpin loop in the N-terminal region folds back onto the DNA-binding face of the finger array, mimicking the charge and shape of DNA. Full-length ZNF410 binds DNA less tightly than the isolated finger array, both in vitro and in cells, consistent with the loop having to be displaced before binding. This is an autoinhibitory mechanism layered on top of ordinary sequence specificity.

## The motif

The element is long for a five-finger protein: a 15-base-pair site, usually written from the CHD4 clusters as CATCCCATAATA with two or three further specified positions at the 5' end (reverse complement TATTATGGGATG). All four databases in this family agree closely on it, and the family is among the most cohesive in the atlas. Five fingers contacting fifteen base pairs is the canonical three-base-pairs-per-finger arrangement, and the element contains no internal repeat or half-site: it is read in one pass, with no spacing rule and no dimerization. Information content is high and spread across the whole word, with the central CCCAT and the 3' AATA both contributing; the AT-rich 3' end is what distinguishes this motif from the many GC-rich promoter motifs it would otherwise resemble. Because ZNF410 has no paralogue, there is no paralogue ambiguity within the family: a strong match means ZNF410 or nothing.

## Where it acts

In erythroid cells, ZNF410 chromatin occupancy is concentrated almost entirely at CHD4. Two regulatory elements, one upstream of the promoter and one intronic, carry 27 ZNF410 motifs between them; no other locus in the human or mouse genome has a comparable cluster, and the two clusters are conserved across mammals. Deleting them reproduces the effect of deleting ZNF410 itself, so essentially all of the factor's relevant output runs through this one gene. Occurrences of the isolated motif do exist elsewhere in the genome, and weak ZNF410 signal has been reported at some of them, but they do not measurably affect transcription. Mechanistically this is thought to be a matter of local concentration: a tight array of sites builds enough occupancy to activate, while single sites do not. The clusters sit in an open, CpG-island-adjacent promoter context rather than in tissue-specific enhancers.

## Biology and disease

ZNF410 came out of CRISPR screens of transcription factors for regulators of fetal haemoglobin (HbF). It is not a direct repressor of HBG1/HBG2; it activates CHD4, and CHD4/NuRD in turn silences the gamma-globin genes. Knocking out ZNF410, or its mouse homolog Zfp410, drops CHD4 protein by roughly 60 percent and raises HbF substantially in adult-type erythroid cultures and in xenotransplantation, without the cellular or organismal toxicity seen when CHD4 itself is removed. That partial, buffered effect is why ZNF410 attracted interest as a therapeutic target for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassaemia, alongside BCL11A and the HBG promoter BCL11A site. Outside erythropoiesis the phenotype is mild, consistent with a factor whose only strong target is a chromatin-remodeler subunit. There is no established human disease caused by ZNF410 mutation, and no recurrent cancer association.

## Reading a hit

A strong match to this 15-base-pair word is good evidence for ZNF410 specifically, because the protein has no paralogue and the motif is long. What a hit does not license is the inference that the site is used. The lesson of this family is that a single occurrence of even a high-information motif is usually not a functional element; what mattered at CHD4 was 27 of them in two clusters. If your hit is a lone site, treat it as a sequence match rather than a regulatory element unless you have occupancy or perturbation data. Conversely, if you find a dense cluster of ZNF410 motifs at a locus, that is worth following up, and genome-wide scans for such clusters have been used to argue that CHD4 really is unique. The database matrices here are a mixture of in vitro (HT-SELEX/methyl-SELEX) and derived archetypes and agree well, so matrix choice matters little.
families.caveats: Trust a hit for the protein but not for function. ZNF410 has no close paralogue, the motif is 15 base pairs long, and the in vitro and ChIP matrices agree, so a strong match is genuinely ZNF410's word rather than a shared GC-rich site. The problem is the opposite of the usual one: isolated matches occur throughout the genome and are largely inert, because ZNF410 needs the dense clusters found only at CHD4 to produce an effect. Do not read a single hit as a regulatory element, and be wary of published ZNF410 peak lists that include weak non-CHD4 sites. Full-length ZNF410 also binds more weakly than its isolated finger array, so in vitro affinities overstate cellular occupancy.

families.name: VEZF1
families.def: CT/GC-rich sites in vascular promoters. VEZF1.
families.short: VEZF1, originally cloned twice as DB1 and as Vezf1, is a broadly expressed six-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger protein first defined on CT/GC-rich promoter elements and on the chicken beta-globin HS4 insulator, where its sites protect against DNA methylation. It has no established consensus sequence: the matrices in motif databases reduce either to a plain poly-C/poly-G run (JASPAR MA1578.2 is six positions long) or to GGGGGAGGGGG, which is the MAZ motif. That is the central problem with this family - the data cannot separate it from MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF281 or ZNF148. Its documented functions are in vascular development, in maintaining DNA methylation levels through Dnmt3b, and in slowing elongating RNA polymerase II.
families.long:
## The factors

VEZF1 is one protein, cloned independently twice. It was first isolated as DB1, one of three Cys2/His2 zinc-finger cDNAs recovered by screening with the CT/GC-rich region (positions -76 to -47) of the human interleukin-3 promoter; the other two clones were EGR1 and EGR2. DB1 encoded a novel 516-residue protein with six zinc fingers, expressed ubiquitously across human tissues, and it bound the IL-3 element constitutively while EGR1 bound only after T-cell activation (Koyano-Nakagawa et al. 1994). Independently, a retroviral entrapment screen in mouse identified Vezf1 (vascular endothelial zinc finger 1) as a gene whose expression is restricted to vascular endothelial cells and their precursors in the yolk sac blood islands (Xiong et al. 1999). The two literatures have not fully merged: one describes a ubiquitous factor, the other an endothelial one, and current work generally treats VEZF1 as broadly expressed with a particular requirement in endothelium. The chicken homolog is BGP1, which has binding sites in the beta-globin locus including the upstream HS4 insulator (Gowher et al. 2008). There are no paralogues; the gene is also catalogued as ZNF161.

## The motif

This family has no consensus sequence that the literature agrees on. The elements VEZF1 was defined on are described only as CT/GC-rich, and the matrices assembled here do not converge. The medoid (CIS-BP M01172_2.00) is CCCCCCAC and the JASPAR profile (MA1578.2) is CCCCCC - six positions, a poly-C run, which will match an enormous number of genomic positions and carries almost no discriminating information. The two HOCOMOCO models are longer but point somewhere else: VEZF1.H14CORE.0.P.C is GGGGGAGGGGG and VEZF1.H14CORE.1.P.B is a 21-position G-run, GGGGGGGGGGGAGGGGGAGGGGG. The first of those has its single best-matching matrix, across all four databases, inside the MAZ family rather than in its own - so as a matter of data, VEZF1's motif is MAZ's motif. The family flags it as a suspect assignment for exactly that reason. Cohesion across the four matrices is 0.69, and label agreement for each of them is 0 to 0.1, meaning that for every one of them the nearest neighbors are mostly labelled with some other factor. Two things follow. First, there is no sequence feature that identifies a VEZF1 site as opposed to a MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF281 or ZNF148 site; the single-base discriminator that separates the GGGAGGG group from the SP1 GC-box (an A where the GC-box has a C, Song et al. 2001) is the only sequence-level distinction available anywhere in this neighborhood, and it does not help here. Second, a poly-C or poly-G match should be treated as a statement about base composition, not about a transcription factor.

## Where it acts

VEZF1 sites were characterized at promoters (IL-3, endothelin-1) and at an insulator. In the chicken beta-globin HS4 element, the VEZF1-binding CT/GC-rich sub-elements are the part that confers protection from DNA methylation: they can defend a transgene from encroaching methylation independently of the enhancer-blocking activity of the same insulator (Dickson et al. 2010). Genome-wide in HeLa S3 cells, VEZF1 binding correlates strongly with peaks of Ser2-phosphorylated elongating RNA polymerase II, reflecting a VEZF1-dependent slowing of elongation (Gowher et al. 2012). That is an unusual place for a zinc-finger factor to act and is one of the few properties that distinguishes VEZF1 functionally from its motif neighbors, though it is a property of the protein, not something readable from a match.

## Biology and disease

Vezf1 is required for vascular development in a dose-dependent manner: targeted inactivation in mice causes vascular defects and embryonic lethality with localized hemorrhage, and heterozygotes are affected (Kuhnert et al. 2005). Vezf1-null embryonic stem cells fail to form normal vascular structures on differentiation (Zou et al. 2010). In endothelial cells VEZF1 acts pro-angiogenically, in part by repressing the anti-angiogenic factor Cited2 (AlAbdi et al. 2018), and it activates the endothelin-1 promoter (Aitsebaomo et al. 2001). Its most striking phenotype is epigenetic: deleting both copies of Vezf1 in mouse embryonic stem cells reduces expression of the full-length active isoform of the Dnmt3b methyltransferase and causes widespread loss of DNA methylation genome-wide (Gowher et al. 2008). So VEZF1 influences methylation both indirectly, through Dnmt3b levels, and locally, through methylation-protecting elements. No human Mendelian disease has been established for VEZF1.

## Reading a hit

Treat a VEZF1 match with more suspicion than almost any other entry in this atlas. All four matrices are derived from binding data in cells (ChIP-seq for both HOCOMOCO models, at grades B and C) and none is an in vitro model, so none of them is evidence that VEZF1 itself prefers that sequence. Two of them are so short or so uniform - CCCCCC, and a 21-base G-run - that they function as composition filters. The longest and most confident model has its best match inside the MAZ family. In practice, then: a VEZF1 hit means "G-rich or C-rich promoter sequence", and the candidate binders include MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF281, ZNF148, the ChIP-derived WT1 models and, one base away, the SP1/KLF GC-box. If you specifically need VEZF1, the useful evidence is not the motif but the context in which VEZF1 has documented function: methylation-protected insulator sub-elements, and regions where elongating Pol II accumulates. Confirm with VEZF1 ChIP or knockdown rather than with a score.
families.caveats: This is the least trustworthy family in the batch. VEZF1 has no agreed literature consensus; its sites are described only as CT/GC-rich. Of the four matrices, JASPAR's is six positions of poly-C, one HOCOMOCO model is a 21-base G-run, and the most informative model has its single best match across all four databases inside the MAZ family - the data cannot tell VEZF1 from MAZ, and flags the assignment as suspect. All models are ChIP-derived; none is in vitro. Read a hit as a statement about G/C-rich composition, not about VEZF1, and confirm by ChIP or knockdown.

families.name: NRF1
families.def: Palindromic GCGCATGCGC at nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene promoters. NRF1.
families.short: NRF1 (nuclear respiratory factor 1, also alpha-PAL) is a single-gene family whose DNA-binding domain belongs to no common fold class, its closest relatives being sea urchin P3A2 and Drosophila Erect wing. It binds as a homodimer to a palindrome, GCGCATGCGC, with each subunit contacting one GCGC half; motif models extend this to TGCGCATGCGC. The site contains two CpG dinucleotides in its most informative positions, so it is strongly associated with CpG-island promoters and is blocked by cytosine methylation. NRF1 sites sit in promoters of nuclear genes for mitochondrial proteins, including cytochrome c, cytochrome c oxidase subunits and TFAM, making NRF1 the main nuclear coordinator of mitochondrial biogenesis. It should not be confused with NFE2L1, also abbreviated Nrf1.
families.long:
## The factors

This family has exactly one human member: NRF1, nuclear respiratory factor 1, also called alpha-PAL for "alpha palindromic-binding protein". It was defined functionally, by mutational and binding analysis of the somatic cytochrome *c* promoter, before it was cloned. Its DNA-binding domain lies in the N-terminal half of the protein and belongs to no previously described class; the closest relatives are the sea urchin developmental regulator P3A2 and the *Drosophila* protein Erect wing (EWG), and the three define a small, conserved family unrelated to zinc fingers, helix-turn-helix, bZIP or any other common fold. The C-terminal half, which carries the activation function, is divergent between the three. NRF1 binds as a homodimer and is broadly expressed; it is a housekeeping factor rather than a tissue-specific one, and its activity is modulated by phosphorylation of an N-terminal serine cluster and by coactivation from the PGC-1 family. Because there is one gene, the usual paralogue problem does not arise — but a nomenclature problem does, described under **Reading a hit**.

## The motif

NRF1 recognizes a palindrome, GCGCATGCGC, and the palindromic character is the defining feature: each subunit of the homodimer contacts one GCGC half, and the guanine contacts on the two strands mirror each other. The motif models in this collection extend it slightly, to an 11- or 12-mer — the HOCOMOCO and Vierstra consensus is TGCGCATGCGC — so the element is equally well described as a tandem pair of TGCGC half-sites separated by a single base. The palindrome is the older rendering; the extended repeat is what the matrices encode. Some models (JASPAR MA0506.3, CIS-BP M08177_2.00) place a C rather than an A/T at the central position, giving TGCGCCTGCGC, which reflects tolerance at the one position that is not part of either half-site.

Two features follow directly from the composition and matter in practice. First, the site contains two CpG dinucleotides, and both fall in the positions that carry the most information. Second, it is therefore methylation-sensitive: cytosine methylation within the site blocks NRF1 binding, and in cells lacking DNA methyltransferases NRF1 gains occupancy at sites it cannot bind in wild-type cells. NRF1 was the factor used to demonstrate this competition genome-wide, and it also scores as methylation-avoiding in systematic methyl-SELEX surveys. Family cohesion is 0.94, the highest tier in this atlas: all four models are effectively the same matrix.

## Where it acts

NRF1 sites are promoter elements, not distal enhancers, and they are strongly associated with CpG islands — which follows from the motif itself, since an unmethylated CpG-rich 10-mer is exactly what a CpG island is made of. The original targets were nuclear genes for mitochondrial proteins: somatic cytochrome *c*, cytochrome *c* oxidase subunits, a ubiquinone-binding subunit of the reductase complex, and the RNA component of RNase MRP, which functions in mitochondrial DNA replication. NRF1 also activates the promoter of *TFAM*, the mitochondrial transcription factor A gene, which is the direct mechanistic link between a nuclear promoter element and mitochondrial genome expression. Beyond respiratory genes, NRF1 sites occur in many broadly expressed promoters, frequently alongside GABP (historically NRF-2), SP1 and YY1 sites. An exact 10-mer of this composition is expected only a few thousand times in 3 Gb of uniform sequence, and because CpGs are depleted outside CpG islands, genuine matches concentrate in island promoters rather than being spread across the genome.

## Biology and disease

NRF1 is the central nuclear factor coordinating expression of the respiratory apparatus with the mitochondrial genome. Mouse *Nrf1* knockouts die at peri-implantation stages with depleted and unstable mitochondrial DNA, a phenotype consistent with loss of *Tfam* and related targets rather than with a single metabolic defect. Through *TFAM*, *TFB1M/TFB2M* and the mitochondrial ribosome and import machinery, NRF1 sets the capacity of oxidative phosphorylation, and its activity is the point at which PGC-1-family coactivators act during mitochondrial biogenesis in muscle and brown fat. The methylation dependence also gives NRF1 a role as a readout of the epigenome: in promoters that become hypermethylated, NRF1 occupancy is lost even though the sequence is intact, so changes in NRF1 target expression can reflect methylation change rather than any change in the factor.

## Reading a hit

The most common error with this family is not motif-related at all, it is naming. "NRF1" in this atlas means nuclear respiratory factor 1 and nothing else. It is not NFE2L1, which is also routinely abbreviated Nrf1 and belongs to the CNC-bZIP antioxidant-response family; it is not NFE2L2/NRF2; and it is not NRF-2, which turned out to be GABP, an ETS-domain factor. A hit on GCGCATGCGC says nothing about antioxidant response elements or the KEAP1-NRF2 pathway.

With one gene in the family, a match is unusually close to a protein-level call, and the evidence supports direct binding: HOCOMOCO's NRF1.H14CORE.0.PS.A combines ChIP-seq with HT-SELEX at grade A, so this is not a ChIP-only inference. The 10-11-mer is long and information-rich enough that a strong match in a CpG-island promoter is genuinely suggestive. What a match does not tell you is occupancy, and here the gap is specific and checkable: because the site carries two CpGs and NRF1 will not bind a methylated site, a perfect match inside a methylated region is probably unbound, so check methylation state. Finally, the Vierstra archetype here is AC0555:NRF:Unknown: the class is recorded as unknown, and the label names clustered factor annotations, not a validated protein.
families.caveats: Two cautions dominate. First, nomenclature: this family is nuclear respiratory factor 1, not NFE2L1 (also abbreviated Nrf1), not NFE2L2/NRF2, and not NRF-2, which is GABP; a hit here has nothing to do with antioxidant response elements. Second, methylation: the palindrome carries two CpGs in its most informative positions and methylation blocks binding, so an intact match inside a methylated region is likely unoccupied — check methylation state, not just sequence. Otherwise this is a strong family. One gene, cohesion 0.94, all four models essentially identical, and HOCOMOCO grade A evidence combining ChIP-seq with HT-SELEX, so the motif is not a ChIP-only inference.

families.name: NPAS3 / NPAS4 / other PAS
families.def: Neuronal PAS-domain bHLH factors binding E-box variants.
families.short: NPAS3 and NPAS4 are neuronal bHLH-PAS transcription factors, relatives of CLOCK, HIF and AHR that heterodimerize with the same shared beta subunits ARNT and ARNT2 and read E-box-like sites built around a CGTG core. NPAS4 is an immediate-early gene induced by neuronal activity rather than by growth factors, and it controls the number of inhibitory synapses formed on excitatory neurons. NPAS3 is a broader brain factor whose disruption segregates with schizophrenia in one family. This is the thinnest family in the group: only three motif models exist, all derived from chromatin immunoprecipitation, and the NPAS4 and NPAS3 models do not actually resemble each other. A match here is best treated as a generic E-box variant unless neuronal, activity-dependent evidence supports more.
families.long:
## The factors

NPAS1 (MOP5) and NPAS3 (MOP6) were cloned together as bHLH-PAS proteins with expression largely restricted to the central nervous system (Zhou et al. 1997). NPAS4, also called NXF, was identified separately as a neuron-specific bHLH-PAS factor that competes with SIM2 at the drebrin promoter (Ooe et al. 2004). All share the class domain layout, a basic helix-loop-helix domain followed by PAS-A and PAS-B, and none binds DNA usefully alone. Co-immunoprecipitation from mouse brain recovers ARNT2 as the major NPAS4 partner with ARNT1 as a minor band; both heterodimers are active in reporter assays, and ARNT1 mRNA is found in some NPAS4-expressing regions lacking ARNT2 (Ooe et al. 2009). ARNT is therefore the shared beta subunit here exactly as it is for HIF and AHR. NPAS4 is an immediate-early gene, unusual in being induced by calcium influx and neuronal activity rather than by growth factors, and its expression is confined to neurons. NPAS3 is more broadly distributed in brain. NPAS1 has no motif model in JASPAR, HOCOMOCO, CIS-BP or the Vierstra archetypes, so it does not appear in this family's data even though it belongs to the group by domain. The family holds only three motifs, one from JASPAR and two from HOCOMOCO.

## The motif

There is no single well-established consensus, and the two members do not share one, so this entry gives no family consensus string. For NPAS4 both available models center on a short CGTG core with a 5' T and a 3' A: HOCOMOCO NPAS4.H14CORE.0.P.B is TCGTGa and JASPAR Npas4 (MA1995.2) is TCGTGAC. That is an E-box-like half-site pair but not a canonical E-box: the position carrying C in CACGTG, or T in the HRE TACGTG, is absent from the core. Read through the pairing rules established for this class, in which the ARNT-type subunit contributes the 3' GTG half-site and the partner supplies the 5' half (Swanson et al. 1995), the NPAS4 model is best understood as ARNT's GTG plus a non-canonical NPAS4 half-site. NPAS3 is different. Its single model, NPAS3.H14CORE.0.P.C, is gkACGTGc, an ordinary ACGTG site, and its nearest neighbor across all four databases lies outside this family: similarity 0.97 to a motif in another family versus 0.81 to the other NPAS models. The pooled consensus for the family, TCGTGa, is essentially the NPAS4 model alone. Recent systematic profiling of prototypical bHLH-PAS proteins including NPAS4 reports footprints of 12-15 bp in which preferences for bases flanking the core, together with DNA shape, carry the discriminating information rather than the core itself (Bersten et al. 2026). The practical consequence is that a 6-7 bp core model for these factors cannot be specific.

## Where it acts

NPAS4 works at activity-regulated promoters and enhancers in neurons, where its induction follows depolarization within minutes and its targets include genes that set the number and distribution of inhibitory synapses on excitatory cells (Lin et al. 2008). In hippocampal CA3 it drives a transcriptional program required for contextual memory formation (Ramamoorthi et al. 2011). Two features limit where these sites matter: expression is restricted to neurons and occupancy requires activity, so in resting neurons and all non-neural tissue nearly all matches are unoccupied. The genome-wide picture is less settled than for the other bHLH-PAS families, and a prominent genome-wide study of NPAS4 heterodimers was retracted in 2024 (Cell 2024), so published site counts and partner-specific cistromes for this family should be treated as provisional. Both HOCOMOCO models here derive from ChIP-seq rather than from in vitro selection.

## Biology and disease

Loss of Npas4 in mice reduces the number of inhibitory synapses formed on excitatory neurons and removes an activity-dependent brake on excitation (Lin et al. 2008); conditional deletion in CA3 impairs contextual fear memory (Ramamoorthi et al. 2011). The factor has since been linked to seizure susceptibility, social behavior and cognitive flexibility (Sun and Lin 2016). For NPAS3, a balanced translocation that disrupts the gene segregates with schizophrenia in an affected family (Kamnasaran et al. 2003), and Npas3-null mice show abnormal neurodevelopment, altered neurotrophin and reelin signaling, and behavioral abnormalities (Brunskill et al. 2005). Neither gene is an established cancer driver.

## Reading a hit

This family has the weakest evidence base of the bHLH-PAS groups in the atlas. All three models are ChIP-derived (HOCOMOCO evidence letter P, grades B and C), so they support "this region was occupied in cells" rather than "this protein binds this sequence"; there is no HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX model for either factor. Because the NPAS4 and NPAS3 models do not resemble each other, a hit should be reported against the specific model, not the family: a match to the NPAS3 model is in practice a match to a generic ACGTG E-box and is closer to the HIF/ARNT class than to NPAS4. The NPAS4 core is five informative base pairs and occurs by chance very often. Cell type and stimulus are more informative than the score: a site is only plausible in neurons and after activity. A hit cannot separate NPAS4 from NPAS3, nor either from HIF, AHR, SIM or ARNT homodimer complexes reading overlapping cores, and it says nothing about which beta subunit, ARNT1 or ARNT2, was present.
families.caveats: Trust this family less than the other bHLH-PAS groups. Only three models exist, all from ChIP-seq at grade B or C, so none is in vitro evidence of direct binding, and indirect or tethered binding cannot be excluded. The two members do not share a motif: the NPAS3 model is a generic ACGTG E-box whose nearest neighbors sit in another family, while the NPAS4 model is a short TCGTG core. Report the model, not the family. NPAS1 has no model at all. A prominent genome-wide study of NPAS4 heterodimers was retracted in 2024, so cistrome-level claims for NPAS4 are provisional. Neuronal identity and recent activity are stronger evidence than any match score.

families.name: Other bHLH
families.def: bHLH factors and archetypes not covered above, incl. MYRF-like and unclassified E-box archetypes.
families.short: A residual bucket rather than a real family: it holds bHLH motifs that could not be placed in any of the defined bHLH families. In the current release that is three models, all labelled SOHLH2, a germ-cell-restricted bHLH protein that heterodimerizes with SOHLH1 and controls spermatogonial differentiation and early folliculogenesis in mice. All three read an ordinary class-B E-box with a G/C flank (CACGTGC), and the data flags each one as resembling MYC/MAX or BHLHE40/41 motifs instead. The family definition also reserves space for MYRF-like factors and unclassified E-box archetypes, though none are assigned here. A hit means "canonical E-box", not SOHLH2.
families.long:
## The factors

This is a residual bucket, not a protein family. The atlas groups bHLH motifs that could not be placed in one of the defined bHLH families - MYC/MAX, USF, MITF/TFE, SREBP, TFAP4, BHLHE40/41, the E-proteins, HES/HEY, MYOD, NEUROD/ATOH, HAND/TWIST, TAL/LYL, CLOCK/BMAL, HIF/ARNT and the others - and in the current release that leaves exactly one gene with motifs: SOHLH2. SOHLH1 and SOHLH2 (spermatogenesis- and oogenesis-specific basic helix-loop-helix 1 and 2) are germ-cell-restricted bHLH proteins. They are expressed in spermatogonia and in oocytes rather than in somatic tissue, they heterodimerize with each other, and they sit outside the well-studied class I/class II pairing scheme because their usual partner is the other SOHLH protein rather than an E-protein. The family definition also reserves this bucket for MYRF-like factors and for unclassified E-box archetypes. MYRF is worth a word because its inclusion in a bHLH-adjacent bucket is a naming accident rather than a structural claim: myelin gene regulatory factor is a membrane-bound, self-cleaving transcription factor whose DNA-binding domain is an Ndt80/PhoG-like beta-sandwich that trimerizes, with no helix-loop-helix at all. No MYRF motif is assigned here in the current data. The atlas assigns 3 motifs to this family: one JASPAR, one HOCOMOCO and one CIS-BP model, all labelled SOHLH2, with SOLH2.H14CORE.0.S.C as the representative.

## The motif

All three models read a class-B E-box with G/C flanks: CACGTGC in HOCOMOCO (HT-SELEX evidence, quality grade C), GCACGTGC in JASPAR (MA1560.2), and a low-information gCACGtG in CIS-BP carrying only 8.1 bits of total information. The data consensus for the family is therefore CACGTGC, which is simply the canonical palindrome CACGTG with one extra flanking base. There is no family-specific motif here, and the family data says so explicitly: each of the three models is flagged as resembling a different family. The HOCOMOCO model's nearest neighbours across all four databases are BHLHE40/41 motifs; the JASPAR and CIS-BP models' nearest neighbours are MYC/MAX motifs. Label agreement - the fraction of a motif's nearest neighbours that carry the same factor label - is 0 to 0.2 for all three. The cohesion figure of 0.92 describes only how similar the three SOHLH2 models are to each other, which is not informative when all three come from the same gene. In short, a SOHLH2 model is a CACGTG E-box that happens to be labelled SOHLH2, and nothing in its information content separates it from the canonical MYC or BHLHE40 site.

## Where it acts

Because the site is an ordinary CACGTG E-box, matches occur throughout the genome: a 6-bp palindrome is expected several hundred thousand times in 3 Gb, reduced somewhat by CpG depletion but still far beyond the number of sites any factor occupies. Nothing is known here about promoter versus enhancer preference or chromatin context, because none of the three models is ChIP-derived - the HOCOMOCO model carries only in vitro (HT-SELEX) evidence, and there is no Vierstra footprint archetype in this family. SOHLH1 and SOHLH2 expression is confined to germ cells, so whatever occupancy exists is restricted to spermatogonia and oocytes and has not been mapped genome-wide at the scale available for the common factors. Reported targets sit in the spermatogonial differentiation program, which the two proteins control jointly.

## Biology and disease

The phenotypes come from mouse genetics. Sohlh1-null mice fail spermatogonial differentiation. Sohlh2-null males are sterile because differentiating type A spermatogonia degenerate, and Sohlh2 is separately required in females for early folliculogenesis and for oocyte-specific gene expression. The two genes act together rather than redundantly: SOHLH1 and SOHLH2 coordinate the spermatogonial differentiation step, consistent with their obligate heterodimerization. Human evidence is thin by comparison and consists largely of individual case reports in infertility cohorts, so the human disease picture should be treated as provisional. There is no cancer or developmental syndrome robustly attributed to either gene.

## Reading a hit

Treat a hit against anything in this bucket as a hit against a generic CACGTG E-box and nothing more. This family exists so that motifs which do not belong to a defined bHLH family are not silently forced into MYC/MAX or BHLHE40/41; it is a holding pen, and membership is expected to change between releases as the assignments are revised. Concretely: do not report a "SOHLH2 site" on the basis of a sequence match. If a BHLH_OTHER model is your top hit, rescore the same sequence against MYC_MAX, USF, MITF_TFE, BHLHE40_41, CLOCK_BMAL and HIF_ARNT and expect comparable scores, then argue from expression - SOHLH2 is only a plausible candidate in germ-cell material. None of these three models has ChIP support, so they say nothing about in vivo occupancy either way.
families.caveats: This bucket has no motif of its own. All three assigned models are CACGTG E-boxes whose nearest neighbours across the four databases belong to other families - BHLHE40/41 for the HOCOMOCO model, MYC/MAX for the JASPAR and CIS-BP models - with label agreement between 0 and 0.2. None is ChIP-derived, and the CIS-BP model carries only 8.1 bits of information. A match therefore licenses no factor assignment at all; report it as a canonical E-box. Membership in a residual bucket is provisional by construction and should be expected to change as the family assignments are revised, so do not build a pipeline that depends on this key's contents.
