families.name: Ndt80/PhoG-like (C11orf9/MYRF)
families.def: Ndt80-like DNA-binding domain archetypes, incl. MYRF.
families.short: This family is named after the budding yeast meiotic activator Ndt80, whose DNA-binding domain defines an immunoglobulin-like fold shared by the human proteins MYRF and MYRFL. MYRF, myelin regulatory factor, is the only well-characterized vertebrate member. It is an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein that trimerizes and cleaves itself using a domain related to bacteriophage tailspike proteins; the released N-terminal fragment enters the nucleus and binds DNA. The measured site is the palindromic eight-base TGGTACCA, consistent with binding by a symmetric oligomer. MYRF is required for oligodendrocyte differentiation and for making and maintaining central nervous system myelin, and human MYRF variants cause a cardiac-urogenital syndrome and disorders of sex development.
families.long:
## The factors

The family is defined by a DNA-binding fold, not by a lineage of related regulators. It takes its
name from Ndt80, the Saccharomyces cerevisiae transcription factor that is activated at pachytene
and turns on roughly 150 middle sporulation genes, including the B-type cyclins, once meiotic
recombination is complete. The crystal structure of the Ndt80 DNA-binding domain showed an
immunoglobulin-like fold, with functional similarities that suggested an evolutionary link to the
p53 family. Human proteins carrying the same Ndt80/PhoG-like domain are MYRF (myelin regulatory
factor, formerly C11orf9 or MRF) and its paralogue MYRFL, which is poorly characterized. MYRF is
unusual for a transcription factor: it is synthesized as a type-2 transmembrane protein in the
endoplasmic reticulum, assembles into a homotrimer, and then cleaves itself through an
autoproteolytic intramolecular chaperone domain that is related to the corresponding domain of
bacteriophage tailspike proteins, the first time that domain was found in a eukaryotic protein.
Cleavage separates the transmembrane C-terminal region from an N-terminal fragment that carries
the DNA-binding domain and a nuclear localization signal. MYRF expression is essentially
restricted to oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system, with some expression in Schwann
cells and other tissues; it is not a broadly expressed factor.

## The motif

All three models in these databases converge on TGGTACCA, an eight-base perfect palindrome, which
is what a symmetric trimeric or dimeric binder would be expected to select: the half-site is TGGT,
read on both strands. The CIS-BP MYRF model and the Vierstra archetype AC0396 are identical to
each other. Chromatin immunoprecipitation of the cleaved N-terminal fragment showed it binding
oligodendrocyte and myelin gene enhancers through a defined consensus, which is consistent with
this palindrome. Information is concentrated in the TGGT/ACCA core; there are no established
spacing rules, and because the site is symmetric, orientation cannot be called from sequence. The
family is not fully coherent here (cohesion 0.73, three motifs). The one discordant model is
HOCOMOCO's MYRFL entry, a long integrative model (GTGCCAGGCNGTGACATCCC) whose best similarity to
any other member of the family is only 0.47, so MYRF and MYRFL should not be assumed to share a
site on the current evidence. The yeast middle sporulation element that Ndt80 reads is a different
sequence again, with a GC-rich 5' half whose pyrimidine-guanine steps are recognized by arginine
side chains through a combination of hydrogen bonding and stacking, and an AT-rich 3' half read
through the minor groove; it is useful as structural background but not as a human motif.

## Where it acts

MYRF sites are found at promoters and, more characteristically, at oligodendrocyte-specific distal
enhancers of myelin genes, including MBP, PLP1, MAG and CNP. Enhancer mapping at the Plp1 locus
identified two oligodendrocyte-specific enhancers, both acted on by MYRF, whose contacts with the
gene are among the strongest in that cell type. MYRF works with SOX10 at many of these elements,
so a MYRF match near a SOX10 dimer site in oligodendrocyte-accessible chromatin is a much stronger
signal than the match alone. As an eight-base fixed palindrome, TGGTACCA is expected by chance on
the order of tens of thousands of times in a human genome, most of them in closed chromatin and in
cell types where MYRF is absent.

## Biology and disease

Mice lacking Myrf in the oligodendrocyte lineage fail to myelinate the central nervous system, and
inducible deletion in adults causes loss of myelin and of mature oligodendrocyte identity, so MYRF
is required for maintenance as well as for differentiation. In humans, de novo MYRF variants cause
a syndrome of congenital cardiac and urogenital anomalies, often with congenital diaphragmatic
hernia, and MYRF haploinsufficiency has been reported in both 46,XY and 46,XX disorders of sex
development. The link between a myelin regulator and cardiac and gonadal development is not
explained by the oligodendrocyte role, and likely reflects earlier developmental expression.

## Reading a hit

The palindrome is short and fully specified, so chance matches are common and the sequence alone
carries no cell-type information. A MYRF match matters only in a cell that expresses MYRF, which
in practice means the oligodendrocyte lineage; elsewhere the same eight bases are inert. Do not
assume that a match to the MYRFL model is equivalent to a MYRF site: that model is discordant with
the MYRF palindrome in these data. Because MYRF requires autoproteolytic release to reach the
nucleus, the presence of MYRF protein in a tissue does not establish that its DNA-binding fragment
is present, which is an unusual extra step between motif and function. Treat the yeast Ndt80 MSE
as a separate element that shares only the fold.
families.caveats: Only three motifs and two proteins sit under this key, and one of them disagrees with the other two: the HOCOMOCO MYRFL model matches the MYRF palindrome at only 0.47, so MYRF and MYRFL cannot be assumed interchangeable. TGGTACCA is eight fixed bases and a perfect palindrome, so chance matches number in the tens of thousands per genome and orientation is undefined. The site is only interpretable in cells expressing MYRF, essentially the oligodendrocyte lineage. MYRF also needs autoproteolytic cleavage before its DNA-binding fragment reaches the nucleus, so protein presence does not imply DNA binding. The yeast Ndt80 MSE shares the fold but not the sequence.

families.name: HMGA (AT-hook)
families.def: AT-rich minor-groove binding. HMGA1, HMGA2.
families.short: HMGA1 and HMGA2 have no sequence specificity worth scanning for. They bind the minor groove of AT-rich DNA through short basic peptides called AT-hooks, which were described from the outset as recognizing DNA structure rather than base sequence, and they will bind essentially any run of A and T. The family holds three motifs, and the data show what that means: the HMGA1 models are ATTTTTA in JASPAR and TAaAATAtAtA in HOCOMOCO, the HMGA2 model is four bases at 2.2 bits, and not one of the three has another model in this family as its nearest neighbour. All three resemble models in other families more than they resemble each other. Do not treat a match here as a binding site.
families.long:
## The factors

HMGA1 and HMGA2 are small, extremely basic, intrinsically disordered nuclear proteins of about 100 residues. They are architectural chromatin factors, among the most abundant non-histone proteins in embryonic and transformed cells, and they work by bending, straightening and unwinding DNA and by making the surrounding chromatin more permissive. HMGA1 exists as two main splice variants, historically called HMG-I and HMG-Y, which differ by an eleven-residue internal segment; HMGA2 was originally called HMGI-C. Both carry three AT-hooks in the N-terminal two-thirds and an acidic C-terminal tail.

The AT-hook itself was defined in 1990 from the mammalian HMG-I proteins as a novel peptide motif for recognizing DNA structure, built around a short palindromic core of the form Arg-Gly-Arg-Pro flanked by lysines and arginines. It was subsequently found in a wide variety of otherwise unrelated DNA-binding proteins - chromatin remodellers, transcription factors and others - where it typically serves as an auxiliary anchor rather than as the specificity-determining module. That is the key point for this page: the AT-hook is an affinity device, not a recognition device.

## The motif

A crystal structure of an HMGA AT-hook bound to AT-rich DNA shows the peptide lying in the narrow minor groove, making van der Waals and water-mediated contacts with the floor of the groove, and the same site can be occupied competitively by small-molecule minor-groove binders. Minor-groove width and narrowness are what the hook reads; the identity of the individual A and T bases is largely irrelevant, and a run of A:T base pairs in almost any arrangement will do. There is no discriminating base pair in the sense that a zinc-finger or homeodomain motif has one.

The three atlas models reflect this exactly. JASPAR MA2124.1 for HMGA1 gives ATTTTTA at 11.9 bits. HOCOMOCO HMGA1.H14CORE.0.P.B gives TAaAATAtAtA at 12.4 bits, but its evidence code is P - ChIP-only - and its grade is B, so there is no in vitro support for it in the atlas. The CIS-BP model M00751 for HMGA2 is the four-base Aata at 2.2 bits, transferred from mouse at 100 percent domain identity, and carries no usable information.

The diagnostic statistic is the nearest-neighbour analysis. For all three models the within-family nearest neighbour is undefined - no model in this family is another's closest match - while the best out-of-family similarity is 0.72 for the HOCOMOCO model, 0.81 for the JASPAR model and 0.80 for the CIS-BP model. Every model here looks more like something in another family than like its own family-mates. Reported cohesion of 0.54 flatters the situation. An ATTTTTA-style heptamer is not distinguishable from a homeodomain TAAT site, an ARID AT core, a FOX forkhead flank, or unremarkable AT-rich intergenic sequence; at human base composition a given AT-only heptamer is expected several hundred thousand times in the genome.

## Where it acts

Because binding is structural, HMGA proteins are found across AT-rich DNA, in nuclear scaffold and matrix-attachment regions, in nucleosome-poor and linker DNA, and at the AT-rich flanks of enhancers. Where they matter functionally, it is through cooperation. The textbook case is the interferon-beta enhancer, where HMG I(Y) is required for NF-kB-dependent virus induction and then for assembly of the complete enhanceosome together with ATF-2/c-Jun and IRF proteins: HMGA bends the DNA into the geometry the other factors need, and its own contribution to sequence recognition is nil. The generalisation is that an HMGA site is defined by its partners, not by its sequence, which is why HMGA occupancy maps are broad and shallow rather than peaked.

## Biology and disease

HMGA2 is the mouse pygmy gene: the pygmy phenotype was mapped to disruption of Hmgi-c, giving small, lean mice and establishing HMGA2 as a growth regulator. In humans, HMGA2 variants and microdeletions cause Silver-Russell syndrome and related growth-restriction phenotypes, and common variants at the locus are associated with adult height. HMGA2 is also one of the most recurrent fusion partners in benign mesenchymal tumours: translocations at 12q14-15 in lipoma, uterine leiomyoma and related lesions repeatedly truncate HMGA2 after its AT-hooks, generating fusions such as HMGA2-SETBP1 that remove the acidic tail while retaining DNA binding. HMGA1 is re-expressed in most aggressive carcinomas, is a driver in breast cancer, and is also involved in insulin receptor regulation and metabolic disease.

## Reading a hit

Effectively, do not read it. If you scan with these models, expect several hundred thousand matches, no ability to separate HMGA1 from HMGA2, and no ability to separate either from any other AT-preferring factor or from bulk AT-rich sequence. HMGA occupancy cannot be predicted from sequence at the resolution a motif scan implies, and a strong score here carries no information about function. If an AT-rich region genuinely matters in your data, the useful questions are whether it is a matrix-attachment or nucleosome-depleted region and which sequence-specific factors bind alongside - HMGA is the geometry, not the address.
families.caveats: HMGA proteins are not sequence-specific: the AT-hook reads minor-groove structure, and any run of A and T will bind. Say it plainly - a match here is not a binding site. All three models are mutually dissimilar enough that none is another's nearest neighbour, while each has an out-of-family match at 0.72 to 0.81, so the family does not cohere. The HOCOMOCO HMGA1 model is ChIP-only (grade B) with no in vitro support in the atlas; the CIS-BP HMGA2 model is four bases at 2.2 bits and unusable. Expect hundreds of thousands of genome-wide matches, indistinguishable from homeodomain, ARID and forkhead AT preferences or from bulk AT-rich sequence.

families.name: Cold-shock domain (YBX)
families.def: Y-box CTGATTGGC. YBX1 and CSD archetypes.
families.short: A one-protein family. YBX1 (YB-1) carries a cold-shock domain, the eukaryotic descendant of the bacterial CspA nucleic-acid-binding fold, and it is at least as much an RNA-binding protein as a transcription factor: it packages messenger RNA, unwinds RNA secondary structure and prefers single-stranded nucleic acid over duplex DNA. Three motifs agree closely with one another - cohesion is 0.95, the highest in this part of the atlas - and all read the same eight base pairs, GATGGTAC, or its reverse complement GTACCATC. Note that this in vitro site is not the classical Y box, CTGATTGGC, with which YB-1 is historically identified; the two should not be conflated.
families.long:
## The factors

The cold-shock domain is one of the oldest nucleic-acid-binding folds, a five-stranded beta-barrel of the OB-fold class, conserved from the bacterial cold-shock proteins such as CspA into eukaryotes. Human cold-shock-domain proteins include the Y-box family YBX1, YBX2 and YBX3, the unrelated CSDE1/UNR and the LIN28 proteins, but only YBX1 contributes motifs to this atlas, so the family is effectively a single-protein entry.

YBX1 was cloned in 1988 as the complementary DNA encoding a protein that binds the Y box of the major histocompatibility complex class II promoter - hence the name Y-box binding protein 1. The Y box itself is an inverted CCAAT element, and Y-box sequences were subsequently shown to be required for basal expression of other promoters, notably the human multidrug resistance gene MDR1. Domain architecture is an alanine/proline N-terminal region, the single cold-shock domain, and a long charged C-terminal region with alternating basic and acidic clusters that does most of the RNA binding and mediates mRNP packaging.

Functionally YBX1 is dual. It acts as a transcription factor at some promoters, but the bulk of the cellular protein is cytoplasmic and bound to messenger RNA, where it packages transcripts, unwinds secondary structure and thereby restrains stress granule assembly. In vitro, YB-1 binds single-stranded nucleic acids in preference to duplex DNA and even displays a 3' to 5' exonuclease activity. Any interpretation of a YBX1 motif has to be made against that background.

## The motif

The three models are essentially the same site read on the two strands. HOCOMOCO YBOX1.H14CORE.0.SM.B gives GTACCATC at 13.0 bits with evidence code SM - HT-SELEX plus methyl-HT-SELEX, so genuine in vitro support - though graded B. The CIS-BP model M04661 and the Vierstra archetype AC0342 both give GATGGtAC, the reverse complement, at 9.9 and 8.8 bits. Pairwise similarity within the family reaches 0.98, and out-of-family similarity stays at 0.63 to 0.65 - the widest margin between within-family and out-of-family matches anywhere in this group of entries. On the internal statistics, this is a clean, well-behaved eight-base-pair motif.

The complication is historical rather than statistical. The site these models describe is built around a CCAT/ATGG core; the classical Y box that gave YBX1 its name is built around CCAAT, one base longer. The atlas ontology labels this family with the Y box CTGATTGGC, and that string does not match the models the family actually contains. Both observations can be true - YB-1 was purified on a Y-box probe, and in vitro selection recovered a CCAT-centred site - but they are not interchangeable, and a scan using these models is not a scan for Y boxes. If your interest is in Y-box or CCAAT-element regulation, the NFY family is the appropriate place to look.

Structural work explains why the duplex-DNA numbers are modest. The solution structure of the YB-1 cold-shock domain identified the canonical aromatic surface that binds nucleic acid, and a later structure of the domain on DNA showed that binding is regulated by phosphorylation, with the phosphorylated protein altering its engagement of the duplex. Comparative work shows the domain discriminates RNA from DNA largely through non-bonded interactions rather than hydrogen-bond readout, which is another way of saying that base identity is not read as strictly as in a classical DNA-binding domain.

## Where it acts

Reported YBX1 promoter targets cluster in proliferation and stress-response genes and in drug-resistance genes such as MDR1, and the protein is recruited to MHC class II and other CCAAT-containing promoters. But most YBX1 in a cell is on messenger RNA, not chromatin, and the genomic occupancy that has been mapped is correspondingly broad. In practice a YBX1 site is defined by the promoter it sits in and the partners present rather than by the eight base pairs alone.

## Biology and disease

YBX1 is essential in mouse: knockout embryos fail in early development with defective neural tube formation and reduced proliferation. In human cancer YBX1 is one of the most consistently overexpressed nucleic-acid-binding proteins, associated with proliferation, drug resistance, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and poor prognosis across many tumour types, and it has been pursued as a therapeutic target. Much of that activity is post-transcriptional - mRNA stabilisation and translational control, including roles in m6A-dependent regulation - rather than transcriptional, which is a further reason not to read YBX1 biology off a DNA motif scan.

## Reading a hit

The motif is technically sound and the family is internally consistent, so a strong GATGGTAC match is a defensible YBX1 candidate site - but only a candidate. Three cautions apply. First, eight base pairs with 10 to 13 bits will still match tens of thousands of times genome-wide, so require promoter context and YBX1 expression. Second, do not treat the hit as a Y box or a CCAAT element; it is neither, and NFY is the family that reads CCAAT. Third, remember what YBX1 mostly does: it binds single-stranded nucleic acid and RNA in preference to duplex DNA, so a sequence match is weak evidence of chromatin occupancy and no evidence at all of transcriptional function. Corroborate with ChIP or footprint data before assigning a regulatory role.
families.caveats: This family is one protein, YBX1, and its three models are the same eight base pairs on opposite strands, so the high cohesion of 0.95 reflects redundancy rather than breadth of support. The models describe a CCAT-centred site, not the CCAAT-based classical Y box CTGATTGGC that the family is named for, and they should not be used to find Y-box or CCAAT elements - that is NFY's motif. The HOCOMOCO model has genuine HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX support but is graded B. Most importantly, YB-1 prefers single-stranded nucleic acids and RNA over duplex DNA and is largely a cytoplasmic mRNA-packaging protein, so a DNA motif match is weak evidence of occupancy and none of function.

families.name: Other / unclassified
families.def: Motifs whose factor has no assigned structural family here: LCOR and LCORL (psq-type HTH) and LRRFIP1. Cofactors without a DBD are in CHROMATIN; unnamed archetypes are in ZNF_UNNAMED.
families.short: This is not a motif family. It is the residual category for motifs whose factor has no assigned structural family in this ontology, and in the current data it holds three matrices for three proteins. Two are the paralogous corepressors LCOR and LCORL, which carry a psq-type helix-turn-helix rather than a homeodomain and whose models are 4-5 bit A-rich strings that carry almost no information. The third is LRRFIP1, cloned as GC-binding factor 2, whose only model is a GC-rich matrix derived from ChIP-seq alone and resembles neither of the others. Internal cohesion is 0.60 and no member has a same-family neighbour that it matches. Read a hit here as unassigned rather than as shared biology, and re-report it to whichever named family the sequence actually matches.
families.long:
## The factors

Three motifs, three proteins. The definition is broader than the contents: it also covers chromatin regulators without a classical DNA-binding domain and unlabelled archetypes, but both of those have entries of their own, so what lands here is proteins believed to bind DNA whose domain has no family of its own.

Two of the three are paralogues. LCOR, ligand-dependent corepressor, is recruited to agonist-bound nuclear receptors through a single LXXLL motif and represses both by binding histone deacetylases directly and by recruiting CtBP corepressors through two consensus motifs; it attenuates receptor signalling rather than activating a programme of its own. LCORL is its larger relative. Both carry a psq-type helix-turn-helix - the pipsqueak fold, a member of the homeodomain-like superfamily - which is a real DNA-binding domain, but this atlas has no pipsqueak family and the fold is not a homeodomain, so neither protein has anywhere else to go.

The third, LRRFIP1, entered the literature as GCF2, found by cross-hybridisation with the cDNA of the GC-rich repressor GCF and shown to bind and repress epidermal growth factor receptor promoter fragments through a major site at nucleotides -249 to -233. It has no recognised DNA-binding domain; the part of it that has been solved is a dimeric coiled coil, and its best-documented activity is cytosolic, as a nucleic-acid-binding protein that drives interferon-beta production through beta-catenin.

## The motif

There is no consensus for this bucket and none should be quoted. The CnAAa string the pipeline reports is only the medoid of three unrelated matrices, and the medoid is the weakest of the three.

The three entries: CIS-BP M02433, labelled LCOR, reads CnAAa and carries 4.1 bits; its provenance record marks it as taken from a Meleagris gallopavo - wild turkey - protein whose DNA-binding domain is 100 percent identical to the human one. CIS-BP M01304, labelled LCORL, reads cchAAa and carries 4.9 bits. The two match each other at 0.97, but each also matches a motif in another family at 0.83-0.84: at five bits an A-rich matrix is not distinguishable from anything else A-rich. LCORL turns up again in the forkhead entry as part of the Vierstra archetype AC0014:FOXR/LCORL, a 3.4-bit AAa matrix pooled with genuine forkhead models. The third entry, HOCOMOCO LRRF1.H14CORE.0.P.B for LRRFIP1, reads aaGCTCGC with 9.6 bits. Its evidence code is P alone - ChIP-seq, with no in vitro assay - and grade B means two experiments of that one type. It has no same-family neighbour anywhere in its top thirty; its best match outside the bucket is only 0.66. Family cohesion is 0.60.

The pipeline treats residual buckets as places where membership says nothing about what a matrix should look like, so it suppresses the suspect flag and reports a resemblance instead; the reported zero suspect motifs is a property of that rule, not a sign that these three belong together.

## Where it acts

Not established as a cis-element for any of the three. LCOR and LCORL act as corepressors recruited by nuclear receptors, so their functional footprint on the genome is at oestrogen, glucocorticoid and related receptor sites, and finding CNAAA under a peak tells you nothing about which receptor brought the corepressor there. The one mapped element for LRRFIP1 is the GC-rich region of the EGFR promoter around -240; its ChIP-derived matrix will pick out promoter-proximal GC-rich sequence, as most ChIP-only GC-rich models do whatever protein they are labelled with. A five- or six-base A-rich matrix of the kind LCOR and LCORL contribute matches several million times in 3.1 Gb on either strand, so a scan against them returns noise at any threshold that returns anything.

## Biology and disease

None of the three has a Mendelian disease attributed to it, but the biology is real. LCOR primes interferon responses in mammary epithelium; miR-199a represses it to protect normal and cancerous mammary stem cells from interferon-induced differentiation and senescence, and that axis is active in poorly differentiated ER-negative breast tumours and associated with poor outcome. LCORL sits in the NCAPG-LCORL interval, one of the most reproducible loci for body size and stature in human and livestock association studies; knockout mice are born small, stay lean, eat less, have reduced circulating IGF-1 and show improved glucose tolerance. LRRFIP1 represses the EGFR and RhoA promoters as GCF2, regulates Wnt/beta-catenin signalling through a specific spliced isoform, and acts in innate immunity as a cytosolic sensor of double-stranded RNA and DNA.

## Reading a hit

Do not report a match here as a match to a family motif. Report the matrix instead, then ask what it is. If the hit is M02433 or M01304, the honest reading is that a four- to five-bit A-rich matrix matched, which is no evidence, and the LCOR matrix is in any case a cross-species transfer from a bird. If it is LRRF1.H14CORE.0.P.B, read it as a GC-rich model built from ChIP-seq alone and compare the sequence against the GC-box families - KLF/SP, MAZ, EGR, NRF1 - before crediting LRRFIP1 with the site. More generally, a residual category exists so that well-supported families are not diluted by unresolved single cases, and a hit in it should be read as unassigned. For LCOR and LCORL the informative question is not what they bind but which nuclear receptor recruited them; for LRRFIP1 it is which GC-box family the sequence belongs to, and whether the protein was in the nucleus at all.
families.caveats: Treat this as an administrative category, not a biological one. It holds three matrices for three proteins whose medoid similarity is 0.60, and the group has no shared consensus: two are 4-5 bit A-rich matrices for the corepressors LCOR and LCORL, one of them transferred from a wild turkey protein, and the third is a 9.6-bit GC-rich model for LRRFIP1 supported by ChIP-seq alone at grade B. No member has a same-family neighbour it actually matches. The reported zero suspect motifs reflects a pipeline rule that suppresses the flag inside residual buckets, not internal agreement. Do not build a consensus, a logo or a representative matrix for this group, and re-report any hit to the named family the sequence matches.

families.name: CTCFL (BORIS)
families.def: CTCF-like core bound by the testis paralogue CTCFL.
aka: Brother of the Regulator of Imprinted Sites
families.short: CTCFL, usually called BORIS, is the single paralogue of CTCF. The two proteins share an almost identical eleven-zinc-finger array and therefore the same DNA sequence preference, so the CTCFL matrices in motif databases are simply shorter, noisier versions of the CTCF core. What differs is the protein outside the fingers and, above all, where and when it is made: CTCFL is normally confined to a narrow window of male germ-cell development, and is re-expressed in many tumors, where it is used as a cancer-testis antigen. A CTCFL motif match is a CTCF-family match; deciding which of the two proteins is bound requires expression data or an antibody, not sequence.
families.long:
## The factors

CTCFL (also BORIS, for Brother of the Regulator of Imprinted Sites) was identified as a paralogue of CTCF whose exons encode the same eleven-zinc-finger domain, and therefore the same DNA-binding potential, attached to entirely different amino- and carboxy-terminal regions (Loukinov et al. 2002). It is the only CTCF paralogue in mammals. Expression is the main distinction. CTCFL is normally restricted to the testis, appearing transiently in male germ cells before the onset of meiosis, at a stage that coincides with erasure of methylation marks; immunohistochemistry on testis sections places it alongside Stra8-positive cells and shows that it overlaps in time with ubiquitously expressed CTCF rather than strictly replacing it (Sleutels et al. 2012). Outside the germ line, CTCFL is silent in normal somatic tissue but is aberrantly activated in a wide range of tumors, which is why it is catalogued as a cancer-testis antigen. Neither protein needs to dimerize to bind DNA; the N and C termini of CTCFL differ from those of CTCF, and it is these regions - not the fingers - that give the two proteins different partners and different outputs.

## The motif

Because the zinc-finger arrays are effectively the same, so is the sequence preference: CTCFL binds the CTCF core. The three CTCFL matrices in this atlas make the point. HOCOMOCO's CTCFL.H14CORE.0.P.B (CCRCCAGGGGGCGC) and CIS-BP's M07930_2.00 (GCGCCCCCTGGCGG, the reverse-complement orientation of the same sequence) both reproduce the CCASYAGRKGGC core that CTCF reads through zinc fingers 3-7, and JASPAR's CTCFL profile (MA1102.3) is only 8 positions long (CAGGGGGC) - a fragment of that core, not a distinct motif. What is *not* captured by any of these matrices is the upstream module that CTCF's fingers 9-11 read, so the CTCFL models are on average shorter and carry less information than the CTCF ones (11.7-15.7 bits here versus up to 22.5 bits for CTCF). That is a property of the models, not evidence of a different specificity. The practical statement is blunt: no position-weight matrix separates CTCFL from CTCF, and none should be expected to. What can be distinguished is site *architecture* rather than site sequence. Comparing CTCF and BORIS occupancy genome-wide, Pugacheva et al. (2015) found that BORIS is largely confined to a subset of regulatory elements containing clustered CTCF motifs, which they called 2xCTS elements, whereas single-motif sites (1xCTS) are bound by CTCF alone; 2xCTS elements are preferentially active promoters and enhancers in both germ cells and BORIS-positive cancer cells. So the discriminating feature is the presence of two adjacent core motifs, not the sequence of either one.

## Where it acts

In germ cells and in BORIS-expressing cancer lines, CTCFL occupies a minority of the CTCF site repertoire, concentrated at the clustered 2xCTS class at active promoters and enhancers, and enriched in regions that escape the histone-to-protamine transition (Pugacheva et al. 2015). Its binding in germ cells is accompanied by testis-specific transcriptional regulators that selectively occupy the BORIS-bound subset (Rivero-Hinojosa et al. 2017). Nucleosome composition matters: CTCFL binding to CTCF-like consensus sites in vivo depends on the local histone variant context, which is one reason its occupancy does not simply mirror CTCF's despite the shared fingers (Sleutels et al. 2012). In cancer, BORIS binding has been mapped to the promoters of cancer-testis antigen genes MAGEA2, MAGEA3 and MAGEA4, where it accompanies their transcriptional activation in lung cancer (Bhan et al. 2011).

## Biology and disease

The germ-line role is the well-supported one: transient CTCFL expression during pre-meiotic male germ-cell development, coincident with epigenetic reprogramming, and regulation of testis-specific genes. Its disease relevance is as an ectopically activated gene. Conditional expression of BORIS in normal cells is sufficient to demethylate and derepress MAGE-A1 and to reactivate other cancer-testis genes (Vatolin et al. 2005), and BORIS occupancy at MAGEA promoters tracks their activation in tumors (Bhan et al. 2011). CTCF and CTCFL are both altered in cancer, but in opposite directions - CTCF behaves as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor while CTCFL is typically gained or de-repressed (Marshall et al. 2014; Debaugny and Skok 2020). Claims that BORIS acts as a simple antagonist of CTCF have not held up cleanly, since the two are co-expressed in germ cells and co-occupy 2xCTS sites.

## Reading a hit

Treat a CTCFL match as a CTCF-family match. The sequence cannot tell you which paralogue is bound, and in almost every human tissue the answer is CTCF, because CTCFL is not expressed: check CTCFL mRNA in your cell type before entertaining it at all. All three database CTCFL matrices derive from chromatin immunoprecipitation in cells where CTCF is also present, so they inherit CTCF's specificity by construction; the HOCOMOCO model carries ChIP-only evidence at grade B. If you have a reason to care about CTCFL specifically, the informative feature is not the motif but whether the region contains two closely spaced core motifs, since the clustered configuration is what BORIS occupancy tracks. And because JASPAR's CTCFL profile is only 8 bp, it will match far more often than a full CTCF core model - do not read those extra hits as CTCFL-specific sites.
families.caveats: CTCFL and CTCF share an almost identical zinc-finger array, so no matrix can separate them and a CTCFL hit is really a CTCF-core hit. In normal somatic tissue CTCFL is not expressed, so the biologically relevant binder is CTCF unless you have expression evidence otherwise. All three database CTCFL models are derived from ChIP in CTCF-containing cells, and JASPAR's is only 8 bp long, which makes it match promiscuously. If CTCFL is genuinely the question, look for two clustered core motifs rather than for a CTCFL-specific sequence, and confirm with an antibody or CTCFL expression data.

families.name: INSM1 / INSM2
families.def: INSM1 and INSM2. The matrices here are GC-rich (TGTCAGGGGGCG) rather than E-box-like, and all three trace back to one compiled model, so the apparent agreement between databases is one matrix repeated.
families.short: INSM1 (originally IA-1, cloned from a human insulinoma) and its paralogue INSM2 are five-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger repressors of neuroendocrine and neuronal differentiation. Despite the family's historical placement alongside the Snail-type repressors, every matrix in this family is a GC-rich, GGGG-containing element - TGTCAGGGGGCG, or GCCCCCTGACA read on the other strand - not a CANNTG E-box. Structural work shows INSM1's fingers bind DNA with little intrinsic specificity for that element and that INSM1 reaches GGGG-containing loci largely by riding with CTCF, and TEAD1 sites through a direct TEAD1 contact. INSM1 is required for pancreatic beta cell and intestinal endocrine development and is now a standard immunohistochemical marker of neuroendocrine tumors.
families.long:
## The factors

INSM1 was isolated as IA-1 from a human insulinoma cDNA library and encodes a roughly 510-residue protein with five C-terminal C2H2 zinc fingers and a proline-rich N terminus. INSM2 is its single paralogue, considerably less studied and without a motif of its own in any of the four databases surveyed here. Recent structural work resolves the whole five-finger module and shows it is unusually flexible: finger 1 adopts a non-canonical CCHC fold and does not contact DNA at all, instead binding the TEAD domain of TEAD1 through hydrophobic contacts, while fingers 2 and 3 bind DNA but, because the interdomain linker is long and flexible, without specificity for the GGGG-containing element that the factor is classically associated with. The functional consequence, as reported in that work, is that INSM1 is recruited to genomic targets substantially through partner proteins - CTCF at GGGG-element loci, TEAD1 at TEAD-target promoters - rather than through autonomous high-affinity recognition. Repression at the insulin promoter involves recruitment of cyclin D1 and HDAC3. INSM1 expression is tightly restricted: transient in neural and endocrine progenitors during development, essentially absent from adult differentiated tissue, and re-expressed in neuroendocrine neoplasia.

## The motif

All three matrices in this family describe the same GC-rich element. JASPAR MA0155.1 renders it TGTCAGGGGGCG, CIS-BP M08445 renders it CGCCCCCTGACA, and the Vierstra archetype AC0533:INSM reads TGCCCCCTGACA; the first is simply the reverse complement of the other two. The informative block is the CCCCC/GGGGG run plus the adjacent TGAC, roughly 15 bits over 11-12 positions. There is no CANNTG E-box anywhere in it. This matters because the family is conventionally described, including in this atlas's own family definition, as carrying "SNAI-like E-box repressor sites": that statement reflects protein-level kinship with the Snail-type C2H2 repressors and the shared habit of repressing differentiation programs, not the matrices, which are unambiguously not E-boxes. Readers looking for an INSM1 E-box will not find one in these data. Two further points constrain how much the consensus is worth. The JASPAR entry is typed COMPILED and traces to literature annotation rather than to a high-throughput binding experiment, and the CIS-BP and Vierstra entries match it at 0.99-1.00 - so the family's apparent perfect internal cohesion is not three independent confirmations but one consensus propagated through three collections. And the structural data argue that fingers 2-3 have limited intrinsic preference for this element, so the matrix is better read as a description of where INSM1 is found than of what it binds tightly in isolation.

## Where it acts

Mapped INSM1 sites are promoter-proximal. The best-characterized single example is the proximal rat insulin I/II promoter, where a GG-to-AT substitution in the INSM1 core site raises promoter activity three- to twenty-fold and abolishes INSM1-dependent repression, and where INSM1 occupancy has been confirmed by chromatin immunoprecipitation in beta cell lines, fetal mouse pancreas and human islets. Genome-wide, INSM1 co-localizes with CTCF at GGGG-element loci and with TEAD1 at TEAD targets, so a large fraction of INSM1 occupancy is expected to be at sites that are primarily another factor's. Because the element is GC- and CpG-rich, it is concentrated in CpG-island promoters, where it competes for space with the many other GC-box-reading C2H2 families.

## Biology and disease

Insm1-null mice fail to make pancreatic beta cells and intestinal endocrine cells in normal numbers, with endocrine progenitors arrested before terminal differentiation. In the developing neocortex Insm1 acts across neurogenic lineages, promoting the generation and expansion of basal progenitors, and in the zebrafish retina insm1a is required for photoreceptor differentiation; in the inner ear Insm1 promotes proliferation of delaminated otic progenitors. The clinical relevance is mostly diagnostic and oncologic. INSM1 protein is now widely used as an immunohistochemical marker of neuroendocrine differentiation across small cell lung carcinoma, neuroendocrine tumors and related neoplasms, generally with better specificity than chromogranin or synaptophysin. In neuroblastoma, INSM1 stabilizes N-MYC protein in a positive-feedback circuit, and INSM1 has been proposed as a therapeutic target and as a promoter for tumor-selective gene delivery.

## Reading a hit

Treat a match here as weak evidence. First, the consensus is GC-rich and CpG-island-like, which means it overlaps the recognition space of SP/KLF, ZBTB7, MAZ, PATZ1 and many other C2H2 GC-box readers; a CCCCC run with a flanking TGAC is not a specific INSM1 signature. Second, the sequence model rests on a single compiled matrix reproduced in three collections, not on independent in vitro determinations: there is no HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX model for INSM1 or INSM2 in HOCOMOCO in these data, so the "this protein binds this sequence" test is not met by the usual standard. Third, the structural evidence indicates that INSM1's fingers lack strong specificity for this element and that genomic recruitment leans on CTCF and TEAD1, which means an INSM1 ChIP peak carrying the motif may well be a CTCF site. Fourth, INSM2 has no motif at all, so nothing here can be attributed to it. If you have an INSM1 hit, the strongest supporting evidence is cell type: transient neural or endocrine progenitors, or a neuroendocrine tumor.
families.caveats: This family's consensus is not an E-box, despite the "SNAI-like" label, which refers to protein kinship rather than to the matrices. The apparent perfect cohesion across JASPAR, CIS-BP and Vierstra reflects one compiled matrix propagated into three collections, not three independent measurements; there is no HOCOMOCO in vitro model here. Structural work indicates INSM1's DNA-binding fingers have little intrinsic specificity for the GGGG element and that occupancy depends heavily on CTCF and TEAD1, so a motif-positive INSM1 peak may belong to a partner. The element is GC-rich and overlaps many other C2H2 GC-box motifs. INSM2 has no motif; do not read a hit as evidence about it.

families.name: ZBTB18 (RP58)
families.def: ZBTB18 (RP58): a C2H2 repressor reading the E-box-like site MACATCTGKM, core CATCTG/CAGATG - an E-box read by zinc fingers rather than by a bHLH.
families.short: ZBTB18, first described as RP58, is a BTB/POZ zinc-finger repressor that binds an E-box-like site, (A/C)ACATCTG(G/T)(A/C), whose CATCTG core reads CAGATG on the opposite strand. It is a C2H2 protein, not a bHLH one, so the E-box it occupies is a site that basic helix-loop-helix activators can also use - which makes competition, not just repression, part of how it works. RP58 concentrates in condensed chromatin and represses target promoters through its POZ domain. In the brain it controls the multipolar-to-bipolar transition of newborn cortical neurons and is required for cerebellar growth; human ZBTB18 mutations cause autosomal dominant intellectual disability and figure in 1q43-q44 deletion syndrome with corpus callosum malformation.
families.long:
## The factors

ZBTB18 is a one-member family in this atlas. The gene, also known as RP58 and ZNF238, encodes a 522-residue protein with an N-terminal POZ/BTB domain - the feature that first placed it alongside BCL6 - and four C-terminal C2H2 zinc fingers. The POZ domain mediates homodimerization and autonomous repression; it does not contact DNA. An early and still striking observation is that almost all RP58 protein localizes to condensed chromatin regions by immunogold electron microscopy, which was the basis for proposing that this factor links sequence-specific repression to chromosome organization. ZBTB18 is expressed most prominently in the developing and adult central nervous system, in cortical and cerebellar neurons, and also in skeletal muscle and other tissues; it is not a lineage-restricted factor in the way GFI1 or ThPOK are. In neurons it behaves as a differentiation-promoting repressor: it shuts down programs belonging to other cell identities rather than activating neuronal genes directly.

## The motif

The binding site was determined by cyclic amplification and selection of targets with recombinant protein, giving the high-affinity consensus (A/C)ACATCTG(G/T)(A/C). The internal CATCTG is a CANNTG E-box variant, and read on the opposite strand the same site presents CAGATG as its core. This is worth stating carefully because the two renderings look like different motifs: the JASPAR HT-SELEX matrix MA0698.2 reads TCCAGATGTT and the HOCOMOCO grade-A model reads CCAGATGTG, both of which are the reverse complement of the selected consensus, not a disagreement with it. Note also that the family definition used in this atlas describes the site as "E-box-like CACATG"; the experimentally selected core is CATCTG (equivalently CAGATG), with an A at the position where CACATG has a C, so the shorter label is slightly off and should not be used for scanning. Information content is 11-15 bits over nine or ten positions - better than a bare 6 bp E-box but still modest. Four adjacent fingers could cover more sequence than the consensus specifies, and the flanking A/C and G/T degeneracies suggest that only two or three fingers contribute strong base contacts. The family data flags one entry as inconsistent: the CIS-BP model M08257 for ZBTB18 reads CGCAGCTGCG, a canonical CAGCTG bHLH E-box whose nearest neighbors across databases fall in the NEUROD/ATOH family rather than with ZBTB18, and which matches no other ZBTB18 model. With only three matrices in the family, that single outlier drags the measured cohesion down to 0.79.

## Where it acts

ZBTB18 acts mainly at promoters of genes belonging to alternative differentiation programs. In developing neurons it represses transcriptional programs linked to non-neuronal cell identity, including programs that correspond to glioblastoma subtypes, and the sites it uses are promoter-proximal E-boxes rather than distal enhancer clusters. Because the core is a CANNTG box with no CpG, matches are not concentrated in CpG islands and occur throughout the genome; a nine-position match with two degenerate positions still arises tens of thousands of times by chance in 3 Gb. The important co-occurrence to keep in mind is with bHLH factors: NEUROG2, NEUROD and ASCL1 bind overlapping CANNTG boxes in the same neuronal promoters, and the sequence alone cannot say which occupied a site.

## Biology and disease

Mouse Rp58 mutants show defective cortical development: newborn neurons fail to complete the multipolar-to-bipolar transition needed for radial migration, and cerebellar growth and patterning are disrupted, with abnormal development of both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons. In humans, heterozygous ZBTB18 loss-of-function and missense variants cause autosomal dominant non-syndromic intellectual disability 22 (MRD22), with developmental delay, seizures and frequent corpus callosum abnormalities; ZBTB18 lies in the critical region of 1q43-q44 deletion syndrome, and its loss is a principal candidate for the corpus callosum and microcephaly phenotypes in that contiguous gene syndrome. Missense variants have been shown to differ in how much they impair DNA binding versus repression, so the allelic series is informative rather than uniform. In glioblastoma, ZBTB18 behaves as a tumor suppressor that is silenced epigenetically, and restoring it represses mesenchymal and lipid-metabolic programs.

## Reading a hit

The CATCTG/CAGATG core makes this an E-box family, with all the attendant ambiguity. Candidates for any CANNTG match include the bHLH factors of the NEUROD/ATOH, ASCL, NEUROG, TCF3/4/12, MYOD and TWIST groups, and among C2H2 proteins the SNAIL, ZEB and INSM-related repressors. An E-box hit is not evidence of a bHLH factor, and equally it is not evidence of ZBTB18. What tilts the balance toward ZBTB18 is the specific internal composition: CATCTG rather than CACCTG, CAGCTG or CACGTG, with the flanking A and G/T. The best-supported matrix here is JASPAR MA0698.2, which is HT-SELEX-derived and thus direct in vitro evidence, and the HOCOMOCO model is grade A with PSM evidence, so "ZBTB18 binds this sequence" is well established. Do not use the CIS-BP entry M08257 (CGCAGCTGCG): it looks like a NEUROD/ATOH-class site, and scanning with it will return bHLH sites labelled as ZBTB18. Finally, since ZBTB18 is one gene, there is no paralogue problem inside the family - but the outside-the-family problem is severe, and a hit should be reported as "E-box consistent with ZBTB18" rather than as a ZBTB18 site.
families.caveats: The site is an E-box variant, so the crowd of bHLH factors plus SNAIL, ZEB and INSM-related C2H2 repressors all compete for interpretation of a match; report an E-box, then argue for ZBTB18 from the internal CATCTG composition and the cell type. The commonly quoted "CACATG" shorthand for this family is not the selected consensus and should not be scanned. Trust JASPAR MA0698.2 (HT-SELEX) and the HOCOMOCO grade-A model, which are reverse-complement renderings of the same site; discard the CIS-BP entry CGCAGCTGCG, which the cross-database analysis places with NEUROD/ATOH and which accounts for this family's low internal cohesion. Single gene, so no paralogue ambiguity within the family.

families.name: SALL
families.def: AT-rich double zinc-finger sites. SALL1-4.
families.short: SALL1 to SALL4 are the human Spalt-like proteins: large C2H2 zinc-finger factors built from several clusters of paired fingers, with a short N-terminal motif that recruits the NuRD corepressor complex. Their DNA binding is unusual in being defined by base composition rather than by a sequence. A single C-terminal pair of fingers in SALL4 reads AT-rich DNA, and a crystal structure shows why it is promiscuous: the contacts use small side chains in the major groove, so many different AT-rich combinations are accepted. There is consequently no reliable consensus string for this family. SALL1 mutations cause Townes-Brocks syndrome and SALL4 mutations Okihiro syndrome; SALL4 is also the cereblon substrate whose degradation explains thalidomide limb teratogenicity.
families.long:
## The factors

The four human SALL genes, SALL1 to SALL4, are homologues of Drosophila spalt. Each protein is large
and built from several clusters of C2H2 zinc fingers, usually a set of paired fingers (three or four
double-finger clusters) plus one unpaired finger, separated by long low-complexity linkers. A short
motif at the extreme N terminus recruits the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase (NuRD) complex,
and NuRD recruitment accounts for much of the repressive activity attributed to these proteins; the
same interaction is required for SALL4's contribution to reprogramming. SALL4 is highly expressed in
embryonic stem cells and in germ-cell and hepatocellular tumors but silenced in most adult tissues,
which is why it is used as an immunohistochemical marker. SALL1 is prominent in kidney and limb,
SALL3 in the nervous system. Mouse work shows Sall1, Sall2 and Sall4 are each required for neural
tube closure.

## The motif

Only one of the SALL clusters binds DNA in SALL4: a pair of fingers near the C terminus (ZFC4).
Inactivating that one cluster drastically reduces SALL4's genome occupancy and reproduces the
phenotype of a complete Sall4 knockout, including precocious differentiation of embryonic stem cells
and embryonic lethality, whereas deleting two of the other clusters is phenotypically neutral. What
that cluster reads is AT-richness rather than a defined word: SALL4 was recovered in a screen for
proteins that bind AT-rich motifs, and genes are de-repressed on SALL4 loss in proportion to their AT
content. Protein-binding-microarray and CUT&RUN experiments define an AT-rich consensus, and the
crystal structure of the C-terminal fingers on AT-rich DNA explains the flexibility: recognition uses
small hydrophobic and polar side chains in the major groove, so many different combinations of A and
T are accepted. We therefore give no consensus string for this family; any single IUPAC word
overstates what the protein specifies.

The database situation reflects this awkwardly. Of the three matrices assigned here, only the SALL3
model (consensus TTATGAATTATGATAT, HOCOMOCO grade A with HT-SELEX, integrative and ChIP support) is
the AT-rich motif the literature describes, and it has no close neighbor among the other family
members. The SALL1 and SALL4 models are ChIP-only (grades C and B) and are GC-rich, with the
consensus GGGTGGGG, which is also the family's data consensus and its medoid. GGGTGGGG is a GC-box-
and KLF/SP-like sequence, and the most economical explanation is that these ChIP-derived models
capture a co-occupancy or promoter signal rather than SALL binding preference. Cohesion in this
family is 0.51, essentially because the literature motif and the database medoid disagree.

## Where it acts

SALL4 occupancy is broad and follows base composition: it accumulates over long AT-rich domains and
at AT-rich genes, a distribution unlike the punctate enhancer occupancy of most transcription
factors, and it acts largely to hold such genes down. That makes the relevant genomic feature a
region rather than a site. Reported partners include NuRD and, in pluripotent cells, the core
pluripotency factors. SALL1 in kidney and limb, and SALL4 in limb and heart development, act at
developmental enhancers, but no well-validated composite element carrying a named SALL site is
established in the way that exists for, say, GATA or ETS composites.

## Biology and disease

Heterozygous truncating SALL1 mutations cause Townes-Brocks syndrome (imperforate anus, thumb
malformations, dysplastic ears and hearing loss, with variable renal and cardiac involvement).
Heterozygous SALL4 mutations cause Okihiro (Duane-radial ray) syndrome, which overlaps the
radial-ray phenotype of Holt-Oram syndrome and includes Duane anomaly. The SALL4 phenotype is
mechanistically informative in two directions. First, the Okihiro missense mutations that fall inside
the C-terminal fingers reduce overall DNA binding without abolishing the AT preference and shift the
protein's association with AT-rich genomic sites, which supports their pathogenicity. Second, SALL4
is a thalidomide-dependent cereblon neosubstrate: thalidomide and its analogs recruit SALL4 to
cereblon for degradation, and this provides a molecular explanation for thalidomide limb
teratogenicity, since chemical SALL4 loss phenocopies genetic SALL4 loss. A crystal structure of the
SALL4-pomalidomide-cereblon-DDB1 complex shows how the degron is presented.

## Reading a hit

There is little to read. This family specifies base composition rather than a word, so a PWM hit is
close to meaningless on its own: an AT-rich match is expected anywhere in AT-rich DNA, and the same
matrices score homeodomain, forkhead and poly-A sequence. The four paralogues are not separable, and
in these databases only SALL1, SALL3 and SALL4 have models at all. The specific trap is the opposite
of the usual one: if your hit came from the GC-rich GGGTGGGG matrices labelled SALL1 or SALL4, you
have almost certainly matched a GC-box-like sequence, and a KLF, SP or other GC-box factor is the
more likely direct binder; those two models are ChIP-only and disagree with every in vitro
measurement of SALL4 specificity. A credible SALL4 claim rests on AT-rich domain-level enrichment,
on the effect of degrading or mutating the ZFC4 cluster, or on the clinical genetics, not on a motif
match.
families.caveats: SALL proteins read base composition, not a word: a C-terminal finger pair in SALL4 binds AT-rich DNA promiscuously, and the crystal structure shows the contacts accept many A/T combinations. We give no consensus for that reason, and an AT-rich hit is expected throughout AT-rich DNA and overlaps homeodomain, forkhead and poly-A signals. The paralogues are indistinguishable, and SALL2 has no model here. Worse, the family's medoid and data consensus come from ChIP-only SALL1 and SALL4 matrices that are GC-rich (GGGTGGGG, a GC-box/KLF-like sequence) and contradict every in vitro measurement; cohesion is 0.51. Matches to those two models are most likely GC-box factors, not SALL.

families.name: RREB1
families.def: RAS-responsive element, GC-rich. RREB1.
families.short: RREB1 is a large C2H2 zinc-finger protein, originally identified as the factor binding the RAS-responsive element of the human calcitonin promoter in medullary thyroid carcinoma cells. It has around fifteen fingers and, in the high-throughput data that define its motif, prefers a long C-rich word usually written CCCCAAACCACCCC. It is a downstream effector of RAS and TGF-beta signalling: in the TGF-beta pathway RREB1 partners with SMAD complexes to direct fibrogenic and developmental epithelial-mesenchymal transitions, and it has been implicated in metastatic enhancer priming. The motif's length is its main virtue and its main problem, since a long C-rich element overlaps several other GC-rich promoter families and no short functional consensus has ever been agreed in the literature.
families.long:
## The factors

RREB1 is a single gene, with no paralogue in the human genome that shares its specificity, and this family therefore has one member and three closely agreeing matrices. The protein is large and carries a long array of C2H2 zinc fingers, on the order of fifteen, which is consistent with the long element the databases recover; as with other very large finger arrays, it is unlikely that all fingers contact DNA in a single binding event. It has appeared under several names: RREB-1, from the RAS-responsive element of the calcitonin promoter; Finb, from work on a Raf-responsive zinc-finger protein that binds divergent sequences; and zinc finger protein 368. Multiple splice variants exist and have been catalogued in urologic cancers. RREB1 is broadly expressed and is not a dedicated tissue-restricted factor.

## The motif

This family needs an explicit statement about what the consensus is and is not. The functional literature never converged on a short IUPAC word: RREB-1 was defined by binding the RAS-responsive element of the human calcitonin gene, the Finb work explicitly reported binding to divergent sequences, and the secretin promoter study described potentiation of BETA2/NeuroD rather than a new consensus. The word given above, CCCCAAACCACCCC, comes from high-throughput in vitro data: the JASPAR MA0073.2 matrix and the CIS-BP M02665 matrix are effectively identical (pairwise similarity 0.998 in this collection), and the Vierstra archetype AC0602 is a slightly shortened version. The full 19-base form CCCCAAACCACCCCCCCCC is C-rich throughout with a short internal A-tract, and the information is carried mainly by the CCCCAAACCA portion; the 3' C-run is low in information and will match almost any C-rich stretch. There is no half-site, no spacing rule and no dimerization requirement described. Since the literature consensus and the data consensus genuinely differ in kind rather than in detail, we quote the data-derived word and label it as such.

Several families in this atlas read C-rich promoter words, and they are easy to confuse. ZNF281/ZNF148 (ZBP-89) read CCCCACCCC; ZBTB7A/B/C read GACCCCCCCC; SP/KLF-type GC boxes are GGGGCGGGGC, that is G-rich on the same strand where RREB1 is C-rich plus CpG-containing; ZBTB17/MIZ1 reads core-promoter GC-rich sites. The RREB1 word's distinguishing feature is the internal AAA: CCCCAAACCACCCC has a purine interruption in the middle of the C-run that GC boxes and ZBTB7 sites lack, and it contains no CpG dinucleotide, which sets it apart from the CpG-island-associated GC-rich families. A hit with no internal A-tract is more likely one of the neighbouring families.

## Where it acts

There is less genomic mapping for RREB1 than for most families of comparable size, and no ChIP-derived matrix appears in HOCOMOCO for it at all, which is itself informative. The characterized sites are promoter-proximal: the calcitonin promoter RAS-responsive element, the secretin promoter, and the SLC39A1/hZIP1 zinc-transporter promoter, where RREB1 overexpression down-regulates the gene in prostate cancer. In the TGF-beta pathway the interesting occupancy is enhancer-associated and combinatorial: RREB1 and SMAD complexes act together at enhancers controlling SNAI1 and other EMT effectors, and RREB1 has been placed in the mechanism by which TGF-beta and RAS jointly unmask primed enhancers to drive metastasis. So the motif can be expected both at C-rich proximal promoters and at signal-dependent enhancers, and in the latter case the relevant unit is a composite RREB1-SMAD arrangement rather than an isolated RREB1 site.

## Biology and disease

RREB1 was found through a differentiation response to RAS in human medullary thyroid carcinoma. Its best-supported function now is as a RAS effector within TGF-beta signalling: it directs the choice between fibrogenic and developmental EMT programs, and in mouse models contributes to enhancer priming for metastasis. Independent lines of work report RREB1 repressing the zinc transporter hZIP1 in prostate cancer, altering p16 expression and proliferation in gastric cancer, and being subject to splice-variant changes in urologic tumours. The RREB1 locus is also recurrently altered in melanoma, and copy-number gain at RREB1 is used diagnostically in melanocytic-lesion FISH panels, which is one of the more concrete clinical connections. Common variants in and near RREB1 appear in genome-wide association studies of type 2 diabetes and birth weight. No Mendelian RREB1 disorder is established.

## Reading a hit

Treat the long C-rich word as a family-level signal at best. The 5' CCCCAAACCA segment carries the discriminating information; the 3' C-run does not, so check that your match covers the informative half rather than sliding along a homopolymeric C stretch. A hit without the internal A-tract is probably a GC box or a ZNF281/ZBTB7-type site. There is no paralogue problem, but there is a provenance problem: the matrices are in vitro high-throughput products that are near-duplicates of each other, so agreement between them is not independent confirmation, and there is no ChIP-derived matrix to check against. For signalling questions, look for a nearby SMAD-binding element, because the functionally demonstrated RREB1 activity in TGF-beta responses is composite. A single promoter-proximal hit does not license the conclusion that a gene is RAS- or TGF-beta-responsive.
families.caveats: The consensus here is data-derived rather than literature-derived, and that matters: the original RAS-responsive element was defined functionally in the calcitonin promoter, and the Finb work reported binding to divergent sequences, so no agreed short consensus exists. The three matrices in this family are near-duplicates from in vitro high-throughput sources, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and no ChIP-derived matrix is available to cross-check. The word is long but much of its length is a low-information C-run that will match many GC-rich promoters, overlapping the ZNF281, ZBTB7, ZBTB17 and SP/KLF families; only the CCCCAAACCA portion discriminates. Functionally demonstrated activity in TGF-beta signalling is composite with SMAD, not standalone.

families.name: MYT1 / ST18 (CCHC zinc finger)
families.def: AAAGTTT core neural repressor sites. MYT1, MYT1L, ST18.
families.short: MYT1, MYT1L and ST18 are the three human members of the MYT/NZF family, which uses an unusual non-classical zinc finger (described as C2HC or CCHHC, not the C2H2 fold of most zinc-finger transcription factors) arranged in two widely separated clusters of fingers. Each cluster binds DNA independently and recognizes the same short AT-rich element, reported as AAAGTTT, and affinity rises sharply when two copies are present, so the functional element is effectively bipartite. The family matters most in neurons: MYT1L is one of the three factors that convert fibroblasts to induced neurons, where it works by repressing non-neuronal programs. MYT1L haploinsufficiency causes a human neurodevelopmental syndrome with obesity. The available motif models for this family are weak.
families.long:
## The factors

MYT1 was cloned in 1992 by its binding to cis-regulatory elements of the myelin proteolipid protein
gene and named myelin transcription factor I. Its zinc fingers do not belong to the classical C2H2
class: the original description assigned them a Cys-X5-Cys-X12-His-X4-Cys arrangement (C2HC), while
later structural work on the same domain in this family describes it as a non-classical CCHHC-type
finger, and both names appear in the literature. MYT1 has six such fingers arranged in two widely
separated clusters. Critically, each cluster binds DNA independently and recognizes the same
sequence, which led to the proposal that one protein can bridge a proximal and a distal site in the
same promoter.

Humans have three members: MYT1 (also MyT1, NZF-2, PLPB1), MYT1L (MYT2) and ST18 (MYT3). ST18 was
cloned as the third member of the neural zinc finger factor family, NZF-3; unlike MyT1 and NZF-1,
which activate transcription in reporter assays, NZF-3 represses. Expression across mouse nervous
system development is broadly overlapping but not identical among the three. MYT1 and MYT1L are the
neural members in practice; MYT1 and ST18 are additionally expressed in pancreatic islet beta cells.
Only MYT1 and MYT1L have motif models in the databases behind this family; ST18 is assigned here on
domain grounds.

## The motif

The consensus reported for these proteins is AAAGTTT, and the key measurement is that a single copy
binds, but a bipartite element containing two copies of the consensus is bound with markedly higher
relative affinity. That is the expected behavior for a protein with two independent finger clusters
of identical specificity, and it means the real recognition unit is a pair of short AT-rich cores
rather than one longer site. Recognition chemistry has been examined for the NZF-1 finger domain,
where hydrogen bonding contributes to base discrimination.

The motifs actually available are thin. HOCOMOCO's MYT1 model, the only one in this family with an A
grade, has the consensus AAACTTTTBNAAA and rests on HT-SELEX plus integrative evidence; its MYT1L
model is ChIP-only at grade C with the consensus AAAGTT; and the CIS-BP human MYT1L motif is not
measured on a human protein at all but inherited from a Caenorhabditis elegans relative at 79%
DNA-binding-domain identity. The data consensus for the family, AAAGTT, therefore reflects six
weakly informative positions, one of them from a nematode. A six- or seven-base AT-rich core carries
roughly the same information as a TATA box, which sets a hard ceiling on what any MYT PWM can
resolve.

## Where it acts

MYT1L occupancy, mapped during fibroblast-to-neuron reprogramming, is unusual in two ways: the
binding sites are largely the same in neurons and in fibroblasts, and they are preferentially in
already-open chromatin. In other words this factor is not selecting sites by cell-type-specific
accessibility; its targets are distributed across the somatic lineage programs it represses. Sites
are found at promoters and in accessible regulatory regions of genes belonging to non-neuronal
lineages, including several components of Notch signaling such as Hes1. Because the core is short and
AT-rich, matches are dense in AT-rich intergenic and intronic DNA and overlap in scoring space with
other AT-preferring models, including homeodomain and forkhead sites and poly-A tracts.

## Biology and disease

MYT1L is one of the three transcription factors, with ASCL1 and POU3F2/BRN2, that convert mouse
fibroblasts into functional induced neurons, and it is dispensable for the initial steps but
important for the quality and stability of the resulting neurons. Its mechanism is repressive: MYT1L
directly represses many different somatic lineage programs while sparing the neuronal program, and it
does so by recruiting a SIN3B-containing complex through an N-terminal domain. That makes it a
counterexample to the assumption that developmental repressors are lineage-specific.

In humans, heterozygous MYT1L deletions and truncating variants (2p25.3) cause MYT1L syndrome:
intellectual disability, autistic features and obesity. Mouse models reproduce the behavioral and
metabolic phenotype, including obesity, and human neuron models show maturation defects, some of
which have been reversed pharmacologically in these systems. On the metabolic side, the Myt factors
act together in beta cells, where their combined loss allows over-activation of stress-response genes
and impairs postnatal beta-cell proliferation and function. ST18 has been studied mainly outside the
nervous system, as a candidate tumor suppressor and in beta-cell function.

## Reading a hit

Be conservative. The motif is a short AT-rich core, so matches are common by chance and cannot be
distinguished from other AT-preferring factors on sequence alone; a single AAAGTTT is weak evidence
even in an otherwise plausible context. A tandem pair of cores in one element is a better signal,
because affinity for the bipartite arrangement is substantially higher. A hit does not identify the
paralogue: MYT1, MYT1L and ST18 share one specificity and the databases cannot separate them, and
ST18 has no measured human matrix here at all. Two provenance problems are worth stating plainly:
the CIS-BP human MYT1L motif is a cross-species transfer from a C. elegans protein, and the HOCOMOCO
MYT1L model is ChIP-only at the lowest quality grade. Given that MYT1L's binding sites are mostly in
pre-existing open chromatin and that its repressive function works through a recruited SIN3B complex,
a MYT1L ChIP peak without a motif is a normal observation rather than an anomaly, and a motif hit
without accessibility is not worth much.
families.caveats: The evidence base is weak for a whole family. The recognition unit is a six- to seven-base AT-rich core, which occurs constantly by chance and overlaps homeodomain, forkhead and poly-A signals; only a tandem pair of cores is a meaningfully specific element. MYT1, MYT1L and ST18 cannot be separated by sequence, and ST18 has no human matrix here. The CIS-BP human MYT1L motif is transferred from a Caenorhabditis elegans protein at 79% DNA-binding-domain identity, and the HOCOMOCO MYT1L model is ChIP-only at grade C; only the MYT1 model has in vitro support. Since MYT1L binds mostly in already-open chromatin and represses via a recruited SIN3B complex, peaks without motifs are expected.

families.name: Other bZIP
families.def: bZIP factors not covered above, e.g. CREBZF, CREBL2, and unclassified bZIP archetypes.
families.short: This is not a family. It is the residual bucket in which bZIP motifs land when they do not belong to any of the defined bZIP families, and in the current data it holds exactly two entries, both from CIS-BP: a cyclic-AMP-response-element-like matrix labelled CREBL2 that was inherited from a Drosophila protein at 64 percent DNA-binding-domain identity, and a short, low-information ACGT-core matrix labelled CREBZF (Zhangfei/SMILE) taken from the mouse ortholog. The two do not resemble each other, and each is closer to a member of another family than to its bucket-mate. Read a hit here as unassigned rather than as a shared motif, and read the underlying proteins as bZIPs that act largely by partnering with, and destabilizing, other bZIPs rather than through a well-mapped element of their own.
families.long:
## The factors

Only two proteins have a motif model in this bucket. CREBZF, also called Zhangfei or SMILE, is a bZIP whose documented mode of action is not sequence-specific activation but interference with other bZIPs. It suppresses CREB3 (Luman) and CREB3L3 (CREBH), both ER-stress transducers in the ATF6/CREB3 family, and it binds XBP1s through its leucine zipper and triggers its proteasomal degradation, reducing induction of unfolded-protein-response genes. Depleting CREBZF has the opposite effect, raising UPR transcript and protein levels. CREBL2 was cloned as a transcript from the chromosome 12p13 interval between ETV6 and CDKN1B, a region recurrently deleted in leukemia, and has since been reported to interact with CREB1 and to promote adipogenesis in 3T3-L1 cells, and to influence metabolism in muscle and liver. Neither protein has an established DNA-binding specificity determined on the human protein. For scale: the human bZIP class has on the order of fifty to sixty members, and the named families in this atlas account for nearly all of the ones with motif models. Several human bZIPs have no model at all in JASPAR 2024, HOCOMOCO v14, CIS-BP or the Vierstra archetypes - ATF5 and NFE2L3 (NRF3) among them - and so appear in no family, including this one.

## The motif

There is no consensus for this bucket and none should be quoted. The two entries are as follows. CIS-BP M03649, labelled CREBL2, reads GTGACGTCAT - a cyclic-AMP response element. Its provenance record marks it as inferred from a Drosophila melanogaster protein at 64 percent DNA-binding-domain identity, and the family data notes that it resembles the CREB/ATF family. CIS-BP M01813, labelled CREBZF, reads AAACGTAK, a short motif carrying 10.8 bits in total, determined on the mouse ortholog, whose DNA-binding domain is 100 percent identical to the human one. The internal cohesion of the pair is 0.60, the lowest of the eight bZIP groups in this atlas, and for each entry the nearest neighbour across all four source databases lies in a different family. In other words the bucket fails the definition of a family used here - a set of motifs it is reasonable to believe are the same motif - and it fails it by design. Averaging these two matrices, or scanning with a single representative for the group, would mix a CRE with an unrelated short ACGT core.

## Where it acts

Not established, for either protein, in the sense that matters for a motif atlas: there is no published genome-wide occupancy map tied to a validated element for CREBZF or CREBL2 in human cells. Scanning with the CREBL2 matrix will return the same promoter-proximal, CpG-island-associated sites that a CREB1 or ATF7 matrix returns, because it is a CRE; that reflects the borrowed Drosophila specificity rather than measured CREBL2 occupancy. The CREBZF matrix is short and will match very frequently, and its hits should not be treated as CREBZF binding sites. Where CREBZF does act functionally is at unfolded-protein-response genes, but as a partner and destabilizer of XBP1s and of CREB3-family activators, so its effect appears at their elements rather than at one of its own.

## Biology and disease

CREBZF behaves as a brake on the unfolded protein response. It reduces induction of UPR genes after thapsigargin treatment, an effect that depends on its leucine zipper and on degradation of XBP1s, and knocking it down in primary sensory neurons increases UPR gene expression. Mouse and cell work has since linked CREBZF to insulin resistance, macrophage inflammatory responses and adipose browning, with its protein level controlled by nutrient state and by reversible acetylation. CREBL2 has no disease attributed to the gene itself; the 12p13 region in which it sits is deleted in leukemia, but the deletions are not mapped to CREBL2, and the functional literature is confined to adipogenesis and to metabolic phenotypes in muscle, liver and Schwann cells. Neither protein has a knockout phenotype that is routinely cited as defining a cis-element.

## Reading a hit

Do not report a match here as a match to a motif. If a scan returns M03649 (CREBL2), read it as a cyclic-AMP response element and report it to the CREB/ATF family, with the caveat that the matrix is a cross-species transfer from an insect protein at 64 percent domain identity and is not evidence about human CREBL2. If it returns M01813 (CREBZF), the match carries little information and no established in vivo target; it does not license the conclusion that CREBZF binds that sequence in human cells. More generally, a residual bucket exists in a motif ontology so that the well-supported families are not diluted by unresolved single cases, and its contents should be read as unassigned rather than as shared biology. If the question is which bZIP is bound at your site, the informative version of that question is which of the named families - AP-1, CREB/ATF, ATF6/CREB3, C/EBP, MAF, NFE2/BACH or PAR bZIP - the sequence best matches, and whether the flanks let you tell them apart at all.
families.caveats: Treat this as an administrative category, not a biological one. It holds two CIS-BP matrices whose internal similarity is the lowest of any bZIP group here (cohesion 0.60), and both are cross-species transfers: the CREBL2 model comes from a Drosophila protein at 64 percent DNA-binding-domain identity and is simply a CRE, and the CREBZF model comes from mouse and carries little information. Neither protein has a validated human element. A hit in this bucket should be re-reported to whichever named family the sequence actually matches, or left unassigned. Do not build a consensus, a logo or a representative matrix for the group, and do not infer that CREBZF and CREBL2 share a site.
